“Puna caparaṃ, brāhmaṇa, yasmiṃ samaye vicikicchāpariyuṭṭhitena cetasā viharati vicikicchāparetena, uppannāya ca vicikicchāya nissaraṇaṃ yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti, attatthampi tasmiṃ samaye yathābhūtaṃ na jānāti na passati, paratthampi…pe… ubhayatthampi… dīgharattaṃ sajjhāyakatāpi mantā nappaṭibhanti, pageva asajjhāyakatā.

Furthermore, Brahmin, when one dwells with a mind beset by doubt, overwhelmed by doubt, and does not know as it really is the escape from arisen doubt, at that time one neither knows nor sees as it really is one's own welfare, nor the welfare of others, nor the welfare of both. Even mantras long recited do not come to mind, let alone those not recited.

“Seyyathāpi, brāhmaṇa, udapatto āvilo luḷito kalalībhūto andhakāre nikkhitto. Tattha cakkhumā puriso sakaṃ mukhanimittaṃ paccavekkhamāno yathābhūtaṃ na jāneyya na [P 5.0124] passeyya. Evameva kho, brāhmaṇa, yasmiṃ samaye vicikicchāpariyuṭṭhitena cetasā viharati vicikicchāparetena, uppannāya ca vicikicchāya nissaraṇaṃ yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti, attatthampi tasmiṃ samaye yathābhūtaṃ na jānāti na passati, paratthampi tasmiṃ samaye yathābhūtaṃ na jānāti [T 5.0171] na passati, ubhayatthampi tasmiṃ samaye yathābhūtaṃ na jānāti na passati; dīgharattaṃ sajjhāyakatāpi mantā nappaṭibhanti, pageva asajjhāyakatā. Ayaṃ kho, brāhmaṇa, hetu ayaṃ paccayo yenekadā dīgharattaṃ sajjhāyakatāpi mantā nappaṭibhanti, pageva asajjhāyakatā.

Just as, brahmin, a bowl of water that is turbid, stirred up, and muddy, is placed in darkness—a person with good eyesight, examining their own facial reflection, would neither know nor see it as it actually is. In the same way, brahmin, when one dwells with a mind beset by doubt, overwhelmed by doubt, and does not understand as it actually is the escape from arisen doubt, at that time one neither knows nor sees as it actually is one's own benefit, nor the benefit of others, nor the benefit of both. Even mantras long recited do not occur to mind, let alone those not recited. This, brahmin, is the cause and this is the reason why sometimes even mantras long recited do not occur to mind, let alone those not recited.

“Yasmiñca kho, brāhmaṇa, samaye na kāmarāgapariyuṭṭhitena cetasā viharati na kāmarāgaparetena, uppannassa ca kāmarāgassa nissaraṇaṃ yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, attatthampi tasmiṃ samaye [V 3.0145] yathābhūtaṃ jānāti passati, paratthampi tasmiṃ samaye yathābhūtaṃ jānāti passati, ubhayatthampi tasmiṃ samaye yathābhūtaṃ jānāti passati; dīgharattaṃ asajjhāyakatāpi mantā paṭibhanti, pageva sajjhāyakatā.

But, brahmin, when one dwells with a mind not beset by sensual lust, not overwhelmed by sensual lust, and understands as it actually is the escape from arisen sensual lust, at that time one knows and sees as it actually is one's own benefit, the benefit of others, and the benefit of both. Even mantras not recited for a long time occur to mind, let alone those recited.

“Seyyathāpi[M 3.0109], brāhmaṇa, udapatto asaṃsaṭṭho lākhāya vā haliddiyā vā nīliyā vā mañjiṭṭhāya vā. Tattha cakkhumā puriso sakaṃ mukhanimittaṃ paccavekkhamāno yathābhūtaṃ jāneyya passeyya. Evameva kho, brāhmaṇa, yasmiṃ samaye na kāmarāgapariyuṭṭhitena cetasā viharati na kāmarāgaparetena, uppannassa ca kāmarāgassa nissaraṇaṃ yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti…pe….

Just as, brahmin, a bowl of water is not mixed with lac, or turmeric, or indigo, or madder—a person with good eyesight, examining their own facial reflection, would know and see it as it actually is. In the same way, brahmin, when one dwells with a mind not beset by sensual lust, not overwhelmed by sensual lust, and understands as it actually is the escape from arisen sensual lust...

“Puna caparaṃ, brāhmaṇa, yasmiṃ samaye na byāpādapariyuṭṭhitena cetasā viharati na byāpādaparetena, uppannassa ca [T 5.0172] byāpādassa nissaraṇaṃ yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, attatthampi tasmiṃ samaye yathābhūtaṃ jānāti passati, paratthampi…pe… ubhayatthampi… dīgharattaṃ asajjhāyakatāpi mantā paṭibhanti, pageva sajjhāyakatā.

Furthermore, brahmin, when one dwells with a mind not beset by ill will, not overwhelmed by ill will, and understands as it actually is the escape from arisen ill will, at that time one knows and sees as it actually is one's own benefit, the benefit of others, and the benefit of both. Even mantras not recited for a long time come to mind, let alone those that have been recited.

“Seyyathāpi, brāhmaṇa, udapatto na agginā santatto na pakkuthito na usmudakajāto, tattha cakkhumā puriso sakaṃ mukhanimittaṃ paccavekkhamāno yathābhūtaṃ jāneyya passeyya[P 5.0125]. Evameva kho, brāhmaṇa, yasmiṃ samaye na byāpādapariyuṭṭhitena cetasā viharati na byāpādaparetena, uppannassa ca byāpādassa nissaraṇaṃ yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, attatthampi tasmiṃ samaye yathābhūtaṃ jānāti passati, paratthampi…pe… ubhayatthampi… dīgharattaṃ asajjhāyakatāpi mantā paṭibhanti, pageva sajjhāyakatā.

Just as, brahmin, a bowl of water is not heated by fire, not boiling, not steaming—a person with good eyesight, examining their own facial reflection, would know and see it as it actually is. In the same way, brahmin, when one dwells with a mind not beset by ill will, not overwhelmed by ill will, and understands as it actually is the escape from arisen ill will, at that time one knows and sees as it actually is one's own benefit, the benefit of others, and the benefit of both. Even mantras not recited for a long time come to mind, let alone those that have been recited.

“Puna caparaṃ, brāhmaṇa, yasmiṃ samaye na thinamiddhapariyuṭṭhitena cetasā viharati na thinamiddhaparetena, uppannassa ca thinamiddhassa nissaraṇaṃ yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, attatthampi tasmiṃ samaye yathābhūtaṃ jānāti passati, paratthampi…pe… ubhayatthampi [V 3.0146]… dīgharattaṃ asajjhāyakatāpi mantā paṭibhanti, pageva sajjhāyakatā.

Furthermore, brahmin, when one dwells with a mind not beset by sloth and torpor, not overwhelmed by sloth and torpor, and understands as it actually is the escape from arisen sloth and torpor, at that time one knows and sees as it actually is one's own benefit, the benefit of others, and the benefit of both. Even mantras not recited for a long time come to mind, let alone those that have been recited.

“Seyyathāpi, brāhmaṇa, udapatto na sevālapaṇakapariyonaddho. Tattha cakkhumā puriso sakaṃ mukhanimittaṃ paccavekkhamāno yathābhūtaṃ [T 5.0173] jāneyya passeyya. Evameva kho, brāhmaṇa, yasmiṃ samaye na thinamiddhapariyuṭṭhitena cetasā viharati na thinamiddhaparetena, uppannassa ca thinamiddhassa nissaraṇaṃ yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, attatthampi tasmiṃ samaye yathābhūtaṃ jānāti passati, paratthampi…pe… ubhayatthampi… dīgharattaṃ asajjhāyakatāpi mantā paṭibhanti, pageva sajjhāyakatā.

Just as, brahmin, a bowl of water is not covered with moss and algae—a person with good eyesight, examining their own facial reflection, would know and see it as it actually is. In the same way, brahmin, when one dwells with a mind not beset by sloth and torpor, not overwhelmed by sloth and torpor, and understands as it actually is the escape from arisen sloth and torpor, at that time one knows and sees as it actually is one's own benefit, the benefit of others, and the benefit of both. Even mantras not recited for a long time occur to mind, let alone those recited.

“Puna [M 3.0110] caparaṃ, brāhmaṇa, yasmiṃ samaye na uddhaccakukkuccapariyuṭṭhitena cetasā viharati na uddhaccakukkuccaparetena, uppannassa ca uddhaccakukkuccassa nissaraṇaṃ yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, attatthampi tasmiṃ samaye yathābhūtaṃ jānāti passati, paratthampi…pe… ubhayatthampi… dīgharattaṃ asajjhāyakatāpi mantā paṭibhanti, pageva sajjhāyakatā.

Furthermore, brahmin, when one dwells with a mind not beset by restlessness and remorse, not overwhelmed by restlessness and remorse, and understands as it actually is the escape from arisen restlessness and remorse, at that time one knows and sees as it actually is one's own benefit, the benefit of others, and the benefit of both. Even mantras not recited for a long time occur to mind, let alone those recited.

“Seyyathāpi, brāhmaṇa, udapatto na vāterito na calito na bhanto na ūmijāto. Tattha cakkhumā puriso sakaṃ mukhanimittaṃ paccavekkhamāno yathābhūtaṃ jāneyya passeyya. Evameva kho, brāhmaṇa, yasmiṃ samaye na uddhaccakukkuccapariyuṭṭhitena cetasā viharati na uddhaccakukkuccaparetena, uppannassa ca uddhaccakukkuccassa nissaraṇaṃ yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, attatthampi tasmiṃ samaye yathābhūtaṃ jānāti passati, paratthampi…pe… ubhayatthampi… dīgharattaṃ asajjhāyakatāpi mantā paṭibhanti, pageva sajjhāyakatā.

Just as, brahmin, a bowl of water is not stirred by the wind, not agitated, not swirling, and has no waves—a person with good eyesight, examining their own facial reflection, would know and see it as it actually is. In the same way, brahmin, when one dwells with a mind not beset by restlessness and remorse, not overwhelmed by restlessness and remorse, and understands as it actually is the escape from arisen restlessness and remorse, at that time one knows and sees as it actually is one's own benefit, the benefit of others, and the benefit of both. Even mantras not recited for a long time occur to mind, let alone those recited.

“Puna [T 5.0174] caparaṃ, brāhmaṇa, yasmiṃ samaye na vicikicchāpariyuṭṭhitena cetasā viharati na vicikicchāparetena, uppannāya ca vicikicchāya nissaraṇaṃ yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti pajānāti passati (syā.), attatthampi tasmiṃ samaye yathābhūtaṃ jānāti passati, paratthampi tasmiṃ samaye yathābhūtaṃ jānāti passati; ubhayatthampi tasmiṃ samaye yathābhūtaṃ jānāti passati; dīgharattaṃ asajjhāyakatāpi mantā paṭibhanti, pageva sajjhāyakatā.

Furthermore, Brahmin, at a time when one dwells with a mind not overcome by doubt, not given over to doubt, and knows as it really is the escape from arisen doubt, at that time one also knows and sees one's own welfare as it really is; at that time one also knows and sees the welfare of others as it really is; at that time one also knows and sees the welfare of both as it really is. Even sacred texts not recited for a long time come to mind, how much more so those that are recited.

“Seyyathāpi[V 3.0147], brāhmaṇa, udapatto accho vippasanno anāvilo āloke nikkhitto. Tattha cakkhumā puriso sakaṃ mukhanimittaṃ paccavekkhamāno yathābhūtaṃ jāneyya passeyya. Evameva kho, brāhmaṇa, yasmiṃ samaye na vicikicchāpariyuṭṭhitena cetasā viharati na vicikicchāparetena, uppannāya ca vicikicchāya nissaraṇaṃ yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, attatthampi tasmiṃ samaye yathābhūtaṃ jānāti passati, paratthampi tasmiṃ samaye yathābhūtaṃ jānāti passati, ubhayatthampi tasmiṃ samaye yathābhūtaṃ jānāti passati; dīgharattaṃ asajjhāyakatāpi mantā paṭibhanti, pageva sajjhāyakatā. Ayaṃ [P 5.0126] kho, brāhmaṇa, hetu ayaṃ paccayo yenekadā dīgharattaṃ asajjhāyakatāpi mantā paṭibhanti, pageva sajjhāyakatā.

Just as, Brahmin, a bowl of water that is clear, limpid, and undisturbed, is placed in the light. There, a man with good eyesight, examining the reflection of his own face, would know and see it as it really is. In the same way, Brahmin, at a time when one dwells with a mind not overcome by doubt, not given over to doubt, and knows as it really is the escape from arisen doubt, at that time one also knows and sees one's own welfare as it really is; at that time one also knows and sees the welfare of others as it really is; at that time one also knows and sees the welfare of both as it really is. Even sacred texts not recited for a long time come to mind, how much more so those that are recited. This, Brahmin, is the cause, this is the condition why at times even sacred texts not recited for a long time come to mind, how much more so those that are recited.

“Sattime[M 3.0111], brāhmaṇa, bojjhaṅgā anāvaraṇā anīvaraṇā cetaso anupakkilesā bhāvitā bahulīkatā vijjāvimuttiphalasacchikiriyāya saṃvattanti. Katame satta? Satisambojjhaṅgo kho, brāhmaṇa, anāvaraṇo [T 5.0175] anīvaraṇo cetaso anupakkileso bhāvito bahulīkato vijjāvimuttiphalasacchikiriyāya saṃvattati…pe… upekkhāsambojjhaṅgo kho, brāhmaṇa, anāvaraṇo anīvaraṇo cetaso anupakkileso bhāvito bahulīkato vijjāvimuttiphalasacchikiriyāya saṃvattati. Ime kho, brāhmaṇa, satta bojjhaṅgā anāvaraṇā anīvaraṇā cetaso anupakkilesā bhāvitā bahulīkatā vijjāvimuttiphalasacchikiriyāya saṃvattantī”ti. Evaṃ vutte saṅgāravo brāhmaṇo bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “abhikkantaṃ, bho gotama…pe… [V 3.0148] upāsakaṃ maṃ bhavaṃ gotamo dhāretu ajjatagge pāṇupetaṃ saraṇaṃ gata”nti. Pañcamaṃ.

Brahmin, these seven factors of awakening are unobstructed, unhindered, not defilements of the mind; when developed and cultivated, they conduce to the realization of the fruit of knowledge and liberation. What seven? The factor of awakening of mindfulness, Brahmin, is unobstructed, unhindered, not a defilement of the mind; when developed and cultivated, it conduces to the realization of the fruit of knowledge and liberation… The factor of awakening of equanimity, Brahmin, is unobstructed, unhindered, not a defilement of the mind; when developed and cultivated, it conduces to the realization of the fruit of knowledge and liberation. These, Brahmin, are the seven factors of awakening that are unobstructed, unhindered, not defilements of the mind; when developed and cultivated, they conduce to the realization of the fruit of knowledge and liberation." When this was said, the brahmin Saṅgārava said this to the Blessed One: "Excellent, Master Gotama!… May Master Gotama remember me as a lay follower who, from this day forward, for as long as life lasts, has gone for refuge." The fifth.

6. Abhayasuttaṃ

6. The Discourse to Abhaya

237. Evaṃ me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā rājagahe viharati gijjhakūṭe pabbate. Atha kho abhayo rājakumāro yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho abhayo rājakumāro bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “pūraṇo, bhante, kassapo evamāha – ‘natthi hetu, natthi paccayo aññāṇāya adassanāya. Ahetu, appaccayo appaccayā (sī.), appaccayaṃ (?) aññāṇaṃ adassanaṃ hoti. Natthi hetu, natthi paccayo ñāṇāya dassanāya. Ahetu, appaccayo ñāṇaṃ dassanaṃ hotī’ti. Idha bhagavā kimāhā”ti? “Atthi, rājakumāra, hetu, atthi paccayo aññāṇāya adassanāya. Sahetu, sappaccayo sappaccayā (sī.), sappaccayaṃ (?) aññāṇaṃ adassanaṃ hoti. Atthi[P 5.0127], rājakumāra, hetu, atthi paccayo ñāṇāya dassanāya. Sahetu, sappaccayo ñāṇaṃ [T 5.0176] dassanaṃ hotī”ti.

237. Thus have I heard. At one time, the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha, on Gijjhakūṭa mountain. Then Prince Abhaya approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, Prince Abhaya said this to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, Pūraṇa Kassapa says this: ‘There is no cause, there is no condition for ignorance and not-seeing. Without cause, without condition, ignorance and not-seeing occur. There is no cause, there is no condition for knowledge and seeing. Without cause, without condition, knowledge and seeing occur.’ What does the Blessed One say in this matter?” “There is, Prince, a cause, there is a condition for ignorance and not-seeing. With cause, with condition, ignorance and not-seeing occur. There is, Prince, a cause, there is a condition for knowledge and seeing. With cause, with condition, knowledge and seeing occur.”

“Katamo pana, bhante, hetu, katamo paccayo aññāṇāya adassanāya? Kathaṃ sahetu, sappaccayo aññāṇaṃ adassanaṃ hotī”ti? “Yasmiṃ kho, rājakumāra, samaye kāmarāgapariyuṭṭhitena cetasā viharati kāmarāgaparetena, uppannassa ca kāmarāgassa nissaraṇaṃ yathābhūtaṃ na jānāti na passati – ayampi kho, rājakumāra, hetu, ayaṃ [M 3.0112] paccayo aññāṇāya adassanāya. Evampi sahetu sappaccayo aññāṇaṃ adassanaṃ hoti.

“Venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the condition for ignorance and not-seeing? How is it that ignorance and not-seeing come to be with cause and with condition?” “When, prince, one dwells with a mind obsessed and overcome by sensual lust, and does not know or see as it really is the escape from that arisen sensual lust—this, prince, is a cause, and this is a condition, for ignorance and not-seeing. In this way, with cause and with condition, ignorance and not-seeing come to be.”

“Puna caparaṃ, rājakumāra, yasmiṃ samaye byāpādapariyuṭṭhitena cetasā viharati byāpādaparetena…pe… thinamiddhapariyuṭṭhitena… uddhaccakukkuccapariyuṭṭhitena… vicikicchāpariyuṭṭhitena cetasā viharati vicikicchāparetena, uppannāya ca vicikicchāya nissaraṇaṃ yathābhūtaṃ na jānāti na passati – ayampi kho, rājakumāra, hetu, ayaṃ [V 3.0149] paccayo aññāṇāya adassanāya. Evampi sahetu sappaccayo aññāṇaṃ adassanaṃ hotī”ti.

“Furthermore, prince, when one dwells with a mind obsessed and overcome by ill will… by sloth and torpor… by restlessness and remorse… or when one dwells with a mind obsessed and overcome by doubt, and does not know or see as it really is the escape from that arisen doubt—this also, prince, is a cause, and this is a condition, for ignorance and not-seeing. In this way, with cause and with condition, ignorance and not-seeing come to be.”

“Ko [T 5.0177] nāmāyaṃ, bhante, dhammapariyāyo”ti? “Nīvaraṇā nāmete, rājakumārā”ti. “Taggha, bhagavā, nīvaraṇā; taggha, sugata, nīvaraṇā! Ekamekenapi kho, bhante, nīvaraṇena abhibhūto yathābhūtaṃ na jāneyya na passeyya, ko pana vādo pañcahi nīvaraṇehi?

“Venerable sir, what is the name of this teaching?” “These, prince, are called the hindrances.” “Indeed, Blessed One, they are hindrances; indeed, Well-farer, they are hindrances! Venerable sir, when one is overcome by even a single hindrance, one would not know or see as it really is; what then is to be said of being overcome by the five hindrances?”

“Katamo pana, bhante, hetu, katamo paccayo ñāṇāya dassanāya? Kathaṃ sahetu, sappaccayo ñāṇaṃ dassanaṃ hotī”ti? “Idha[P 5.0128], rājakumāra, bhikkhu satisambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti vivekanissitaṃ virāganissitaṃ nirodhanissitaṃ vossaggapariṇāmiṃ. So satisambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāvitena cittena yathābhūtaṃ jānāti passati – ayampi kho, rājakumāra, hetu, ayaṃ paccayo ñāṇāya dassanāya. Evampi sahetu, sappaccayo ñāṇaṃ dassanaṃ hoti.

“Venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the condition for knowledge and seeing? How is it that knowledge and seeing come to be with cause and with condition?” “Here, prince, a bhikkhu develops the enlightenment factor of mindfulness, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and culminates in relinquishment. With a mind in which the enlightenment factor of mindfulness has been developed, he knows and sees things as they really are. This, prince, is a cause, and this is a condition, for knowledge and seeing. In this way, with cause and with condition, knowledge and seeing come to be.”

“Puna caparaṃ, rājakumāra, bhikkhu…pe… upekkhāsambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti vivekanissitaṃ virāganissitaṃ nirodhanissitaṃ vossaggapariṇāmiṃ. So upekkhāsambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāvitena cittena yathābhūtaṃ jānāti passati – ayampi kho, rājakumāra, hetu, ayaṃ paccayo ñāṇāya dassanāya. Evaṃ sahetu, sappaccayo ñāṇaṃ dassanaṃ hotī”ti.

“Furthermore, prince, a bhikkhu… develops the enlightenment factor of equanimity, which is based on seclusion, dispassion, and cessation, culminating in relinquishment. With a mind that has developed the enlightenment factor of equanimity, he knows and sees things as they really are. This, prince, is a cause, this is a condition for knowledge and vision. Thus, with a cause and with a condition, knowledge and vision come to be.”

“Ko nāmāyaṃ, bhante, dhammapariyāyo”ti? “Bojjhaṅgā nāmete, rājakumārā”ti. “Taggha, bhagavā, bojjhaṅgā; taggha, sugata, bojjhaṅgā! Ekamekenapi kho, bhante, bojjhaṅgena samannāgato yathābhūtaṃ [T 5.0178] jāneyya passeyya, ko pana vādo sattahi bojjhaṅgehi? Yopi me, bhante, gijjhakūṭaṃ pabbataṃ ārohantassa [M 3.0113] kāyakilamatho cittakilamatho, sopi me paṭippassaddho, dhammo ca me abhisamito”ti. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

“Venerable sir, what is the name of this discourse on the Dhamma?” “These are called the enlightenment factors, prince.” “Indeed, Blessed One, they are enlightenment factors; indeed, Sugata, they are enlightenment factors! If one endowed with even a single enlightenment factor, venerable sir, would know and see things as they really are, what is to be said of one endowed with all seven enlightenment factors? Venerable sir, whatever bodily fatigue and mental fatigue I had while climbing Vulture Peak Mountain, that too has subsided for me, and the Dhamma has been realized by me.” Sixth.

Sākacchavaggo chaṭṭho.

The Sixth Chapter on Discussion.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary for this is:

Āhārā [V 3.0150] pariyāyamaggi, mettaṃ saṅgāravena ca;

Abhayo pucchito pañhaṃ, gijjhakūṭamhi pabbateti.

Nutriments, Sequence, Fire, Loving-kindness, and with Saṅgārava; Abhaya asked a question on Vulture Peak Mountain.

7. Ānāpānavaggo

7. The Chapter on Mindfulness of Breathing

1. Aṭṭhikamahapphalasuttaṃ

1. The Discourse on the Great Fruit of the Perception of a Skeleton

238. Sāvatthinidānaṃ[T 5.0179][P 5.0129]. “Aṭṭhikasaññā, bhikkhave, bhāvitā bahulīkatā mahapphalā hoti mahānisaṃsā. Kathaṃ bhāvitā ca, bhikkhave, aṭṭhikasaññā kathaṃ bahulīkatā mahapphalā hoti mahānisaṃsā? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu aṭṭhikasaññāsahagataṃ satisambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti vivekanissitaṃ virāganissitaṃ nirodhanissitaṃ vossaggapariṇāmiṃ…pe… aṭṭhikasaññāsahagataṃ upekkhāsambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti vivekanissitaṃ virāganissitaṃ nirodhanissitaṃ vossaggapariṇāmiṃ. Evaṃ bhāvitā kho, bhikkhave, aṭṭhikasaññā evaṃ bahulīkatā mahapphalā hoti mahānisaṃsā”ti.

238. At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, the perception of a skeleton, when developed and cultivated, is of great fruit and great benefit. And how, bhikkhus, is the perception of a skeleton developed and cultivated so that it is of great fruit and great benefit? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu develops the enlightenment factor of mindfulness accompanied by the perception of a skeleton, which is based on seclusion, dispassion, and cessation, culminating in relinquishment… he develops the enlightenment factor of equanimity accompanied by the perception of a skeleton, which is based on seclusion, dispassion, and cessation, culminating in relinquishment. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that the perception of a skeleton, when developed and cultivated, is of great fruit and great benefit.”

Aññataraphalasuttaṃ

The Discourse on One of the Fruits

“Aṭṭhikasaññāya, bhikkhave, bhāvitāya bahulīkatāya dvinnaṃ phalānaṃ aññataraṃ phalaṃ pāṭikaṅkhaṃ – diṭṭheva dhamme aññā, sati vā upādisese anāgāmitā. Kathaṃ bhāvitāya ca kho[V 3.0151], bhikkhave, aṭṭhikasaññāya kathaṃ bahulīkatāya dvinnaṃ phalānaṃ aññataraṃ phalaṃ pāṭikaṅkhaṃ – diṭṭheva dhamme aññā, sati vā upādisese anāgāmitā? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu aṭṭhikasaññāsahagataṃ satisambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti…pe… aṭṭhikasaññāsahagataṃ upekkhāsambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti vivekanissitaṃ virāganissitaṃ nirodhanissitaṃ vossaggapariṇāmiṃ. Evaṃ bhāvitāya kho, bhikkhave, aṭṭhikasaññāya evaṃ bahulīkatāya [M 3.0114] dvinnaṃ phalānaṃ aññataraṃ phalaṃ [T 5.0180] pāṭikaṅkhaṃ – diṭṭheva dhamme aññā, sati vā upādisese anāgāmitā”ti.

“Bhikkhus, when the perception of a skeleton is developed and cultivated, one of two fruits is to be expected: either final knowledge in this very life or, if there is a remnant of clinging, the state of non-returning. And how, bhikkhus, is the perception of a skeleton developed and cultivated so that one of two fruits is to be expected: either final knowledge in this very life or, if there is a remnant of clinging, the state of non-returning? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu develops the enlightenment factor of mindfulness accompanied by the perception of a skeleton… he develops the enlightenment factor of equanimity accompanied by the perception of a skeleton, which is based on seclusion, dispassion, and cessation, culminating in relinquishment. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that when the perception of a skeleton is developed and cultivated, one of these two fruits is to be expected: either final knowledge in this very life or, if there is a remnant of clinging, the state of non-returning.”

Mahatthasuttaṃ

The Discourse on Great Benefit

“Aṭṭhikasaññā[P 5.0130], bhikkhave, bhāvitā bahulīkatā mahato atthāya saṃvattati. Kathaṃ bhāvitā ca, bhikkhave, aṭṭhikasaññā kathaṃ bahulīkatā mahato atthāya saṃvattati? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu aṭṭhikasaññāsahagataṃ satisambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti…pe… aṭṭhikasaññāsahagataṃ upekkhāsambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti vivekanissitaṃ virāganissitaṃ nirodhanissitaṃ vossaggapariṇāmiṃ. Evaṃ bhāvitā kho, bhikkhave, aṭṭhikasaññā evaṃ bahulīkatā mahato atthāya saṃvattatī”ti.

“Bhikkhus, the perception of a skeleton, when developed and cultivated, conduces to great benefit. And how, bhikkhus, is the perception of a skeleton developed and cultivated so that it conduces to great benefit? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu develops the enlightenment factor of mindfulness accompanied by the perception of a skeleton… he develops the enlightenment factor of equanimity accompanied by the perception of a skeleton, which is based on seclusion, dispassion, and cessation, culminating in relinquishment. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that the perception of a skeleton, when developed and cultivated, conduces to great benefit.”

Yogakkhemasuttaṃ

The Discourse on Security From Bondage

“Aṭṭhikasaññā, bhikkhave, bhāvitā bahulīkatā mahato yogakkhemāya saṃvattati. Kathaṃ bhāvitā ca, bhikkhave, aṭṭhikasaññā kathaṃ bahulīkatā mahato yogakkhemāya saṃvattati? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu aṭṭhikasaññāsahagataṃ satisambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti…pe… aṭṭhikasaññāsahagataṃ upekkhāsambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti vivekanissitaṃ virāganissitaṃ nirodhanissitaṃ vossaggapariṇāmiṃ. Evaṃ bhāvitā kho, bhikkhave, aṭṭhikasaññā evaṃ bahulīkatā mahato yogakkhemāya saṃvattatī”ti.

“Bhikkhus, the perception of a skeleton, when developed and cultivated, conduces to the great security from bondage. And how, bhikkhus, is the perception of a skeleton, when developed and cultivated, conducive to the great security from bondage? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu develops the enlightenment factor of mindfulness accompanied by the perception of a skeleton... he develops the enlightenment factor of equanimity accompanied by the perception of a skeleton, which is based on seclusion, dispassion, and cessation, culminating in relinquishment. In this way, bhikkhus, the perception of a skeleton, when thus developed and thus cultivated, conduces to the great security from bondage.”

Saṃvegasuttaṃ

The Discourse on Trepidation

“Aṭṭhikasaññā[V 3.0152], bhikkhave, bhāvitā bahulīkatā mahato saṃvegāya saṃvattati. Kathaṃ bhāvitā ca, bhikkhave, aṭṭhikasaññā kathaṃ bahulīkatā mahato saṃvegāya saṃvattati? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu aṭṭhikasaññāsahagataṃ satisambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti…pe… aṭṭhikasaññāsahagataṃ [T 5.0181] upekkhāsambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti vivekanissitaṃ virāganissitaṃ nirodhanissitaṃ vossaggapariṇāmiṃ. Evaṃ bhāvitā kho, bhikkhave, aṭṭhikasaññā evaṃ bahulīkatā mahato saṃvegāya saṃvattatī”ti.

“Bhikkhus, the perception of a skeleton, when developed and cultivated, conduces to great trepidation. And how, bhikkhus, is the perception of a skeleton, when developed and cultivated, conducive to great trepidation? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu develops the enlightenment factor of mindfulness accompanied by the perception of a skeleton... he develops the enlightenment factor of equanimity accompanied by the perception of a skeleton, which is based on seclusion, dispassion, and cessation, culminating in relinquishment. In this way, bhikkhus, the perception of a skeleton, when thus developed and thus cultivated, conduces to great trepidation.”

Phāsuvihārasuttaṃ

The Discourse on Dwelling in Comfort

“Aṭṭhikasaññā[M 3.0115][P 5.0131], bhikkhave, bhāvitā bahulīkatā mahato phāsuvihārāya saṃvattati. Kathaṃ bhāvitā ca, bhikkhave, aṭṭhikasaññā kathaṃ bahulīkatā mahato phāsuvihārāya saṃvattati? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu aṭṭhikasaññāsahagataṃ satisambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti…pe… aṭṭhikasaññāsahagataṃ upekkhāsambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti vivekanissitaṃ virāganissitaṃ nirodhanissitaṃ vossaggapariṇāmiṃ. Evaṃ bhāvitā kho, bhikkhave, aṭṭhikasaññā evaṃ bahulīkatā mahato phāsuvihārāya saṃvattatī”ti. Paṭhamaṃ.

“Bhikkhus, the perception of a skeleton, when developed and cultivated, conduces to a great dwelling in comfort. And how, bhikkhus, is the perception of a skeleton, when developed and cultivated, conducive to a great dwelling in comfort? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu develops the enlightenment factor of mindfulness accompanied by the perception of a skeleton... he develops the enlightenment factor of equanimity accompanied by the perception of a skeleton, which is based on seclusion, dispassion, and cessation, culminating in relinquishment. In this way, bhikkhus, the perception of a skeleton, when thus developed and thus cultivated, conduces to a great dwelling in comfort.” First.

Ānāpānavaggo sattamo.

The Chapter on Breathing, the Seventh.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary verse is:

Aṭṭhikapuḷavakaṃ vinīlakaṃ, vicchiddakaṃ uddhumātena pañcamaṃ;

Mettā karuṇā muditā upekkhā, ānāpānena te dasāti.

The Skeleton, the worm-infested, the livid, the fissured, and with the bloated as the fifth; loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, equanimity, and with breathing—these are the ten.

10. Nirodhasuttaṃ

10. The Discourse on Cessation

257. “Nirodhasaññā, bhikkhave, bhāvitā bahulīkatā mahapphalā hoti mahānisaṃsā. Kathaṃ bhāvitā ca, bhikkhave, nirodhasaññā kathaṃ bahulīkatā mahapphalā hoti mahānisaṃsā? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu nirodhasaññāsahagataṃ satisambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti…pe… nirodhasaññāsahagataṃ upekkhāsambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti vivekanissitaṃ virāganissitaṃ nirodhanissitaṃ vossaggapariṇāmiṃ. Evaṃ bhāvitā kho, bhikkhave, nirodhasaññā evaṃ bahulīkatā mahapphalā hoti mahānisaṃsāti.

257. “The perception of cessation, monks, when developed and cultivated, is of great fruit and great benefit. And how, monks, is the perception of cessation developed and cultivated so as to be of great fruit and great benefit? Here, monks, a monk develops the enlightenment factor of mindfulness accompanied by the perception of cessation… he develops the enlightenment factor of equanimity accompanied by the perception of cessation, based on seclusion, dispassion, and cessation, culminating in relinquishment. Thus developed and cultivated, monks, the perception of cessation is of great fruit and great benefit.”

“Nirodhasaññāya, bhikkhave, bhāvitāya bahulīkatāya dvinnaṃ phalānaṃ aññataraṃ phalaṃ pāṭikaṅkhaṃ – diṭṭheva dhamme aññā, sati vā upādisese anāgāmitā. Kathaṃ bhāvitāya, bhikkhave, nirodhasaññāya kathaṃ bahulīkatāya dvinnaṃ phalānaṃ aññataraṃ phalaṃ pāṭikaṅkhaṃ – diṭṭheva dhamme aññā, sati vā upādisese anāgāmitā? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu [T 5.0183] nirodhasaññāsahagataṃ satisambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti…pe… nirodhasaññāsahagataṃ upekkhāsambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti vivekanissitaṃ virāganissitaṃ nirodhanissitaṃ vossaggapariṇāmiṃ. Evaṃ bhāvitāya kho, bhikkhave, nirodhasaññāya evaṃ bahulīkatāya dvinnaṃ phalānaṃ aññataraṃ phalaṃ pāṭikaṅkhaṃ – diṭṭheva dhamme aññā, sati vā upādisese anāgāmitā”ti.

“Monks, when the perception of cessation has been developed and cultivated, one of two fruits is to be expected: either final knowledge in this very life or, if there is a residue of clinging, non-returning. And how is the perception of cessation developed and cultivated so that one of two fruits is to be expected: either final knowledge in this very life or, if there is a residue of clinging, non-returning? Here, monks, a monk develops the enlightenment factor of mindfulness accompanied by the perception of cessation… he develops the enlightenment factor of equanimity accompanied by the perception of cessation, based on seclusion, dispassion, and cessation, culminating in relinquishment. It is in this way, monks, that when the perception of cessation has been developed and cultivated, one of two fruits is to be expected: either final knowledge in this very life or, if there is a residue of clinging, non-returning.”

“Nirodhasaññā, bhikkhave, bhāvitā bahulīkatā mahato atthāya saṃvattati, mahato yogakkhemāya saṃvattati, mahato saṃvegāya saṃvattati, mahato phāsuvihārāya saṃvattati. Kathaṃ bhāvitā ca, bhikkhave, nirodhasaññā kathaṃ bahulīkatā [P 5.0134] mahato atthāya saṃvattati, mahato yogakkhemāya [M 3.0118] saṃvattati, mahato saṃvegāya saṃvattati, mahato phāsuvihārāya saṃvattati? Idha, bhikkhave[V 3.0164], bhikkhu nirodhasaññāsahagataṃ satisambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti…pe… nirodhasaññāsahagataṃ upekkhāsambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti vivekanissitaṃ virāganissitaṃ nirodhanissitaṃ vossaggapariṇāmiṃ. Evaṃ bhāvitā kho, bhikkhave, nirodhasaññā evaṃ bahulīkatā mahato atthāya saṃvattati, mahato yogakkhemāya saṃvattati, mahato saṃvegāya saṃvattati, mahato phāsuvihārāya saṃvattatī”ti. Dasamaṃ.

“The perception of cessation, monks, when developed and cultivated, conduces to great benefit, conduces to great security from bondage, conduces to great spiritual urgency, conduces to a comfortable abiding. And how, monks, is the perception of cessation developed and cultivated so that it conduces to great benefit, conduces to great security from bondage, conduces to great spiritual urgency, conduces to a comfortable abiding? Here, monks, a monk develops the enlightenment factor of mindfulness accompanied by the perception of cessation… he develops the enlightenment factor of equanimity accompanied by the perception of cessation, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and culminates in relinquishment. When the perception of cessation is developed and cultivated in this way, monks, it conduces to great benefit, conduces to great security from bondage, conduces to great spiritual urgency, and conduces to a comfortable abiding.” Tenth.

Nirodhavaggo aṭṭhamo.

The Chapter on Cessation, the Eighth.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary verse:

Asubhamaraṇaāhāre, paṭikūlaanabhiratena paṭikūlena ca sabbaloke (syā.);

Aniccadukkhaanattapahānaṃ, virāganirodhena te dasāti.

Foulness, Death, Repulsiveness in Food, and Lack of Delight; Impermanence, Suffering, Not-Self, Abandonment, Dispassion, and Cessation—these are the ten.

9. Gaṅgāpeyyālavaggo

9. 9. The Ganges Repetition Series Chapter

1-12. Gaṅgānadīādisuttaṃ

1–12. The Discourses Beginning with the River Ganges

258-269. “Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, gaṅgā nadī pācīnaninnā pācīnapoṇā pācīnapabbhārā; evameva kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu satta bojjhaṅge bhāvento satta bojjhaṅge bahulīkaronto nibbānaninno hoti nibbānapoṇo [T 5.0184] nibbānapabbhāro. Kathañca, bhikkhave, bhikkhu satta bojjhaṅge bhāvento satta bojjhaṅge bahulīkaronto nibbānaninno hoti nibbānapoṇo nibbānapabbhāro? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu satisambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti…pe… upekkhāsambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti vivekanissitaṃ virāganissitaṃ nirodhanissitaṃ vossaggapariṇāmiṃ…pe… evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu satta bojjhaṅge bhāvento satta bojjhaṅge bahulīkaronto nibbānaninno hoti nibbānapoṇo nibbānapabbhāro”ti. (Yāva esanā pāḷi vitthāretabbā).

“Monks, just as the river Ganges slopes, inclines, and tends towards the east, so too a monk who develops and cultivates the seven factors of enlightenment slopes, inclines, and tends towards Nibbāna. And how, monks, does a monk who develops and cultivates the seven factors of enlightenment slope, incline, and tend towards Nibbāna? Here, monks, a monk develops the enlightenment factor of mindfulness… he develops the enlightenment factor of equanimity, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, culminating in relinquishment… Thus, monks, a monk who develops and cultivates the seven factors of enlightenment slopes, inclines, and tends towards Nibbāna.” (The Pāli should be expanded up to the Esanā Sutta).

Gaṅgāpeyyālavaggo navamo.

The Ganges Repetition Series Chapter, the Ninth.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary verse:

Cha [V 3.0165][M 3.0119][P 5.0135] pācīnato ninnā, cha ninnā ca samuddato;

Dvete cha dvādasa honti, vaggo tena pavuccatīti.

Six sloping to the east, and six sloping to the ocean; these two sets of six become twelve, therefore it is called a chapter.

10. Uddhambhāgiyasuttaṃ

13. 10. The Discourse on the Higher Fetters

311. Sāvatthinidānaṃ. “Pañcimāni, bhikkhave, uddhambhāgiyāni saṃyojanāni. Katamāni pañca? Rūparāgo, arūparāgo, māno, uddhaccaṃ, avijjā [P 5.0137] – imāni kho, bhikkhave[V 3.0190], pañcuddhambhāgiyāni saṃyojanāni. Imesaṃ kho, bhikkhave, pañcannaṃ uddhambhāgiyānaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ abhiññāya pariññāya parikkhayāya pahānāya satta bojjhaṅgā bhāvetabbā. Katame satta? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu satisambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti vivekanissitaṃ virāganissitaṃ nirodhanissitaṃ vossaggapariṇāmiṃ…pe… upekkhāsambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti rāgavinayapariyosānaṃ dosavinayapariyosānaṃ mohavinayapariyosānaṃ… amatogadhaṃ amataparāyanaṃ amatapariyosānaṃ… nibbānaninnaṃ nibbānapoṇaṃ nibbānapabbhāraṃ. Imesaṃ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu pañcannaṃ uddhambhāgiyānaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ abhiññāya pariññāya parikkhayāya pahānāya ime satta bojjhaṅgā bhāvetabbā”ti. Dasamaṃ.

311. At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, there are these five higher fetters. What five? Lust for form, lust for the formless, conceit, restlessness, and ignorance. These, Bhikkhus, are the five higher fetters. For the direct knowledge, full understanding, utter destruction, and abandonment of these five higher fetters, the seven enlightenment factors should be developed. What seven? Here, Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu develops the enlightenment factor of mindfulness, which is based upon seclusion, based upon dispassion, based upon cessation, culminating in relinquishment… he develops the enlightenment factor of equanimity, which has the removal of lust as its culmination, the removal of hatred as its culmination, the removal of delusion as its culmination… which is immersed in the Deathless, has the Deathless as its destination, has the Deathless as its culmination… which slopes, inclines, and tends towards Nibbāna. Bhikkhus, for the direct knowledge, full understanding, utter destruction, and abandonment of these five higher fetters, these seven enlightenment factors should be developed.”

Oghavaggo terasamo.

The Chapter on Floods is the thirteenth.

Floods, Yokes, Clinging, Bonds, and Latent Tendencies; Sensual Pleasures, Hindrances, Aggregates, Lower and Higher Fetters.

The Second Connected Discourses on the Enlightenment Factors.

3. Satipaṭṭhānasaṃyuttaṃ

3. 3. The Connected Discourses on the Foundations of Mindfulness

1. Ambapālivaggo

1. 1. The Chapter on Ambapālī

1. Ambapālisuttaṃ

1. 1. The Discourse at Ambapālī's Grove

367. Evaṃ [T 5.0190][V 3.0220][M 3.0123][P 5.0141] me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā vesāliyaṃ viharati ambapālivane. Tatra kho bhagavā bhikkhū āmantesi – “bhikkhavo”ti. “Bhadante”ti te bhikkhū bhagavato paccassosuṃ. Bhagavā etadavoca –

367. Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Vesālī, in Ambapālī’s Grove. There, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus!” “Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:

“Ekāyano ayaṃ, bhikkhave, maggo sattānaṃ visuddhiyā sokaparidevānaṃ samatikkamāya dukkhadomanassānaṃ atthaṅgamāya ñāyassa adhigamāya nibbānassa sacchikiriyāya, yadidaṃ – cattāro satipaṭṭhānā. Katame cattāro? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ; vedanāsu vedanānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ; citte cittānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ; dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ. Ekāyano ayaṃ, bhikkhave, maggo sattānaṃ visuddhiyā sokaparidevānaṃ samatikkamāya dukkhadomanassānaṃ atthaṅgamāya ñāyassa adhigamāya nibbānassa sacchikiriyāya, yadidaṃ – cattāro satipaṭṭhānā”ti.

“Bhikkhus, this is the direct path for the purification of beings, for the overcoming of sorrow and lamentation, for the cessation of suffering and displeasure, for the attainment of the noble path, for the realization of Nibbāna—that is, the four foundations of mindfulness. What are the four? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in the world. He dwells contemplating the mind in the mind, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in the world. He dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in the world. Bhikkhus, this is the direct path for the purification of beings, for the overcoming of sorrow and lamentation, for the cessation of suffering and displeasure, for the attainment of the noble path, for the realization of Nibbāna—that is, the four foundations of mindfulness.”

Idamavoca [T 5.0191] bhagavā. Attamanā te bhikkhū bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinandunti. Paṭhamaṃ.

The Blessed One said this. Those bhikkhus, being pleased, greatly delighted in the Blessed One’s words. The first.

2. Satisuttaṃ

2. 2. The Discourse on Mindfulness

368. Ekaṃ [V 3.0221][P 5.0142] samayaṃ bhagavā vesāliyaṃ viharati ambapālivane. Tatra kho bhagavā bhikkhū āmantesi – “bhikkhavo”ti. “Bhadante”ti te bhikkhū bhagavato paccassosuṃ. Bhagavā etadavoca –

368. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Vesālī, in Ambapālī’s Grove. There, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus!” “Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:

“Sato, bhikkhave, bhikkhu vihareyya sampajāno. Ayaṃ vo amhākaṃ anusāsanī. Kathañca, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sato hoti? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya [M 3.0124] loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ; vedanāsu…pe… citte…pe… dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sato hoti.

“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu should dwell mindful and clearly comprehending. This is our instruction to you. And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu mindful? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings... the mind in the mind... phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in the world. Thus, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is mindful.”

“Kathañca, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sampajāno hoti? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu abhikkante paṭikkante sampajānakārī hoti, ālokite vilokite sampajānakārī hoti, samiñjite pasārite sampajānakārī hoti, saṅghāṭipattacīvaradhāraṇe sampajānakārī hoti, asite pīte khāyite sāyite sampajānakārī hoti, uccārapassāvakamme sampajānakārī hoti, gate ṭhite nisinne sutte jāgarite bhāsite tuṇhībhāve sampajānakārī hoti. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sampajānakārī hoti. Sato, bhikkhave, bhikkhu vihareyya sampajāno. Ayaṃ vo amhākaṃ anusāsanī”ti. Dutiyaṃ.

“And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu clearly comprehending? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu acts with clear comprehension when going forward and returning; when looking ahead and looking around; when bending and stretching; when bearing the outer robe, bowl, and robes; when eating, drinking, chewing, and savoring; when defecating and urinating; when walking, standing, sitting, sleeping, waking, speaking, and in being silent. Thus, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu acts with clear comprehension. Mindful and clearly comprehending, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu should dwell. This is our instruction to you.”

3. Bhikkhusuttaṃ

3. The Bhikkhu Discourse

369. Ekaṃ [T 5.0192] samayaṃ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme. Atha kho aññataro bhikkhu yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho so bhikkhu bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “sādhu me, bhante, bhagavā saṃkhittena dhammaṃ desetu, yamahaṃ bhagavato dhammaṃ sutvā eko vūpakaṭṭho [P 5.0143] appamatto ātāpī [V 3.0222] pahitatto vihareyya”nti. “Evameva panidhekacce moghapurisā mañceva mameva (sī.) ajjhesanti, dhamme ca bhāsite mameva anubandhitabbaṃ maññantī”ti. “Desetu me, bhante, bhagavā saṃkhittena dhammaṃ, desetu sugato saṃkhittena dhammaṃ. Appeva nāmāhaṃ bhagavato bhāsitassa atthaṃ jāneyyaṃ, appeva nāmāhaṃ bhagavato bhāsitassa dāyādo assa”nti. “Tasmātiha tvaṃ, bhikkhu, ādimeva visodhehi kusalesu dhammesu. Ko cādi kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ? Sīlañca suvisuddhaṃ, diṭṭhi ca ujukā. Yato kho te, bhikkhu, sīlañca suvisuddhaṃ bhavissati diṭṭhi ca ujukā, tato tvaṃ, bhikkhu, sīlaṃ nissāya sīle patiṭṭhāya cattāro satipaṭṭhāne tividhena bhāveyyāsi.

369. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. Then a certain bhikkhu approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, that bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it would be good if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that, having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, secluded, diligent, ardent, and resolute.” “In this very way, some foolish men here make this request of me, and after the Dhamma has been spoken, they think that they should just keep following me.” “Venerable sir, let the Blessed One teach me the Dhamma in brief; let the Well-spoken One teach the Dhamma in brief. It may be that I will understand the meaning of the Blessed One’s utterance; it may be that I will become an heir to the Blessed One’s utterance.” “Therefore, bhikkhu, you should first of all purify the very beginning in wholesome qualities. And what is the beginning of wholesome qualities? Virtue well purified and a view that is straight. When, bhikkhu, your virtue is well purified and your view is straight, then, bhikkhu, based on virtue, established in virtue, you should develop the four foundations of mindfulness in three ways.”

Katame [M 3.0125] cattāro? Idha tvaṃ, bhikkhu, ajjhattaṃ vā kāye kāyānupassī viharāhi ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ; bahiddhā vā kāye kāyānupassī viharāhi ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ; ajjhattabahiddhā [T 5.0193] vā kāye kāyānupassī viharāhi ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ. Ajjhattaṃ vā vedanāsu…pe… bahiddhā vā vedanāsu…pe… ajjhattabahiddhā vā vedanāsu vedanānupassī viharāhi ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ. Ajjhattaṃ vā citte…pe… bahiddhā vā citte…pe… ajjhattabahiddhā vā citte cittānupassī viharāhi ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ. Ajjhattaṃ vā dhammesu…pe… bahiddhā vā dhammesu…pe… ajjhattabahiddhā vā dhammesu dhammānupassī viharāhi ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ. Yato kho tvaṃ, bhikkhu, sīlaṃ nissāya sīle patiṭṭhāya ime cattāro satipaṭṭhāne evaṃ tividhena bhāvessasi, tato tuyhaṃ, bhikkhu, yā ratti vā divaso vā āgamissati vuddhiyeva pāṭikaṅkhā kusalesu dhammesu, no parihānī”ti.

“What are the four? Here, bhikkhu, you should dwell contemplating the body in the body internally—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having subdued covetousness and displeasure in the world. You should dwell contemplating the body in the body externally—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having subdued covetousness and displeasure in the world. You should dwell contemplating the body in the body both internally and externally—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having subdued covetousness and displeasure in the world. You should dwell contemplating feelings in feelings internally… externally… both internally and externally—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having subdued covetousness and displeasure in the world. You should dwell contemplating the mind in the mind internally… externally… both internally and externally—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having subdued covetousness and displeasure in the world. You should dwell contemplating phenomena in phenomena internally… externally… both internally and externally—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having subdued covetousness and displeasure in the world. When, bhikkhu, relying on virtue and established in virtue, you develop these four foundations of mindfulness in this threefold way, then for you, bhikkhu, for whatever night or day that comes, only growth in wholesome states is to be expected, not decline.”

Atha kho so bhikkhu bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinanditvā [P 5.0144] anumoditvā uṭṭhāyāsanā bhagavantaṃ [V 3.0223] abhivādetvā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā pakkāmi. Atha kho so bhikkhu eko vūpakaṭṭho appamatto ātāpī pahitatto viharanto nacirasseva – yassatthāya kulaputtā sammadeva agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajanti, tadanuttaraṃ – brahmacariyapariyosānaṃ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharati[T 5.0194]. “Khīṇā jāti, vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ, kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ, nāparaṃ itthattāyā”ti abbhaññāsi. Aññataro ca pana so bhikkhu arahataṃ ahosīti. Tatiyaṃ.

Then that bhikkhu, having greatly delighted in and rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him keeping the right side toward him, and departed. Then that bhikkhu, dwelling alone, secluded, diligent, ardent, and resolute, before long, in this very life, realized for himself with direct knowledge the unsurpassed consummation of the holy life for which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness, and having attained it, he dwelled therein. He understood: “Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.” And that bhikkhu became one of the arahants.

4. Sālasuttaṃ

4. The Sāla Discourse

370. Ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā kosalesu viharati sālāya brāhmaṇagāme. Tatra kho bhagavā bhikkhū āmantesi…pe… etadavoca –

370. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling among the Kosalans at Sālā, a brahmin village. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus … and said:

“Ye te, bhikkhave, bhikkhū navā acirapabbajitā adhunāgatā imaṃ dhammavinayaṃ, te vo, bhikkhave, bhikkhū catunnaṃ satipaṭṭhānānaṃ bhāvanāya samādapetabbā nivesetabbā patiṭṭhāpetabbā. Katamesaṃ catunnaṃ? Etha tumhe, āvuso, kāye [M 3.0126] kāyānupassino viharatha ātāpino sampajānā ekodibhūtā vippasannacittā samāhitā ekaggacittā, kāyassa yathābhūtaṃ ñāṇāya; vedanāsu vedanānupassino viharatha ātāpino sampajānā ekodibhūtā vippasannacittā samāhitā ekaggacittā, vedanānaṃ yathābhūtaṃ ñāṇāya; citte cittānupassino viharatha ātāpino sampajānā ekodibhūtā vippasannacittā samāhitā ekaggacittā, cittassa yathābhūtaṃ ñāṇāya; dhammesu dhammānupassino viharatha ātāpino sampajānā ekodibhūtā vippasannacittā samāhitā ekaggacittā, dhammānaṃ yathābhūtaṃ ñāṇāya. Yepi [P 5.0145] te, bhikkhave, bhikkhū sekhā appattamānasā anuttaraṃ yogakkhemaṃ patthayamānā viharanti, tepi kāye kāyānupassino viharanti ātāpino sampajānā ekodibhūtā vippasannacittā samāhitā ekaggacittā[T 5.0195], kāyassa pariññāya; vedanāsu vedanānupassino viharanti ātāpino sampajānā ekodibhūtā vippasannacittā samāhitā ekaggacittā, vedanānaṃ pariññāya; citte cittānupassino viharanti ātāpino sampajānā ekodibhūtā vippasannacittā samāhitā ekaggacittā, cittassa pariññāya; dhammesu dhammānupassino viharanti ātāpino sampajānā ekodibhūtā vippasannacittā samāhitā ekaggacittā, dhammānaṃ pariññāya.

“Bhikkhus, those bhikkhus who are new, not long ordained, recently come to this Dhamma and Discipline—those bhikkhus should be incited by you, settled, and established in the development of the four establishments of mindfulness. In which four? ‘Come, friends, dwell contemplating the body in the body—ardent, clearly comprehending, unified, with a lucid mind, concentrated, with a one-pointed mind—for the sake of knowing the body as it really is. Dwell contemplating feelings in feelings—ardent, clearly comprehending, unified, with a lucid mind, concentrated, with a one-pointed mind—for the sake of knowing feelings as they really are. Dwell contemplating the mind in the mind—ardent, clearly comprehending, unified, with a lucid mind, concentrated, with a one-pointed mind—for the sake of knowing the mind as it really is. Dwell contemplating dhammas in dhammas—ardent, clearly comprehending, unified, with a lucid mind, concentrated, with a one-pointed mind—for the sake of knowing dhammas as they really are.’ And those bhikkhus, bhikkhus, who are trainees, who have not yet attained the goal, who dwell aspiring for the unsurpassed security from bondage—they too dwell contemplating the body in the body—ardent, clearly comprehending, unified, with a lucid mind, concentrated, with a one-pointed mind—for the full understanding of the body. They dwell contemplating feelings in feelings—ardent, clearly comprehending, unified, with a lucid mind, concentrated, with a one-pointed mind—for the full understanding of feelings. They dwell contemplating the mind in the mind—ardent, clearly comprehending, unified, with a lucid mind, concentrated, with a one-pointed mind—for the full understanding of the mind. They dwell contemplating dhammas in dhammas—ardent, clearly comprehending, unified, with a lucid mind, concentrated, with a one-pointed mind—for the full understanding of dhammas.”

“Yepi [V 3.0224] te, bhikkhave, bhikkhū arahanto khīṇāsavā vusitavanto katakaraṇīyā ohitabhārā anuppattasadatthā parikkhīṇabhavasaṃyojanā sammadaññā vimuttā, tepi kāye kāyānupassino viharanti ātāpino sampajānā ekodibhūtā vippasannacittā samāhitā ekaggacittā, kāyena visaṃyuttā; vedanāsu vedanānupassino viharanti ātāpino sampajānā ekodibhūtā vippasannacittā samāhitā ekaggacittā, vedanāhi visaṃyuttā; citte cittānupassino viharanti ātāpino sampajānā ekodibhūtā vippasannacittā samāhitā ekaggacittā, cittena visaṃyuttā; dhammesu dhammānupassino viharanti ātāpino sampajānā ekodibhūtā vippasannacittā samāhitā ekaggacittā, dhammehi visaṃyuttā.

“Bhikkhus, even those bhikkhus who are arahants, whose taints are destroyed, who have lived the holy life, who have done what was to be done, who have laid down the burden, who have attained their own welfare, whose fetters of existence are utterly destroyed, and who are liberated through right knowledge—they too dwell contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, unified, with a lucid mind, concentrated, with a one-pointed mind, being disjoined from the body. They dwell contemplating feelings in feelings, ardent, clearly comprehending, unified, with a lucid mind, concentrated, with a one-pointed mind, being disjoined from feelings. They dwell contemplating the mind in the mind, ardent, clearly comprehending, unified, with a lucid mind, concentrated, with a one-pointed mind, being disjoined from the mind. They dwell contemplating dhammas in dhammas, ardent, clearly comprehending, unified, with a lucid mind, concentrated, with a one-pointed mind, being disjoined from dhammas.”

“Yepi te, bhikkhave, bhikkhū navā acirapabbajitā adhunāgatā imaṃ dhammavinayaṃ, te vo, bhikkhave, bhikkhū imesaṃ catunnaṃ satipaṭṭhānānaṃ bhāvanāya [T 5.0196] samādapetabbā nivesetabbā patiṭṭhāpetabbā”ti. Catutthaṃ.

“Bhikkhus, those bhikkhus who are new, not long gone forth, and have recently come to this Dhamma and Discipline—those bhikkhus should be made by you to undertake, to enter into, and to be established in the development of these four establishments of mindfulness.” Fourth.

5. Akusalarāsisuttaṃ

5. The Sutta on the Heap of the Unwholesome

371. Sāvatthinidānaṃ[M 3.0127]. Tatra kho bhagavā etadavoca – “‘akusalarāsī’ti, bhikkhave, vadamāno pañca nīvaraṇe sammā vadamāno vadeyya. Kevalo hāyaṃ, bhikkhave, akusalarāsi, yadidaṃ – pañca nīvaraṇā. Katame pañca? Kāmacchandanīvaraṇaṃ[P 5.0146], byāpādanīvaraṇaṃ, thinamiddhanīvaraṇaṃ, uddhaccakukkuccanīvaraṇaṃ, vicikicchānīvaraṇaṃ. ‘Akusalarāsī’ti, bhikkhave, vadamāno ime pañca nīvaraṇe sammā vadamāno vadeyya. Kevalo hāyaṃ, bhikkhave, akusalarāsi, yadidaṃ – pañca nīvaraṇā.

371. At Sāvatthī. There, the Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, one who, speaking of ‘a heap of the unwholesome,’ would be speaking rightly if one were to speak of the five hindrances. For this, bhikkhus, is entirely a heap of the unwholesome, that is, the five hindrances. What are the five? The hindrance of sensual desire, the hindrance of ill will, the hindrance of sloth and torpor, the hindrance of restlessness and remorse, and the hindrance of doubt. Bhikkhus, one who, speaking of ‘a heap of the unwholesome,’ would be speaking rightly if one were to speak of these five hindrances. For this, bhikkhus, is entirely a heap of the unwholesome, that is, the five hindrances.”

“‘Kusalarāsī’ti, bhikkhave, vadamāno cattāro satipaṭṭhāne sammā vadamāno vadeyya. Kevalo hāyaṃ, bhikkhave, kusalarāsi, yadidaṃ – cattāro satipaṭṭhānā. Katame cattāro? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ; vedanāsu…pe… citte…pe… dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ[V 3.0225]. ‘Kusalarāsī’ti, bhikkhave, vadamāno ime cattāro satipaṭṭhāne sammā vadamāno vadeyya. Kevalo hāyaṃ, bhikkhave, kusalarāsi, yadidaṃ – cattāro satipaṭṭhānā”ti. Pañcamaṃ.

“Bhikkhus, one who, when saying ‘a heap of the wholesome,’ would be speaking rightly if one were to speak of the four establishments of mindfulness. For this, bhikkhus, is entirely a heap of the wholesome, that is, the four establishments of mindfulness. Which four? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having subdued covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings… mind in mind… dhammas in dhammas, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having subdued covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. Bhikkhus, one who, when saying ‘a heap of the wholesome,’ would be speaking rightly if one were to speak of these four establishments of mindfulness. For this, bhikkhus, is entirely a heap of the wholesome, that is, the four establishments of mindfulness.” Fifth.

6. Sakuṇagghisuttaṃ

6. The Sutta on the Hawk

372. “Bhūtapubbaṃ, bhikkhave, sakuṇagghi lāpaṃ sakuṇaṃ sahasā ajjhappattā aggahesi. Atha kho, bhikkhave, lāpo sakuṇo sakuṇagghiyā hariyamāno evaṃ paridevasi – ‘mayamevamha mayamevāmha (ka.) alakkhikā, mayaṃ [T 5.0197] appapuññā, ye mayaṃ agocare carimha paravisaye. Sacejja mayaṃ gocare careyyāma sake pettike visaye, na myāyaṃ na cāyaṃ (sī.), sakuṇagghi, alaṃ abhavissa, yadidaṃ – yuddhāyā’ti. ‘Ko pana te, lāpa, gocaro sako pettiko visayo’ti? ‘Yadidaṃ – naṅgalakaṭṭhakaraṇaṃ leḍḍuṭṭhāna’”nti. “Atha [P 5.0147] kho, bhikkhave, sakuṇagghi sake bale apatthaddhā sake bale asaṃvadamānā avacamānā (sī.) lāpaṃ sakuṇaṃ pamuñci – ‘gaccha kho tvaṃ, lāpa, tatrapi me gantvā na mokkhasī’”ti.

372. “Once upon a time, bhikkhus, a hawk suddenly swooped down and seized a quail. Then, bhikkhus, as the hawk was carrying him off, the quail lamented thus: ‘How unfortunate we are! How little merit we have, that we wandered in what is not our feeding ground, in another’s domain. If today we were wandering in our own feeding ground, in our own ancestral domain, this hawk would not have been a match for me in battle.’ ‘But what, quail, is your own feeding ground, your own ancestral domain?’ ‘It is a ploughed field with turned-up clods.’ Then, bhikkhus, the hawk, not arrogant about her own strength and not boasting of her own strength, released the quail, saying: ‘Go now, quail, but even having gone there, you will not escape from me!’”

“Atha [M 3.0128] kho, bhikkhave, lāpo sakuṇo naṅgalakaṭṭhakaraṇaṃ leḍḍuṭṭhānaṃ gantvā mahantaṃ leḍḍuṃ abhiruhitvā sakuṇagghiṃ vadamāno aṭṭhāsi – ‘ehi kho dāni me, sakuṇagghi, ehi kho dāni me, sakuṇagghī’ti. Atha kho sā, bhikkhave, sakuṇagghi sake bale apatthaddhā sake bale asaṃvadamānā ubho pakkhe sannayha sandhāya (sī. syā.) lāpaṃ sakuṇaṃ sahasā ajjhappattā. Yadā kho, bhikkhave, aññāsi lāpo sakuṇo ‘bahuāgato kho myāyaṃ sakuṇagghī’ti, atha tasseva leḍḍussa antaraṃ paccupādi. Atha kho, bhikkhave, sakuṇagghi tattheva uraṃ paccatāḷesi. Evañhi taṃ evaṃ hetaṃ (sī.), bhikkhave, hoti yo agocare carati paravisaye.

“Then, monks, the quail went to a place of clods made by a plough, climbed onto a large clod, and stood there saying to the hawk: ‘Come now indeed to my presence, O hawk! Come now indeed to my presence, O hawk!’ Then, monks, that hawk, confident in her own strength and unrestrained, gathered both wings and suddenly swooped down upon the quail. When, monks, the quail knew, ‘This hawk has come at me with great force,’ he then entered the space within that very clod. Then, monks, the hawk struck her breast against that very clod. Thus it is, monks, for one who wanders in an improper range, in another’s territory.”

“Tasmātiha, bhikkhave, mā agocare carittha paravisaye. Agocare, bhikkhave, carataṃ paravisaye lacchati māro otāraṃ, lacchati māro ārammaṇaṃ. Ko ca, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno agocaro paravisayo? Yadidaṃ – pañca kāmaguṇā. Katame pañca? Cakkhuviññeyyā rūpā iṭṭhā kantā manāpā piyarūpā kāmūpasaṃhitā rajanīyā, sotaviññeyyā [T 5.0198] saddā…pe… ghānaviññeyyā [V 3.0226] gandhā… jivhāviññeyyā rasā… kāyaviññeyyā phoṭṭhabbā iṭṭhā kantā manāpā piyarūpā kāmūpasaṃhitā rajanīyā – ayaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno agocaro paravisayo.

“Therefore, monks, do not wander in an improper range, in another’s territory. For those who wander in an improper range, in another’s territory, Māra will gain an opportunity, Māra will gain a footing. And what, monks, is a monk's improper range and another’s territory? It is the five strands of sensual pleasure. Which five? Forms cognizable by the eye—desirable, pleasing, charming, beloved, connected with sensual pleasure, and enticing; sounds cognizable by the ear… smells cognizable by the nose… tastes cognizable by the tongue… tangible objects cognizable by the body—desirable, pleasing, charming, beloved, connected with sensual pleasure, and enticing. This, monks, is a monk's improper range and another’s territory.”

“Gocare, bhikkhave, caratha sake pettike visaye. Gocare, bhikkhave, carataṃ sake pettike visaye na lacchati māro otāraṃ, na lacchati māro ārammaṇaṃ. Ko [P 5.0148] ca, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno gocaro sako pettiko visayo? Yadidaṃ – cattāro satipaṭṭhānā. Katame cattāro? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ; vedanāsu…pe… citte…pe… dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ – ayaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno gocaro sako pettiko visayo”ti. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

“Dwell, monks, in your own resort, your ancestral domain. For those who dwell in their own resort, their ancestral domain, Māra will not gain an opportunity; Māra will not find a support. And what, monks, is a monk’s own resort, his ancestral domain? It is these four establishments of mindfulness. Which four? Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having subdued covetousness and displeasure in the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings… the mind in the mind… phenomena in phenomena—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having subdued covetousness and displeasure in the world. This, monks, is a monk’s own resort, his ancestral domain.” Sixth.

7. Makkaṭasuttaṃ

7. The Discourse on the Monkey

373. “Atthi, bhikkhave, himavato pabbatarājassa duggā visamā desā, yattha neva makkaṭānaṃ cārī na manussānaṃ. Atthi, bhikkhave, himavato pabbatarājassa [M 3.0129] duggā visamā desā, yattha makkaṭānañhi kho cārī, na manussānaṃ. Atthi, bhikkhave, himavato pabbatarājassa samā bhūmibhāgā ramaṇīyā, yattha makkaṭānañceva cārī manussānañca. Tatra, bhikkhave, luddā makkaṭavīthīsu lepaṃ oḍḍenti makkaṭānaṃ bādhanāya.

373. “Monks, in Himavat, the king of mountains, there are difficult, uneven regions which are not the resort of monkeys nor of humans. There are, monks, in Himavat, the king of mountains, difficult, uneven regions which are the resort of monkeys, but not of humans. There are, monks, in Himavat, the king of mountains, level, delightful tracts of land which are the resort of both monkeys and humans. There, monks, hunters set a sticky trap on the monkey trails for the purpose of capturing the monkeys.

“Tatra, bhikkhave, ye te makkaṭā abālajātikā alolajātikā, te taṃ lepaṃ disvā ārakā parivajjanti. Yo pana so hoti [T 5.0199] makkaṭo bālajātiko lolajātiko, so taṃ lepaṃ upasaṅkamitvā hatthena gaṇhāti. So tattha bajjhati. ‘Hatthaṃ mocessāmī’ti dutiyena hatthena gaṇhāti. So tattha bajjhati. ‘Ubho hatthe mocessāmī’ti pādena gaṇhāti. So tattha bajjhati. ‘Ubho hatthe mocessāmi pādañcā’ti dutiyena pādena gaṇhāti. So tattha bajjhati. ‘Ubho hatthe mocessāmi pāde cā’ti tuṇḍena gaṇhāti. So tattha bajjhati. Evañhi so, bhikkhave, makkaṭo pañcoḍḍito thunaṃ seti anayaṃ āpanno byasanaṃ āpanno yathākāmakaraṇīyo [V 3.0227][P 5.0149] luddassa. Tamenaṃ, bhikkhave, luddo vijjhitvā tasmiṃyeva kaṭṭhakataṅgāre tasmiṃyeva makkaṭaṃ uddharitvā (sī. syā.) avassajjetvā yena kāmaṃ pakkamati. Evaṃ so taṃ, bhikkhave, hoti yo agocare carati paravisaye.

“There, monks, those monkeys that are not foolish and reckless, upon seeing that sticky trap, avoid it from afar. But a monkey that is foolish and reckless approaches that sticky trap and grabs it with its hand. It gets stuck there. Thinking, ‘I will free my hand,’ it grabs the trap with its other hand. It gets stuck there. Thinking, ‘I will free both hands,’ it grabs the trap with its foot. It gets stuck there. Thinking, ‘I will free both hands and a foot,’ it grabs the trap with its other foot. It gets stuck there. Thinking, ‘I will free both hands and both feet,’ it grabs the trap with its snout. It gets stuck there. Thus, monks, that monkey, trapped in five places, lies there groaning, having met with misfortune, having met with ruin, to be dealt with as the hunter wishes. Then, monks, the hunter, having struck it, leaves it on that very woodpile and departs wherever he pleases. Thus it is, monks, for one who wanders in an improper range, in another’s territory.”

“Tasmātiha, bhikkhave, mā agocare carittha paravisaye. Agocare, bhikkhave, carataṃ paravisaye lacchati māro otāraṃ, lacchati māro ārammaṇaṃ. Ko ca, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno agocaro paravisayo? Yadidaṃ – pañca kāmaguṇā. Katame pañca? Cakkhuviññeyyā rūpā iṭṭhā kantā manāpā piyarūpā kāmūpasaṃhitā rajanīyā, sotaviññeyyā saddā…pe… ghānaviññeyyā gandhā… jivhāviññeyyā rasā… kāyaviññeyyā phoṭṭhabbā iṭṭhā kantā manāpā piyarūpā kāmūpasaṃhitā rajanīyā. Ayaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno agocaro paravisayo.

“Therefore, monks, do not wander in an improper range, in another’s territory. For those who wander in an improper range, in another’s territory, Māra will gain an opportunity, Māra will gain a footing. And what, monks, is a monk's improper range and another’s territory? It is the five strands of sensual pleasure. Which five? Forms cognizable by the eye—desirable, pleasing, charming, beloved, connected with sensual pleasure, and enticing; sounds cognizable by the ear… smells cognizable by the nose… tastes cognizable by the tongue… tangible objects cognizable by the body—desirable, pleasing, charming, beloved, connected with sensual pleasure, and enticing. This, monks, is a monk's improper range and another’s territory.”

“Gocare, bhikkhave, caratha sake pettike visaye. Gocare, bhikkhave[T 5.0200], carataṃ sake pettike visaye na lacchati māro otāraṃ, na lacchati māro ārammaṇaṃ. Ko ca, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno gocaro sako pettiko visayo? Yadidaṃ – cattāro satipaṭṭhānā. Katame cattāro[M 3.0130]? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ; vedanāsu…pe… citte…pe… dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ. Ayaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno gocaro sako pettiko visayo”ti. Sattamaṃ.

“Dwell, monks, in your own resort, your ancestral domain. For those who dwell in their own resort, their ancestral domain, Māra will not gain an opportunity; Māra will not find a support. And what, monks, is a monk’s own resort, his ancestral domain? It is these four establishments of mindfulness. Which four? Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having subdued covetousness and displeasure in the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings… the mind in the mind… phenomena in phenomena—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having subdued covetousness and displeasure in the world. This, monks, is a monk’s own resort, his ancestral domain.” Seventh.

8. Sūdasuttaṃ

8. The Discourse on the Cook

374. “Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, bālo abyatto akusalo sūdo rājānaṃ vā rājamahāmattaṃ vā rājamahāmattānaṃ vā (sī.) nānaccayehi sūpehi paccupaṭṭhito assa – ambilaggehipi, tittakaggehipi, kaṭukaggehipi, madhuraggehipi, khārikehipi, akhārikehipi, loṇikehipi, aloṇikehipi.

374. “Suppose, bhikkhus, a foolish, inexpert, unskilled cook were to present a king or a royal minister with various kinds of curries: predominantly sour, predominantly bitter, predominantly pungent, predominantly sweet, alkaline, non-alkaline, salty, and unsalty.

“Sa [P 5.0150] kho so, bhikkhave, bālo abyatto akusalo sūdo sakassa bhattu nimittaṃ na uggaṇhāti – ‘idaṃ vā me ajja bhattu sūpeyyaṃ ruccati, imassa vā abhiharati, imassa vā bahuṃ gaṇhāti, imassa vā vaṇṇaṃ bhāsati. Ambilaggaṃ vā me ajja bhattu sūpeyyaṃ ruccati[V 3.0228], ambilaggassa vā abhiharati, ambilaggassa vā bahuṃ gaṇhāti, ambilaggassa vā vaṇṇaṃ bhāsati. Tittakaggaṃ vā me ajja… kaṭukaggaṃ vā me ajja… madhuraggaṃ vā me ajja… khārikaṃ vā me ajja… akhārikaṃ vā me ajja… loṇikaṃ [T 5.0201] vā me ajja… aloṇikaṃ vā me ajja bhattu sūpeyyaṃ ruccati, aloṇikassa vā abhiharati, aloṇikassa vā bahuṃ gaṇhāti, aloṇikassa vā vaṇṇaṃ bhāsatī’”ti.

“Bhikkhus, that foolish, inexpert, unskilled cook does not grasp his master’s sign: ‘Today my master likes this curry, or he reaches for this one, or he takes a lot of this one, or he speaks in praise of this one. Today my master likes the predominantly sour curry, or he reaches for the predominantly sour one, or he takes a lot of the predominantly sour one, or he speaks in praise of the predominantly sour one. Today my master likes the predominantly bitter one… or the predominantly pungent one… or the predominantly sweet one… or the alkaline one… or the non-alkaline one… or the salty one… or today my master likes the unsalty curry, or he reaches for the unsalty one, or he takes a lot of the unsalty one, or he speaks in praise of the unsalty one.’”

“Sa kho so, bhikkhave, bālo abyatto akusalo sūdo na ceva lābhī hoti acchādanassa, na lābhī vetanassa, na lābhī abhihārānaṃ. Taṃ kissa hetu? Tathā hi so, bhikkhave, bālo abyatto akusalo sūdo sakassa bhattu nimittaṃ na uggaṇhāti. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, idhekacco bālo abyatto akusalo bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ. Tassa kāye kāyānupassino viharato cittaṃ na samādhiyati, upakkilesā na pahīyanti. So taṃ nimittaṃ na uggaṇhāti. Vedanāsu vedanānupassī viharati…pe… citte cittānupassī viharati [M 3.0131] …pe… dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ. Tassa dhammesu dhammānupassino viharato cittaṃ na samādhiyati, upakkilesā na pahīyanti. So taṃ nimittaṃ na uggaṇhāti.

“Bhikkhus, that foolish, inexpert, and unskilled cook gains neither clothing, wages, nor gratuities. For what reason? Because, bhikkhus, that foolish, inexpert, and unskilled cook does not grasp the sign of his master. Even so, bhikkhus, here some foolish, inexpert, and unskilled bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. While he dwells contemplating the body in the body, his mind does not become concentrated, and the defilements are not abandoned. He does not grasp that sign. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings… he dwells contemplating the mind in the mind… he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. While he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, his mind does not become concentrated, and the defilements are not abandoned. He does not grasp that sign.”

“Sa kho so, bhikkhave, bālo abyatto akusalo bhikkhu na ceva lābhī hoti diṭṭheva dhamme sukhavihārānaṃ, na lābhī satisampajaññassa[P 5.0151]. Taṃ kissa hetu? Tathā hi so, bhikkhave, bālo abyatto akusalo bhikkhu sakassa cittassa nimittaṃ na uggaṇhāti.

“Bhikkhus, that foolish, inexpert, and unskilled bhikkhu gains neither pleasant abidings in this very life, nor mindfulness and clear comprehension. For what reason? Because, bhikkhus, that foolish, inexpert, and unskilled bhikkhu does not grasp the sign of his own mind.”

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, paṇḍito byatto kusalo sūdo rājānaṃ [T 5.0202] vā rājamahāmattaṃ vā nānaccayehi sūpehi paccupaṭṭhito assa – ambilaggehipi, tittakaggehipi, kaṭukaggehipi, madhuraggehipi, khārikehipi, akhārikehipi, loṇikehipi, aloṇikehipi.

“Suppose, bhikkhus, a wise, astute, and skillful cook were to attend upon a king or a king's great minister with various kinds of curries—predominantly sour, predominantly bitter, predominantly pungent, predominantly sweet, alkaline, non-alkaline, salty, and unsalty.”

“Sa kho so, bhikkhave, paṇḍito byatto kusalo sūdo sakassa bhattu nimittaṃ uggaṇhāti – ‘idaṃ vā me ajja bhattu sūpeyyaṃ ruccati, imassa vā abhiharati, imassa vā bahuṃ gaṇhāti, imassa vā vaṇṇaṃ bhāsati. Ambilaggaṃ vā me ajja bhattu sūpeyyaṃ ruccati[V 3.0229], ambilaggassa vā abhiharati, ambilaggassa vā bahuṃ gaṇhāti, ambilaggassa vā vaṇṇaṃ bhāsati. Tittakaggaṃ vā me ajja… kaṭukaggaṃ vā me ajja… madhuraggaṃ vā me ajja… khārikaṃ vā me ajja… akhārikaṃ vā me ajja… loṇikaṃ vā me ajja… aloṇikaṃ vā me ajja bhattu sūpeyyaṃ ruccati, aloṇikassa vā abhiharati, aloṇikassa vā bahuṃ gaṇhāti, aloṇikassa vā vaṇṇaṃ bhāsatī’”ti.

“Bhikkhus, that wise, astute, and skillful cook grasps his master’s sign: ‘Today my master likes this curry; he reaches for this, he takes much of this, and he speaks in its praise. Today my master likes the predominantly sour curry; he reaches for the predominantly sour one, he takes much of the predominantly sour one, and he speaks in its praise. Today the predominantly bitter one… the predominantly pungent one… the predominantly sweet one… the alkaline one… the non-alkaline one… the salty one… today my master likes the unsalty curry; he reaches for the unsalty one, he takes much of the unsalty one, and he speaks in its praise.’”

“Sa kho so, bhikkhave, paṇḍito byatto kusalo sūdo lābhī ceva hoti acchādanassa, lābhī vetanassa, lābhī abhihārānaṃ. Taṃ kissa hetu? Tathā hi so, bhikkhave, paṇḍito byatto kusalo sūdo sakassa bhattu nimittaṃ uggaṇhāti. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, idhekacco paṇḍito byatto kusalo bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ. Tassa kāye kāyānupassino viharato [T 5.0203] cittaṃ samādhiyati, upakkilesā pahīyanti[P 5.0152]. So taṃ nimittaṃ uggaṇhāti. Vedanāsu vedanānupassī viharati…pe… citte cittānupassī viharati…pe… dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati [M 3.0132] ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ. Tassa dhammesu dhammānupassino viharato cittaṃ samādhiyati, upakkilesā pahīyanti. So taṃ nimittaṃ uggaṇhāti.

“Indeed, bhikkhus, that wise, astute, and skillful cook gains clothing, wages, and gifts. For what reason? Because, bhikkhus, that wise, astute, and skillful cook grasps his master’s sign. Even so, bhikkhus, here some wise, astute, and skillful bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. As he dwells contemplating the body in the body, his mind becomes concentrated and the defilements are abandoned. He grasps that sign. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings… mind in mind… phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. As he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, his mind becomes concentrated and the defilements are abandoned. He grasps that sign.”

“Sa kho so, bhikkhave, paṇḍito byatto kusalo bhikkhu lābhī ceva hoti diṭṭheva dhamme sukhavihārānaṃ, lābhī hoti satisampajaññassa. Taṃ kissa hetu? Tathā hi so, bhikkhave, paṇḍito byatto kusalo bhikkhu sakassa cittassa nimittaṃ uggaṇhātī”ti. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

“Indeed, bhikkhus, that wise, astute, and skillful bhikkhu gains pleasant abidings in this very life, and he gains mindfulness and clear comprehension. For what reason? Because, bhikkhus, that wise, astute, and skillful bhikkhu grasps the sign of his own mind.” Eighth.

9. Gilānasuttaṃ

9. The Discourse on the Sick Person

375. Evaṃ me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā vesāliyaṃ viharati veḷuvagāmake beluvagāmake (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.). Tatra kho bhagavā bhikkhū āmantesi – “etha tumhe, bhikkhave, samantā vesāliyā yathāmittaṃ yathāsandiṭṭhaṃ yathāsambhattaṃ vassaṃ upetha. Idhevāhaṃ veḷuvagāmake vassaṃ upagacchāmī”ti. “Evaṃ, bhante”ti [V 3.0230] kho te bhikkhū bhagavato paṭissutvā samantā vesāliyā yathāmittaṃ yathāsandiṭṭhaṃ yathāsambhattaṃ vassaṃ upagacchuṃ. Bhagavā pana tattheva veḷuvagāmake vassaṃ upagacchi upagañchi (sī. pī.).

375. Thus have I heard: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Vesālī in the village of Veḷuva. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Come, bhikkhus, enter the rains retreat around Vesālī, wherever you have friends, wherever you have acquaintances, wherever you have companions. I shall enter the rains retreat right here in the village of Veḷuva.” “Yes, Venerable Sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One, and they entered the rains retreat around Vesālī, wherever they had friends, wherever they had acquaintances, wherever they had companions. The Blessed One, however, entered the rains retreat right there in the village of Veḷuva.

Atha kho bhagavato vassūpagatassa kharo ābādho uppajji, bāḷhā vedanā vattanti māraṇantikā. Tatra sudaṃ bhagavā sato sampajāno adhivāsesi avihaññamāno. Atha kho bhagavato etadahosi – “na kho [T 5.0204] me taṃ patirūpaṃ, yohaṃ anāmantetvā upaṭṭhāke anapaloketvā bhikkhusaṅghaṃ parinibbāyeyyaṃ. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ imaṃ ābādhaṃ vīriyena paṭipaṇāmetvā jīvitasaṅkhāraṃ adhiṭṭhāya [P 5.0153] vihareyya”nti. Atha kho bhagavā taṃ ābādhaṃ vīriyena paṭipaṇāmetvā jīvitasaṅkhāraṃ adhiṭṭhāya vihāsi. (Atha kho bhagavato so ābādho paṭippassambhi) ( ) dī. ni. 2.164 dissati.

Then, after the Blessed One had entered the rains retreat, a severe illness arose in him, and strong, deadly pains occurred. The Blessed One endured them, mindful and clearly comprehending, without being afflicted. Then it occurred to the Blessed One: “It would not be fitting for me to attain final Nibbāna without addressing the attendants and taking leave of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. What if I were to suppress this illness with effort and, having resolved upon the life-force, continue to dwell?” Then the Blessed One suppressed that illness with effort and, having resolved upon the life-force, continued to dwell. Then that illness of the Blessed One subsided.

Atha kho bhagavā gilānā vuṭṭhito gilānavuṭṭhito (saddanīti) aciravuṭṭhito gelaññā vihārā nikkhamitvā vihārapacchāyāyaṃ vihārapacchāchāyāyaṃ (bahūsu) paññatte āsane nisīdi. Atha kho āyasmā ānando yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho āyasmā ānando bhagavantaṃ [M 3.0133] etadavoca – “diṭṭho me, bhante, bhagavato phāsu; diṭṭhaṃ, bhante, bhagavato khamanīyaṃ; diṭṭhaṃ, bhante, bhagavato yāpanīyaṃ. Api ca me, bhante, madhurakajāto viya kāyo, disāpi me na pakkhāyanti, dhammāpi maṃ nappaṭibhanti bhagavato gelaññena. Api ca me, bhante, ahosi kācideva assāsamattā – ‘na tāva bhagavā parinibbāyissati, na yāva bhagavā bhikkhusaṅghaṃ ārabbha kiñcideva udāharatī’”ti.
