Idhāvuso, bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ; vedanāsu…pe… [V 3.0250] citte…pe… dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ. Imesaṃ kho, āvuso, catunnaṃ satipaṭṭhānānaṃ padesaṃ bhāvitattā sekho hotī”ti. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

“Which four? Here, friend, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body as a body—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in the world. He dwells contemplating feelings as feelings… mind as mind… phenomena as phenomena—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in the world. Friend, one is a trainee because of having developed a portion of these four foundations of mindfulness.”

7. Samattasuttaṃ

7. Completeness

393. Taṃyeva nidānaṃ. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho āyasmā sāriputto āyasmantaṃ anuruddhaṃ etadavoca – “‘asekho[T 5.0234], asekho’ti, āvuso anuruddha, vuccati. Kittāvatā nu kho, āvuso, asekho hotī”ti? “Catunnaṃ kho, āvuso, satipaṭṭhānānaṃ samattaṃ bhāvitattā asekho hoti”.

393. The setting is the same. Seated to one side, the Venerable Sāriputta said this to the Venerable Anuruddha: “Friend Anuruddha, it is said, ‘an adept, an adept.’ To what extent, friend, is one an adept?” “Friend, one is an adept because of having developed the four foundations of mindfulness to completion.”

“Katamesaṃ catunnaṃ? Idhāvuso, bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ; vedanāsu…pe… citte…pe… dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ. Imesaṃ kho[M 3.0153], āvuso, catunnaṃ satipaṭṭhānānaṃ samattaṃ bhāvitattā asekho hotī”ti. Sattamaṃ.

“Which four? Here, friend, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body as a body, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in the world; he dwells contemplating feelings as feelings… mind as mind… phenomena as phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in the world. It is, friend, by the complete development of these four foundations of mindfulness that one becomes an adept.”

8. Lokasuttaṃ

8. The World

394. Taṃyeva nidānaṃ. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho āyasmā sāriputto āyasmantaṃ anuruddhaṃ etadavoca – “katamesaṃ, āvuso anuruddha, dhammānaṃ bhāvitattā bahulīkatattā mahābhiññataṃ mahābhiññātaṃ (pī.) patto”ti? “Catunnaṃ[P 5.0176], āvuso, satipaṭṭhānānaṃ bhāvitattā bahulīkatattā mahābhiññataṃ patto”.

394. The setting is the same. Seated to one side, the Venerable Sāriputta said this to the Venerable Anuruddha: “Friend Anuruddha, by developing and frequently practicing which qualities have you attained great direct knowledge?” “Friend, it is by developing and frequently practicing the four foundations of mindfulness that I have attained great direct knowledge.”

“Katamesaṃ catunnaṃ? Idhāhaṃ, āvuso, kāye kāyānupassī viharāmi ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ; vedanāsu…pe… citte…pe… dhammesu dhammānupassī viharāmi ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ. Imesaṃ khvāhaṃ, āvuso[V 3.0251], catunnaṃ satipaṭṭhānānaṃ bhāvitattā bahulīkatattā mahābhiññataṃ patto. Imesañca panāhaṃ, āvuso, catunnaṃ satipaṭṭhānānaṃ bhāvitattā bahulīkatattā sahassaṃ lokaṃ [T 5.0235] abhijānāmī”ti. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

“Which four? Here, friend, I dwell contemplating the body as a body, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in the world; I dwell contemplating feelings as feelings… mind as mind… phenomena as phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in the world. It is, friend, because I have developed and frequently practiced these four foundations of mindfulness that I have attained great direct knowledge. And furthermore, friend, it is because I have developed and frequently practiced these four foundations of mindfulness that I directly know a thousand worlds.”

9. Sirivaḍḍhasuttaṃ

9. The Discourse on Sirivaḍḍha

395. Ekaṃ samayaṃ āyasmā ānando rājagahe viharati veḷuvane kalandakanivāpe. Tena kho pana samayena sirivaḍḍho sirīvaḍḍho (ka.) gahapati ābādhiko hoti dukkhito bāḷhagilāno. Atha kho sirivaḍḍho gahapati aññataraṃ purisaṃ āmantesi – “ehi tvaṃ, ambho purisa, yenāyasmā ānando tenupasaṅkama; upasaṅkamitvā mama vacanena āyasmato ānandassa pāde sirasā vanda – ‘sirivaḍḍho, bhante, gahapati ābādhiko dukkhito bāḷhagilāno. So āyasmato ānandassa pāde sirasā vandatī’ti. Evañca vadehi – ‘sādhu kira, bhante, āyasmā ānando yena sirivaḍḍhassa gahapatissa nivesanaṃ tenupasaṅkamatu anukampaṃ upādāyā’”ti. “Evaṃ, bhante”ti kho so puriso sirivaḍḍhassa gahapatissa paṭissutvā yenāyasmā ānando tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho [M 3.0154] so puriso āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ etadavoca – “sirivaḍḍho, bhante, gahapati ābādhiko dukkhito bāḷhagilāno, so āyasmato ānandassa pāde sirasā vandati. Evañca vadeti – ‘sādhu kira, bhante, āyasmā ānando yena sirivaḍḍhassa gahapatissa nivesanaṃ tenupasaṅkamatu anukampaṃ upādāyā’”ti. Adhivāsesi [P 5.0177] kho āyasmā ānando tuṇhībhāvena.

395. At one time, the Venerable Ānanda was staying in Rājagaha, in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place. At that time, the householder Sirivaḍḍha was sick, suffering, and gravely ill. Then the householder Sirivaḍḍha addressed a certain man: “Come, good man, go to the Venerable Ānanda. Having approached, venerate the Venerable Ānanda’s feet with your head in my name, saying, ‘Venerable sir, the householder Sirivaḍḍha is sick, suffering, and gravely ill. He venerates the Venerable Ānanda’s feet with his head.’ And say this: ‘It would be good, venerable sir, if the Venerable Ānanda would approach the residence of the householder Sirivaḍḍha, out of compassion.’” “Yes, sir,” that man replied to the householder Sirivaḍḍha. Then he went to the Venerable Ānanda, and after paying homage to him, sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, he said to the Venerable Ānanda: “Venerable sir, the householder Sirivaḍḍha is sick, suffering, and gravely ill. He venerates the Venerable Ānanda’s feet with his head, and says, ‘It would be good, venerable sir, if the Venerable Ānanda would approach the residence of the householder Sirivaḍḍha, out of compassion.’” The Venerable Ānanda consented by silence.

Atha kho āyasmā ānando pubbaṇhasamayaṃ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya [T 5.0236] yena sirivaḍḍhassa gahapatissa nivesanaṃ tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā paññatte āsane nisīdi. Nisajja kho āyasmā ānando sirivaḍḍhaṃ gahapatiṃ etadavoca – “kacci te, gahapati, khamanīyaṃ kacci yāpanīyaṃ, kacci dukkhā vedanā paṭikkamanti, no abhikkamanti; paṭikkamosānaṃ paññāyati, no abhikkamo”ti? “Na me, bhante, khamanīyaṃ na yāpanīyaṃ. Bāḷhā me dukkhā vedanā abhikkamanti, no paṭikkamanti; abhikkamosānaṃ paññāyati, no paṭikkamo”ti.

Then, in the morning, the Venerable Ānanda, having dressed, took his bowl and robe, and went to the residence of the householder Sirivaḍḍha. Having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat. Sitting there, the Venerable Ānanda said to the householder Sirivaḍḍha: “Householder, are you enduring? Are you getting by? Are your painful feelings subsiding and not increasing? Is their subsiding apparent, and not their increasing?” “Venerable sir, I am not enduring, I am not getting by. My strong painful feelings are increasing, not subsiding; their increasing is apparent, not their subsiding.”

“Tasmātiha te, gahapati, evaṃ sikkhitabbaṃ – ‘kāye kāyānupassī viharissāmi ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ; vedanāsu…pe… [V 3.0252] citte…pe… dhammesu dhammānupassī viharissāmi ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassa’nti. Evañhi te, gahapati, sikkhitabba”nti.

“Therefore, householder, you should train yourself thus: ‘I will dwell contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in the world. In feelings… in mind… in phenomena, I will dwell contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in the world.’ Thus, householder, you should train yourself.”

“Yeme, bhante, bhagavatā cattāro satipaṭṭhānā desitā saṃvijjanti, te dhammā saṃvijjante ratanadhammā (sī.) mayi, ahañca tesu dhammesu sandissāmi. Ahañhi, bhante, kāye kāyānupassī viharāmi ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ; vedanāsu…pe… citte…pe… dhammesu dhammānupassī viharāmi ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ. Yāni cimāni, bhante, bhagavatā pañcorambhāgiyāni saṃyojanāni [T 5.0237] desitāni, nāhaṃ, bhante, tesaṃ kiñci attani appahīnaṃ samanupassāmī”ti. “Lābhā te, gahapati, suladdhaṃ te, gahapati! Anāgāmiphalaṃ tayā, gahapati, byākata”nti. Navamaṃ.

“Venerable sir, these four foundations of mindfulness taught by the Blessed One are found in me, and I am found in those teachings. For, venerable sir, I dwell contemplating the body in the body—ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful—having removed covetousness and displeasure in the world. In feelings… in mind… in phenomena, I dwell contemplating phenomena in phenomena—ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful—having removed covetousness and displeasure in the world. And, venerable sir, as for these five lower fetters taught by the Blessed One, I do not perceive any of them unabandoned in myself.” “It is your gain, householder, it is well gained by you, householder! The fruit of non-returning has been declared by you, householder.” The ninth.

10. Mānadinnasuttaṃ

10. The Discourse on Mānadinna

396. Taṃyeva [M 3.0155][P 5.0178] nidānaṃ. Tena kho pana samayena mānadinno gahapati ābādhiko hoti dukkhito bāḷhagilāno. Atha kho mānadinno gahapati aññataraṃ purisaṃ āmantesi – “ehi tvaṃ, ambho purisa…pe… na me, bhante, khamanīyaṃ na yāpanīyaṃ. Bāḷhā me dukkhā vedanā abhikkamanti, no paṭikkamanti; abhikkamosānaṃ paññāyati, no paṭikkamoti. Evarūpāya cāhaṃ, bhante, dukkhāya vedanāya phuṭṭho samāno kāye kāyānupassī viharāmi ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ; vedanāsu…pe… citte…pe… dhammesu dhammānupassī viharāmi ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ. Yāni cimāni, bhante, bhagavatā pañcorambhāgiyāni saṃyojanāni desitāni, nāhaṃ, bhante, tesaṃ kiñci attani appahīnaṃ samanupassāmī”ti. “Lābhā te, gahapati, suladdhaṃ te, gahapati! Anāgāmiphalaṃ tayā, gahapati, byākata”nti. Dasamaṃ.

396. The same setting. At that time, the householder Mānadinna was sick, suffering, and gravely ill. Then the householder Mānadinna addressed a certain man: “Come, good man…” … “Venerable sir, I am not enduring, I am not getting by. My strong painful feelings are increasing, not subsiding; their increasing is apparent, not their subsiding. Though afflicted by such a painful feeling, I dwell contemplating the body in the body—ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful—having removed covetousness and displeasure in the world. In feelings… in mind… in phenomena, I dwell contemplating phenomena in phenomena—ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful—having removed covetousness and displeasure in the world. And, venerable sir, as for these five lower fetters taught by the Blessed One, I do not perceive any of them unabandoned in myself.” “It is your gain, householder, it is well-gained by you, householder! The fruit of non-returning has been declared by you, householder.” The tenth.

Sīlaṭṭhitivaggo tatiyo.

The Chapter on Virtue and Stability, the third.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary of that:

Sīlaṃ [T 5.0238][V 3.0253] ṭhiti parihānaṃ, suddhaṃ brāhmaṇapadesaṃ;

Samattaṃ loko sirivaḍḍho, mānadinnena te dasāti.

Virtue, Stability, Decline, Purity, Brahmin, and Designation; Completeness, World, Sirivaḍḍha, and Mānadinna—these are the ten.

4. Ananussutavaggo

4. The Chapter on the Unheard

1. Ananussutasuttaṃ

1. The Discourse on the Unheard

397. Sāvatthinidānaṃ[T 5.0239]. “‘Ayaṃ kāye kāyānupassanā’ti me, bhikkhave, pubbe ananussutesu [P 5.0179] dhammesu cakkhuṃ udapādi, ñāṇaṃ udapādi, paññā udapādi, vijjā udapādi, āloko udapādi. ‘Sā kho panāyaṃ kāye kāyānupassanā bhāvetabbā’ti me, bhikkhave…pe… bhāvitā’ti me, bhikkhave, pubbe ananussutesu dhammesu cakkhuṃ udapādi, ñāṇaṃ udapādi, paññā udapādi, vijjā udapādi, āloko udapādi”.

397. At Sāvatthī. “‘This is contemplation of the body in the body’—thus, bhikkhus, in regard to dhammas unheard before, the eye of wisdom arose in me, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true knowledge arose, and light arose. ‘Indeed, that contemplation of the body in the body is to be developed’—thus, bhikkhus… ‘It has been developed’—thus, bhikkhus, in regard to dhammas unheard before, the eye of wisdom arose in me, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true knowledge arose, and light arose.”

“‘Ayaṃ [M 3.0156] vedanāsu vedanānupassanā’ti me, bhikkhave, pubbe ananussutesu dhammesu cakkhuṃ udapādi, ñāṇaṃ udapādi, paññā udapādi, vijjā udapādi, āloko udapādi. ‘Sā kho panāyaṃ vedanāsu vedanānupassanā bhāvetabbā’ti me, bhikkhave…pe… bhāvitā’ti me, bhikkhave, pubbe ananussutesu dhammesu cakkhuṃ udapādi, ñāṇaṃ udapādi, paññā udapādi, vijjā udapādi, āloko udapādi.

‘Bhikkhus, “This is the contemplation of feelings in feelings”—thus, regarding dhammas unheard before, the eye arose in me, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, higher knowledge arose, and light arose. “Bhikkhus, that contemplation of feelings in feelings is to be developed”—thus… “it has been developed”—thus, regarding dhammas unheard before, the eye arose in me, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, higher knowledge arose, and light arose.

“‘Ayaṃ citte cittānupassanā’ti me, bhikkhave, pubbe ananussutesu dhammesu cakkhuṃ udapādi, ñāṇaṃ udapādi, paññā udapādi, vijjā udapādi, āloko udapādi. ‘Sā kho panāyaṃ citte cittānupassanā bhāvetabbā’ti me, bhikkhave…pe… bhāvitā’ti me, bhikkhave, pubbe ananussutesu dhammesu cakkhuṃ udapādi, ñāṇaṃ udapādi, paññā udapādi, vijjā udapādi, āloko udapādi.

‘Bhikkhus, “This is the contemplation of the mind in the mind”—thus, regarding dhammas unheard before, the eye arose in me, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, higher knowledge arose, and light arose. “Bhikkhus, that contemplation of the mind in the mind is to be developed”—thus… “it has been developed”—thus, regarding dhammas unheard before, the eye arose in me, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, higher knowledge arose, and light arose.

“‘Ayaṃ [T 5.0240][V 3.0254] dhammesu dhammānupassanā’ti me, bhikkhave, pubbe ananussutesu dhammesu cakkhuṃ udapādi, ñāṇaṃ udapādi, paññā udapādi, vijjā udapādi, āloko udapādi. ‘Sā kho panāyaṃ dhammesu dhammānupassanā bhāvetabbā’ti me, bhikkhave…pe… bhāvitā’ti me, bhikkhave, pubbe ananussutesu dhammesu cakkhuṃ udapādi, ñāṇaṃ udapādi, paññā udapādi, vijjā udapādi, āloko udapādī”ti. Paṭhamaṃ.

‘Bhikkhus, “This is the contemplation of dhammas in dhammas”—thus, regarding dhammas unheard before, the eye arose in me, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, higher knowledge arose, and light arose. “Bhikkhus, that contemplation of dhammas in dhammas is to be developed”—thus… “it has been developed”—thus, regarding dhammas unheard before, the eye arose in me, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, higher knowledge arose, and light arose.’ First.

2. Virāgasuttaṃ

2. The Discourse on Dispassion

398. “Cattārome, bhikkhave, satipaṭṭhānā bhāvitā bahulīkatā ekantanibbidāya virāgāya nirodhāya upasamāya abhiññāya sambodhāya nibbānāya saṃvattanti.

398. ‘Bhikkhus, these four establishments of mindfulness, when developed and frequently practiced, conduce to utter disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to pacification, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, and to Nibbāna.

“Katame cattāro? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ; vedanāsu…pe… citte…pe… dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ. Ime kho, bhikkhave, cattāro satipaṭṭhānā bhāvitā bahulīkatā ekantanibbidāya virāgāya nirodhāya upasamāya abhiññāya sambodhāya nibbānāya saṃvattantī”ti. Dutiyaṃ.

‘What four? Here, Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having subdued covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings… mind in mind… dhammas in dhammas, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having subdued covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. These, Bhikkhus, are the four establishments of mindfulness that, when developed and frequently practiced, conduce to utter disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to pacification, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, and to Nibbāna.’ Second.

3. Viraddhasuttaṃ

3. The Discourse on Failure

399. “Yesaṃ [M 3.0157] kesañci, bhikkhave, cattāro satipaṭṭhānā viraddhā, viraddho tesaṃ ariyo maggo ariyo aṭṭhaṅkiko maggo (ka.) imasmiṃ yeva sutte dissati aṭṭhaṅgikotipadaṃ, na panāññattha iddhipāda anuruddhādīsu sammā dukkhakkhayagāmī. Yesaṃ [P 5.0180] kesañci, bhikkhave, cattāro satipaṭṭhānā āraddhā, āraddho tesaṃ ariyo maggo sammā dukkhakkhayagāmī.

399. ‘Bhikkhus, for whomever the four establishments of mindfulness are neglected, for them the noble path that leads rightly to the destruction of suffering is neglected. Bhikkhus, for whomever the four establishments of mindfulness are undertaken, for them the noble path that leads rightly to the destruction of suffering is undertaken.

“Katame cattāro? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno [T 5.0241] satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ; vedanāsu…pe… citte…pe… dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ. Yesaṃ kesañci[V 3.0255], bhikkhave, ime cattāro satipaṭṭhānā viraddhā, viraddho tesaṃ ariyo maggo sammā dukkhakkhayagāmī. Yesaṃ kesañci, bhikkhave, ime cattāro satipaṭṭhānā āraddhā, āraddho tesaṃ ariyo maggo sammā dukkhakkhayagāmī”ti. Tatiyaṃ.

‘What four? Here, Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having subdued covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings… mind in mind… dhammas in dhammas, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having subdued covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. For whomever, Bhikkhus, these four establishments of mindfulness are neglected, for them the noble path that leads rightly to the destruction of suffering is neglected. For whomever, Bhikkhus, these four establishments of mindfulness are undertaken, for them the noble path that leads rightly to the destruction of suffering is undertaken.’ Third.

4. Bhāvitasuttaṃ

4. The Discourse on Development

400. “Cattārome, bhikkhave, satipaṭṭhānā bhāvitā bahulīkatā apārā pāraṃ gamanāya saṃvattanti.

400. ‘Bhikkhus, these four establishments of mindfulness, when developed and frequently practiced, lead to going from the near shore to the far shore.

“Katame cattāro? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ; vedanāsu…pe… citte…pe… dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ. Ime kho, bhikkhave, cattāro satipaṭṭhānā bhāvitā bahulīkatā apārā pāraṃ gamanāya saṃvattantī”ti. Catutthaṃ.

‘What four? Here, Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having subdued covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings… mind in mind… dhammas in dhammas, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having subdued covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. These, Bhikkhus, are the four establishments of mindfulness which, when developed and frequently practiced, lead to going from the near shore to the far shore.’ Fourth.

5. Satisuttaṃ

5. The Discourse on Mindfulness

401. Sāvatthinidānaṃ. “Sato, bhikkhave, bhikkhu vihareyya sampajāno. Ayaṃ vo amhākaṃ anusāsanī”.

401. At Sāvatthī. ‘Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu should dwell mindful and clearly comprehending. This is our instruction to you.’

“Kathañca, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sato hoti? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ[M 3.0158]; vedanāsu…pe… citte…pe… dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sato hoti.

‘And how, Bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu mindful? Here, Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having subdued covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings… mind in mind… dhammas in dhammas, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having subdued covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. Thus, Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is mindful.

“Kathañca[T 5.0242], bhikkhave, bhikkhu sampajāno hoti? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno viditā vedanā uppajjanti, viditā upaṭṭhahanti[P 5.0181], viditā abbhatthaṃ gacchanti. Viditā vitakkā uppajjanti[V 3.0256], viditā upaṭṭhahanti, viditā abbhatthaṃ gacchanti. Viditā saññā uppajjanti, viditā upaṭṭhahanti, viditā abbhatthaṃ gacchanti. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sampajāno hoti. Sato, bhikkhave, bhikkhu vihareyya sampajāno. Ayaṃ vo amhākaṃ anusāsanī”ti. Pañcamaṃ.

‘And how, Bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu clearly comprehending? Here, Bhikkhus, for a bhikkhu, feelings are known as they arise, known as they are present, and known as they cease. Thoughts are known as they arise, known as they are present, and known as they cease. Perceptions are known as they arise, known as they are present, and known as they cease. Thus, Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is clearly comprehending. Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu should dwell mindful and clearly comprehending. This is our instruction to you.’ Fifth.

6. Aññāsuttaṃ

6. The Discourse on Final Knowledge

402. “Cattārome, bhikkhave, satipaṭṭhānā. Katame cattāro? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ; vedanāsu…pe… citte…pe… dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ. Ime kho, bhikkhave, cattāro satipaṭṭhānā. Imesaṃ kho, bhikkhave, catunnaṃ satipaṭṭhānānaṃ bhāvitattā bahulīkatattā dvinnaṃ phalānaṃ aññataraṃ phalaṃ pāṭikaṅkhaṃ – diṭṭheva dhamme aññā, sati vā upādisese anāgāmitā”ti. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

402. “O monks, these are the four foundations of mindfulness. What are the four? Here, O monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in the world; he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings… mind in mind… phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in the world. These, O monks, are the four foundations of mindfulness. Because of the development and cultivation of these four foundations of mindfulness, one of two fruits is to be expected: either final knowledge in this very life or, if there is a remainder of clinging, the state of non-return.” The Sixth.

7. Chandasuttaṃ

7. The Discourse on Desire

403. “Cattārome, bhikkhave, satipaṭṭhānā. Katame cattāro? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ. Tassa kāye kāyānupassino viharato yo kāyasmiṃ chando so pahīyati. Chandassa pahānā amataṃ sacchikataṃ hoti.

403. “O monks, these are the four foundations of mindfulness. What are the four? Here, O monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in the world. For him who dwells contemplating the body in the body, whatever desire there is in regard to the body is abandoned. Through the abandoning of desire, the Deathless is realized.

“Vedanāsu [T 5.0243] vedanānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ. Tassa vedanāsu vedanānupassino viharato yo vedanāsu chando so pahīyati. Chandassa pahānā amataṃ sacchikataṃ hoti.

“He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in the world. For him who dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, whatever desire there is in regard to feelings is abandoned. Through the abandoning of desire, the Deathless is realized.

“Citte [M 3.0159][P 5.0182] cittānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ. Tassa citte cittānupassino viharato yo cittamhi chando so pahīyati. Chandassa pahānā amataṃ sacchikataṃ hoti.

“He dwells contemplating the mind in the mind, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in the world. For him who dwells contemplating the mind in the mind, whatever desire there is in regard to the mind is abandoned. Through the abandoning of desire, the Deathless is realized.

“Dhammesu [V 3.0257] dhammānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ. Tassa dhammesu dhammānupassino viharato yo dhammesu chando so pahīyati. Chandassa pahānā amataṃ sacchikataṃ hotī”ti. Sattamaṃ.

“He dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in the world. For him who dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, whatever desire there is in regard to phenomena is abandoned. Through the abandoning of desire, the Deathless is realized.” The Seventh.

8. Pariññātasuttaṃ

8. The Discourse on Full Understanding

404. “Cattārome, bhikkhave, satipaṭṭhānā. Katame cattāro? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ. Tassa kāye kāyānupassino viharato kāyo pariññāto hoti. Kāyassa pariññātattā amataṃ sacchikataṃ hoti.

404. “O monks, these are the four foundations of mindfulness. What are the four? Here, O monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in the world. For him who dwells contemplating the body in the body, the body is fully understood. Because the body is fully understood, the Deathless is realized.

“Vedanāsu vedanānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ. Tassa vedanāsu vedanānupassino viharato vedanā pariññātā honti. Vedanānaṃ pariññātattā [T 5.0244] amataṃ sacchikataṃ hoti.

“He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in the world. For him who dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, feelings are fully understood. Because feelings are fully understood, the Deathless is realized.

“Citte cittānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ. Tassa citte cittānupassino viharato cittaṃ pariññātaṃ hoti. Cittassa pariññātattā amataṃ sacchikataṃ hoti.

“He dwells contemplating the mind in the mind, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in the world. For him who dwells contemplating the mind in the mind, the mind is fully understood. Because the mind is fully understood, the Deathless is realized.

“Dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ. Tassa dhammesu dhammānupassino viharato dhammā pariññātā honti. Dhammānaṃ pariññātattā amataṃ sacchikataṃ hotī”ti. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

“He dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in the world. For him who dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, phenomena are fully understood. Because phenomena are fully understood, the Deathless is realized.” The Eighth.

9. Bhāvanāsuttaṃ

9. The Discourse on Development

405. “Catunnaṃ[M 3.0160], bhikkhave, satipaṭṭhānānaṃ bhāvanaṃ desessāmi. Taṃ suṇātha”. “Katamā, bhikkhave, catunnaṃ satipaṭṭhānānaṃ bhāvanā? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ; vedanāsu…pe… citte…pe… dhammesu dhammānupassī [V 3.0258] viharati ātāpī [P 5.0183] sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ. Ayaṃ kho, bhikkhave, catunnaṃ satipaṭṭhānānaṃ bhāvanā”ti. Navamaṃ.

405. “O monks, I will teach the development of the four foundations of mindfulness. Listen to that. What, O monks, is the development of the four foundations of mindfulness? Here, O monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in the world; he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings… mind in mind… phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in the world. This, O monks, is the development of the four foundations of mindfulness.” The Ninth.

10. Vibhaṅgasuttaṃ

10. The Discourse on Analysis

406. “Satipaṭṭhānañca vo, bhikkhave, desessāmi satipaṭṭhānabhāvanañca satipaṭṭhānabhāvanāgāminiñca paṭipadaṃ. Taṃ suṇātha”. “Katamañca, bhikkhave, satipaṭṭhānaṃ? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ; vedanāsu vedanānupassī viharati…pe… citte cittānupassī viharati…pe… dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati ātāpī [T 5.0245] sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ. Idaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, satipaṭṭhānaṃ”.

406. “O monks, I shall teach you the foundation of mindfulness, the development of the foundation of mindfulness, and the practice leading to the development of the foundation of mindfulness. Listen to that. And what, O monks, is the foundation of mindfulness? Here, O monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in the world; he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings… he dwells contemplating the mind in the mind… he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in the world. This, O monks, is called the foundation of mindfulness.”

“Katamā ca, bhikkhave, satipaṭṭhānabhāvanā? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu samudayadhammānupassī kāyasmiṃ viharati, vayadhammānupassī kāyasmiṃ viharati, samudayavayadhammānupassī kāyasmiṃ viharati, ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ. Samudayadhammānupassī vedanāsu viharati…pe… samudayadhammānupassī citte viharati… samudayadhammānupassī dhammesu viharati, vayadhammānupassī dhammesu viharati, samudayavayadhammānupassī dhammesu viharati, ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, satipaṭṭhānabhāvanā.

“And what, O monks, is the development of the foundation of mindfulness? Here, O monks, a monk dwells contemplating the nature of arising in the body, he dwells contemplating the nature of passing away in the body, and he dwells contemplating the nature of arising and passing away in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in the world. He dwells contemplating the nature of arising in feelings… he dwells contemplating the nature of arising in the mind… he dwells contemplating the nature of arising in phenomena, he dwells contemplating the nature of passing away in phenomena, and he dwells contemplating the nature of arising and passing away in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in the world. This, O monks, is called the development of the foundation of mindfulness.”

“Katamā ca, bhikkhave, satipaṭṭhānabhāvanāgāminī paṭipadā? Ayameva ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo, seyyathidaṃ – sammādiṭṭhi, sammāsaṅkappo, sammāvācā, sammākammanto, sammāājīvo, sammāvāyāmo, sammāsati, sammāsamādhi. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, satipaṭṭhānabhāvanāgāminī paṭipadā”ti. Dasamaṃ.

“And what, bhikkhus, is the practice leading to the development of the foundations of mindfulness? It is this very Noble Eightfold Path, that is: right view, right thought, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration. This, bhikkhus, is called the practice leading to the development of the foundations of mindfulness.”

Ananussutavaggo catuttho.

The Ananussuta Chapter is the fourth.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary of that is:

Ananussutaṃ [M 3.0161][V 3.0259][P 5.0184] virāgo, viraddho bhāvanā sati;

Aññā chandaṃ pariññāya, bhāvanā vibhaṅgena cāti.

Ananussuta, Virāga, Viraddha, Bhāvanā, Sati; Aññā, Chanda, Pariññā, Bhāvanā, and Vibhaṅga.

5. Amatavaggo

5. The Amata Chapter

1. Amatasuttaṃ

1. The Amata Sutta

407. Sāvatthinidānaṃ[T 5.0246]. “Catūsu, bhikkhave, satipaṭṭhānesu suppatiṭṭhitacittā viharatha. Mā vo amataṃ panassa. Katamesu catūsu? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ; vedanāsu…pe… citte…pe… dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ. Imesu, bhikkhave, catūsu satipaṭṭhānesu suppatiṭṭhitacittā viharatha. Mā vo amataṃ panassā”ti. Paṭhamaṃ.

407. At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, dwell with your minds well established in the four foundations of mindfulness. Let the Deathless not be lost to you. In which four? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings… mind in mind… dhammas in dhammas, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. Bhikkhus, dwell with your minds well established in these four foundations of mindfulness. Let the Deathless not be lost to you.”

2. Samudayasuttaṃ

2. The Discourse on Arising

408. “Catunnaṃ, bhikkhave, satipaṭṭhānānaṃ samudayañca atthaṅgamañca desessāmi. Taṃ suṇātha. Ko ca, bhikkhave, kāyassa samudayo? Āhārasamudayā kāyassa samudayo; āhāranirodhā kāyassa atthaṅgamo. Phassasamudayā vedanānaṃ samudayo; phassanirodhā vedanānaṃ atthaṅgamo. Nāmarūpasamudayā cittassa samudayo; nāmarūpanirodhā cittassa atthaṅgamo. Manasikārasamudayā dhammānaṃ samudayo; manasikāranirodhā dhammānaṃ atthaṅgamo”ti. Dutiyaṃ.

408. “Bhikkhus, I shall teach you the arising and the cessation of the four foundations of mindfulness. Listen to that. And what, bhikkhus, is the arising of the body? From the arising of nutriment comes the arising of the body; from the cessation of nutriment comes the cessation of the body. From the arising of contact comes the arising of feelings; from the cessation of contact comes the cessation of feelings. From the arising of name-and-form comes the arising of the mind; from the cessation of name-and-form comes the cessation of the mind. From the arising of attention comes the arising of dhammas; from the cessation of attention comes the cessation of dhammas.”

3. Maggasuttaṃ

3. The Discourse on the Path

409. Sāvatthinidānaṃ[V 3.0260][P 5.0185]. Tatra kho bhagavā bhikkhū āmantesi – “ekamidāhaṃ, bhikkhave, samayaṃ uruvelāyaṃ viharāmi najjā nerañjarāya tīre ajapālanigrodhe paṭhamābhisambuddho. Tassa mayhaṃ, bhikkhave, rahogatassa paṭisallīnassa evaṃ cetaso parivitakko udapādi – ‘ekāyano [T 5.0247] ayaṃ maggo sattānaṃ [M 3.0162] visuddhiyā sokaparidevānaṃ samatikkamāya dukkhadomanassānaṃ atthaṅgamāya ñāyassa adhigamāya nibbānassa sacchikiriyāya, yadidaṃ – cattāro satipaṭṭhānā’”.

409. At Sāvatthī. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, on one occasion, when I was newly enlightened, I was dwelling at Uruvelā on the bank of the Nerañjarā River, at the foot of the Goatherd’s Banyan Tree. Then, bhikkhus, while I was alone in seclusion, this thought arose in my mind: ‘This is the direct path for the purification of beings, for the overcoming of sorrow and lamentation, for the cessation of suffering and displeasure, for the attainment of the noble path, for the realization of Nibbāna—namely, the four foundations of mindfulness.’”

“Katame cattāro? Kāye vā bhikkhu kāyānupassī vihareyya ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ; vedanāsu vā bhikkhu vedanānupassī vihareyya…pe… citte vā bhikkhu cittānupassī vihareyya…pe… dhammesu vā bhikkhu dhammānupassī vihareyya ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ. Ekāyano ayaṃ maggo sattānaṃ visuddhiyā sokaparidevānaṃ samatikkamāya dukkhadomanassānaṃ atthaṅgamāya ñāyassa adhigamāya nibbānassa sacchikiriyāya, yadidaṃ – cattāro satipaṭṭhānā”ti.

“What are the four? A bhikkhu should dwell contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. He should dwell contemplating feelings in feelings… mind in mind… dhammas in dhammas, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. This is the direct path for the purification of beings, for the overcoming of sorrow and lamentation, for the cessation of suffering and displeasure, for the attainment of the noble path, for the realization of Nibbāna—namely, the four foundations of mindfulness.”

“Atha kho, bhikkhave, brahmā sahampati mama cetasā cetoparivitakkamaññāya – seyyathāpi nāma balavā puriso samiñjitaṃ vā bāhaṃ pasāreyya, pasāritaṃ vā bāhaṃ samiñjeyya, evameva – brahmaloke antarahito mama purato pāturahosi. Atha kho, bhikkhave, brahmā sahampati ekaṃsaṃ uttarāsaṅgaṃ karitvā yenāhaṃ tenañjaliṃ paṇāmetvā maṃ etadavoca – ‘evametaṃ, bhagavā, evametaṃ, sugata! Ekāyano ayaṃ, bhante, maggo sattānaṃ visuddhiyā sokaparidevānaṃ samatikkamāya dukkhadomanassānaṃ atthaṅgamāya ñāyassa adhigamāya nibbānassa sacchikiriyāya, yadidaṃ – cattāro [P 5.0186] satipaṭṭhānā’”.

“Then, bhikkhus, Brahmā Sahampati, having known with his mind the reflection in my mind—just as a strong man might extend his bent arm or bend his extended arm—disappeared from the Brahmā world and appeared before me. Then, bhikkhus, Brahmā Sahampati arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, extended his joined hands in reverence towards me, and said this to me: ‘So it is, Blessed One! So it is, Well-Gone One! This, venerable sir, is the direct path for the purification of beings, for the overcoming of sorrow and lamentation, for the cessation of suffering and displeasure, for the attainment of the noble path, for the realization of Nibbāna—namely, the four foundations of mindfulness.’”

“Katame cattāro? Kāye [T 5.0248] vā, bhante, bhikkhu kāyānupassī vihareyya ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ; vedanāsu vā…pe… citte vā [V 3.0261] …pe… dhammesu vā, bhante, bhikkhu dhammānupassī vihareyya ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ. Ekāyano ayaṃ, bhante, maggo sattānaṃ visuddhiyā sokaparidevānaṃ samatikkamāya dukkhadomanassānaṃ atthaṅgamāya ñāyassa adhigamāya nibbānassa sacchikiriyāya, yadidaṃ – cattāro satipaṭṭhānā”ti.

“What are the four? Here, venerable sir, a bhikkhu should dwell contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. He should dwell contemplating feelings in feelings… mind in mind… dhammas in dhammas, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. This, venerable sir, is the direct path for the purification of beings, for the overcoming of sorrow and lamentation, for the cessation of suffering and displeasure, for the attainment of the noble path, for the realization of Nibbāna—namely, the four foundations of mindfulness.”

“Idamavoca, bhikkhave, brahmā sahampati. Idaṃ vatvā athāparaṃ etadavoca –

“This, bhikkhus, Brahmā Sahampati said. Having said this, he spoke further:

‘Ekāyanaṃ jātikhayantadassī, maggaṃ pajānāti hitānukampī;

Etena maggena tariṃsu pubbe, tarissanti ye ca taranti ogha’”nti. tatiyaṃ;

‘The one who sees the end of birth, compassionate for the welfare of beings, knows the direct path. By this path they crossed over the flood in the past, they will cross over, and they are crossing over now.’

4. Satisuttaṃ

4. The Discourse on Mindfulness

410. “Sato[M 3.0163], bhikkhave, bhikkhu vihareyya. Ayaṃ vo amhākaṃ anusāsanī. Kathañca, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sato hoti? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ; vedanāsu…pe… citte…pe… dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sato hoti. Sato, bhikkhave, bhikkhu vihareyya. Ayaṃ vo amhākaṃ anusāsanī”ti. Catutthaṃ.

410. “A bhikkhu should dwell mindful, bhikkhus. This is our instruction to you. And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu mindful? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world; he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings… mind in mind… dhammas in dhammas, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that a bhikkhu is mindful. A bhikkhu should dwell mindful, bhikkhus. This is our instruction to you.”

5. Kusalarāsisuttaṃ

5. The Discourse on the Heap of the Wholesome

411. “‘Kusalarāsī’ti, bhikkhave, vadamāno cattāro satipaṭṭhāne sammā vadamāno vadeyya. Kevalo hāyaṃ, bhikkhave, kusalarāsi, yadidaṃ – cattāro satipaṭṭhānā.

411. “Bhikkhus, one who says, ‘a heap of the wholesome,’ would be speaking rightly if they were to speak of the four establishments of mindfulness. For this, bhikkhus, is the entire heap of the wholesome, that is to say, the four establishments of mindfulness.”

“Katame cattāro? Idha[P 5.0187], bhikkhave, bhikkhu [T 5.0249] kāye kāyānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ; vedanāsu…pe… citte…pe… cittānupassī…pe… dhammesu dhammānupassī [V 3.0262] viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ. ‘Kusalarāsī’ti, bhikkhave, vadamāno ime cattāro satipaṭṭhāne sammā vadamāno vadeyya. Kevalo hāyaṃ, bhikkhave, kusalarāsi, yadidaṃ – cattāro satipaṭṭhānā”ti. Pañcamaṃ.

“What four? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having subdued covetousness and displeasure in the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings… the mind in the mind… phenomena in phenomena—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having subdued covetousness and displeasure in the world. Bhikkhus, one who says, ‘a heap of the wholesome,’ would be speaking rightly if they were to speak of these four establishments of mindfulness. For this, bhikkhus, is the entire heap of the wholesome, that is to say, the four establishments of mindfulness.”

6. Pātimokkhasaṃvarasuttaṃ

6. 6. The Discourse on the Pātimokkha Restraint

412. Atha kho aññataro bhikkhu yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami…pe… ekamantaṃ nisinno kho so bhikkhu bhagavantaṃ etadavoca –

412. Then a certain bhikkhu approached the Blessed One… Seated to one side, that bhikkhu said this to the Blessed One:

“Sādhu me, bhante, bhagavā saṃkhittena dhammaṃ desetu, yamahaṃ bhagavato dhammaṃ sutvā eko vūpakaṭṭho appamatto ātāpī pahitatto vihareyya”nti. “Tasmātiha tvaṃ, bhikkhu, ādimeva visodhehi kusalesu dhammesu. Ko cādi kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ? Idha tvaṃ, bhikkhu, pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvuto viharāhi ācāragocarasampanno aṇumattesu vajjesu bhayadassāvī, samādāya sikkhassu sikkhāpadesu. Yato kho tvaṃ, bhikkhu, pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvuto viharissasi ācāragocarasampanno aṇumattesu vajjesu [M 3.0164] bhayadassāvī samādāya sikkhissu sikkhāpadesu; tato tvaṃ, bhikkhu, sīlaṃ nissāya sīle patiṭṭhāya cattāro satipaṭṭhāne bhāveyyāsi”.

“Venerable sir, it would be good if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that, having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute.” “Therefore, bhikkhu, you should first purify the very beginning in regard to wholesome qualities. And what is the beginning of wholesome qualities? Here, bhikkhu, you should dwell restrained by the Pātimokkha restraint, accomplished in conduct and resort, seeing danger in the slightest faults, undertaking and training in the training rules. When, bhikkhu, you dwell restrained by the Pātimokkha restraint, accomplished in conduct and resort, seeing danger in the slightest faults, undertaking and training in the training rules, then, bhikkhu, relying on virtue and established in virtue, you should develop the four establishments of mindfulness.”

“Katame cattāro? Idha tvaṃ, bhikkhu, kāye kāyānupassī viharāhi ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ; vedanāsu…pe… citte…pe… dhammesu dhammānupassī viharāhi ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ[T 5.0250]. Yato kho tvaṃ, bhikkhu, sīlaṃ nissāya sīle patiṭṭhāya ime cattāro satipaṭṭhāne evaṃ bhāvessasi, tato tuyhaṃ, bhikkhu, yā ratti vā divaso vā āgamissati vuddhiyeva pāṭikaṅkhā kusalesu dhammesu, no parihānī”ti.

“What four? Here, bhikkhu, you should dwell contemplating the body in the body—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having subdued covetousness and displeasure in the world. You should dwell contemplating feelings in feelings… the mind in the mind… phenomena in phenomena—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having subdued covetousness and displeasure in the world. When, bhikkhu, relying on virtue and established in virtue, you develop these four establishments of mindfulness in this way, then for you, bhikkhu, whether night or day comes, only growth in wholesome qualities is to be expected, not decline.”

Atha kho so bhikkhu bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinanditvā anumoditvā uṭṭhāyāsanā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā pakkāmi. Atha [P 5.0188] kho so bhikkhu eko vūpakaṭṭho appamatto ātāpī pahitatto viharanto nacirasseva – yassatthāya kulaputtā sammadeva agārasmā anagāriyaṃ [V 3.0263] pabbajanti, tadanuttaraṃ – brahmacariyapariyosānaṃ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharati. “Khīṇā jāti, vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ, kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ, nāparaṃ itthattāyā”ti abbhaññāsi. Aññataro ca pana so bhikkhu arahataṃ ahosīti. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

Then that bhikkhu, having delighted in and rejoiced at the Blessed One’s words, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him respectfully, and departed. Then that bhikkhu, dwelling alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, before long realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, that unsurpassed culmination of the holy life for the sake of which sons of good families rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness, and having attained it, he dwelt therein. He knew directly: “Destroyed is birth, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.” And that bhikkhu became one of the arahants.

7. Duccaritasuttaṃ

7. 7. The Discourse on Misconduct

413. Atha kho aññataro bhikkhu yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami…pe… “sādhu me, bhante, bhagavā saṃkhittena dhammaṃ desetu, yamahaṃ bhagavato dhammaṃ sutvā eko vūpakaṭṭho appamatto ātāpī pahitatto vihareyya”nti. “Tasmātiha tvaṃ, bhikkhu, ādimeva visodhehi kusalesu dhammesu. Ko cādi kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ? Idha tvaṃ, bhikkhu, kāyaduccaritaṃ pahāya kāyasucaritaṃ bhāvessasi. Vacīduccaritaṃ pahāya vacīsucaritaṃ [T 5.0251] bhāvessasi. Manoduccaritaṃ pahāya manosucaritaṃ bhāvessasi. Yato kho tvaṃ, bhikkhu, kāyaduccaritaṃ pahāya kāyasucaritaṃ bhāvessasi, vacīduccaritaṃ pahāya vacīsucaritaṃ bhāvessasi, manoduccaritaṃ pahāya manosucaritaṃ bhāvessasi, tato tvaṃ, bhikkhu, sīlaṃ nissāya sīle patiṭṭhāya cattāro satipaṭṭhāne bhāveyyāsi”.

413. Then a certain bhikkhu approached the Blessed One… and said: “Venerable sir, it would be good if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that, having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute.” “Therefore, bhikkhu, you should first purify the very beginning in regard to wholesome qualities. And what is the beginning of wholesome qualities? Here, bhikkhu, having abandoned bodily misconduct, you should cultivate wholesome bodily conduct; having abandoned verbal misconduct, you should cultivate wholesome verbal conduct; having abandoned mental misconduct, you should cultivate wholesome mental conduct. When, bhikkhu, having abandoned bodily misconduct, you cultivate wholesome bodily conduct; having abandoned verbal misconduct, you cultivate wholesome verbal conduct; and having abandoned mental misconduct, you cultivate wholesome mental conduct—then, bhikkhu, relying on virtue, established in virtue, you should develop the four establishments of mindfulness.”

“Katame [M 3.0165] cattāro? Idha tvaṃ, bhikkhu, kāye kāyānupassī viharāhi ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ; vedanāsu…pe… citte…pe… dhammesu dhammānupassī viharāhi ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ. Yato kho tvaṃ, bhikkhu, sīlaṃ nissāya sīle patiṭṭhāya ime cattāro satipaṭṭhāne evaṃ bhāvessasi, tato tuyhaṃ, bhikkhu, yā ratti vā divaso vā āgamissati vuddhiyeva pāṭikaṅkhā kusalesu dhammesu, no parihānī”ti…pe… aññataro ca pana so bhikkhu arahataṃ ahosīti. Sattamaṃ.

“What four? Here, bhikkhu, you should dwell contemplating the body in the body—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having subdued covetousness and displeasure in the world. You should dwell contemplating feelings in feelings… the mind in the mind… phenomena in phenomena—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having subdued covetousness and displeasure in the world. When you, bhikkhu, relying on virtue, established in virtue, develop these four establishments of mindfulness in this way, then, bhikkhu, for you, whatever night or day may come, only growth in wholesome qualities is to be expected, not decline.” … And that bhikkhu became one of the arahants.

8. Mittasuttaṃ

8. 8. The Discourse on Friends

414. “Ye[P 5.0189], bhikkhave, anukampeyyātha, ye ca kho sotabbaṃ maññeyyuṃ mittā vā amaccā [V 3.0264] vā ñātī vā sālohitā vā, te vo, bhikkhave, catunnaṃ satipaṭṭhānānaṃ bhāvanāya samādapetabbā nivesetabbā patiṭṭhāpetabbā.

414. “Bhikkhus, those for whom you would have compassion, and those who might think they should be listened to—whether they be friends, associates, relatives, or kinsmen—should be encouraged, settled, and established by you in the development of the four establishments of mindfulness.

“Katamesaṃ, catunnaṃ? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ; vedanāsu…pe… citte…pe… dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ. Ye, bhikkhave, anukampeyyātha, ye ca sotabbaṃ maññeyyuṃ mittā vā [T 5.0252] amaccā vā ñātī vā sālohitā vā, te vo, bhikkhave, imesaṃ catunnaṃ satipaṭṭhānānaṃ bhāvanāya samādapetabbā nivesetabbā patiṭṭhāpetabbā”ti. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

“What four? Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body as a body, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in the world. In feelings [...], in mind [...], in phenomena, he dwells contemplating phenomena as phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in the world. Monks, those for whom you might have compassion, and those who might think they should listen—whether friends, colleagues, relatives, or blood relatives—they should be encouraged, settled, and established by you in the development of these four foundations of mindfulness.” The eighth.

9. Vedanāsuttaṃ

9. The Discourse on Feeling

415. “Tisso imā, bhikkhave, vedanā. Katamā tisso? Sukhā vedanā, dukkhā vedanā, adukkhamasukhā vedanā – imā kho, bhikkhave, tisso vedanā. Imāsaṃ kho, bhikkhave, tissannaṃ vedanānaṃ pariññāya cattāro satipaṭṭhānā bhāvetabbā.

415. “Monks, there are these three feelings. Which three? Pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. These, monks, are the three feelings. For the full understanding of these three feelings, the four foundations of mindfulness should be developed.”

“Katame cattāro? Idha bhikkhave, bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ; vedanāsu…pe… citte…pe… dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ. Imāsaṃ kho, bhikkhave, tissannaṃ vedanānaṃ pariññāya ime cattāro satipaṭṭhānā bhāvetabbā”ti. Navamaṃ.

“What four? Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body as a body, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in the world. In feelings [...], in mind [...], in phenomena, he dwells contemplating phenomena as phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in the world. For the full understanding of these three feelings, these four foundations of mindfulness should be developed.” The ninth.

10. Āsavasuttaṃ

10. The Discourse on the Taints

416. “Tayome[M 3.0166], bhikkhave āsavā. Katame tayo? Kāmāsavo, bhavāsavo, avijjāsavo [V 3.0265] – ime kho, bhikkhave, tayo āsavā. Imesaṃ [P 5.0190] kho, bhikkhave, tiṇṇannaṃ āsavānaṃ pahānāya cattāro satipaṭṭhānā bhāvetabbā.

416. “Monks, there are these three taints. Which three? The taint of sensual desire, the taint of becoming, and the taint of ignorance. These, monks, are the three taints. For the abandoning of these three taints, the four foundations of mindfulness should be developed.”

“Katame cattāro? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ; vedanāsu…pe… citte…pe… dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke [T 5.0253] abhijjhādomanassaṃ. Imesaṃ kho, bhikkhave, tiṇṇannaṃ āsavānaṃ pahānāya ime cattāro satipaṭṭhānā bhāvetabbā”ti. Dasamaṃ.

“What four? Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body as a body, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in the world. In feelings [...], in mind [...], in phenomena, he dwells contemplating phenomena as phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in the world. For the abandoning of these three taints, these four foundations of mindfulness should be developed.” The tenth.

Amatavaggo pañcamo.

The Chapter on the Deathless, the Fifth.

Tassuddānaṃ –

Its Summary:

Amataṃ samudayo maggo, sati kusalarāsi ca;

Pātimokkhaṃ duccaritaṃ, mittavedanā āsavena cāti.

Deathless, Origin, Path, Mindfulness, Heap of Wholesome States; The Pātimokkha, Misconduct, Friend, Feeling, and the Taints.

6. Gaṅgāpeyyālavaggo

6. The Chapter on the Ganges Repetition Series

1-12. Gaṅgānadīādisuttadvādasakaṃ

1–12. The Group of Twelve Discourses Beginning with the Ganges River

417-428. “Seyyathāpi[T 5.0254], bhikkhave, gaṅgā nadī pācīnaninnā pācīnapoṇā pācīnapabbhārā; evameva kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu cattāro satipaṭṭhāne bhāvento cattāro satipaṭṭhāne bahulīkaronto nibbānaninno hoti nibbānapoṇo nibbānapabbhāro.

417–428. “Just as, monks, the Ganges River inclines to the east, slopes to the east, and tends to the east; in the same way, monks, a monk who develops and cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness inclines toward Nibbāna, slopes toward Nibbāna, and tends toward Nibbāna.”

“Kathañca, bhikkhave, bhikkhu cattāro satipaṭṭhāne bhāvento cattāro satipaṭṭhāne bahulīkaronto nibbānaninno hoti nibbānapoṇo nibbānapabbhāro? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ; vedanāsu [M 3.0167] …pe… citte [V 3.0266] …pe… dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu cattāro satipaṭṭhāne bhāvento cattāro satipaṭṭhāne bahulīkaronto nibbānaninno hoti nibbānapoṇo nibbānapabbhāro”ti vitthāretabbaṃ.

“And how, monks, does a monk, by developing and cultivating the four foundations of mindfulness, incline toward Nibbāna, slope toward Nibbāna, and tend toward Nibbāna? Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body as a body, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in the world. In feelings [...], in mind [...], in phenomena, he dwells contemplating phenomena as phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in the world. It is in this way, monks, that a monk, by developing and cultivating the four foundations of mindfulness, inclines toward Nibbāna, slopes toward Nibbāna, and tends toward Nibbāna.” This should be elaborated.

Gaṅgāpeyyālavaggo chaṭṭho.

The Chapter on the Ganges Repetition Series, the Sixth.

Tassuddānaṃ –

Its Summary:

Cha pācīnato ninnā, cha ninnā ca samuddato;

Ete dve cha dvādasa honti, vaggo tena pavuccatīti.

Six inclining to the east, and six inclining to the ocean; these two sets of six make twelve, thus the chapter is called.

7. Appamādavaggo

7. The Chapter on Heedfulness

1-10. Tathāgatādisuttadasakaṃ

1–10. The Decad of Discourses Beginning with the Tathāgata

429-438. Yāvatā, bhikkhave, sattā apadā vā dvipadā vā catuppadā vā bahuppadā vāti vitthāretabbaṃ.

429–438. “Monks, as far as there are beings, whether footless, two-footed, four-footed, or many-footed—this should be expanded.”

Appamādavaggo sattamo.

The Chapter on Heedfulness, the Seventh.

Tassuddānaṃ –

Its Summary:

Tathāgataṃ [P 5.0191] padaṃ kūṭaṃ, mūlaṃ sāro ca vassikaṃ;

Rājā candimasūriyā, vatthena dasamaṃ padanti.

The Tathāgata, the Footprint, the Peak, the Root, the Essence, and the Rain-cloth; The King, the Moon, and the Sun, and the tenth is declared with the Cloth.

8. Balakaraṇīyavaggo

8. The Chapter on What Requires Strength

1-12. Balādisuttadvādasakaṃ

1–12. The Group of Twelve Discourses Beginning with Strength

439-450. Seyyathāpi[V 3.0267], bhikkhave, ye keci balakaraṇīyā kammantā karīyantīti vitthāretabbaṃ.

439–450. “Just as, monks, whatever tasks requiring strength are done—this should be expanded.”

Balakaraṇīyavaggo aṭṭhamo.

The Chapter on What Requires Strength, the Eighth.

Tassuddānaṃ –

Its Summary:

Balaṃ [M 3.0168] bījañca nāgo ca, rukkho kumbhena sūkiyā;

Ākāsena ca dve meghā, nāvā āgantukā nadīti.

Strength, Seed, Elephant, Tree, Pot, Needle, Sky, Two Clouds, Boat, Visitor, and River.

9. Esanāvaggo

9. The Chapter on Seeking

1-10. Esanādisuttadasakaṃ

1–10. The Decad of Discourses Beginning with Seeking

451-460. Tisso imā, bhikkhave, esanā. Katamā tisso? Kāmesanā, bhavesanā, brahmacariyesanāti vitthāretabbaṃ.

451–460. “Monks, there are these three kinds of seeking. Which three? Seeking for sensual pleasures, seeking for existence, and seeking for the holy life.” This should be elaborated.

Esanāvaggo navamo.

The Chapter on Seeking, the Ninth.

Tassuddānaṃ –

Its Summary:

Esanā vidhā āsavo, bhavo ca dukkhatā tisso;

Khilaṃ malañca nīgho ca, vedanā taṇhā tasināya cāti.

Seeking, Modes, Taints, Existence, and the three Sufferings; Barrenness, Stains, Afflictions, Feelings, Craving, and Thirst.

10. Oghavaggo

10. The Chapter on Floods

1-10. Uddhambhāgiyādisuttadasakaṃ

1–10. The Decad of Discourses Beginning with the Higher Fetters

461-470. “Pañcimāni[V 3.0268], bhikkhave, uddhambhāgiyāni saṃyojanāni. Katamāni pañca? Rūparāgo, arūparāgo, māno, uddhaccaṃ, avijjā [P 5.0192] – imāni kho, bhikkhave, pañcuddhambhāgiyāni saṃyojanāni. Imesaṃ kho, bhikkhave, pañcannaṃ uddhambhāgiyānaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ abhiññāya pariññāya parikkhayāya pahānāya cattāro satipaṭṭhānā bhāvetabbā.

461–470. “Monks, there are these five higher fetters. Which five? Lust for form, lust for the formless, conceit, restlessness, and ignorance. These, monks, are the five higher fetters. For the higher knowledge, full understanding, utter destruction, and abandonment of these five higher fetters, the four foundations of mindfulness should be developed.”

“Katame [M 3.0169] cattāro? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu kāye [T 5.0255] kāyānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ; vedanāsu…pe… citte…pe… dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ. Imesaṃ kho, bhikkhave, pañcannaṃ uddhambhāgiyānaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ abhiññāya pariññāya parikkhayāya pahānāya ime cattāro satipaṭṭhānā bhāvetabbā”ti.

“Which four? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings… contemplating mind in mind… contemplating phenomena in phenomena—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. For the higher knowledge, full understanding, utter destruction, and abandonment of these five higher fetters, these four foundations of mindfulness should be developed.”

(Yathā maggasaṃyuttaṃ tathā satipaṭṭhānasaṃyuttaṃ vitthāretabbaṃ).

(As with the Connected Discourses on the Path, so the Connected Discourses on the Foundations of Mindfulness should be elaborated.)

Oghavaggo dasamo.

The Flood Division, the Tenth.

Tassuddānaṃ –

Its Summary:

Ogho yogo upādānaṃ, ganthā anusayena ca;

Kāmaguṇā nīvaraṇā, khandhā oruddhambhāgiyāti.

Floods, yokes, clinging, bonds, and latent tendencies; Sensual pleasures, hindrances, aggregates, and lower fetters.

Satipaṭṭhānasaṃyuttaṃ tatiyaṃ.

The Connected Discourses on the Foundations of Mindfulness, the Third.

4. Indriyasaṃyuttaṃ

4. The Connected Discourses on the Faculties

1. Suddhikavaggo

1. The Pure Division

1. Suddhikasuttaṃ

1. The Pure Discourse

471. Sāvatthinidānaṃ[T 5.0256][M 3.0170][V 3.0269][P 5.0193]. “Pañcimāni, bhikkhave, indriyāni. Katamāni pañca? Saddhindriyaṃ, vīriyindriyaṃ, satindriyaṃ, samādhindriyaṃ, paññindriyaṃ – imāni kho, bhikkhave, pañcindriyānī”ti. Paṭhamaṃ.

471. At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, there are these five faculties. What five? The faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom. These, bhikkhus, are the five faculties.” The first.

2. Paṭhamasotāpannasuttaṃ

2. The First Discourse on the Stream-Enterer

472. “Pañcimāni, bhikkhave, indriyāni. Katamāni pañca? Saddhindriyaṃ, vīriyindriyaṃ, satindriyaṃ, samādhindriyaṃ, paññindriyaṃ. Yato kho, bhikkhave, ariyasāvako imesaṃ pañcannaṃ indriyānaṃ assādañca samudayañca atthaṅgamañca assādañca (syā. kaṃ. pī. ka.) saṃ. ni. 2.175 ādīnavañca nissaraṇañca yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti – ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, ariyasāvako sotāpanno avinipātadhammo niyato sambodhiparāyaṇo”ti. Dutiyaṃ.

472. “Bhikkhus, there are these five faculties. What five? The faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom. When, bhikkhus, a noble disciple understands as it actually is the gratification, the danger, and the escape in regard to these five faculties, this one, bhikkhus, is called a noble disciple who is a stream-enterer, not subject to falling into the lower realms, assured, and destined for enlightenment.” The second.

3. Dutiyasotāpannasuttaṃ

3. The Second Discourse on the Stream-Enterer

473. “Pañcimāni, bhikkhave, indriyāni. Katamāni pañca? Saddhindriyaṃ, vīriyindriyaṃ, satindriyaṃ, samādhindriyaṃ, paññindriyaṃ. Yato kho, bhikkhave, ariyasāvako imesaṃ pañcannaṃ indriyānaṃ samudayañca atthaṅgamañca assādañca ādīnavañca [P 5.0194] nissaraṇañca yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti [V 3.0270] – ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, ariyasāvako sotāpanno avinipātadhammo [T 5.0257] niyato sambodhiparāyaṇo”ti. Tatiyaṃ.

473. “Bhikkhus, there are these five faculties. What five? The faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom. When, bhikkhus, a noble disciple understands as it actually is the origination and the cessation, the gratification, the danger, and the escape in regard to these five faculties, this one, bhikkhus, is called a noble disciple who is a stream-enterer, not subject to falling into the lower realms, assured, and destined for enlightenment.” The third.

4. Paṭhamaarahantasuttaṃ

4. The First Discourse on the Arahant

474. “Pañcimāni, bhikkhave, indriyāni. Katamāni pañca? Saddhindriyaṃ, vīriyindriyaṃ, satindriyaṃ, samādhindriyaṃ, paññindriyaṃ. Yato kho, bhikkhave, ariyasāvako imesaṃ pañcannaṃ indriyānaṃ assādañca samudayañca atthaṅgamañca assādañca (syā. kaṃ. pī. ka.) saṃ. ni. 2.175 ādīnavañca nissaraṇañca yathābhūtaṃ viditvā [M 3.0171] anupādāvimutto hoti – ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, bhikkhu arahaṃ khīṇāsavo vusitavā katakaraṇīyo ohitabhāro anuppattasadattho parikkhīṇabhavasaṃyojano sammadaññā vimutto”ti. Catutthaṃ.

474. “Bhikkhus, there are these five faculties. What five? The faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom. When, bhikkhus, a noble disciple, having known as it actually is the gratification, the danger, and the escape in regard to these five faculties, is liberated without clinging, this one, bhikkhus, is called a bhikkhu who is an arahant, whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, has done what was to be done, has laid down the burden, has attained his own welfare, has utterly destroyed the fetters of becoming, and is liberated through perfect direct knowledge.” The fourth.

5. Dutiyaarahantasuttaṃ

5. The Second Discourse on the Arahant

475. “Pañcimāni, bhikkhave, indriyāni. Katamāni pañca? Saddhindriyaṃ, vīriyindriyaṃ, satindriyaṃ, samādhindriyaṃ, paññindriyaṃ. Yato kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu imesaṃ pañcannaṃ indriyānaṃ samudayañca atthaṅgamañca assādañca ādīnavañca nissaraṇañca yathābhūtaṃ viditvā anupādāvimutto hoti – ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, bhikkhu arahaṃ khīṇāsavo vusitavā katakaraṇīyo ohitabhāro anuppattasadattho parikkhīṇabhavasaṃyojano sammadaññā vimutto”ti. Pañcamaṃ.

475. “Bhikkhus, there are these five faculties. What five? The faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom. When, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, having known as it actually is the arising, the cessation, the gratification, the danger, and the escape in regard to these five faculties, is liberated without clinging, this one, bhikkhus, is called a bhikkhu who is an arahant, whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, has done what was to be done, has laid down the burden, has attained his own welfare, has utterly destroyed the fetters of becoming, and is liberated through perfect direct knowledge.” The fifth.

6. Paṭhamasamaṇabrāhmaṇasuttaṃ

6. The First Discourse on Recluses and Brahmins

476. “Pañcimāni, bhikkhave, indriyāni. Katamāni pañca? Saddhindriyaṃ…pe… paññindriyaṃ. Ye hi keci, bhikkhave, samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā imesaṃ pañcannaṃ indriyānaṃ assādañca ādīnavañca nissaraṇañca yathābhūtaṃ nappajānanti, na me te, bhikkhave, samaṇā vā [T 5.0258] brāhmaṇā vā samaṇesu vā samaṇasammatā brāhmaṇesu vā brāhmaṇasammatā, na ca panete [P 5.0195] āyasmanto sāmaññatthaṃ vā brahmaññatthaṃ vā diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharanti.

476. “Bhikkhus, there are these five faculties. What five? The faculty of faith… the faculty of wisdom. Bhikkhus, whatever recluses or brahmins do not understand as it actually is the gratification, the danger, and the escape in regard to these five faculties, they are not reckoned by me as recluses among recluses or as brahmins among brahmins. Nor do those venerable ones, in this very life, realize for themselves with direct knowledge the goal of recluseship or the goal of brahminhood and dwell having attained it.

“Ye [V 3.0271] ca kho keci ye ca kho te (syā. kaṃ. ka.) saṃ. ni. 2.174, bhikkhave, samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā imesaṃ pañcannaṃ indriyānaṃ samudayañca atthaṅgamañca assādañca ādīnavañca nissaraṇañca yathābhūtaṃ pajānanti, te kho me, bhikkhave, samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā samaṇesu ceva samaṇasammatā brāhmaṇesu ca brāhmaṇasammatā; te ca panāyasmanto sāmaññatthañca brahmaññatthañca diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharantī”ti. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

“But, bhikkhus, whatever recluses or brahmins understand as it actually is the arising, the cessation, the gratification, the danger, and the escape in regard to these five faculties, they are reckoned by me as recluses among recluses and as brahmins among brahmins. And those venerable ones, in this very life, realize for themselves with direct knowledge the goal of recluseship and the goal of brahminhood and dwell having attained it.” The sixth.

7. Dutiyasamaṇabrāhmaṇasuttaṃ

7. The Second Discourse on Recluses and Brahmins

477. “Ye hi keci, bhikkhave, samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā saddhindriyaṃ nappajānanti, saddhindriyasamudayaṃ nappajānanti, saddhindriyanirodhaṃ nappajānanti, saddhindriyanirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadaṃ nappajānanti; vīriyindriyaṃ nappajānanti…pe… satindriyaṃ nappajānanti [M 3.0172] …pe… samādhindriyaṃ nappajānanti…pe… paññindriyaṃ nappajānanti, paññindriyasamudayaṃ nappajānanti, paññindriyanirodhaṃ nappajānanti, paññindriyanirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadaṃ nappajānanti, na me te, bhikkhave samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā samaṇesu vā samaṇasammatā brāhmaṇesu vā brāhmaṇasammatā, na ca panete āyasmanto sāmaññatthaṃ vā brahmaññatthaṃ [T 5.0259] vā diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharanti.

477. Monks, any recluses or brahmins who do not understand the faculty of faith, do not understand the arising of the faculty of faith, do not understand the cessation of the faculty of faith, do not understand the practice leading to the cessation of the faculty of faith; who do not understand the faculty of energy... who do not understand the faculty of mindfulness... who do not understand the faculty of concentration... who do not understand the faculty of wisdom, do not understand the arising of the faculty of wisdom, do not understand the cessation of the faculty of wisdom, do not understand the practice leading to the cessation of the faculty of wisdom—I do not consider them recluses among recluses or brahmins among brahmins. Nor do those venerable ones, having realized it for themselves with direct knowledge, dwell having attained the goal of recluseship or the goal of brahminhood in this very life.

“Ye ca kho keci, bhikkhave, samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā saddhindriyaṃ pajānanti, saddhindriyasamudayaṃ pajānanti, saddhindriyanirodhaṃ pajānanti, saddhindriyanirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadaṃ pajānanti; vīriyindriyaṃ pajānanti, vīriyindriyasamudayaṃ pajānanti, vīriyindriyanirodhaṃ pajānanti, vīriyindriyanirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadaṃ pajānanti; satindriyaṃ pajānanti…pe… samādhindriyaṃ pajānanti…pe… paññindriyaṃ [P 5.0196] pajānanti, paññindriyasamudayaṃ pajānanti, paññindriyanirodhaṃ pajānanti, paññindriyanirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadaṃ pajānanti[V 3.0272], te kho me, bhikkhave, samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā samaṇesu ceva samaṇasammatā brāhmaṇesu ca brāhmaṇasammatā, te ca panāyasmanto sāmaññatthañca brahmaññatthañca diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharantī”ti. Sattamaṃ.

Indeed, monks, whatever recluses or brahmins understand the faculty of faith, understand the arising of the faculty of faith, understand the cessation of the faculty of faith, and understand the path leading to the cessation of the faculty of faith; understand the faculty of energy... understand the faculty of mindfulness... understand the faculty of concentration... understand the faculty of wisdom, understand the arising of the faculty of wisdom, understand the cessation of the faculty of wisdom, and understand the path leading to the cessation of the faculty of wisdom—I consider them recluses among recluses and brahmins among brahmins. And those venerable ones, having realized for themselves with direct knowledge in this very life, abide having attained the goal of recluseship and the goal of brahminhood. Seventh.

8. Daṭṭhabbasuttaṃ

8. The Sutta on What is to be Seen

478. “Pañcimāni, bhikkhave, indriyāni. Katamāni pañca? Saddhindriyaṃ…pe… paññindriyaṃ. Kattha ca, bhikkhave, saddhindriyaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ? Catūsu sotāpattiyaṅgesu – ettha saddhindriyaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Kattha ca, bhikkhave, vīriyindriyaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ? Catūsu sammappadhānesu – ettha vīriyindriyaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Kattha [T 5.0260] ca, bhikkhave, satindriyaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ? Catūsu satipaṭṭhānesu – ettha satindriyaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Kattha ca, bhikkhave, samādhindriyaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ? Catūsu jhānesu – ettha samādhindriyaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Kattha ca, bhikkhave, paññindriyaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ? Catūsu ariyasaccesu – ettha paññindriyaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Imāni kho, bhikkhave, pañcindriyānī”ti. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

478. Monks, there are these five faculties. Which five? The faculty of faith... the faculty of wisdom. And where, monks, is the faculty of faith to be seen? In the four factors of stream-entry—herein the faculty of faith is to be seen. And where, monks, is the faculty of energy to be seen? In the four right exertions—herein the faculty of energy is to be seen. And where, monks, is the faculty of mindfulness to be seen? In the four foundations of mindfulness—herein the faculty of mindfulness is to be seen. And where, monks, is the faculty of concentration to be seen? In the four jhānas—herein the faculty of concentration is to be seen. And where, monks, is the faculty of wisdom to be seen? In the four noble truths—herein the faculty of wisdom is to be seen. These, indeed, monks, are the five faculties. Eighth.

9. Paṭhamavibhaṅgasuttaṃ

9. The First Sutta on Analysis

479. “Pañcimāni, bhikkhave, indriyāni. Katamāni pañca? Saddhindriyaṃ…pe… paññindriyaṃ. Katamañca, bhikkhave, saddhindriyaṃ? Idha, bhikkhave, ariyasāvako saddho hoti, saddahati tathāgatassa bodhiṃ [P 5.0197] – ‘itipi so bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho vijjācaraṇasampanno [M 3.0173] sugato lokavidū anuttaro purisadammasārathi satthā devamanussānaṃ buddho bhagavā’ti – idaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, saddhindriyaṃ.

479. Monks, there are these five faculties. Which five? The faculty of faith... the faculty of wisdom. And what, monks, is the faculty of faith? Here, monks, a noble disciple has faith; he places his faith in the enlightenment of the Tathāgata: 'Indeed, the Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, the Well-Gone, knower of the world, an unsurpassed trainer of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Enlightened One, the Blessed One.' This, monks, is called the faculty of faith.

“Katamañca, bhikkhave, vīriyindriyaṃ? Idha, bhikkhave, ariyasāvako āraddhavīriyo viharati akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ pahānāya, kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ upasampadāya, thāmavā daḷhaparakkamo anikkhittadhuro kusalesu dhammesu – idaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, vīriyindriyaṃ.

And what, monks, is the faculty of energy? Here, monks, a noble disciple dwells with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome qualities and for the attainment of wholesome qualities; he is strong, firm in his effort, not shirking his duty in regard to wholesome qualities. This, monks, is called the faculty of energy.

“Katamañca, bhikkhave, satindriyaṃ? Idha, bhikkhave, ariyasāvako satimā hoti paramena [V 3.0273] satinepakkena samannāgato cirakatampi cirabhāsitampi saritā [T 5.0261] anussaritā – idaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, satindriyaṃ.

And what, monks, is the faculty of mindfulness? Here, monks, a noble disciple is mindful, possessing supreme mindfulness and discernment, one who remembers and recollects what was done long ago and spoken long ago. This, monks, is called the faculty of mindfulness.

“Katamañca, bhikkhave, samādhindriyaṃ? Idha, bhikkhave, ariyasāvako vossaggārammaṇaṃ karitvā labhati samādhiṃ, labhati cittassa ekaggataṃ – idaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, samādhindriyaṃ.

And what, monks, is the faculty of concentration? Here, monks, a noble disciple, having made relinquishment the object, gains concentration, gains one-pointedness of mind. This, monks, is called the faculty of concentration.

“Katamañca, bhikkhave, paññindriyaṃ? Idha, bhikkhave, ariyasāvako paññavā hoti udayatthagāminiyā paññāya samannāgato ariyāya nibbedhikāya, sammā dukkhakkhayagāminiyā – idaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, paññindriyaṃ. Imāni kho, bhikkhave, pañcindriyānī”ti. Navamaṃ.

And what, monks, is the faculty of wisdom? Here, monks, a noble disciple is wise, possessing the wisdom that discerns arising and passing away, which is noble, penetrative, and leads rightly to the complete destruction of suffering. This, monks, is called the faculty of wisdom. These, indeed, monks, are the five faculties. Ninth.

10. Dutiyavibhaṅgasuttaṃ

10. The Second Sutta on Analysis

480. “Pañcimāni, bhikkhave, indriyāni. Katamāni pañca? Saddhindriyaṃ…pe… paññindriyaṃ. Katamañca, bhikkhave, saddhindriyaṃ? Idha, bhikkhave, ariyasāvako saddho hoti, saddahati tathāgatassa bodhiṃ – ‘itipi so bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho vijjācaraṇasampanno sugato lokavidū anuttaro purisadammasārathi satthā devamanussānaṃ buddho bhagavā’ti – idaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, saddhindriyaṃ.

480. Monks, there are these five faculties. Which five? The faculty of faith... the faculty of wisdom. And what, monks, is the faculty of faith? Here, monks, a noble disciple has faith; he places his faith in the Tathāgata’s enlightenment: ‘Indeed, the Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, the Well-Gone, knower of the world, an unsurpassed trainer of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Enlightened One, the Blessed One.’ This, monks, is called the faculty of faith.

“Katamañca[P 5.0198], bhikkhave, vīriyindriyaṃ? Idha, bhikkhave, ariyasāvako āraddhavīriyo viharati akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ pahānāya, kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ upasampadāya, thāmavā daḷhaparakkamo anikkhittadhuro kusalesu dhammesu. So anuppannānaṃ pāpakānaṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ anuppādāya chandaṃ janeti vāyamati vīriyaṃ ārabhati cittaṃ paggaṇhāti padahati; uppannānaṃ [T 5.0262] pāpakānaṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ pahānāya chandaṃ janeti vāyamati vīriyaṃ [M 3.0174] ārabhati cittaṃ paggaṇhāti padahati; anuppannānaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ uppādāya chandaṃ janeti vāyamati vīriyaṃ ārabhati cittaṃ paggaṇhāti padahati; uppannānaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ ṭhitiyā samāpattiyā (syā. kaṃ. ka.) asammosāya bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā chandaṃ janeti vāyamati vīriyaṃ ārabhati cittaṃ paggaṇhāti padahati – idaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, vīriyindriyaṃ.

“And what, Bhikkhus, is the faculty of energy? Here, Bhikkhus, a noble disciple dwells with energy aroused for abandoning unwholesome qualities and for acquiring wholesome qualities; he is strong, firm in exertion, not laying down the burden in regard to wholesome qualities. He generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts his mind, and strives for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome qualities. He generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts his mind, and strives for the abandoning of arisen evil, unwholesome qualities. He generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts his mind, and strives for the arising of unarisen wholesome qualities. He generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts his mind, and strives for the maintenance, non-confusion, increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment of arisen wholesome qualities. This, Bhikkhus, is called the faculty of energy.”

“Katamañca[V 3.0274], bhikkhave, satindriyaṃ? Idha, bhikkhave, ariyasāvako satimā hoti paramena satinepakkena samannāgato, cirakatampi cirabhāsitampi saritā anussaritā. So kāye kāyānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ; vedanāsu…pe… citte…pe… dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ – idaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, satindriyaṃ.

“And what, Bhikkhus, is the faculty of mindfulness?
