5. The Connected Discourses on the Right Strivings

1. Gaṅgāpeyyālavaggo

1. The Chapter with the Ganges Repetition Series

1-12. Pācīnādisuttadvādasakaṃ

1–12. The Twelve Suttas Beginning with the East

651-662. Sāvatthinidānaṃ[T 5.0319][V 3.0318][M 3.0214][P 5.0244]. Tatra kho bhagavā etadavoca – “cattārome, bhikkhave, sammappadhānā. Katame cattāro? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu anuppannānaṃ pāpakānaṃ akusalānaṃ [T 5.0320] dhammānaṃ anuppādāya chandaṃ janeti vāyamati vīriyaṃ ārabhati cittaṃ paggaṇhāti padahati. Uppannānaṃ pāpakānaṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ pahānāya chandaṃ janeti vāyamati vīriyaṃ ārabhati cittaṃ paggaṇhāti padahati. Anuppannānaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ uppādāya chandaṃ janeti vāyamati vīriyaṃ ārabhati cittaṃ paggaṇhāti padahati. Uppannānaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ ṭhitiyā asammosāya bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā chandaṃ janeti vāyamati vīriyaṃ ārabhati cittaṃ paggaṇhāti padahati. Ime kho, bhikkhave, cattāro sammappadhānāti”.

651–662. At Sāvatthī. There the Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, there are these four right strivings. Which four? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts his mind, and strives for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states. He generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts his mind, and strives for the abandoning of arisen evil, unwholesome states. He generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts his mind, and strives for the arising of unarisen wholesome states. He generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts his mind, and strives for the maintenance, non-degeneration, increase, abundance, development, and perfection of arisen wholesome states. These, bhikkhus, are the four right strivings.”

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, gaṅgā nadī pācīnaninnā pācīnapoṇā pācīnapabbhārā; evameva kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu cattāro sammappadhāne bhāvento cattāro sammappadhāne bahulīkaronto nibbānaninno hoti nibbānapoṇo nibbānapabbhāro. Kathañca, bhikkhave, bhikkhu cattāro sammappadhāne bhāvento cattāro sammappadhāne bahulīkaronto nibbānaninno hoti nibbānapoṇo nibbānapabbhāro? Idha[P 5.0245], bhikkhave, bhikkhu anuppannānaṃ pāpakānaṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ anuppādāya chandaṃ janeti vāyamati vīriyaṃ ārabhati cittaṃ paggaṇhāti padahati. Uppannānaṃ pāpakānaṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ pahānāya chandaṃ janeti vāyamati vīriyaṃ ārabhati cittaṃ paggaṇhāti padahati. Anuppannānaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ uppādāya chandaṃ janeti vāyamati vīriyaṃ ārabhati cittaṃ paggaṇhāti padahati. Uppannānaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ ṭhitiyā asammosāya bhiyyobhāvāya [V 3.0319] vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā chandaṃ janeti vāyamati vīriyaṃ ārabhati cittaṃ paggaṇhāti padahati. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu cattāro sammappadhāne bhāvento cattāro sammappadhāne bahulīkaronto nibbānaninno hoti nibbānapoṇo nibbānapabbhāro”ti. Dvādasamaṃ. (Sammappadhānasaṃyuttassa gaṅgāpeyyālī sammappadhānavasena vitthāretabbā).

“Just as, monks, the river Ganges flows eastward, inclines eastward, and slopes eastward; even so, a monk who develops and cultivates the four right strivings flows towards Nibbāna, inclines towards Nibbāna, and slopes towards Nibbāna. And how, monks, does a monk who develops and cultivates the four right strivings flow towards Nibbāna, incline towards Nibbāna, and slope towards Nibbāna? Here, monks, a monk generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts his mind, and strives for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states. He generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts his mind, and strives for the abandoning of arisen evil, unwholesome states. He generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts his mind, and strives for the arising of unarisen wholesome states. He generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts his mind, and strives for the maintenance, non-disappearance, increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment of arisen wholesome states. It is in this way, monks, that a monk who develops and cultivates the four right strivings flows towards Nibbāna, inclines towards Nibbāna, and slopes towards Nibbāna.” The twelfth. (The Ganges Repetition Section of the Connected Discourses on the Right Strivings should be elaborated by means of the right strivings.)

Gaṅgāpeyyālavaggo paṭhamo.

The First Chapter: The Ganges Repetition Series.

Tassuddānaṃ –

Its summary:

Cha [M 3.0215] pācīnato ninnā, cha ninnā ca samuddato;

Dvete cha dvādasa honti, vaggo tena pavuccatīti.

Six slope to the east, six slope to the ocean; twice six make twelve, thus the chapter is called.

673-684. “Seyyathāpi[P 5.0246], bhikkhave, ye keci balakaraṇīyā kammantā kayiranti, sabbe [V 3.0320] te pathaviṃ nissāya pathaviyaṃ patiṭṭhāya evamete balakaraṇīyā kammantā kayiranti; evameva kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sīlaṃ [T 5.0321] nissāya sīle patiṭṭhāya cattāro sammappadhāne bhāveti, cattāro sammappadhāne bahulīkaroti. Kathañca, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sīlaṃ nissāya sīle patiṭṭhāya cattāro sammappadhāne bhāveti, cattāro sammappadhāne bahulīkaroti? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu anuppannānaṃ pāpakānaṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ anuppādāya chandaṃ janeti vāyamati vīriyaṃ ārabhati cittaṃ paggaṇhāti padahati…pe… uppannānaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ ṭhitiyā asammosāya bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā chandaṃ janeti vāyamati vīriyaṃ ārabhati cittaṃ paggaṇhāti padahati. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sīlaṃ nissāya [M 3.0216] sīle patiṭṭhāya cattāro sammappadhāne bhāveti, cattāro sammappadhāne bahulīkarotī”ti. (Evaṃ balakaraṇīyavaggo sammappadhānavasena vitthāretabbo). Dvādasamaṃ.

“Just as, monks, whatever strenuous tasks are performed, they are all performed in reliance on the earth, established on the earth; even so, a monk, in reliance on virtue, established in virtue, develops the four right strivings and cultivates them. And how, monks, does a monk, in reliance on virtue, established in virtue, develop the four right strivings and cultivate them? Here, monks, a monk generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts his mind, and strives for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states… for the maintenance, non-disappearance, increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment of arisen wholesome states, he generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts his mind, and strives. It is in this way, monks, that a monk, in reliance on virtue, established in virtue, develops the four right strivings and cultivates them.” (Thus the Chapter on Strenuous Tasks should be elaborated by means of the right strivings). The twelfth.

Balakaraṇīyavaggo tatiyo.

The Third Chapter: Strenuous Tasks.

Strength, the seed, and the nāga; the tree, the pot, and the spike; the sky and the two clouds; the boat, the visitor, and the river.

685-694. “Tisso imā, bhikkhave, esanā. Katamā tisso? Kāmesanā, bhavesanā, brahmacariyesanā – imā kho, bhikkhave, tisso esanā. Imāsaṃ [P 5.0247] kho, bhikkhave, tissannaṃ esanānaṃ abhiññāya pariññāya parikkhayāya pahānāya cattāro sammappadhānā bhāvetabbā. Katame cattāro? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu anuppannānaṃ…pe… uppannānaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ ṭhitiyā asammosāya bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā chandaṃ janeti vāyamati vīriyaṃ ārabhati [T 5.0322] cittaṃ paggaṇhāti padahati. Imāsaṃ kho, bhikkhave, tissannaṃ esanānaṃ [V 3.0321] abhiññāya pariññāya parikkhayāya pahānāya ime cattāro sammappadhānā bhāvetabbā”ti. (Vitthāretabbaṃ). Dasamaṃ.

“Monks, there are these three searches. What three? The search for sensual pleasures, the search for existence, and the search for a holy life. These, monks, are the three searches. For the direct knowledge, full understanding, utter destruction, and abandonment of these three searches, the four right strivings should be developed. What four? Here, monks, a monk generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts his mind, and strives… for the maintenance, non-disappearance, increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment of arisen wholesome states. For the direct knowledge, full understanding, utter destruction, and abandonment of these three searches, these four right strivings should be developed.” (This should be elaborated.) The tenth.

The search, kinds, taints, existence, and the three sufferings; barrenness, stain, and affliction; feeling, craving, and thirst.

Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu saddhābalaṃ bhāveti vivekanissitaṃ virāganissitaṃ nirodhanissitaṃ vossaggapariṇāmiṃ, vīriyabalaṃ…pe… satibalaṃ… samādhibalaṃ… paññābalaṃ bhāveti vivekanissitaṃ virāganissitaṃ nirodhanissitaṃ vossaggapariṇāmiṃ. 705-716. "Monks, there are these five powers. What five? Just as, monks, the river Ganges slopes towards the east, inclines towards the east, and tends towards the east; even so, a monk who develops and cultivates these five powers slopes towards Nibbāna, inclines towards Nibbāna, and tends towards Nibbāna. He develops the power of energy... pe ... the power of mindfulness... the power of concentration... he develops the power of wisdom, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and culminates in relinquishment. It is in this way, monks, that a monk who develops and cultivates these five powers slopes towards Nibbāna, inclines towards Nibbāna, and tends towards Nibbāna." The twelfth.

6. The Ganges Repetition Section

1-12. Pācīnādisuttadvādasakaṃ

1–12. The Dozen Discourses Beginning with the Eastern Direction

759-770. “Seyyathāpi[M 3.0220], bhikkhave, gaṅgā nadī pācīnaninnā pācīnapoṇā pācīnapabbhārā[V 3.0325]; evameva [P 5.0252] kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu pañca balāni bhāvento pañca balāni bahulīkaronto nibbānaninno hoti nibbānapoṇo nibbānapabbhāro. Kathañca, bhikkhave, bhikkhu pañca balāni bhāvento pañca balāni bahulīkaronto nibbānaninno hoti nibbānapoṇo nibbānapabbhāro? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu, saddhābalaṃ bhāveti rāgavinayapariyosānaṃ dosavinayapariyosānaṃ mohavinayapariyosānaṃ…pe… evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu pañca balāni bhāvento pañca balāni bahulīkaronto nibbānaninno hoti nibbānapoṇo nibbānapabbhāro”ti. (Vitthāretabbā) dvādasamaṃ.

“Just as, monks, the river Ganges slopes towards the east, inclines towards the east, and tends towards the east; even so, monks, a monk, by developing the five powers and by cultivating the five powers, slopes towards Nibbāna, inclines towards Nibbāna, and tends towards Nibbāna. And how, monks, does a monk, by developing the five powers and by cultivating the five powers, slope towards Nibbāna, incline towards Nibbāna, and tend towards Nibbāna? Here, monks, a monk develops the power of faith, which has the removal of lust as its culmination, the removal of hatred as its culmination, and the removal of delusion as its culmination… pe … Thus, monks, a monk, by developing the five powers and by cultivating the five powers, slopes towards Nibbāna, inclines towards Nibbāna, and tends towards Nibbāna.” (This is to be expanded). The twelfth.

Gaṅgāpeyyālavaggo chaṭṭho.

The Ganges Repetition Section is the sixth.

Tassuddānaṃ –

Its summary:

Cha pācīnato ninnā, cha ninnā ca samuddato;

Dvete cha dvādasa honti, vaggo tena pavuccatīti.

Six slope towards the east, and six slope towards the ocean; these two sixes become twelve, thus the section is called.

Appamāda-balakaraṇīyavaggā vitthāretabbā.

The Heedfulness Chapter and the What is to be Done with the Powers Chapter are to be expanded.

9. Esanāvaggo

9. The Chapter on Seeking

1-12. Esanādisuttadvādasakaṃ

1–12. The Dozen Suttas Beginning with Seeking

792-802. Evaṃ esanāpāḷi vitthāretabbā – rāgavinayapariyosānaṃ dosavinayapariyosānaṃ mohavinayapariyosānaṃ.

Thus, the text on seeking is to be expanded: having the removal of lust as its culmination, the removal of hatred as its culmination, and the removal of delusion as its culmination.

Esanāvaggo navamo.

The ninth, the Chapter on Seeking, is finished.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary thereof:

Esanā vidhā āsavo, bhavo ca dukkhatā tisso;

Khilaṃ malañca nīgho ca, vedanā taṇhā tasinā cāti.

Seeking, modes, corruptions, becoming, and the three sufferings; barrenness, defilement, and affliction, feeling, craving, and thirst.

10. Oghavaggo

10. The Chapter on Floods

1-10. Oghādisuttadasakaṃ

1–10. The Decade of Suttas Beginning with the Flood

803-812. “Pañcimāni[V 3.0327][M 3.0221][P 5.0253][T 5.0325], bhikkhave, uddhambhāgiyāni saṃyojanāni. Katamāni pañca? Rūparāgo, arūparāgo, māno, uddhaccaṃ avijjā – imāni kho, bhikkhave, pañcuddhambhāgiyāni saṃyojanāni. Imesaṃ kho, bhikkhave, pañcannaṃ uddhambhāgiyānaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ abhiññāya pariññāya parikkhayāya pahānāya pañca balāni bhāvetabbāni. Katamāni pañca? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu saddhābalaṃ bhāveti…pe… paññābalaṃ bhāveti rāgavinayapariyosānaṃ dosavinayapariyosānaṃ mohavinayapariyosānaṃ. Imesaṃ kho, bhikkhave, pañcannaṃ uddhambhāgiyānaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ abhiññāya pariññāya parikkhayāya pahānāya imāni pañca balāni bhāvetabbānī”ti. Dasamaṃ.

“Monks, there are these five higher fetters. What five? Lust for form, lust for the formless, conceit, restlessness, and ignorance—these, monks, are the five higher fetters. For the direct knowledge, full understanding, utter destruction, and abandoning of these five higher fetters, five powers are to be developed. What five? Here, monks, a monk develops the power of faith… he develops the power of wisdom which has as its culmination the removal of lust, the removal of hatred, and the removal of delusion. For the direct knowledge, full understanding, utter destruction, and abandoning of these five higher fetters, these five powers are to be developed.”

Oghavaggo dasamo.

The tenth, the Chapter on Floods, is finished.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary thereof:

Ogho yogo upādānaṃ, ganthā anusayena ca;

Kāmaguṇā nīvaraṇā, khandhā oruddhambhāgiyāti.

Floods, yokes, clinging, bonds, and latent tendencies; sensual pleasures, hindrances, aggregates, and the lower fetters.

Balasaṃyuttaṃ chaṭṭhaṃ.

The sixth, the Connected Discourses on the Powers, is finished.

7. Iddhipādasaṃyuttaṃ

7. The Connected Discourses on the Bases of Spiritual Power

1. Cāpālavaggo

1. The Cāpāla Chapter

1. Apārasuttaṃ

1. From the Near Shore

813. “Cattārome [T 5.0326][V 3.0328][M 3.0222][P 5.0254] bhikkhave, iddhipādā bhāvitā bahulīkatā apārā pāraṃ gamanāya saṃvattanti. Katame cattāro? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu chandasamādhippadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgataṃ iddhipādaṃ bhāveti, vīriyasamādhippadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgataṃ iddhipādaṃ bhāveti, cittasamādhippadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgataṃ iddhipādaṃ bhāveti, vīmaṃsāsamādhippadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgataṃ iddhipādaṃ bhāveti. Ime kho, bhikkhave, cattāro iddhipādā bhāvitā bahulīkatā apārā pāraṃ gamanāya saṃvattantī”ti. Paṭhamaṃ.

813. “Monks, these four bases of spiritual power, when developed and cultivated, lead to going from the near shore to the far shore. What four? Here, monks, a monk develops the basis of spiritual power that is possessed of concentration due to desire and the formations of striving. He develops the basis of spiritual power that is possessed of concentration due to energy and the formations of striving. He develops the basis of spiritual power that is possessed of concentration due to mind and the formations of striving. He develops the basis of spiritual power that is possessed of concentration due to investigation and the formations of striving. These, monks, are the four bases of spiritual power that, when developed and cultivated, lead to going from the near shore to the far shore.”

2. Viraddhasuttaṃ

2. Neglected

814. “Yesaṃ kesañci, bhikkhave, cattāro iddhipādā viraddhā, viraddho tesaṃ ariyo maggo sammā dukkhakkhayagāmī. Yesaṃ kesañci, bhikkhave, cattāro iddhipādā āraddhā, āraddho tesaṃ ariyo maggo sammā dukkhakkhayagāmī. Katame cattāro? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu chandasamādhippadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgataṃ iddhipādaṃ bhāveti, vīriyasamādhi…pe… cittasamādhi…pe… vīmaṃsāsamādhippadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgataṃ iddhipādaṃ bhāveti. Yesaṃ [P 5.0255] kesañci, bhikkhave, ime cattāro iddhipādā viraddhā, viraddho tesaṃ ariyo maggo sammā dukkhakkhayagāmī. Yesaṃ kesañci, bhikkhave, ime cattāro iddhipādā āraddhā, āraddho tesaṃ ariyo [T 5.0327] maggo sammā dukkhakkhayagāmī”ti. Dutiyaṃ.

814. “Monks, for anyone for whom the four bases of spiritual power are neglected, for them the noble path leading rightly to the destruction of suffering is neglected. For anyone, monks, for whom the four bases of spiritual power are undertaken, for them the noble path leading rightly to the destruction of suffering is undertaken. What are the four? Here, monks, a monk develops the basis of spiritual power that is endowed with concentration due to zeal and volitional formations of striving. He develops the basis of spiritual power that is endowed with concentration due to energy… that is endowed with concentration due to mind… that is endowed with concentration due to investigation and volitional formations of striving. Monks, for anyone for whom these four bases of spiritual power are neglected, for them the noble path leading rightly to the destruction of suffering is neglected. For anyone, monks, for whom these four bases of spiritual power are undertaken, for them the noble path leading rightly to the destruction of suffering is undertaken.”

3. Ariyasuttaṃ

3. Noble

815. “Cattārome[V 3.0329], bhikkhave, iddhipādā bhāvitā bahulīkatā ariyā niyyānikā niyyanti takkarassa sammā dukkhakkhayāya. Katame cattāro? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu chandasamādhippadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgataṃ iddhipādaṃ bhāveti, vīriyasamādhi…pe… cittasamādhi…pe… iddhipādaṃ bhāveti, vīmaṃsāsamādhippadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgataṃ iddhipādaṃ bhāveti. Ime kho, bhikkhave, cattāro iddhipādā bhāvitā [M 3.0223] bahulīkatā ariyā niyyānikā niyyanti takkarassa sammā dukkhakkhayāyā”ti. Tatiyaṃ.

815. “Monks, these four bases of spiritual power, when developed and cultivated, are noble and lead to deliverance; they lead one who practices them to the right destruction of suffering. What are the four? Here, monks, a monk develops the basis of spiritual power that is endowed with concentration due to zeal and volitional formations of striving. He develops the basis of spiritual power that is endowed with concentration due to energy… that is endowed with concentration due to mind… He develops the basis of spiritual power that is endowed with concentration due to investigation and volitional formations of striving. These, monks, are the four bases of spiritual power that, when developed and cultivated, are noble and lead to deliverance; they lead one who practices them to the right destruction of suffering.”

4. Nibbidāsuttaṃ

4. Disenchantment

816. “Cattārome, bhikkhave, iddhipādā bhāvitā bahulīkatā ekantanibbidāya virāgāya nirodhāya upasamāya abhiññāya sambodhāya nibbānāya saṃvattanti. Katame cattāro? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu chandasamādhippadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgataṃ iddhipādaṃ bhāveti, vīriyasamādhi…pe… cittasamādhi…pe… vīmaṃsāsamādhippadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgataṃ iddhipādaṃ bhāveti. Ime kho, bhikkhave, cattāro iddhipādā bhāvitā bahulīkatā ekantanibbidāya virāgāya nirodhāya upasamāya abhiññāya sambodhāya nibbānāya saṃvattantī”ti. Catutthaṃ.

816. “Monks, these four bases of spiritual power, when developed and cultivated, conduce to utter disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, peace, direct knowledge, enlightenment, and Nibbāna. What are the four? Here, monks, a monk develops the basis of spiritual power endowed with concentration due to zeal and volitional formations of striving. He develops the basis of spiritual power endowed with concentration due to energy and volitional formations of striving. He develops the basis of spiritual power endowed with concentration due to mind and volitional formations of striving. He develops the basis of spiritual power endowed with concentration due to investigation and volitional formations of striving. These, monks, are the four bases of spiritual power that, when developed and cultivated, conduce to utter disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, peace, direct knowledge, enlightenment, and Nibbāna.”

5. Iddhipadesasuttaṃ

5. A Portion of Spiritual Power

817. “Ye hi keci, bhikkhave, atītamaddhānaṃ samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā iddhipadesaṃ abhinipphādesuṃ sabbe te catunnaṃ iddhipādānaṃ bhāvitattā bahulīkatattā. Ye hi keci[P 5.0256], bhikkhave, anāgatamaddhānaṃ samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā iddhipadesaṃ abhinipphādessanti sabbe te [T 5.0328] catunnaṃ iddhipādānaṃ bhāvitattā bahulīkatattā. Ye hi keci, bhikkhave, etarahi samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā iddhipadesaṃ abhinipphādenti sabbe te catunnaṃ iddhipādānaṃ bhāvitattā bahulīkatattā.

817. “Monks, whatever ascetics or brahmins in the past accomplished a portion of spiritual power, all of them did so by developing and cultivating the four bases of spiritual power. Whatever ascetics or brahmins in the future will accomplish a portion of spiritual power, all of them will do so by developing and cultivating the four bases of spiritual power. Whatever ascetics or brahmins in the present accomplish a portion of spiritual power, all of them do so by developing and cultivating the four bases of spiritual power.”

“Katamesaṃ [V 3.0330] catunnaṃ? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu chandasamādhippadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgataṃ iddhipādaṃ bhāveti, vīriyasamādhi…pe… cittasamādhi…pe… vīmaṃsāsamādhippadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgataṃ iddhipādaṃ bhāveti. Ye hi keci, bhikkhave, atītamaddhānaṃ samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā iddhipadesaṃ abhinipphādesuṃ, sabbe te imesaṃyeva catunnaṃ iddhipādānaṃ bhāvitattā bahulīkatattā. Ye hi keci, bhikkhave, anāgatamaddhānaṃ samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā iddhipadesaṃ abhinipphādessanti, sabbe te imesaṃyeva catunnaṃ iddhipādānaṃ bhāvitattā bahulīkatattā. Ye hi keci, bhikkhave, etarahi samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā iddhipadesaṃ abhinipphādenti, sabbe te imesaṃyeva catunnaṃ iddhipādānaṃ bhāvitattā bahulīkatattā”ti. Pañcamaṃ.

Which four? Here, monks, a monk develops the basis of spiritual power endowed with concentration due to zeal and with striving-formations; he develops the basis of spiritual power endowed with concentration due to energy... with concentration due to mind... with concentration due to investigation and with striving-formations. Monks, whatever ascetics or brahmins in the past accomplished a portion of spiritual power, all of them did so by developing and cultivating these same four bases of spiritual power. Whatever ascetics or brahmins in the future will accomplish a portion of spiritual power, all of them will do so by developing and cultivating these same four bases of spiritual power. Whatever ascetics or brahmins in the present accomplish a portion of spiritual power, all of them do so by developing and cultivating these same four bases of spiritual power.” The fifth.

6. Samattasuttaṃ

6. The Discourse on Completion

818. “Ye [M 3.0224] hi keci, bhikkhave, atītamaddhānaṃ samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā samattaṃ iddhiṃ abhinipphādesuṃ, sabbe te catunnaṃ iddhipādānaṃ bhāvitattā bahulīkatattā. Ye hi keci, bhikkhave, anāgatamaddhānaṃ samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā samattaṃ iddhiṃ abhinipphādessanti, sabbe te catunnaṃ iddhipādānaṃ bhāvitattā bahulīkatattā. Ye hi keci, bhikkhave, etarahi samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā samattaṃ iddhiṃ abhinipphādenti[T 5.0329], sabbe te catunnaṃ iddhipādānaṃ bhāvitattā bahulīkatattā.

818. Monks, whatever ascetics or brahmins in the past accomplished complete spiritual power, all of them did so by developing and cultivating the four bases of spiritual power. Whatever ascetics or brahmins in the future will accomplish complete spiritual power, all of them will do so by developing and cultivating the four bases of spiritual power. Whatever ascetics or brahmins at present accomplish complete spiritual power, all of them do so by developing and cultivating the four bases of spiritual power.

“Katamesaṃ catunnaṃ? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu chandasamādhippadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgataṃ iddhipādaṃ bhāveti, vīriyasamādhi…pe… cittasamādhi…pe… vīmaṃsāsamādhippadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgataṃ iddhipādaṃ bhāveti. Ye hi keci, bhikkhave, atītamaddhānaṃ samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā samattaṃ iddhiṃ abhinipphādesuṃ, sabbe te imesaṃyeva catunnaṃ iddhipādānaṃ bhāvitattā bahulīkatattā. Ye hi keci, bhikkhave, anāgatamaddhānaṃ samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā samattaṃ iddhiṃ abhinipphādessanti, sabbe te imesaṃyeva catunnaṃ iddhipādānaṃ bhāvitattā bahulīkatattā. Ye hi keci, bhikkhave, etarahi samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā samattaṃ iddhiṃ abhinipphādenti, sabbe te imesaṃyeva catunnaṃ iddhipādānaṃ bhāvitattā bahulīkatattā”ti. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

Of which four? Here, monks, a monk develops the basis of spiritual power endowed with concentration due to zeal and with striving-formations; he develops the basis of spiritual power endowed with concentration due to energy... with concentration due to mind... with concentration due to investigation and with striving-formations. Monks, whatever ascetics or brahmins in the past accomplished complete spiritual power, all of them did so by developing and cultivating these very four bases of spiritual power. Whatever ascetics or brahmins in the future will accomplish complete spiritual power, all of them will do so by developing and cultivating these very four bases of spiritual power. Whatever ascetics or brahmins in the present accomplish complete spiritual power, all of them do so by developing and cultivating these very four bases of spiritual power.” The sixth.

7. Bhikkhusuttaṃ

7. The Discourse on the Monk

819. “Ye [V 3.0331][P 5.0257] hi keci, bhikkhave, atītamaddhānaṃ bhikkhū āsavānaṃ khayā anāsavaṃ cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttiṃ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja vihariṃsu, sabbe te catunnaṃ iddhipādānaṃ bhāvitattā bahulīkatattā. Ye hi keci, bhikkhave, anāgatamaddhānaṃ bhikkhū āsavānaṃ khayā anāsavaṃ cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttiṃ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharissanti, sabbe te catunnaṃ iddhipādānaṃ bhāvitattā bahulīkatattā. Ye hi keci, bhikkhave, etarahi bhikkhū āsavānaṃ khayā anāsavaṃ cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttiṃ [T 5.0330] diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharanti, sabbe te catunnaṃ iddhipādānaṃ bhāvitattā bahulīkatattā.

819. Monks, whatever monks in the past, through the destruction of the taints, having realized it for themselves with direct knowledge, attained and dwelt in the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom in this very life—all of them did so by developing and cultivating the four bases of spiritual power. Monks, whatever monks in the future, through the destruction of the taints, having realized it for themselves with direct knowledge, will attain and dwell in the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom in this very life—all of them will do so by developing and cultivating the four bases of spiritual power. Monks, whatever monks in the present, through the destruction of the taints, having realized it for themselves with direct knowledge, attain and dwell in the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom in this very life—all of them do so by developing and cultivating the four bases of spiritual power.

“Katamesaṃ [M 3.0225] catunnaṃ? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu chandasamādhippadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgataṃ iddhipādaṃ bhāveti, vīriyasamādhi…pe… cittasamādhi…pe… vīmaṃsāsamādhippadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgataṃ iddhipādaṃ bhāveti. Ye hi keci, bhikkhave, atītamaddhānaṃ bhikkhū āsavānaṃ khayā anāsavaṃ cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttiṃ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja vihariṃsu sabbe te imesaṃyeva catunnaṃ iddhipādānaṃ bhāvitattā bahulīkatattā. Ye hi keci, bhikkhave, anāgatamaddhānaṃ bhikkhū āsavānaṃ khayā anāsavaṃ cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttiṃ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharissanti, sabbe te imesaṃyeva catunnaṃ iddhipādānaṃ bhāvitattā bahulīkatattā. Ye hi keci, bhikkhave, etarahi bhikkhū āsavānaṃ khayā anāsavaṃ cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttiṃ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharanti, sabbe te imesaṃyeva catunnaṃ iddhipādānaṃ bhāvitattā bahulīkatattā”ti. Sattamaṃ.

Of which four? Here, monks, a monk develops the basis of spiritual power endowed with concentration due to zeal and with striving-formations; he develops the basis of spiritual power endowed with concentration due to energy... with concentration due to mind... with concentration due to investigation and with striving-formations. Monks, whatever monks in the past, through the destruction of the taints, having realized it for themselves with direct knowledge, attained and dwelt in the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom in this very life—all of them did so by developing and cultivating these very four bases of spiritual power. Whatever monks in the future, through the destruction of the taints, having realized it for themselves with direct knowledge, will attain and dwell in the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom in this very life—all of them will do so by developing and cultivating these very four bases of spiritual power. Whatever monks in the present, through the destruction of the taints, having realized it for themselves with direct knowledge, attain and dwell in the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom in this very life—all of them do so by developing and cultivating these very four bases of spiritual power.” The seventh.

8. Buddhasuttaṃ

8. The Discourse on the Buddha

820. “Cattārome, bhikkhave, iddhipādā. Katame cattāro? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu chandasamādhippadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgataṃ iddhipādaṃ bhāveti, vīriyasamādhi…pe… cittasamādhi …pe… vīmaṃsāsamādhippadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgataṃ iddhipādaṃ bhāveti. Ime kho, bhikkhave, cattāro iddhipādā[V 3.0332]. Imesaṃ [T 5.0331] kho, bhikkhave, catunnaṃ iddhipādānaṃ bhāvitattā bahulīkatattā tathāgato ‘arahaṃ sammāsambuddho’ti vuccatī”ti. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

820. Monks, there are these four bases of spiritual power. What four? Here, monks, a monk develops the basis of spiritual power endowed with concentration due to zeal and with striving-formations; he develops the basis of spiritual power endowed with concentration due to energy... with concentration due to mind... with concentration due to investigation and with striving-formations. These, monks, are the four bases of spiritual power. It is because of having developed and cultivated these four bases of spiritual power, monks, that the Tathāgata is called ‘the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One’.” The eighth.

9. Ñāṇasuttaṃ

9. The Discourse on Knowledge

821. “‘Ayaṃ [P 5.0258] chandasamādhippadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgato iddhipādo’ti me bhikkhave, pubbe ananussutesu dhammesu cakkhuṃ udapādi, ñāṇaṃ udapādi, paññā udapādi, vijjā udapādi, āloko udapādi. ‘So kho panāyaṃ chandasamādhippadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgato iddhipādo bhāvetabbo’ti me, bhikkhave…pe… ‘bhāvito’ti me, bhikkhave, pubbe ananussutesu dhammesu cakkhuṃ udapādi, ñāṇaṃ udapādi, paññā udapādi, vijjā udapādi, āloko udapādi.

821. “‘This is the basis of spiritual power endowed with concentration based on desire and with formations of striving’—thus, monks, concerning things unheard before, vision arose in me, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true knowledge arose, light arose. ‘Indeed, that basis of spiritual power endowed with concentration based on desire and with formations of striving is to be developed’—thus, monks… ‘It has been developed’—thus, monks, concerning things unheard before, vision arose in me, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true knowledge arose, light arose.

“‘Ayaṃ [M 3.0226] vīriyasamādhippadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgato iddhipādo’ti me, bhikkhave, pubbe ananussutesu dhammesu cakkhuṃ udapādi, ñāṇaṃ udapādi, paññā udapādi, vijjā udapādi, āloko udapādi. ‘So kho panāyaṃ vīriyasamādhippadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgato iddhipādo bhāvetabbo’ti me, bhikkhave…pe… ‘bhāvito’ti me, bhikkhave, pubbe ananussutesu dhammesu cakkhuṃ udapādi, ñāṇaṃ udapādi, paññā udapādi, vijjā udapādi, āloko udapādi.

“‘This is the basis of spiritual power endowed with concentration based on energy and with formations of striving’—thus, monks, concerning things unheard before, vision arose in me, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true knowledge arose, light arose. ‘Indeed, that basis of spiritual power endowed with concentration based on energy and with formations of striving is to be developed’—thus, monks… ‘It has been developed’—thus, monks, concerning things unheard before, vision arose in me, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true knowledge arose, light arose.

“‘Ayaṃ cittasamādhippadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgato iddhipādo’ti me, bhikkhave, pubbe ananussutesu dhammesu cakkhuṃ udapādi, ñāṇaṃ udapādi, paññā udapādi, vijjā udapādi, āloko udapādi. ‘So kho panāyaṃ cittasamādhippadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgato iddhipādo bhāvetabbo’ti [T 5.0332] me, bhikkhave…pe… ‘bhāvito’ti me, bhikkhave, pubbe ananussutesu dhammesu cakkhuṃ udapādi, ñāṇaṃ udapādi, paññā udapādi, vijjā udapādi, āloko udapādi.

“‘This is the basis of spiritual power endowed with concentration based on mind and with formations of striving’—thus, monks, concerning things unheard before, vision arose in me, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true knowledge arose, light arose. ‘Indeed, that basis of spiritual power endowed with concentration based on mind and with formations of striving is to be developed’—thus, monks… ‘It has been developed’—thus, monks, concerning things unheard before, vision arose in me, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true knowledge arose, light arose.

“‘Ayaṃ vīmaṃsāsamādhippadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgato iddhipādo’ti me, bhikkhave, pubbe ananussutesu dhammesu cakkhuṃ udapādi, ñāṇaṃ udapādi, paññā udapādi, vijjā udapādi, āloko udapādi. ‘So kho panāyaṃ vīmaṃsāsamādhippadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgato iddhipādo bhāvetabbo’ti me, bhikkhave…pe… ‘bhāvito’ti me, bhikkhave, pubbe ananussutesu dhammesu cakkhuṃ [V 3.0333] udapādi, ñāṇaṃ udapādi, paññā udapādi, vijjā udapādi, āloko udapādī”ti. Navamaṃ.

“‘This is the basis of spiritual power endowed with concentration based on investigation and with formations of striving’—thus, monks, concerning things unheard before, vision arose in me, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true knowledge arose, light arose. ‘Indeed, that basis of spiritual power endowed with concentration based on investigation and with formations of striving is to be developed’—thus, monks… ‘It has been developed’—thus, monks, concerning things unheard before, vision arose in me, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true knowledge arose, light arose.” The ninth.

10. Cetiyasuttaṃ

10. The Discourse on Shrines

822. Evaṃ me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā vesāliyaṃ viharati mahāvane kūṭāgārasālāyaṃ. Atha [P 5.0259] kho bhagavā pubbaṇhasamayaṃ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya vesāliṃ piṇḍāya pāvisi. Vesāliyaṃ piṇḍāya caritvā pacchābhattaṃ piṇḍapātapaṭikkanto āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ āmantesi – “gaṇhāhi, ānanda, nisīdanaṃ. Yena cāpālaṃ cetiyaṃ pāvālacetiyaṃ (syā. kaṃ.) tenupasaṅkamissāma divāvihārāyā”ti. “Evaṃ bhante”ti kho āyasmā ānando bhagavato paṭissutvā nisīdanaṃ ādāya bhagavantaṃ piṭṭhito piṭṭhito anubandhi. Atha kho bhagavā yena cāpālaṃ cetiyaṃ tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā [T 5.0333][M 3.0227] paññatte āsane nisīdi. Āyasmāpi kho ānando bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinnaṃ kho āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ bhagavā etadavoca –

822. Thus have I heard: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Vesālī in the Great Wood at the Kūṭāgāra Hall. Then the Blessed One, having dressed in the morning, took his bowl and robe and entered Vesālī for alms. Having wandered for alms in Vesālī and returned from the alms round after the meal, he addressed Venerable Ānanda: “Take a sitting cloth, Ānanda. Let us go to the Cāpāla Shrine for the day’s sojourn.” “Yes, venerable sir,” replied Venerable Ānanda, and taking a sitting cloth, he followed behind the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One went to the Cāpāla Shrine, and upon arrival, sat down on the prepared seat. Venerable Ānanda also, having paid homage to the Blessed One, sat down to one side. To Venerable Ānanda, who was sitting to one side, the Blessed One said this:

“Ramaṇīyā, ānanda, vesālī, ramaṇīyaṃ udenaṃ cetiyaṃ, ramaṇīyaṃ gotamakaṃ cetiyaṃ, ramaṇīyaṃ sattambaṃ cetiyaṃ, ramaṇīyaṃ bahuputtaṃ cetiyaṃ bahuputtakacetiyaṃ (syā. kaṃ. pī. ka.), ramaṇīyaṃ sārandadaṃ cetiyaṃ ānandacetiyaṃ (ka.), sānandaraṃ (ka.), ramaṇīyaṃ cāpālaṃ cetiyaṃ. Yassa kassaci, ānanda, cattāro iddhipādā bhāvitā bahulīkatā yānīkatā vatthukatā anuṭṭhitā paricitā susamāraddhā, so ākaṅkhamāno kappaṃ vā tiṭṭheyya kappāvasesaṃ vā. Tathāgatassa kho, ānanda, cattāro iddhipādā bhāvitā bahulīkatā yānīkatā vatthukatā anuṭṭhitā paricitā susamāraddhā. Ākaṅkhamāno, ānanda, tathāgato kappaṃ vā tiṭṭheyya kappāvasesaṃ vā”ti.

“Delightful, Ānanda, is Vesālī; delightful is the Udena Shrine; delightful is the Gotamaka Shrine; delightful is the Sattamba Shrine; delightful is the Bahuputta Shrine; delightful is the Sārandada Shrine; delightful is the Cāpāla Shrine. Anyone, Ānanda, who has developed, cultivated, made a vehicle of it, made it a basis, sustained it, consolidated it, and properly undertaken it, could, if he wished, remain for an aeon or for the remainder of the aeon. The Tathāgata, Ānanda, has developed, cultivated, made a vehicle of, made a basis of, sustained, consolidated, and properly undertaken the four bases of spiritual power. If he wished, Ānanda, the Tathāgata could remain for an aeon or for the remainder of the aeon.”

Evampi kho āyasmā ānando bhagavatā oḷārike nimitte kayiramāne oḷārike obhāse kayiramāne nāsakkhi paṭivijjhituṃ; na bhagavantaṃ yāci – “tiṭṭhatu, bhante, bhagavā kappaṃ, tiṭṭhatu sugato kappaṃ sugato kappāvasesaṃ (pī. ka.) dī. ni. 2.167 bahujanahitāya bahujanasukhāya lokānukampāya atthāya hitāya sukhāya devamanussāna”nti yathā taṃ mārena pariyuṭṭhitacitto.

Even so, though the Blessed One gave such a plain sign, made such a clear indication, Venerable Ānanda was not able to comprehend it. He did not beseech the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, may the Blessed One remain for an aeon, may the Sugata remain for an aeon, for the welfare and happiness of the many, out of compassion for the world, for the good, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans”—so much was his mind possessed by Māra.

Dutiyampi [V 3.0334] kho bhagavā…pe… tatiyampi [P 5.0260] kho bhagavā āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ āmantesi – “ramaṇīyā, ānanda, vesālī, ramaṇīyaṃ udenaṃ cetiyaṃ, ramaṇīyaṃ gotamakaṃ cetiyaṃ, ramaṇīyaṃ sattambaṃ cetiyaṃ, ramaṇīyaṃ [T 5.0334] bahuputtaṃ cetiyaṃ, ramaṇīyaṃ sārandadaṃ cetiyaṃ, ramaṇīyaṃ cāpālaṃ cetiyaṃ. Yassa kassaci, ānanda, cattāro iddhipādā bhāvitā bahulīkatā yānīkatā vatthukatā anuṭṭhitā paricitā susamāraddhā, so ākaṅkhamāno kappaṃ vā tiṭṭheyya kappāvasesaṃ vā. Tathāgatassa kho, ānanda, cattāro iddhipādā bhāvitā bahulīkatā yānīkatā vatthukatā anuṭṭhitā paricitā susamāraddhā. Ākaṅkhamāno, ānanda, tathāgato kappaṃ vā tiṭṭheyya kappāvasesaṃ vā”ti.

A second time the Blessed One … A third time the Blessed One addressed Venerable Ānanda: “Delightful, Ānanda, is Vesālī; delightful is the Udena Shrine; delightful is the Gotamaka Shrine; delightful is the Sattamba Shrine; delightful is the Bahuputta Shrine; delightful is the Sārandada Shrine; delightful is the Cāpāla Shrine. Anyone, Ānanda, who has developed, cultivated, made a vehicle of it, made it a basis, sustained it, consolidated it, and properly undertaken it, could, if he wished, remain for an aeon or for the remainder of the aeon. The Tathāgata, Ānanda, has developed, cultivated, made a vehicle of, made a basis of, sustained, consolidated, and properly undertaken the four bases of spiritual power. If he wished, Ānanda, the Tathāgata could remain for an aeon or for the remainder of the aeon.”

Evampi [M 3.0228] kho āyasmā ānando bhagavatā oḷārike nimitte kayiramāne oḷārike obhāse kayiramāne nāsakkhi paṭivijjhituṃ; na bhagavantaṃ yāci – “tiṭṭhatu, bhante, bhagavā kappaṃ, tiṭṭhatu sugato kappaṃ bahujanahitāya bahujanasukhāya lokānukampāya atthāya hitāya sukhāya devamanussāna”nti yathā taṃ mārena pariyuṭṭhitacitto.

Even so, indeed, although the Blessed One was making such a gross hint, making such a gross sign, the Venerable Ānanda was not able to penetrate it. He did not beseech the Blessed One: 'Venerable sir, may the Blessed One remain for an aeon, may the Sugata remain for an aeon for the welfare of the many, for the happiness of the many, out of compassion for the world, for the good, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans'—so possessed was his mind by Māra.

Atha kho bhagavā āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ āmantesi – “gaccha kho tvaṃ, ānanda, yassa dāni kālaṃ maññasī”ti. “Evaṃ, bhante”ti kho āyasmā ānando bhagavato paṭissutvā uṭṭhāyāsanā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā avidūre aññatarasmiṃ rukkhamūle nisīdi. Atha kho māro pāpimā, acirapakkante āyasmante ānande, yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “parinibbātu [T 5.0335] dāni, bhante, bhagavā, parinibbātu dāni sugato parinibbātu sugato (sī. syā. kaṃ.) evamuparipi! Parinibbānakālo dāni, bhante, bhagavato. Bhāsitā kho panesā, bhante, bhagavatā vācā – ‘na tāvāhaṃ, pāpima[P 5.0261], parinibbāyissāmi yāva me bhikkhū na sāvakā bhavissanti viyattā vinītā visāradā bahussutā dhammadharā dhammānudhammappaṭipannā sāmīcippaṭipannā anudhammacārino, sakaṃ ācariyakaṃ uggahetvā ācikkhissanti desessanti paññapessanti paṭṭhapessanti vivarissanti vibhajissanti uttānīkarissanti uttāniṃ karissanti (ka.), uttānikarissanti (pī.), uppannaṃ parappavādaṃ sahadhammena suniggahitaṃ niggahetvā sappāṭihāriyaṃ dhammaṃ desessantī’”ti.

Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda: 'Go now, Ānanda, for what you deem it is time.' 'Very well, venerable sir,' the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One, and having risen from his seat, he paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him to the right, and sat down at the foot of a certain tree not far away. Then, not long after the Venerable Ānanda had departed, Māra the Evil One approached the Blessed One. Having approached, he said this to the Blessed One: 'Venerable sir, may the Blessed One now attain Parinibbāna! May the Sugata now attain Parinibbāna! Now, venerable sir, is the time for the Blessed One’s Parinibbāna. For, venerable sir, these words were spoken by the Blessed One: “I will not attain Parinibbāna, Evil One, so long as my bhikkhu disciples have not become skilled, disciplined, confident, learned, upholders of the Dhamma, practicing in accordance with the Dhamma, practicing fittingly, and practicing in conformity with the Dhamma; so long as they have not, after learning their own teacher's doctrine, declared it, taught it, proclaimed it, established it, revealed it, analyzed it, and made it clear; and so long as they have not, having thoroughly refuted with reason an opposing doctrine that has arisen, taught the Dhamma with its marvels.”'”

Santi kho pana, bhante, etarahi bhikkhū bhagavato sāvakā viyattā vinītā visāradā bahussutā dhammadharā dhammānudhammappaṭipannā sāmīcippaṭipannā anudhammacārino, sakaṃ ācariyakaṃ uggahetvā [V 3.0335] ācikkhanti desenti paññapenti paṭṭhapenti vivaranti vibhajanti uttānīkaronti, uppannaṃ parappavādaṃ sahadhammena suniggahitaṃ niggahetvā sappāṭihāriyaṃ dhammaṃ desenti. Parinibbātu dāni, bhante, bhagavā, parinibbātu dāni, sugato! Parinibbānakālo dāni, bhante, bhagavato.

Venerable sir, now there are monks, disciples of the Blessed One, who are skilled, disciplined, confident, learned, upholders of the Dhamma, practicing in accordance with the Dhamma, practicing fittingly, and practicing in conformity with the Dhamma. Having learned their own teacher's doctrine, they declare, teach, proclaim, establish, reveal, analyze, and make it clear. Having thoroughly refuted with reason an opposing doctrine that has arisen, they teach the Dhamma with its marvels. Let the Blessed One now attain Parinibbāna, venerable sir! Let the Sugata now attain Parinibbāna! It is now the time, venerable sir, for the Blessed One's Parinibbāna.

“Bhāsitā kho panesā, bhante, bhagavatā vācā – ‘na tāvāhaṃ, pāpima, parinibbāyissāmi yāva me bhikkhuniyo na sāvikā bhavissanti viyattā vinītā [M 3.0229] visāradā bahussutā dhammadharā dhammānudhammappaṭipannā sāmīcippaṭipannā anudhammacāriniyo, sakaṃ ācariyakaṃ uggahetvā ācikkhissanti desessanti paññapessanti paṭṭhapessanti vivarissanti vibhajissanti [T 5.0336] uttānīkarissanti, uppannaṃ parappavādaṃ sahadhammena suniggahitaṃ niggahetvā sappāṭihāriyaṃ dhammaṃ desessantī’”ti.

Venerable sir, this word was indeed spoken by the Blessed One: ‘I will not attain Parinibbāna, Evil One, so long as my bhikkhunī disciples have not become skilled, disciplined, confident, learned, upholders of the Dhamma, practicing in accordance with the Dhamma, practicing fittingly, and practicing in conformity with the Dhamma; so long as they have not, after learning their own teacher's doctrine, declared it, taught it, proclaimed it, established it, revealed it, analyzed it, and made it clear; and so long as they have not, having thoroughly refuted with reason an opposing doctrine that has arisen, taught the Dhamma with its marvels.’

“Santi kho pana, bhante, etarahi bhikkhuniyo bhagavato sāvikā viyattā vinītā visāradā bahussutā dhammadharā dhammānudhammappaṭipannā sāmīcippaṭipannā anudhammacāriniyo, sakaṃ ācariyakaṃ uggahetvā ācikkhanti desenti paññapenti paṭṭhapenti vivaranti vibhajanti uttānīkaronti, uppannaṃ parappavādaṃ sahadhammena suniggahitaṃ niggahetvā sappāṭihāriyaṃ dhammaṃ desenti. Parinibbātu dāni, bhante, bhagavā, parinibbātu dāni, sugato! Parinibbānakālo dāni, bhante, bhagavato.

Venerable sir, now there are bhikkhunīs, disciples of the Blessed One, who are skilled, disciplined, confident, learned, upholders of the Dhamma, practicing in accordance with the Dhamma, practicing fittingly, and practicing in conformity with the Dhamma. Having learned their own teacher's doctrine, they declare, teach, proclaim, establish, reveal, analyze, and make it clear. Having thoroughly refuted with reason an opposing doctrine that has arisen, they teach the Dhamma with its marvels. Let the Blessed One now attain Parinibbāna, venerable sir! Let the Sugata now attain Parinibbāna! It is now the time, venerable sir, for the Blessed One's Parinibbāna.

“Bhāsitā kho panesā, bhante, bhagavatā vācā – ‘na tāvāhaṃ, pāpima, parinibbāyissāmi yāva me upāsakā…pe… yāva me upāsikā na sāvikā bhavissanti viyattā vinītā visāradā bahussutā dhammadharā dhammānudhammappaṭipannā sāmīcippaṭipannā anudhammacāriniyo, sakaṃ ācariyakaṃ uggahetvā ācikkhissanti desessanti paññapessanti paṭṭhapessanti vivarissanti vibhajissanti uttānīkarissanti, uppannaṃ parappavādaṃ sahadhammena suniggahitaṃ niggahetvā sappāṭihāriyaṃ dhammaṃ desessantī’”ti.

Venerable sir, this word was indeed spoken by the Blessed One: ‘I will not attain Parinibbāna, Evil One, so long as my upāsaka disciples... so long as my upāsikā disciples have not become skilled, disciplined, confident, learned, upholders of the Dhamma, practicing in accordance with the Dhamma, practicing fittingly, and practicing in conformity with the Dhamma; so long as they have not, after learning their own teacher's doctrine, declared it, taught it, proclaimed it, established it, revealed it, analyzed it, and made it clear; and so long as they have not, having thoroughly refuted with reason an opposing doctrine that has arisen, taught the Dhamma with its marvels.’

“Santi kho pana, bhante, etarahi upāsakā…pe… upāsikā bhagavato sāvikā viyattā vinītā visāradā bahussutā dhammadharā dhammānudhammappaṭipannā [P 5.0262] sāmīcippaṭipannā anudhammacāriniyo[V 3.0336], sakaṃ ācariyakaṃ uggahetvā ācikkhanti desenti paññapenti paṭṭhapenti vivaranti vibhajanti [T 5.0337] uttānīkaronti, uppannaṃ parappavādaṃ sahadhammena suniggahitaṃ niggahetvā sappāṭihāriyaṃ dhammaṃ desenti. Parinibbātu dāni, bhante, bhagavā, parinibbātu dāni, sugato! Parinibbānakālo dāni, bhante, bhagavato.

Venerable sir, now there are upāsakas... upāsikās, disciples of the Blessed One, who are skilled, disciplined, confident, learned, upholders of the Dhamma, practicing in accordance with the Dhamma, practicing fittingly, and practicing in conformity with the Dhamma. Having learned their own teacher's doctrine, they declare, teach, proclaim, establish, reveal, analyze, and make it clear. Having thoroughly refuted with reason an opposing doctrine that has arisen, they teach the Dhamma with its marvels. Now, venerable sir, let the Blessed One attain Parinibbāna! Now, let the Sugata attain Parinibbāna! It is now the time, venerable sir, for the Blessed One’s Parinibbāna.

“Bhāsitā kho panesā, bhante, bhagavatā vācā – ‘na tāvāhaṃ, pāpima, parinibbāyissāmi yāva me idaṃ brahmacariyaṃ na iddhañceva bhavissati phītañca vitthāritaṃ bāhujaññaṃ puthubhūtaṃ yāva devamanussehi suppakāsita’nti. Tayidaṃ, bhante, bhagavato brahmacariyaṃ iddhañceva phītañca vitthāritaṃ bāhujaññaṃ puthubhūtaṃ [M 3.0230] yāva devamanussehi suppakāsitaṃ. Parinibbātu dāni, bhante, bhagavā, parinibbātu dāni sugato. Parinibbānakālo dāni, bhante, bhagavato”ti.

Venerable sir, this word was indeed spoken by the Blessed One: ‘Evil One, I will not attain final Nibbāna so long as this holy life of mine has not become prosperous, flourishing, widespread, known to many, vast, and well-proclaimed among gods and humans.’ Now, venerable sir, this holy life of the Blessed One is prosperous, flourishing, widespread, known to many, vast, and well-proclaimed among gods and humans. Let the Blessed One now attain final Nibbāna, venerable sir! Let the Sugata now attain final Nibbāna! Now, venerable sir, is the time for the Blessed One’s final Nibbāna.”

Evaṃ vutte bhagavā māraṃ pāpimantaṃ etadavoca – “appossukko tvaṃ, pāpima, hohi. Na ciraṃ nacirasseva (ka.) tathāgatassa parinibbānaṃ bhavissati. Ito tiṇṇaṃ māsānaṃ accayena tathāgato parinibbāyissatī”ti. Atha kho bhagavā cāpāle cetiye sato sampajāno āyusaṅkhāraṃ ossaji. Ossaṭṭhe ca osajje pana (ka.) bhagavatā āyusaṅkhāre mahābhūmicālo ahosi bhiṃsanako lomahaṃso, devadundubhiyo devadudrabhiyo (ka.) ca phaliṃsu. Atha kho bhagavā etamatthaṃ viditvā tāyaṃ velāyaṃ imaṃ udānaṃ udānesi –

When this was said, the Blessed One said this to Māra the Evil One: “Be at ease, Evil One. The Tathāgata’s final Nibbāna will not be long delayed. Three months from now, the Tathāgata will attain final Nibbāna.” Then, at the Cāpāla Shrine, the Blessed One, mindful and clearly comprehending, relinquished the life-sustaining volition. And when the life-sustaining volition was relinquished by the Blessed One, there was a great earthquake, terrible and hair-raising, and the celestial drums resounded. Then, having understood this matter, the Blessed One on that occasion uttered this inspired utterance:

“Tulamatulañca [T 5.0338][P 5.0263] sambhavaṃ, bhavasaṅkhāramavassaji muni;

Ajjhattarato samāhito, abhindi kavacamivattasambhava”nti. dasamaṃ;

The Sage relinquished the comparable and the incomparable, the cause of becoming, and the volitional formation of existence. Delighting inwardly, concentrated, he shattered his self-originated being like a suit of armor.

Cāpālavaggo paṭhamo.

The Cāpāla Chapter, the First.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary verse for this chapter:

Apārāpi viraddho ca, ariyā nibbidāpi ca;

Padesaṃ samattaṃ bhikkhu, buddhaṃ ñāṇañca cetiyanti.

Apāra, Viraddha, Ariyā, and Nibbidā; Padesa, Samatta, Bhikkhu, Buddha, Ñāṇa, and Cetiya.

2. Pāsādakampanavaggo

2. The Chapter on the Shaking of the Mansion

1. Pubbasuttaṃ

1. The Sutta on the Past

823. Sāvatthinidānaṃ[T 5.0339][V 3.0337]. “Pubbeva me, bhikkhave, sambodhā anabhisambuddhassa bodhisattasseva sato etadahosi – ‘ko nu kho hetu, ko paccayo iddhipādabhāvanāyā’ti? Tassa mayhaṃ, bhikkhave, etadahosi – ‘idha bhikkhu chandasamādhippadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgataṃ iddhipādaṃ bhāveti – iti me chando na ca atilīno bhavissati, na ca atippaggahito bhavissati, na ca ajjhattaṃ saṃkhitto bhavissati, na ca bahiddhā vikkhitto bhavissati. Pacchāpuresaññī ca viharati – yathā pure tathā pacchā, yathā pacchā tathā pure; yathā [M 3.0231] adho tathā uddhaṃ, yathā uddhaṃ tathā adho; yathā divā tathā rattiṃ, yathā rattiṃ tathā divā. Iti vivaṭena cetasā apariyonaddhena sappabhāsaṃ cittaṃ bhāveti’”.

823. At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, before my enlightenment, while I was still an unenlightened Bodhisatta, this thought occurred to me: ‘What is the cause, what is the condition, for the development of the bases for spiritual power?’ Then, bhikkhus, this thought occurred to me: ‘Here, a bhikkhu develops the basis for spiritual power that is endowed with concentration due to desire and the formations of striving, thinking: “Thus my desire will be neither too lax nor too strained; it will be neither inwardly constricted nor outwardly scattered.” He dwells perceiving what is after and what was before: as before, so after; as after, so before; as below, so above; as above, so below; as by day, so by night; as by night, so by day. Thus, with a mind that is open and unenveloped, he develops a mind imbued with luminosity.’

“Vīriyasamādhippadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgataṃ [P 5.0264] iddhipādaṃ bhāveti – iti me vīriyaṃ na ca atilīnaṃ bhavissati, na ca atippaggahitaṃ bhavissati, na ca ajjhattaṃ saṃkhittaṃ bhavissati, na ca bahiddhā vikkhittaṃ bhavissati. Pacchāpuresaññī ca viharati – yathā pure tathā pacchā, yathā pacchā tathā pure; yathā adho tathā uddhaṃ, yathā uddhaṃ tathā adho; yathā divā tathā rattiṃ, yathā rattiṃ tathā divā. Iti vivaṭena cetasā apariyonaddhena sappabhāsaṃ cittaṃ bhāveti.

“He develops the basis for spiritual power that is endowed with concentration due to energy and the formations of striving, thinking: ‘Thus my energy will be neither too slack nor too tense; it will be neither inwardly constricted nor outwardly scattered.’ He dwells perceiving what is after and what was before: as before, so after; as after, so before; as below, so above; as above, so below; as by day, so by night; as by night, so by day. Thus, with a mind that is open and unenveloped, he develops a mind imbued with luminosity.

“Cittasamādhippadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgataṃ [T 5.0340] iddhipādaṃ bhāveti – iti me cittaṃ na ca atilīnaṃ bhavissati, na ca atippaggahitaṃ bhavissati, na ca ajjhattaṃ saṃkhittaṃ bhavissati, na ca bahiddhā vikkhittaṃ bhavissati. Pacchāpuresaññī ca viharati – yathā pure tathā pacchā, yathā pacchā tathā pure; yathā adho tathā uddhaṃ, yathā uddhaṃ tathā adho; yathā divā tathā rattiṃ, yathā rattiṃ tathā divā. Iti vivaṭena cetasā apariyonaddhena sappabhāsaṃ cittaṃ bhāveti.

“He develops the basis for spiritual power that is endowed with concentration due to mind and the formations of striving, thinking: ‘Thus my mind will be neither too sluggish nor too agitated; it will be neither inwardly constricted nor outwardly scattered.’ He dwells perceiving what is after and what was before: as before, so after; as after, so before; as below, so above; as above, so below; as by day, so by night; as by night, so by day. Thus, with a mind that is open and unenveloped, he develops a mind imbued with luminosity.

“Vīmaṃsāsamādhippadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgataṃ iddhipādaṃ bhāveti – iti me vīmaṃsā na ca atilīnā bhavissati, na ca atippaggahitā bhavissati, na ca ajjhattaṃ saṃkhittā bhavissati[V 3.0338], na ca bahiddhā vikkhittā bhavissati. Pacchāpuresaññī ca viharati – yathā pure tathā pacchā, yathā pacchā tathā pure; yathā adho tathā uddhaṃ, yathā uddhaṃ tathā adho; yathā divā tathā rattiṃ, yathā rattiṃ tathā divā. Iti vivaṭena cetasā apariyonaddhena sappabhāsaṃ cittaṃ bhāveti.

“He develops the basis for spiritual power that is endowed with concentration due to investigation and the formations of striving, thinking: ‘Thus my investigation will be neither too slack nor too tense; it will be neither inwardly constricted nor outwardly scattered.’ He dwells perceiving what is after and what was before: as before, so after; as after, so before; as below, so above; as above, so below; as by day, so by night; as by night, so by day. Thus, with a mind that is open and unenveloped, he develops a mind imbued with luminosity.

“Evaṃ bhāvitesu kho, bhikkhu, catūsu iddhipādesu evaṃ bahulīkatesu, anekavihitaṃ iddhividhaṃ paccanubhoti – ekopi hutvā bahudhā hoti, bahudhāpi hutvā eko hoti; āvibhāvaṃ, tirobhāvaṃ; tirokuṭṭaṃ tiropākāraṃ tiropabbataṃ asajjamāno gacchati, seyyathāpi ākāse; pathaviyāpi ummujjanimujjaṃ karoti, seyyathāpi udake; udakepi abhijjamāne [M 3.0232] abhijjamāno (sī. pī. ka.) gacchati, seyyathāpi pathaviyaṃ; ākāsepi pallaṅkena [P 5.0265] kamati, seyyathāpi [T 5.0341] pakkhī sakuṇo; imepi candimasūriye evaṃmahiddhike evaṃmahānubhāve pāṇinā parimasati parāmasati (sī. syā. kaṃ.) parimajjati; yāva brahmalokāpi kāyena vasaṃ vatteti.

“When, bhikkhu, these four bases for spiritual power have been developed and cultivated in this way, he experiences the various kinds of spiritual power: having been one, he becomes many; having been many, he becomes one; he appears and vanishes; he goes unhindered through a wall, a rampart, or a mountain as if through space; he dives in and out of the earth as if in water; he walks on water without breaking the surface as if on land; he travels through the sky cross-legged like a winged bird; he touches and strokes with his hand the sun and moon, so mighty and powerful; he wields bodily mastery even as far as the Brahmā world.

“Evaṃ bhāvitesu kho, bhikkhu, catūsu iddhipādesu evaṃ bahulīkatesu dibbāya sotadhātuyā visuddhāya atikkantamānusikāya ubho sadde suṇāti – dibbe ca mānuse ca, dūre santike cāti.

“When, bhikkhu, these four bases for spiritual power have been developed and cultivated in this way, with the divine ear element, which is purified and surpasses the human, he hears both kinds of sounds—divine and human, whether far or near.”

“Evaṃ bhāvitesu kho, bhikkhu, catūsu iddhipādesu evaṃ bahulīkatesu, parasattānaṃ parapuggalānaṃ cetasā ceto paricca pajānāti. Sarāgaṃ vā cittaṃ ‘sarāgaṃ citta’nti pajānāti; vītarāgaṃ vā cittaṃ ‘vītarāgaṃ citta’nti pajānāti; sadosaṃ vā cittaṃ ‘sadosaṃ citta’nti pajānāti; vītadosaṃ vā cittaṃ ‘vītadosaṃ citta’nti pajānāti; samohaṃ vā cittaṃ ‘samohaṃ citta’nti pajānāti; vītamohaṃ vā cittaṃ ‘vītamohaṃ citta’nti pajānāti; saṃkhittaṃ vā cittaṃ ‘saṃkhittaṃ citta’nti pajānāti; vikkhittaṃ vā cittaṃ ‘vikkhittaṃ citta’nti pajānāti; mahaggataṃ vā cittaṃ ‘mahaggataṃ citta’nti pajānāti; amahaggataṃ vā cittaṃ ‘amahaggataṃ citta’nti pajānāti; sauttaraṃ vā cittaṃ ‘sauttaraṃ citta’nti pajānāti; anuttaraṃ vā cittaṃ ‘anuttaraṃ citta’nti pajānāti; samāhitaṃ vā cittaṃ ‘samāhitaṃ citta’nti pajānāti; asamāhitaṃ vā cittaṃ ‘asamāhitaṃ citta’nti pajānāti; vimuttaṃ vā cittaṃ ‘vimuttaṃ citta’nti pajānāti; avimuttaṃ vā cittaṃ ‘avimuttaṃ citta’nti pajānāti”.

O bhikkhu, when these four bases of psychic power have been thus developed and cultivated, a bhikkhu indeed understands the minds of other beings, of other persons, having encompassed them with his own mind. He understands a mind with lust as ‘a mind with lust’; a mind without lust as ‘a mind without lust’; a mind with hate as ‘a mind with hate’; a mind without hate as ‘a mind without hate’; a mind with delusion as ‘a mind with delusion’; a mind without delusion as ‘a mind without delusion’; a constricted mind as ‘a constricted mind’; a scattered mind as ‘a scattered mind’; an exalted mind as ‘an exalted mind’; an unexalted mind as ‘an unexalted mind’; a surpassable mind as ‘a surpassable mind’; an unsurpassed mind as ‘an unsurpassed mind’; a concentrated mind as ‘a concentrated mind’; an unconcentrated mind as ‘an unconcentrated mind’; a liberated mind as ‘a liberated mind’; an unliberated mind as ‘an unliberated mind.’

“Evaṃ [T 5.0342][V 3.0339] bhāvitesu kho, bhikkhu, catūsu iddhipādesu evaṃ bahulīkatesu, anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussarati, seyyathidaṃ – ekampi jātiṃ dvepi jātiyo tissopi jātiyo catassopi jātiyo pañcapi jātiyo dasapi jātiyo vīsampi jātiyo tiṃsampi jātiyo cattālīsampi jātiyo paññāsampi [P 5.0266] jātiyo jātisatampi jātisahassampi jātisatasahassampi anekepi saṃvaṭṭakappe anekepi vivaṭṭakappe anekepi saṃvaṭṭavivaṭṭakappe – ‘amutrāsiṃ evaṃnāmo evaṃgotto evaṃvaṇṇo evamāhāro evaṃsukhadukkhappaṭisaṃvedī evamāyupariyanto, so tato cuto amutra udapādiṃ uppādiṃ (sī.); tatrāpāsiṃ evaṃnāmo [M 3.0233] evaṃgotto evaṃvaṇṇo evamāhāro evaṃsukhadukkhappaṭisaṃvedī evamāyupariyanto, so tato cuto idhūpapanno’ti. Iti sākāraṃ sauddesaṃ anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussarati.

O bhikkhu, when these four bases of psychic power have been thus developed and cultivated, he recollects his manifold past lives, that is to say: one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, many eons of contraction, many eons of expansion, many eons of contraction and expansion: ‘There I was with such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, experiencing such pleasure and pain, with such a lifespan. Passing away from there, I reappeared elsewhere. There too I was with such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, experiencing such pleasure and pain, with such a lifespan. Passing away from there, I have been reborn here.’ Thus he recollects his manifold past lives with their aspects and details.

“Evaṃ bhāvitesu kho bhikkhu, catūsu iddhipādesu evaṃ bahulīkatesu, dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena satte passati cavamāne upapajjamāne hīne paṇīte suvaṇṇe dubbaṇṇe, sugate duggate yathākammūpage satte pajānāti – ‘ime vata, bhonto, sattā kāyaduccaritena samannāgatā vacīduccaritena samannāgatā manoduccaritena samannāgatā ariyānaṃ upavādakā micchādiṭṭhikā micchādiṭṭhikammasamādānā; te kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapannā. Ime vā pana, bhonto, sattā kāyasucaritena samannāgatā vacīsucaritena samannāgatā manosucaritena samannāgatā ariyānaṃ [T 5.0343] anupavādakā sammādiṭṭhikā sammādiṭṭhikammasamādānā; te kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapannā’ti. Iti dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena satte passati cavamāne upapajjamāne hīne paṇīte suvaṇṇe dubbaṇṇe, sugate duggate yathākammūpage satte pajānāti.

Indeed, a bhikkhu, when these four bases of psychic power have been thus developed and thus cultivated, with the divine eye—which is purified and surpasses the human—sees beings passing away and being reborn, inferior and superior, of good complexion and bad complexion, in a good destination and a bad destination, and knows beings who fare according to their kamma: ‘Indeed, venerable sirs, these beings were endowed with misconduct of body, speech, and mind, reviled the noble ones, held wrong view, and undertook actions based on wrong view. With the breakup of the body, after death, they have been reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a state of ruin, in hell. But indeed, venerable sirs, these other beings were endowed with good conduct of body, speech, and mind, did not revile the noble ones, held right view, and undertook actions based on right view. With the breakup of the body, after death, they have been reborn in a good destination, the heavenly world.’ Thus, with the divine eye—which is purified and surpasses the human—he sees beings passing away and being reborn, inferior and superior, of good complexion and bad complexion, in a good destination and a bad destination, and knows beings who fare according to their kamma.

“Evaṃ bhāvitesu kho, bhikkhu, catūsu iddhipādesu evaṃ bahulīkatesu, āsavānaṃ khayā anāsavaṃ cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttiṃ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharatī”ti. Paṭhamaṃ.

O bhikkhu, when these four bases of psychic power have been thus developed and cultivated, with the destruction of the taints, a bhikkhu enters and abides in the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having realized it for himself with direct knowledge in this very life. The First.

2. Mahapphalasuttaṃ

2. The Discourse on Great Fruit

824. “Cattārome[P 5.0267], bhikkhave, iddhipādā bhāvitā bahulīkatā mahapphalā honti mahānisaṃsā. Kathaṃ bhāvitā ca, bhikkhave, cattāro iddhipādā kathaṃ bahulīkatā mahapphalā honti [V 3.0340] mahānisaṃsā? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu chandasamādhippadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgataṃ iddhipādaṃ bhāveti – ‘iti me chando na ca atilīno bhavissati, na ca atippaggahito bhavissati, na ca ajjhattaṃ saṃkhitto bhavissati, na ca bahiddhā vikkhitto bhavissati’. Pacchāpuresaññī ca viharati – yathā pure tathā pacchā, yathā pacchā tathā pure; yathā adho tathā uddhaṃ, yathā uddhaṃ tathā adho; yathā divā tathā rattiṃ, yathā rattiṃ tathā [M 3.0234] divā. Iti vivaṭena cetasā apariyonaddhena sappabhāsaṃ cittaṃ bhāveti.

824. Bhikkhus, these four bases of psychic power, when developed and cultivated, are of great fruit and great benefit. And how, bhikkhus, are the four bases of psychic power, when developed and cultivated, of great fruit and great benefit? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu develops the basis of psychic power endowed with concentration founded on desire, along with volitional formations of exertion, thinking: ‘Thus my desire will be neither too slack nor too strained, neither inwardly constricted nor outwardly scattered.’ And he dwells with the perception of ‘after’ and ‘before’: as before, so after; as after, so before; as below, so above; as above, so below; as by day, so by night; as by night, so by day. Thus, with an open and uncovered mind, he develops a mind imbued with radiance.

“Vīriyasamādhi…pe… cittasamādhi…pe… vīmaṃsāsamādhippadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgataṃ iddhipādaṃ bhāveti – ‘iti me vīmaṃsā na ca atilīnā bhavissati, na ca atippaggahitā [T 5.0344] bhavissati, na ca ajjhattaṃ saṃkhittā bhavissati, na ca bahiddhā vikkhittā bhavissati’. Pacchāpuresaññī ca viharati – yathā pure tathā pacchā, yathā pacchā tathā pure; yathā adho tathā uddhaṃ, yathā uddhaṃ tathā adho; yathā divā tathā rattiṃ, yathā rattiṃ tathā divā. Iti vivaṭena cetasā apariyonaddhena sappabhāsaṃ cittaṃ bhāveti. Evaṃ bhāvitā kho, bhikkhave, cattāro iddhipādā evaṃ bahulīkatā mahapphalā honti mahānisaṃsā.

He develops the basis of psychic power endowed with concentration founded on energy… endowed with concentration founded on mind… endowed with concentration founded on investigation, along with volitional formations of exertion, thinking: ‘Thus my investigation will be neither too slack nor too strained, neither inwardly constricted nor outwardly scattered.’ And he dwells with the perception of ‘after’ and ‘before’: as before, so after; as after, so before; as below, so above; as above, so below; as by day, so by night; as by night, so by day. Thus, with an open and uncovered mind, he develops a mind imbued with radiance. Bhikkhus, when these four bases of psychic power are developed and cultivated in this way, they are indeed of great fruit and great benefit.

“Evaṃ bhāvitesu kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu catūsu iddhipādesu evaṃ bahulīkatesu anekavihitaṃ iddhividhaṃ paccanubhoti – ekopi hutvā bahudhā hoti…pe… yāva brahmalokāpi kāyena vasaṃ vatteti…pe….

“Bhikkhus, when these four bases of spiritual power have been thus developed and cultivated, a bhikkhu indeed experiences the various kinds of spiritual power: having been one, he becomes many… he wields mastery with his body even as far as the Brahma world…”

“Evaṃ [P 5.0268] bhāvitesu kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu catūsu iddhipādesu evaṃ bahulīkatesu, āsavānaṃ khayā anāsavaṃ cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttiṃ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharatī”ti. Dutiyaṃ.

“Indeed, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu has developed and cultivated the four bases of spiritual power in this way, through the destruction of the taints, he, in this very life, realizes for himself with direct knowledge the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having attained it, abides therein. Second.”

3. Chandasamādhisuttaṃ

3. The Discourse on Concentration Due to Desire

825. “Chandaṃ ce, bhikkhave, bhikkhu nissāya labhati samādhiṃ, labhati cittassa ekaggataṃ – ayaṃ vuccati chandasamādhi. So anuppannānaṃ pāpakānaṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ anuppādāya chandaṃ janeti vāyamati vīriyaṃ ārabhati cittaṃ paggaṇhāti padahati. Uppannānaṃ pāpakānaṃ [V 3.0341] akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ pahānāya chandaṃ janeti vāyamati vīriyaṃ ārabhati cittaṃ paggaṇhāti padahati. Anuppannānaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ uppādāya chandaṃ janeti vāyamati vīriyaṃ ārabhati cittaṃ paggaṇhāti padahati. Uppannānaṃ [T 5.0345] kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ ṭhitiyā asammosāya bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā chandaṃ janeti vāyamati vīriyaṃ ārabhati cittaṃ paggaṇhāti padahati. Ime vuccanti ‘padhānasaṅkhārā’ti. Iti ayañca chando, ayañca chandasamādhi, ime ca padhānasaṅkhārā – ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, ‘chandasamādhippadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgato iddhipādo’”.

825. “Bhikkhus, if a bhikkhu, relying on desire, gains concentration, gains one-pointedness of mind—this is called concentration due to desire. He generates desire for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states; he endeavors, arouses energy, exerts his mind, and strives. He generates desire for the abandoning of arisen evil, unwholesome states; he endeavors, arouses energy, exerts his mind, and strives. He generates desire for the arising of unarisen wholesome states; he endeavors, arouses energy, exerts his mind, and strives. He generates desire for the maintenance, non-disappearance, increase, abundance, development, and completion of arisen wholesome states; he endeavors, arouses energy, exerts his mind, and strives. These are called ‘formations of exertion.’ Thus, this desire, this concentration due to desire, and these formations of exertion—this, bhikkhus, is called ‘the basis of spiritual power endowed with concentration due to desire and formations of exertion.’”

“Vīriyaṃ [M 3.0235] ce, bhikkhave, bhikkhu nissāya labhati samādhiṃ, labhati cittassa ekaggataṃ – ayaṃ vuccati ‘vīriyasamādhi’. So anuppannānaṃ…pe… uppannānaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ ṭhitiyā asammosāya bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā chandaṃ janeti vāyamati vīriyaṃ ārabhati cittaṃ paggaṇhāti padahati. Ime vuccanti ‘padhānasaṅkhārā’ti. Iti idañca vīriyaṃ, ayañca vīriyasamādhi, ime ca padhānasaṅkhārā – ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, ‘vīriyasamādhippadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgato iddhipādo’”.

“Bhikkhus, if a bhikkhu, relying on energy, gains concentration, gains one-pointedness of mind—this is called ‘concentration due to energy.’ He generates desire, endeavors, arouses energy, exerts his mind, and strives for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states… for the maintenance, non-disappearance, increase, abundance, development, and completion of arisen wholesome states. These are called ‘formations of exertion.’ Thus, this energy, this concentration due to energy, and these formations of exertion—this, bhikkhus, is called ‘the basis of spiritual power endowed with concentration due to energy and the formations of exertion.’”

“Cittaṃ [P 5.0269] ce, bhikkhave, bhikkhu nissāya labhati samādhiṃ, labhati cittassa ekaggataṃ – ayaṃ vuccati ‘cittasamādhi’. So anuppannānaṃ pāpakānaṃ…pe… uppannānaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ ṭhitiyā asammosāya bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā chandaṃ janeti vāyamati vīriyaṃ ārabhati cittaṃ paggaṇhāti padahati. Ime vuccanti ‘padhānasaṅkhārā’ti. Iti idañca cittaṃ, ayañca cittasamādhi, ime ca padhānasaṅkhārā – ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, ‘cittasamādhippadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgato [T 5.0346] iddhipādo’”.

“Bhikkhus, if a bhikkhu, relying on the mind, gains concentration, gains one-pointedness of mind—this is called ‘concentration due to mind.’ He generates desire, endeavors, arouses energy, exerts his mind, and strives for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states… for the maintenance, non-disappearance, increase, abundance, development, and completion of arisen wholesome states. These are called ‘formations of exertion.’ Thus, this mind, this concentration due to mind, and these formations of exertion—this, bhikkhus, is called ‘the basis of spiritual power endowed with concentration due to mind and the formations of exertion.’”

“Vīmaṃsaṃ ce, bhikkhave, bhikkhu nissāya labhati samādhiṃ, labhati cittassa ekaggataṃ – ayaṃ vuccati ‘vīmaṃsāsamādhi’. So anuppannānaṃ pāpakānaṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ anuppādāya chandaṃ janeti vāyamati vīriyaṃ ārabhati cittaṃ paggaṇhāti padahati…pe… uppannānaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ ṭhitiyā asammosāya bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā chandaṃ janeti vāyamati vīriyaṃ ārabhati cittaṃ paggaṇhāti padahati. Ime vuccanti ‘padhānasaṅkhārā’ti[V 3.0342]. Iti ayañca vīmaṃsā, ayañca vīmaṃsāsamādhi, ime ca padhānasaṅkhārā – ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, ‘vīmaṃsāsamādhippadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgato iddhipādo’”ti. Tatiyaṃ.

“Bhikkhus, if a bhikkhu, relying on investigation, gains concentration, gains one-pointedness of mind—this is called ‘concentration due to investigation.’ He generates desire, endeavors, arouses energy, exerts his mind, and strives for the non-arising of unarisen, evil, unwholesome states… for the maintenance, non-disappearance, increase, abundance, development, and completion of arisen wholesome states, he generates desire, endeavors, arouses energy, exerts his mind, and strives. These are called ‘the formations of exertion.’ Thus, this investigation, this concentration due to investigation, and these formations of exertion—this, bhikkhus, is called ‘the basis of spiritual power endowed with concentration due to investigation and the formations of exertion.’ Third.”

4. Moggallānasuttaṃ

4. The Moggallāna Sutta

826. Evaṃ me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati pubbārāme migāramātupāsāde. Tena kho pana samayena sambahulā bhikkhū heṭṭhāmigāramātupāsāde viharanti uddhatā unnaḷā capalā mukharā vikiṇṇavācā muṭṭhassatino asampajānā asamāhitā bhantacittā vibbhantacittā (sī. syā. kaṃ.) pākatindriyā.

826. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī, in the Eastern Park, at the mansion of Migāra’s mother. Now at that time, many bhikkhus were dwelling below the mansion of Migāra’s mother—restless, haughty, fickle, harsh-spoken, scattered in speech, of lapsed mindfulness, without clear comprehension, unconcentrated, with agitated minds, and with unguarded faculties.

Atha [M 3.0236] kho bhagavā āyasmantaṃ mahāmoggallānaṃ āmantesi – “ete kho, moggallāna, sabrahmacārino heṭṭhāmigāramātupāsāde [P 5.0270] viharanti uddhatā unnaḷā capalā mukharā vikiṇṇavācā muṭṭhassatino asampajānā asamāhitā bhantacittā pākatindriyā. Gaccha, moggallāna, te bhikkhū saṃvejehī”ti.

Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna: “Moggallāna, these fellow practitioners of the holy life dwelling below the mansion of Migāra’s mother are restless, haughty, fickle, harsh-spoken, scattered in speech, of lapsed mindfulness, without clear comprehension, unconcentrated, with agitated minds, and with unguarded faculties. Go, Moggallāna, and stir those bhikkhus with a sense of urgency.”

“Evaṃ, bhante”ti kho āyasmā mahāmoggallāno [T 5.0347] bhagavato paṭissutvā tathārūpaṃ iddhābhisaṅkhāraṃ abhisaṅkhāresi abhisaṅkharesi (syā. pī. ka.) yathā pādaṅguṭṭhakena migāramātupāsādaṃ saṅkampesi sampakampesi sampacālesi. Atha kho te bhikkhū saṃviggā lomahaṭṭhajātā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhaṃsu – “acchariyaṃ vata, bho, abbhutaṃ vata, bho! Nivātañca vata ayañca migāramātupāsādo gambhīranemo sunikhāto acalo asampakampī, atha ca pana saṅkampito sampakampito sampacālito”ti!

“Very well, venerable sir.” Thus, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, having assented to the Blessed One, created such a formation of spiritual power that with his big toe he made the mansion of Migāra's mother shake up and down, tremble from below upwards, and quake all around. Then those bhikkhus, being alarmed and with their hair standing on end, stood to one side, saying: “Sirs, it is indeed astonishing! Sirs, it is indeed marvelous! Indeed, it is windless, and this mansion of Migāra's mother is deeply founded, well-fixed, immovable, and unshakable. And yet, it has been shaken up and down, trembled from below upwards, and quaked all around!”

Atha kho bhagavā yena te bhikkhū tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā te bhikkhū bhagavā etadavoca – “kiṃ nu tumhe, bhikkhave, saṃviggā lomahaṭṭhajātā ekamantaṃ ṭhitā”ti? “Acchariyaṃ, bhante, abbhutaṃ bhante! Nivātañca vata ayañca migāramātupāsādo gambhīranemo sunikhāto acalo asampakampī, atha ca pana saṅkampito sampakampito sampacālito”ti! “Tumheva kho, bhikkhave, saṃvejetukāmena moggallānena bhikkhunā pādaṅguṭṭhakena migāramātupāsādo, saṅkampito sampakampito sampacālito. Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, katamesaṃ dhammānaṃ bhāvitattā bahulīkatattā moggallāno bhikkhu evaṃmahiddhiko evaṃmahānubhāvo”ti[V 3.0343]? “Bhagavaṃmūlakā no, bhante, dhammā, bhagavaṃnettikā bhagavaṃpaṭisaraṇā. Sādhu vata, bhante, bhagavantaṃyeva paṭibhātu etassa bhāsitassa attho. Bhagavato sutvā bhikkhū dhāressantī”ti.

Then the Blessed One approached those monks. Having approached, the Blessed One said this to those monks: “Why now, monks, do you stand to one side, alarmed and with your hair standing on end?” “Venerable sir, it is astonishing! Venerable sir, it is marvelous! Indeed, it is windless, and this mansion of Migāra's mother is deeply founded, well-fixed, immovable, and unshakable. And yet, it has been shaken, trembled, and quaked!” “Monks, indeed, it was by the monk Moggallāna, wishing to stir you, that the mansion of Migāra's mother was shaken, trembled, and quaked with his big toe. What do you think of this, monks? Because of having developed and cultivated which qualities is the monk Moggallāna of such great psychic power, of such great might?” “Venerable sir, for us, the teachings have the Blessed One as their root, the Blessed One as their guide, the Blessed One as their refuge. It would be good, venerable sir, if the meaning of this statement would occur to the Blessed One himself. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the monks will remember it.”

“Tena [P 5.0271] hi, bhikkhave, suṇātha. Catunnaṃ kho, bhikkhave, iddhipādānaṃ [T 5.0348] bhāvitattā bahulīkatattā moggallāno bhikkhu evaṃmahiddhiko evaṃmahānubhāvo. Katamesaṃ catunnaṃ? Idha, bhikkhave, moggallāno bhikkhu chandasamādhippadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgataṃ iddhipādaṃ bhāveti, vīriyasamādhi…pe… cittasamādhi…pe… vīmaṃsāsamādhippadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgataṃ iddhipādaṃ bhāveti – ‘iti me vīmaṃsā na ca [M 3.0237] atilīnā bhavissati, na ca atippaggahitā bhavissati; na ca ajjhattaṃ saṃkhittā bhavissati, na ca bahiddhā vikkhittā bhavissati’. Pacchāpuresaññī ca viharati – yathā pure tathā pacchā, yathā pacchā tathā pure; yathā adho tathā uddhaṃ yathā uddhaṃ tathā adho; yathā divā tathā rattiṃ, yathā rattiṃ tathā divā. Iti vivaṭena cetasā apariyonaddhena sappabhāsaṃ cittaṃ bhāveti. Imesaṃ kho, bhikkhave, catunnaṃ iddhipādānaṃ bhāvitattā bahulīkatattā moggallāno bhikkhu evaṃmahiddhiko evaṃmahānubhāvo. Imesañca pana, bhikkhave, catunnaṃ iddhipādānaṃ bhāvitattā bahulīkatattā moggallāno bhikkhu anekavihitaṃ iddhividhaṃ paccanubhoti…pe… yāva brahmalokāpi kāyena vasaṃ vatteti…pe… imesañca pana, bhikkhave, catunnaṃ iddhipādānaṃ bhāvitattā bahulīkatattā moggallāno bhikkhu āsavānaṃ khayā anāsavaṃ cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttiṃ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharatī”ti. Catutthaṃ.

“In that case, monks, listen. It is through the development and cultivation of the four bases of psychic power that the monk Moggallāna possesses such great psychic power and might. Which four? Here, monks, the monk Moggallāna develops the base of psychic power endowed with concentration founded on desire and with striving formations; he develops the base of psychic power endowed with concentration founded on energy… he develops the base of psychic power endowed with concentration founded on mind… he develops the base of psychic power endowed with concentration founded on investigation and with striving formations, thinking: ‘Thus my investigation will not be too slack nor too strained; it will not be constricted internally nor scattered externally.’ He dwells perceiving before and after: as before, so after; as after, so before. As below, so above; as above, so below. As by day, so by night; as by night, so by day. Thus, with an open and unenclosed mind, he develops a luminous mind. It is through the development and cultivation of these four bases of psychic power that the monk Moggallāna possesses such great psychic power and might.
