He dwells contemplating the nature of arising in the body externally; he dwells contemplating the nature of passing away in the body externally; he dwells contemplating the nature of arising and passing away in the body externally—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in the world. He dwells contemplating the nature of arising in the body both internally and externally; he dwells contemplating the nature of passing away in the body both internally and externally; he dwells contemplating the nature of arising and passing away in the body both internally and externally—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in the world.

“So [M 3.0258] sace ākaṅkhati – ‘appaṭikūle paṭikūlasaññī vihareyya’nti, paṭikūlasaññī tattha viharati; sace ākaṅkhati – ‘paṭikūle appaṭikūlasaññī vihareyya’nti, appaṭikūlasaññī tattha viharati; sace ākaṅkhati – ‘appaṭikūle ca paṭikūle ca paṭikūlasaññī vihareyya’nti, paṭikūlasaññī tattha viharati; sace ākaṅkhati – ‘paṭikūle ca appaṭikūle ca appaṭikūlasaññī vihareyya’nti, appaṭikūlasaññī tattha viharati; sace ākaṅkhati – ‘appaṭikūlañca paṭikūlañca tadubhayaṃ abhinivajjetvā upekkhako vihareyyaṃ sato sampajāno’ti, upekkhako tattha viharati sato sampajāno.

If he wishes, ‘May I dwell perceiving the repulsive in the unrepulsive,’ he dwells therein perceiving the repulsive. If he wishes, ‘May I dwell perceiving the unrepulsive in the repulsive,’ he dwells therein perceiving the unrepulsive. If he wishes, ‘May I dwell perceiving the repulsive in both the unrepulsive and the repulsive,’ he dwells therein perceiving the repulsive. If he wishes, ‘May I dwell perceiving the unrepulsive in both the repulsive and the unrepulsive,’ he dwells therein perceiving the unrepulsive. If he wishes, ‘Having avoided both the unrepulsive and the repulsive, may I dwell equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending,’ he dwells therein equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending.

“Ajjhattaṃ vedanāsu samudayadhammānupassī viharati, ajjhattaṃ vedanāsu vayadhammānupassī viharati, ajjhattaṃ vedanāsu samudayavayadhammānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ[T 5.0378]. Bahiddhā vedanāsu samudayadhammānupassī viharati, bahiddhā vedanāsu vayadhammānupassī viharati, bahiddhā vedanāsu samudayavayadhammānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ. Ajjhattabahiddhā vedanāsu samudayadhammānupassī viharati, ajjhattabahiddhā vedanāsu vayadhammānupassī viharati, ajjhattabahiddhā vedanāsu samudayavayadhammānupassī [P 5.0296] viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ.

He dwells contemplating the nature of arising in feelings internally; he dwells contemplating the nature of passing away in feelings internally; he dwells contemplating the nature of arising and passing away in feelings internally—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in the world. He dwells contemplating the nature of arising in feelings externally; he dwells contemplating the nature of passing away in feelings externally; he dwells contemplating the nature of arising and passing away in feelings externally—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in the world. He dwells contemplating the nature of arising in feelings both internally and externally; he dwells contemplating the nature of passing away in feelings both internally and externally; he dwells contemplating the nature of arising and passing away in feelings both internally and externally—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in the world.

“So sace ākaṅkhati – ‘appaṭikūle paṭikūlasaññī vihareyya’nti, paṭikūlasaññī tattha viharati; sace ākaṅkhati – ‘paṭikūle appaṭikūlasaññī vihareyya’nti, appaṭikūlasaññī tattha viharati; sace ākaṅkhati – ‘appaṭikūle ca paṭikūle ca paṭikūlasaññī vihareyya’nti, paṭikūlasaññī tattha viharati; sace ākaṅkhati – ‘paṭikūle ca appaṭikūle ca appaṭikūlasaññī vihareyya’nti, appaṭikūlasaññī tattha viharati; sace ākaṅkhati – ‘appaṭikūlañca paṭikūlañca tadubhayaṃ abhinivajjetvā upekkhako vihareyyaṃ sato sampajāno’ti, upekkhako tattha viharati sato sampajāno.

If he wishes, ‘May I dwell perceiving the repulsive in the unrepulsive,’ he dwells therein perceiving the repulsive. If he wishes, ‘May I dwell perceiving the unrepulsive in the repulsive,’ he dwells therein perceiving the unrepulsive. If he wishes, ‘May I dwell perceiving the repulsive in both the unrepulsive and the repulsive,’ he dwells therein perceiving the repulsive. If he wishes, ‘May I dwell perceiving the unrepulsive in both the repulsive and the unrepulsive,’ he dwells therein perceiving the unrepulsive. If he wishes, ‘Having avoided both the unrepulsive and the repulsive, may I dwell equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending,’ he dwells therein equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending.

“Ajjhattaṃ citte…pe… bahiddhā citte…pe… ajjhattabahiddhā citte samudayadhammānupassī [V 3.0367] viharati… ajjhattabahiddhā citte vayadhammānupassī viharati… ajjhattabahiddhā citte samudayavayadhammānupassī viharati ātāpī…pe… abhijjhādomanassaṃ.

Internally in the mind… externally in the mind… both internally and externally in the mind, he dwells contemplating the nature of arising… he dwells contemplating the nature of passing away… he dwells contemplating the nature of arising and passing away—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in the world.

“So [T 5.0379] sace ākaṅkhati – ‘appaṭikūle paṭikūlasaññī vihareyya’nti[M 3.0259], paṭikūlasaññī tattha viharati…pe… upekkhako tattha viharati sato sampajāno.

If he wishes, ‘May I dwell perceiving the repulsive in the unrepulsive,’ he dwells therein perceiving the repulsive… and so on… he dwells therein equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending.

“Ajjhattaṃ dhammesu…pe… bahiddhā dhammesu…pe… ajjhattabahiddhā dhammesu samudayadhammānupassī viharati… ajjhattabahiddhā dhammesu vayadhammānupassī viharati… ajjhattabahiddhā dhammesu samudayavayadhammānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ.

Internally in phenomena… externally in phenomena… He dwells contemplating the nature of arising in phenomena both internally and externally… he dwells contemplating the nature of passing away in phenomena both internally and externally… he dwells contemplating the nature of arising and passing away in phenomena both internally and externally—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in the world.

“So sace ākaṅkhati – ‘appaṭikūle paṭikūlasaññī vihareyya’nti, paṭikūlasaññī tattha viharati…pe… upekkhako tattha viharati sato sampajāno. Ettāvatā kho, āvuso, bhikkhuno cattāro satipaṭṭhānā āraddhā hontī”ti. Paṭhamaṃ.

If he wishes, ‘May I dwell perceiving the repulsive in the non-repulsive,’ he dwells therein perceiving the repulsive... he dwells therein equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending. To this extent, friend, the four establishments of mindfulness are undertaken by a bhikkhu. First.

2. Dutiyarahogatasuttaṃ

2. The Second Discourse on Seclusion

900. Sāvatthinidānaṃ. Atha kho āyasmato anuruddhassa rahogatassa paṭisallīnassa evaṃ cetaso parivitakko udapādi – “yesaṃ kesañci cattāro satipaṭṭhānā viraddhā, viraddho tesaṃ ariyo maggo sammā dukkhakkhayagāmī; yesaṃ kesañci cattāro satipaṭṭhānā āraddhā, āraddho tesaṃ ariyo maggo sammā dukkhakkhayagāmī”ti.

900. At Sāvatthī. Then, while the Venerable Anuruddha was alone and in seclusion, this thought arose in his mind: “For whomever the four establishments of mindfulness are neglected, for them the noble path that rightly leads to the destruction of suffering is neglected; for whomever the four establishments of mindfulness are undertaken, for them the noble path that rightly leads to the destruction of suffering is undertaken.”

Atha kho āyasmā mahāmoggallāno āyasmato anuruddhassa cetasā cetoparivitakkamaññāya – seyyathāpi nāma [P 5.0297] balavā puriso samiñjitaṃ vā bāhaṃ pasāreyya[T 5.0380], pasāritaṃ vā bāhaṃ samiñjeyya, evameva – āyasmato anuruddhassa sammukhe pāturahosi.

Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, having known with his mind the thought in the Venerable Anuruddha’s mind, just as a strong man might extend his flexed arm or flex his extended arm, appeared before the Venerable Anuruddha.

Atha kho āyasmā mahāmoggallāno āyasmantaṃ anuruddhaṃ etadavoca – “kittāvatā nu kho, āvuso anuruddha, bhikkhuno cattāro satipaṭṭhānā āraddhā hontī”ti?

Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said this to the Venerable Anuruddha: “To what extent, friend Anuruddha, are the four establishments of mindfulness undertaken by a bhikkhu?”

“Idhāvuso[V 3.0368], bhikkhu ajjhattaṃ kāye kāyānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ. Bahiddhā kāye kāyānupassī viharati…pe… ajjhattabahiddhā kāye kāyānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ.

“Here, friend, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body internally, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having subdued covetousness and displeasure in the world. He dwells contemplating the body in the body externally… and both internally and externally, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having subdued covetousness and displeasure in the world.

“Ajjhattaṃ vedanāsu vedanānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ. Bahiddhā vedanāsu vedanānupassī [M 3.0260] viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ. Ajjhattabahiddhā vedanāsu vedanānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ.

“He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings internally, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having subdued covetousness and displeasure in the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings externally, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having subdued covetousness and displeasure in the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings both internally and externally, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having subdued covetousness and displeasure in the world.

“Ajjhattaṃ citte…pe… bahiddhā citte…pe… ajjhattabahiddhā citte cittānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ.

“He dwells contemplating mind in mind internally… externally… and both internally and externally, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having subdued covetousness and displeasure in the world.

“Ajjhattaṃ dhammesu…pe… bahiddhā dhammesu…pe… ajjhattabahiddhā dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ. Ettāvatā kho, āvuso, bhikkhuno [T 5.0381] cattāro satipaṭṭhānā āraddhā hontī”ti. Dutiyaṃ.

“He dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena internally... externally... and both internally and externally, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having subdued covetousness and displeasure in the world. To this extent, friend, the four establishments of mindfulness are undertaken by a bhikkhu.” The second.

3. Sutanusuttaṃ

3. The Sutanu Discourse

901. Ekaṃ samayaṃ āyasmā anuruddho sāvatthiyaṃ viharati sutanutīre. Atha kho sambahulā bhikkhū yenāyasmā anuruddho tenupasaṅkamiṃsu; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmatā anuruddhena saddhiṃ sammodiṃsu. Sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Ekamantaṃ [P 5.0298] nisinnā kho te bhikkhū āyasmantaṃ anuruddhaṃ etadavocuṃ – “katamesaṃ āyasmā anuruddho dhammānaṃ bhāvitattā bahulīkatattā mahābhiññataṃ patto”ti?

901. At one time the Venerable Anuruddha was dwelling at Sāvatthī on the bank of the Sutanu River. Then many bhikkhus approached the Venerable Anuruddha; having approached, they exchanged greetings with him. Having concluded their courteous and memorable conversation, they sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, those bhikkhus said to the Venerable Anuruddha: “Venerable Anuruddha, due to having developed and cultivated which phenomena have you attained great higher knowledge?”

“Catunnaṃ khvāhaṃ, āvuso, satipaṭṭhānānaṃ bhāvitattā bahulīkatattā mahābhiññataṃ patto. Katamesaṃ catunnaṃ? Idhāhaṃ, āvuso, kāye kāyānupassī viharāmi ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ; vedanāsu…pe… [V 3.0369] citte…pe… dhammesu dhammānupassī viharāmi ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ – imesaṃ khvāhaṃ, āvuso, catunnaṃ satipaṭṭhānānaṃ bhāvitattā bahulīkatattā mahābhiññataṃ patto. Imesañca panāhaṃ, āvuso, catunnaṃ satipaṭṭhānānaṃ bhāvitattā bahulīkatattā hīnaṃ dhammaṃ hīnato abbhaññāsiṃ, majjhimaṃ dhammaṃ majjhimato abbhaññāsiṃ, paṇītaṃ dhammaṃ paṇītato abbhaññāsi”nti. Tatiyaṃ.

“Friends, it is due to having developed and cultivated the four establishments of mindfulness that I have attained great higher knowledge. Which four? Here, friends, I dwell contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having subdued covetousness and displeasure in the world; in feelings… in mind… in phenomena, I dwell contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having subdued covetousness and displeasure in the world. Friends, it is due to having developed and cultivated these four establishments of mindfulness that I have attained great higher knowledge. And furthermore, friends, due to having developed and cultivated these four establishments of mindfulness, I have directly known inferior phenomena as inferior, middling phenomena as middling, and superior phenomena as superior.” The third.

4. Paṭhamakaṇḍakīsuttaṃ

4. The First Discourse at Kaṇḍakī

902. Ekaṃ samayaṃ āyasmā ca anuruddho āyasmā ca sāriputto āyasmā ca mahāmoggallāno sākete viharanti kaṇḍakīvane[T 5.0382]. Atha [M 3.0261] kho āyasmā ca sāriputto āyasmā ca mahāmoggallāno sāyanhasamayaṃ paṭisallānā vuṭṭhitā yenāyasmā anuruddho tenupasaṅkamiṃsu; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmatā anuruddhena saddhiṃ sammodiṃsu. Sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho āyasmā sāriputto āyasmantaṃ anuruddhaṃ etadavoca – “sekhenāvuso anuruddha, bhikkhunā katame dhammā upasampajja vihātabbā”ti?

902. At one time the Venerable Anuruddha, the Venerable Sāriputta, and the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna were dwelling at Sāketa in the Kaṇḍakī Grove. Then, in the evening, having emerged from seclusion, the Venerable Sāriputta and the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna approached the Venerable Anuruddha; having approached, they exchanged greetings with the Venerable Anuruddha. After concluding their courteous and memorable conversation, they sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Venerable Sāriputta said this to the Venerable Anuruddha: “Friend Anuruddha, having undertaken which phenomena should a bhikkhu who is a learner dwell?”

“Sekhenāvuso sāriputta, bhikkhunā cattāro satipaṭṭhānā upasampajja vihātabbā. Katame cattāro? Idhāvuso, bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ; vedanāsu [P 5.0299] …pe… citte…pe… dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ – sekhenāvuso sāriputta, bhikkhunā ime cattāro satipaṭṭhānā upasampajja vihātabbā”ti. Catutthaṃ.

“Friend Sāriputta, a bhikkhu who is a learner should dwell having undertaken the four establishments of mindfulness. Which four? Here, friend, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having subdued covetousness and displeasure in the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings… mind in mind… phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having subdued covetousness and displeasure in the world. Friend Sāriputta, a bhikkhu who is a learner should dwell having undertaken these four establishments of mindfulness.” The fourth.

5. Dutiyakaṇḍakīsuttaṃ

5. The Second Discourse at Kaṇḍakī

903. Sāketanidānaṃ. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho āyasmā sāriputto āyasmantaṃ anuruddhaṃ [V 3.0370] etadavoca – “asekhenāvuso anuruddha, bhikkhunā katame dhammā upasampajja vihātabbā”ti? “Asekhenāvuso sāriputta, bhikkhunā cattāro satipaṭṭhānā upasampajja vihātabbā. Katame cattāro? Idhāvuso, bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ[T 5.0383]; vedanāsu…pe… citte…pe… dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ – asekhenāvuso sāriputta, bhikkhunā ime cattāro satipaṭṭhānā upasampajja vihātabbā”ti. Pañcamaṃ.

903. At Sāketa. Seated to one side, the Venerable Sāriputta said this to the Venerable Anuruddha: “Friend Anuruddha, having accomplished which dhammas should a bhikkhu who is a non-learner dwell?” “Friend Sāriputta, a bhikkhu who is a non-learner should dwell having accomplished the four foundations of mindfulness. Which four? Here, friend, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having subdued covetousness and displeasure in the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings… mind in mind… phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having subdued covetousness and displeasure in the world. Friend Sāriputta, a bhikkhu who is a non-learner should dwell having accomplished these four foundations of mindfulness.”

6. Tatiyakaṇḍakīsuttaṃ

6. The Third Kaṇḍakī Sutta

904. Sāketanidānaṃ. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho āyasmā sāriputto āyasmantaṃ anuruddhaṃ etadavoca – “katamesaṃ āyasmā anuruddho dhammānaṃ bhāvitattā bahulīkatattā mahābhiññataṃ patto”ti? “Catunnaṃ khvāhaṃ, āvuso, satipaṭṭhānānaṃ bhāvitattā bahulīkatattā mahābhiññataṃ patto[M 3.0262]. Katamesaṃ catunnaṃ? Idhāhaṃ, āvuso, kāye kāyānupassī viharāmi ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ; vedanāsu…pe… citte…pe… dhammesu dhammānupassī viharāmi ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ – imesaṃ khvāhaṃ, āvuso, catunnaṃ satipaṭṭhānānaṃ bhāvitattā bahulīkatattā mahābhiññataṃ patto. Imesañca panāhaṃ, āvuso, catunnaṃ satipaṭṭhānānaṃ bhāvitattā bahulīkatattā sahassaṃ lokaṃ abhijānāmī”ti. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

904. At Sāketa. Seated to one side, the Venerable Sāriputta said this to the Venerable Anuruddha: “Venerable Anuruddha, through having developed and cultivated which dhammas have you attained great direct knowledge?” “Friend, it is through having developed and cultivated the four foundations of mindfulness that I have attained great direct knowledge. Which four? Here, friend, I dwell contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having subdued covetousness and displeasure in the world; …on feelings… on the mind… I dwell contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having subdued covetousness and displeasure in the world. Friend, it is through having developed and cultivated these four foundations of mindfulness that I have attained great direct knowledge. And further, friend, through having developed and cultivated these four foundations of mindfulness, I directly know the thousandfold world-system.”

7. Taṇhakkhayasuttaṃ

7. The Discourse on the Destruction of Craving

905. Sāvatthinidānaṃ[P 5.0300]. Tatra kho āyasmā anuruddho bhikkhū āmantesi – “āvuso bhikkhavo”ti. “Āvuso”ti kho te bhikkhū āyasmato anuruddhassa paccassosuṃ. Āyasmā anuruddho etadavoca –

905. At Sāvatthī. There, the Venerable Anuruddha addressed the bhikkhus: “Friends, bhikkhus!” “Friend,” those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Anuruddha. The Venerable Anuruddha said this:

“Cattārome[V 3.0371], āvuso, satipaṭṭhānā bhāvitā bahulīkatā taṇhakkhayāya saṃvattanti. Katame cattāro? Idhāvuso, bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharati…pe… [T 5.0384] vedanāsu…pe… citte…pe… dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ – ime kho, āvuso, cattāro satipaṭṭhānā bhāvitā bahulīkatā taṇhakkhayāya saṃvattantī”ti. Sattamaṃ.

“Friends, these four foundations of mindfulness, when developed and cultivated, conduce to the destruction of craving. Which four? Here, friends, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body… on feelings… on the mind… he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having subdued covetousness and displeasure in the world. These four foundations of mindfulness, friends, when developed and cultivated, conduce to the destruction of craving.”

8. Salaḷāgārasuttaṃ

8. The Discourse at the Salaḷa Hut

906. Ekaṃ samayaṃ āyasmā anuruddho sāvatthiyaṃ viharati salaḷāgāre. Tatra kho āyasmā anuruddho bhikkhū āmantesi…pe… etadavoca – “seyyathāpi, āvuso, gaṅgā nadī pācīnaninnā pācīnapoṇā pācīnapabbhārā. Atha mahājanakāyo āgaccheyya kuddālapiṭakaṃ kuddālapiṭakaṃ (bahūsu) ādāya – ‘mayaṃ imaṃ gaṅgānadiṃ pacchāninnaṃ karissāma pacchāpoṇaṃ pacchāpabbhāra’nti. Taṃ kiṃ maññathāvuso, api nu so mahājanakāyo gaṅgānadiṃ pacchāninnaṃ kareyya pacchāpoṇaṃ pacchāpabbhāra”nti? “No hetaṃ, āvuso”. “Taṃ kissa hetu”? “Gaṅgā, āvuso, nadī pācīnaninnā pācīnapoṇā pācīnapabbhārā. Sā na sukarā pacchāninnaṃ kātuṃ pacchāpoṇaṃ pacchāpabbhāraṃ. Yāvadeva ca pana so mahājanakāyo kilamathassa vighātassa bhāgī assā”ti.

906. On one occasion, the Venerable Anuruddha was dwelling at Sāvatthī in the Salaḷa Hut. There, the Venerable Anuruddha addressed the bhikkhus… and said this: “Suppose, friends, the river Ganges slants to the east, slopes to the east, and inclines to the east. Then a great crowd of people would come with spades and baskets, saying: ‘We will make this river Ganges slant to the west, slope to the west, and incline to the west.’ What do you think, friends? Could that great crowd of people make the river Ganges slant to the west, slope to the west, and incline to the west?” “Certainly not, friend.” “For what reason?” “Friend, the river Ganges slants to the east, slopes to the east, and inclines to the east. It is not easy to make it slant to the west, slope to the west, and incline to the west. That great crowd of people would only become partakers of weariness and distress.”

“Evameva [M 3.0263] kho, āvuso, bhikkhuṃ cattāro satipaṭṭhāne bhāventaṃ cattāro satipaṭṭhāne bahulīkarontaṃ rājāno vā rājamahāmattā vā mittā vā amaccā vā ñātī vā sālohitā vā [P 5.0301] bhogehi abhihaṭṭhuṃ pavāreyyuṃ – ‘ehambho purisa, kiṃ te ime kāsāvā anudahanti? Kiṃ muṇḍo kapālamanusañcarasi? Ehi hīnāyāvattitvā bhoge ca bhuñjassu puññāni ca karohī’”ti.

“In the same way, friends, when a bhikkhu is developing and cultivating the four foundations of mindfulness, kings or great royal ministers, friends or associates, kinsmen or blood relatives might invite him, enticing him with wealth, saying: ‘Come, good man! What good are these ochre robes to you? Why wander about shaven-headed, with bowl in hand, being tormented? Come, return to the lower life, enjoy wealth, and make merit.’”

“So vata, āvuso, bhikkhu cattāro satipaṭṭhāne [T 5.0385] bhāvento cattāro satipaṭṭhāne bahulīkaronto sikkhaṃ paccakkhāya hīnāyāvattissatīti – netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati. Taṃ kissa hetu? Yañhi taṃ, āvuso, cittaṃ dīgharattaṃ vivekaninnaṃ vivekapoṇaṃ vivekapabbhāraṃ taṃ vata hīnāyāvattissatīti [V 3.0372] – netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati. Kathañcāvuso, bhikkhu cattāro satipaṭṭhāne bhāveti, cattāro satipaṭṭhāne bahulīkarotīti? Idhāvuso, bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharati…pe… vedanāsu…pe… citte…pe… dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ. Evaṃ kho, āvuso, bhikkhu cattāro satipaṭṭhāne bhāveti, cattāro satipaṭṭhāne bahulīkarotī”ti. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

“Friends, that a bhikkhu who develops and cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness would renounce the training and return to the lower life—this is impossible. For what reason? Friends, that a mind which for a long time has been inclined towards seclusion, sloped towards seclusion, and bent towards seclusion would return to the lower life—this is impossible. And how, friends, does a bhikkhu develop and cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness? Here, friends, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body… on feelings… on the mind… he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having subdued covetousness and displeasure in the world. It is in this way, friends, that a bhikkhu develops and cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness.”

9. Ambapālivanasuttaṃ

9. The Discourse in Ambapālī's Grove

907. Ekaṃ samayaṃ āyasmā ca anuruddho āyasmā ca sāriputto vesāliyaṃ viharanti ambapālivane. Atha kho āyasmā sāriputto sāyanhasamayaṃ paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito…pe… ekamantaṃ nisinno kho āyasmā sāriputto āyasmantaṃ anuruddhaṃ etadavoca –

907. On one occasion, the Venerable Anuruddha and the Venerable Sāriputta were dwelling in Vesālī in Ambapālī's Grove. Then, in the evening, the Venerable Sāriputta rose from seclusion... Seated to one side, the Venerable Sāriputta said this to the Venerable Anuruddha:

“Vippasannāni kho te, āvuso anuruddha, indriyāni, parisuddho mukhavaṇṇo pariyodāto. Katamenāyasmā anuruddho vihārena etarahi bahulaṃ viharatī”ti? “Catūsu khvāhaṃ, āvuso, satipaṭṭhānesu suppatiṭṭhitacitto etarahi bahulaṃ viharāmi. Katamesu catūsu? Idhāhaṃ, āvuso, kāye kāyānupassī [T 5.0386] viharāmi ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ; vedanāsu…pe… citte…pe… dhammesu dhammānupassī viharāmi ātāpī [M 3.0264] sampajāno [P 5.0302] satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ – imesu khvāhaṃ, āvuso, catūsu satipaṭṭhānesu suppatiṭṭhitacitto etarahi bahulaṃ viharāmi. Yo so, āvuso, bhikkhu arahaṃ khīṇāsavo vusitavā katakaraṇīyo ohitabhāro anuppattasadattho parikkhīṇabhavasaṃyojano sammadaññā vimutto, so imesu catūsu satipaṭṭhānesu suppatiṭṭhitacitto bahulaṃ viharatī”ti.

“Friend Anuruddha, your faculties are clear, your complexion pure and bright. In what dwelling does the Venerable Anuruddha now frequently abide?” “I now frequently abide, friend, with a well-established mind in the four foundations of mindfulness. Which four? Here, friend, I dwell contemplating the body in the body—ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. I dwell contemplating feelings in feelings... mind in mind... phenomena in phenomena—ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. It is in these four foundations of mindfulness, friend, that I now frequently abide with a well-established mind. Friend, any bhikkhu who is an arahant, one whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, attained his own welfare, utterly destroyed the fetters of being, and is completely liberated through right knowledge—he too frequently abides with a well-established mind in these four foundations of mindfulness.”

“Lābhā vata no, āvuso, suladdhaṃ vata no, āvuso! Ye mayaṃ āyasmato anuruddhassa sammukhāva assumha āsabhiṃ vācaṃ bhāsamānassā”ti. Navamaṃ.

“It is a gain for us, friends, truly well-gained for us, that we were in the very presence of the Venerable Anuruddha as he was speaking a heroic utterance.” Ninth.

10. Bāḷhagilānasuttaṃ

10. The Discourse on Being Gravely Ill

908. Ekaṃ [V 3.0373] samayaṃ āyasmā anuruddho sāvatthiyaṃ viharati andhavanasmiṃ ābādhiko dukkhito bāḷhagilāno. Atha kho sambahulā bhikkhū yenāyasmā anuruddho tenupasaṅkamiṃsu; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmantaṃ anuruddhaṃ etadavocuṃ –

908. At one time, the Venerable Anuruddha was staying at Sāvatthī in the Blind Men's Grove, afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill. Then a number of bhikkhus approached the Venerable Anuruddha and said this to him:

“Katamenāyasmato anuruddhassa vihārena viharato uppannā sārīrikā dukkhā vedanā cittaṃ na pariyādāya tiṭṭhantī”ti? “Catūsu kho me, āvuso, satipaṭṭhānesu suppatiṭṭhitacittassa viharato uppannā sārīrikā dukkhā vedanā cittaṃ na pariyādāya tiṭṭhanti. Katamesu catūsu? Idhāhaṃ, āvuso, kāye kāyānupassī viharāmi…pe… vedanāsu…pe… citte…pe… dhammesu dhammānupassī viharāmi ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ – imesu [T 5.0387] kho me, āvuso, catūsu satipaṭṭhānesu suppatiṭṭhitacittassa viharato uppannā sārīrikā dukkhā vedanā cittaṃ na pariyādāya tiṭṭhantī”ti. Dasamaṃ.

“By what manner of dwelling, Venerable Anuruddha, do bodily painful feelings that have arisen not overwhelm your mind and persist?” “Friends, it is when I dwell with my mind well-established in the four foundations of mindfulness that bodily painful feelings that have arisen do not overwhelm my mind and persist. In which four? Here, friends, I dwell contemplating the body in the body... feelings in feelings... mind in mind... phenomena in phenomena—ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in the world. It is, friends, because I dwell with my mind well-established in these four foundations of mindfulness that bodily painful feelings that have arisen do not overwhelm my mind and persist.” Tenth.

Rahogatavaggo paṭhamo.

The First Chapter on Seclusion.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary of this is:

Rahogatena [P 5.0303] dve vuttā, sutanu kaṇḍakī tayo;

Taṇhakkhayasalaḷāgāraṃ, ambapāli ca gilānanti.

Two are spoken with Rahogata; Sutanu, Kaṇḍakī, three; Taṇhakkhaya, Salaḷāgāra; Ambapāli and Gilāna.

2. Dutiyavaggo

2. The Second Chapter.

1. Kappasahassasuttaṃ

1. The Discourse on a Thousand Eons.

909. Ekaṃ [T 5.0388][M 3.0265] samayaṃ āyasmā anuruddho sāvatthiyaṃ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme. Atha kho sambahulā bhikkhū yenāyasmā anuruddho tenupasaṅkamiṃsu; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmatā [V 3.0374] anuruddhena saddhiṃ…pe… ekamantaṃ nisinnā kho te bhikkhū āyasmantaṃ anuruddhaṃ etadavocuṃ –

909. At one time the Venerable Anuruddha was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. Then a number of bhikkhus approached the Venerable Anuruddha. Having approached, they exchanged greetings with the Venerable Anuruddha and, when the courteous and amiable talk was finished, sat down to one side. Seated to one side, those bhikkhus said this to the Venerable Anuruddha:

“Katamesaṃ āyasmā anuruddho dhammānaṃ bhāvitattā bahulīkatattā mahābhiññataṃ patto”ti? “Catunnaṃ khvāhaṃ, āvuso, satipaṭṭhānānaṃ bhāvitattā bahulīkatattā mahābhiññataṃ patto. Katamesaṃ catunnaṃ? Idhāhaṃ, āvuso, kāye kāyānupassī viharāmi…pe… vedanāsu…pe… citte…pe… dhammesu dhammānupassī viharāmi ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ – imesaṃ khvāhaṃ, āvuso, catunnaṃ satipaṭṭhānānaṃ bhāvitattā bahulīkatattā mahābhiññataṃ patto. Imesañca panāhaṃ, āvuso, catunnaṃ satipaṭṭhānānaṃ bhāvitattā bahulīkatattā kappasahassaṃ anussarāmī”ti. Paṭhamaṃ.

“Venerable Anuruddha, by developing and cultivating which phenomena have you attained great direct knowledge?” “Friends, it is by developing and cultivating the four foundations of mindfulness that I have attained great direct knowledge. Which four? Here, friends, I dwell contemplating the body in the body… in feelings… in the mind… I dwell contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. It is, friends, by developing and cultivating these four foundations of mindfulness that I have attained great direct knowledge. And furthermore, friends, it is by developing and cultivating these four foundations of mindfulness that I recollect a thousand eons.” First.

2. Iddhividhasuttaṃ

2. The Discourse on Psychic Powers

910. “Imesañca panāhaṃ, āvuso, catunnaṃ satipaṭṭhānānaṃ bhāvitattā bahulīkatattā anekavihitaṃ iddhividhaṃ paccanubhomi – ekopi hutvā bahudhā homi…pe… yāva brahmalokāpi kāyena vasaṃ vattemī”ti. Dutiyaṃ.

910. “And furthermore, friends, it is by developing and cultivating these four foundations of mindfulness that I experience various kinds of psychic power: having been one, I become many… and I wield mastery with the body even as far as the Brahma-world.” Second.

3. Dibbasotasuttaṃ

3. The Discourse on the Divine Ear

911. “Imesañca [T 5.0389][P 5.0304] panāhaṃ, āvuso, catunnaṃ satipaṭṭhānānaṃ bhāvitattā bahulīkatattā dibbāya sotadhātuyā visuddhāya atikkantamānusikāya ubho sadde suṇāmi dibbe ca mānuse ca ye dūre santike cā”ti. Tatiyaṃ.

911. “And furthermore, friends, it is by developing and cultivating these four foundations of mindfulness that with the divine ear-element, which is purified and surpasses the human, I hear both kinds of sounds, divine and human, whether far or near.” Third.

4. Cetopariyasuttaṃ

4. The Discourse on Encompassing the Mind

912. “Imesañca panāhaṃ, āvuso, catunnaṃ satipaṭṭhānānaṃ bhāvitattā bahulīkatattā parasattānaṃ parapuggalānaṃ cetasā ceto paricca pajānāmi [M 3.0266] – sarāgaṃ vā cittaṃ ‘sarāgaṃ [V 3.0375] citta’nti pajānāmi…pe… avimuttaṃ vā cittaṃ ‘avimuttaṃ citta’nti pajānāmī”ti. Catutthaṃ.

912. “And furthermore, friends, it is by developing and cultivating these four foundations of mindfulness that, having encompassed with my own mind the minds of other beings and other persons, I know them: I know a mind with lust as ‘a mind with lust’… and I know an unliberated mind as ‘an unliberated mind.’” Fourth.

5. Ṭhānasuttaṃ

5. The Discourse on the Possible

913. “Imesañca panāhaṃ, āvuso, catunnaṃ satipaṭṭhānānaṃ bhāvitattā bahulīkatattā ṭhānañca ṭhānato aṭṭhānañca aṭṭhānato yathābhūtaṃ pajānāmī”ti. Pañcamaṃ.

913. “And furthermore, friends, it is by developing and cultivating these four foundations of mindfulness that I know as it really is the possible as possible and the impossible as impossible.” Fifth.

6. Kammasamādānasuttaṃ

6. The Discourse on the Undertaking of Kamma

914. “Imesañca panāhaṃ, āvuso, catunnaṃ satipaṭṭhānānaṃ bhāvitattā bahulīkatattā atītānāgatapaccuppannānaṃ kammasamādānānaṃ ṭhānaso hetuso vipākaṃ yathābhūtaṃ pajānāmī”ti. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

914. “And furthermore, friends, it is by developing and cultivating these four foundations of mindfulness that I know as it really is, with its conditions and its causes, the result of past, future, and present kamma undertakings.” Sixth.

7. Sabbatthagāminisuttaṃ

7. The Discourse on the All-Reaching Path

915. “Imesañca panāhaṃ, āvuso, catunnaṃ satipaṭṭhānānaṃ bhāvitattā bahulīkatattā sabbatthagāminippaṭipadaṃ yathābhūtaṃ pajānāmī”ti. Sattamaṃ.

915. “And furthermore, friends, it is by developing and cultivating these four foundations of mindfulness that I know as it really is the practice that leads everywhere.” Seventh.

8. Nānādhātusuttaṃ

8. The Discourse on Diverse Elements

916. “Imesañca panāhaṃ, āvuso, catunnaṃ satipaṭṭhānānaṃ bhāvitattā bahulīkatattā anekadhātunānādhātulokaṃ yathābhūtaṃ pajānāmī”ti. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

916. Furthermore, friends, because I have developed and cultivated these four establishments of mindfulness, I know as it really is the world with its many and diverse elements.

9. Nānādhimuttisuttaṃ

9. The Discourse on Diverse Inclinations

917. “Imesañca [T 5.0390][P 5.0305] panāhaṃ, āvuso, catunnaṃ satipaṭṭhānānaṃ bhāvitattā bahulīkatattā sattānaṃ nānādhimuttikataṃ yathābhūtaṃ pajānāmī”ti. Navamaṃ.

917. Furthermore, friends, because I have developed and cultivated these four establishments of mindfulness, I know as it really is the diverse inclinations of beings.

10. Indriyaparopariyattasuttaṃ

10. The Discourse on the Varying Faculties

918. “Imesañca [V 3.0376] panāhaṃ, āvuso, catunnaṃ satipaṭṭhānānaṃ bhāvitattā bahulīkatattā parasattānaṃ parapuggalānaṃ indriyaparopariyattaṃ yathābhūtaṃ pajānāmī”ti. Dasamaṃ.

918. Furthermore, friends, because I have developed and cultivated these four establishments of mindfulness, I know as it really is the varying degrees of faculties in other beings and other individuals.

11. Jhānādisuttaṃ

11. The Discourse on Jhāna and so forth

919. “Imesañca [M 3.0267] panāhaṃ, āvuso, catunnaṃ satipaṭṭhānānaṃ bhāvitattā bahulīkatattā jhānavimokkhasamādhisamāpattīnaṃ saṃkilesaṃ vodānaṃ vuṭṭhānaṃ yathābhūtaṃ pajānāmī”ti. Ekādasamaṃ.

919. Furthermore, friends, because I have developed and cultivated these four establishments of mindfulness, I know as it really is the defilement, purification, and emergence regarding the jhānas, liberations, concentrations, and attainments.

12. Pubbenivāsasuttaṃ

12. The Discourse on Past Lives

920. “Imesañca panāhaṃ, āvuso, catunnaṃ satipaṭṭhānānaṃ bhāvitattā bahulīkatattā anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussarāmi, seyyathidaṃ – ekampi jātiṃ dvepi jātiyo…pe… iti sākāraṃ sauddesaṃ anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussarāmī”ti. Dvādasamaṃ.

920. Furthermore, friends, because I have developed and cultivated these four establishments of mindfulness, I recollect my manifold past lives, that is, one birth, two births… Thus with their aspects and details, I recollect my manifold past lives.

13. Dibbacakkhusuttaṃ

13. The Discourse on the Divine Eye

921. “Imesañca panāhaṃ, āvuso, catunnaṃ satipaṭṭhānānaṃ bhāvitattā bahulīkatattā dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena satte passāmi cavamāne upapajjamāne…pe… iti dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena yathākammūpage satte pajānāmī”ti. Terasamaṃ.

921. Furthermore, friends, because I have developed and cultivated these four establishments of mindfulness, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, I see beings passing away and reappearing… Thus with the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, I understand beings who fare according to their kamma.

14. Āsavakkhayasuttaṃ

14. The Discourse on the Destruction of the Taints

922. “Imesañca panāhaṃ, āvuso, catunnaṃ satipaṭṭhānānaṃ bhāvitattā bahulīkatattā āsavānaṃ khayā anāsavaṃ cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttiṃ diṭṭhe [P 5.0306] dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharāmī”ti. Cuddasamaṃ.

922. Furthermore, friends, because I have developed and cultivated these four establishments of mindfulness, through the destruction of the taints, I dwell having attained the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having realized it for myself with direct knowledge in this very life.

Dutiyo vaggo.

The Second Section.

Tassuddānaṃ –

Its summary:

Mahābhiññaṃ [T 5.0391][V 3.0377] iddhi dibbaṃ, cetopariyaṃ ṭhānaṃ kammaṃ;

Sabbatthadhātudhimutti, indriyaṃ jhānaṃ tisso vijjāti.

Great Direct Knowledge, psychic power, the divine ear, penetration of minds, the possible, kamma; the all-reaching, elements, inclinations, faculties, jhāna, the three knowledges.

Anuruddhasaṃyuttaṃ aṭṭhamaṃ.

The Connected Discourses on Anuruddha, the Eighth.

9. Jhānasaṃyuttaṃ

9. The Connected Discourses on Jhāna

1. Gaṅgāpeyyālavaggo

1. The Ganges Repetition Section

1-12. Jhānādisuttadvādasakaṃ

1-12. Twelve Discourses on Jhāna and So Forth

923-934. Sāvatthinidānaṃ [T 5.0392][V 3.0378][M 3.0268][P 5.0307] “cattāro me, bhikkhave, jhānā. Katame cattāro? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu vivicceva kāmehi vivicca akusalehi dhammehi savitakkaṃ savicāraṃ vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā ajjhattaṃ sampasādanaṃ cetaso ekodibhāvaṃ avitakkaṃ avicāraṃ samādhijaṃ pītisukhaṃ dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Pītiyā ca virāgā upekkhako ca viharati sato ca sampajāno sukhañca kāyena paṭisaṃvedeti, yaṃ taṃ ariyā ācikkhanti – ‘upekkhako satimā sukhavihārī’ti tatiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Sukhassa ca pahānā dukkhassa ca pahānā pubbeva somanassadomanassānaṃ atthaṅgamā adukkhamasukhaṃ upekkhāsatipārisuddhiṃ catutthaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Ime kho, bhikkhave, cattāro jhānā”ti.

923-934. At Sāvatthī. "Bhikkhus, there are these four jhānas. What four? Here, bhikkhus, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. With the stilling of applied and sustained thought, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without applied and sustained thought, and has rapture and pleasure born of concentration. With the fading away of rapture, he dwells equanimously, mindful, and clearly comprehending, and he experiences pleasure with the body; he enters and dwells in the third jhāna, of which the noble ones declare: 'He is equanimous, mindful, and dwells happily.' With the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous passing away of joy and grief, he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and has purity of mindfulness due to equanimity. These, bhikkhus, are the four jhānas."

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, gaṅgā nadī pācīnaninnā pācīnapoṇā pācīnapabbhārā; evameva kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu cattāro [P 5.0308] jhāne bhāvento cattāro jhāne bahulīkaronto nibbānaninno hoti nibbānapoṇo nibbānapabbhāro. Kathañca, bhikkhave, bhikkhu cattāro jhāne bhāvento cattāro jhāne bahulīkaronto nibbānaninno hoti nibbānapoṇo nibbānapabbhāro? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu vivicceva kāmehi vivicca akusalehi dhammehi savitakkaṃ savicāraṃ vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja [T 5.0393] viharati. Vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā…pe… dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ…pe… [V 3.0379] tatiyaṃ jhānaṃ…pe… catutthaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu cattāro jhāne bhāvento cattāro jhāne bahulīkaronto nibbānaninno hoti nibbānapoṇo nibbānapabbhāro”ti. Dvādasamaṃ.

“Just as, bhikkhus, the river Ganges slants, slopes, and inclines to the east; so too, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who develops and cultivates the four jhānas slants, slopes, and inclines towards Nibbāna. And how, bhikkhus, does a bhikkhu who develops and cultivates the four jhānas slant, slope, and incline towards Nibbāna? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. With the stilling of applied and sustained thought... he enters and dwells in the second jhāna... the third jhāna... the fourth jhāna. Thus, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who develops and cultivates the four jhānas slants, slopes, and inclines towards Nibbāna.” Twelfth.

Gaṅgāpeyyālavaggo paṭhamo.

The First Ganges Repetition Section.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary:

Cha [M 3.0269] pācīnato ninnā, cha ninnā ca samuddato;

Dvete cha dvādasa honti, vaggo tena pavuccatīti.

Six slanting towards the east, and six slanting towards the sea; these two sixes become twelve, therefore the chapter is so called.

Appamādavaggo vitthāretabbo.

The Chapter on Heedfulness should be expanded.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary:

Tathāgataṃ padaṃ kūṭaṃ, mūlaṃ sāro ca vassikaṃ;

Rājā candimasūriyā, vatthena dasamaṃ padanti.

The Tathāgata, the footprint, the peak, the root, the heartwood, and the jasmine; the king, the moon and sun, with the cloth as the tenth.

Balakaraṇīyavaggo vitthāretabbo.

The Chapter on Exertion should be elaborated.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary:

Balaṃ [V 3.0380][P 5.0309] bījañca nāgo ca, rukkho kumbhena sūkiyā;

Ākāsena ca dve meghā, nāvā āgantukā nadīti.

Strength, the seed, and the nāga, the tree, with the pot and the needle; and with the sky, two clouds, the boat, the guest, and the river.

Esanāvaggo vitthāretabbo.

The Chapter on Seeking should be elaborated.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary:

Esanā vidhā āsavo, bhavo ca dukkhatā tisso;

Khilaṃ malañca nīgho ca, vedanā taṇhā tasinā cāti.

Seeking, modes, taints, and becoming, the three sufferings; barrenness, stain, and affliction, feeling, craving, and thirst.

5. Oghavaggo

5. The Chapter on Floods

1-10. Oghādisuttaṃ

1-10. The Discourses on Floods and So Forth

967-976. “Pañcimāni, bhikkhave, uddhambhāgiyāni saṃyojanāni. Katamāni pañca? Rūparāgo, arūparāgo, māno, uddhaccaṃ, avijjā – imāni kho, bhikkhave, pañcuddhambhāgiyāni [M 3.0270] saṃyojanāni. Imesaṃ kho, bhikkhave, pañcannaṃ uddhambhāgiyānaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ abhiññāya pariññāya parikkhayāya pahānāya cattāro jhānā bhāvetabbā. Katame cattāro? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu vivicceva kāmehi vivicca akusalehi dhammehi savitakkaṃ savicāraṃ vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā ajjhattaṃ sampasādanaṃ cetaso ekodibhāvaṃ avitakkaṃ avicāraṃ samādhijaṃ pītisukhaṃ dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ…pe… [V 3.0381] tatiyaṃ jhānaṃ…pe… catutthaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Imesaṃ [P 5.0310] kho, bhikkhave, pañcannaṃ uddhambhāgiyānaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ abhiññāya pariññāya parikkhayāya pahānāya ime cattāro jhānā bhāvetabbā”ti vitthāretabbaṃ. Dasamaṃ. (Yathā maggasaṃyuttaṃ tathā vitthāretabbaṃ).

“Bhikkhus, there are these five higher fetters. Which five? Lust for form, lust for the formless, conceit, restlessness, and ignorance. These, bhikkhus, are the five higher fetters. For the direct knowledge, full understanding, destruction, and abandonment of these five higher fetters, the four jhānas are to be developed. Which four? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. With the stilling of applied and sustained thought, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without applied and sustained thought, and is filled with rapture and pleasure born of concentration… the third jhāna… the fourth jhāna. For the direct knowledge, full understanding, destruction, and abandonment of these five higher fetters, these four jhānas are to be developed.” This is to be elaborated. Tenth. (It should be elaborated just as in the Maggasaṃyutta).

Oghavaggo pañcamo.

The Chapter on Floods, the Fifth.

Tassuddānaṃ –

Its summary:

Ogho yogo upādānaṃ, ganthā anusayena ca;

Kāmaguṇā nīvaraṇā, khandhā oruddhambhāgiyāti.

Floods, yokes, clinging, bonds, and latent tendencies; strands of sensual pleasure, hindrances, aggregates, and the lower and higher fetters.

Jhānasaṃyuttaṃ navamaṃ.

The Connected Discourses on Jhāna, the Ninth.

10. Ānāpānasaṃyuttaṃ

The Connected Discourses on Breathing

1. Ekadhammavaggo

The Chapter on One Thing

1. Ekadhammasuttaṃ

The Discourse on One Thing

977. Sāvatthinidānaṃ[T 5.0394][V 3.0382][M 3.0271][P 5.0311]. Tatra kho…pe… etadavoca – “ekadhammo, bhikkhave, bhāvito bahulīkato mahapphalo hoti mahānisaṃso. Katamo ekadhammo? Ānāpānassati ānāpānasati (sī. pī.). Kathaṃ bhāvitā ca, bhikkhave, ānāpānassati kathaṃ bahulīkatā mahapphalā hoti mahānisaṃsā? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu araññagato vā rukkhamūlagato vā suññāgāragato vā nisīdati pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā ujuṃ kāyaṃ paṇidhāya parimukhaṃ satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā. So satova assasati, satova sato (bahūsu) tatiyapārājikepi passasati. Dīghaṃ vā assasanto ‘dīghaṃ assasāmī’ti pajānāti, dīghaṃ vā passasanto ‘dīghaṃ passasāmī’ti pajānāti; rassaṃ vā assasanto ‘rassaṃ assasāmī’ti pajānāti, rassaṃ vā passasanto ‘rassaṃ passasāmī’ti pajānāti; ‘sabbakāyappaṭisaṃvedī assasissāmī’ti sikkhati, ‘sabbakāyappaṭisaṃvedī passasissāmī’ti sikkhati; ‘passambhayaṃ kāyasaṅkhāraṃ assasissāmī’ti sikkhati, ‘passambhayaṃ kāyasaṅkhāraṃ passasissāmī’ti sikkhati; ‘pītippaṭisaṃvedī [P 5.0312] assasissāmī’ti sikkhati, ‘pītippaṭisaṃvedī passasissāmī’ti sikkhati; ‘sukhappaṭisaṃvedī assasissāmī’ti sikkhati, ‘sukhappaṭisaṃvedī passasissāmī’ti sikkhati; ‘cittasaṅkhārappaṭisaṃvedī assasissāmī’ti sikkhati, ‘cittasaṅkhārappaṭisaṃvedī [T 5.0395] passasissāmī’ti sikkhati; ‘passambhayaṃ cittasaṅkhāraṃ assasissāmī’ti sikkhati, ‘passambhayaṃ cittasaṅkhāraṃ passasissāmī’ti sikkhati; ‘cittappaṭisaṃvedī assasissāmī’ti sikkhati, ‘cittappaṭisaṃvedī passasissāmī’ti sikkhati; ‘abhippamodayaṃ cittaṃ assasissāmī’ti sikkhati, ‘abhippamodayaṃ cittaṃ passasissāmī’ti sikkhati; ‘samādahaṃ cittaṃ assasissāmī’ti sikkhati[V 3.0383], ‘samādahaṃ cittaṃ passasissāmī’ti sikkhati; ‘vimocayaṃ cittaṃ assasissāmī’ti sikkhati, ‘vimocayaṃ [M 3.0272] cittaṃ passasissāmī’ti sikkhati; ‘aniccānupassī assasissāmī’ti sikkhati, ‘aniccānupassī passasissāmī’ti sikkhati; ‘virāgānupassī assasissāmī’ti sikkhati, ‘virāgānupassī passasissāmī’ti sikkhati; ‘nirodhānupassī assasissāmī’ti sikkhati, ‘nirodhānupassī passasissāmī’ti sikkhati; ‘paṭinissaggānupassī assasissāmī’ti sikkhati, ‘paṭinissaggānupassī passasissāmī’ti sikkhati. Evaṃ bhāvitā kho, bhikkhave, ānāpānassati evaṃ bahulīkatā mahapphalā hoti mahānisaṃsā”ti. Paṭhamaṃ.

10. At Sāvatthī. There… he said this: “Bhikkhus, one thing, when developed and cultivated, is of great fruit and great benefit. What is that one thing? Mindfulness of in-breathing and out-breathing. And how, bhikkhus, is mindfulness of in-breathing and out-breathing developed and cultivated so that it is of great fruit and great benefit? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, having gone to the forest, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty dwelling, sits down; having folded his legs crosswise, set his body erect, and established mindfulness before him. Mindful he breathes out, mindful he breathes in. Breathing out long, he knows, ‘I breathe out long’; or breathing in long, he knows, ‘I breathe in long.’ Breathing out short, he knows, ‘I breathe out short’; or breathing in short, he knows, ‘I breathe in short.’ He trains, ‘I will breathe out experiencing the whole body’; he trains, ‘I will breathe in experiencing the whole body.’ He trains, ‘Calming the bodily formation, I will breathe out’; he trains, ‘Calming the bodily formation, I will breathe in.’ He trains, ‘Experiencing rapture, I will breathe out’; he trains, ‘Experiencing rapture, I will breathe in.’ He trains, ‘Experiencing pleasure, I will breathe out’; he trains, ‘Experiencing pleasure, I will breathe in.’ He trains, ‘Experiencing the mental formation, I will breathe out’; he trains, ‘Experiencing the mental formation, I will breathe in.’ He trains, ‘Calming the mental formation, I will breathe out’; he trains, ‘Calming the mental formation, I will breathe in.’ He trains, ‘Experiencing the mind, I will breathe out’; he trains, ‘Experiencing the mind, I will breathe in.’ He trains, ‘Gladdening the mind, I will breathe out’; he trains, ‘Gladdening the mind, I will breathe in.’ He trains, ‘Concentrating the mind, I will breathe out’; he trains, ‘Concentrating the mind, I will breathe in.’ He trains, ‘Liberating the mind, I will breathe out’; he trains, ‘Liberating the mind, I will breathe in.’ He trains, ‘Contemplating impermanence, I will breathe out’; he trains, ‘Contemplating impermanence, I will breathe in.’ He trains, ‘Contemplating dispassion, I will breathe out’; he trains, ‘Contemplating dispassion, I will breathe in.’ He trains, ‘Contemplating cessation, I will breathe out’; he trains, ‘Contemplating cessation, I will breathe in.’ He trains, ‘Contemplating relinquishment, I will breathe out’; he trains, ‘Contemplating relinquishment, I will breathe in.’ Bhikkhus, when mindfulness of in-breathing and out-breathing is developed and cultivated in this way, it is of great fruit and great benefit.” First.

2. Bojjhaṅgasuttaṃ

1. The Discourse on the Factors of Enlightenment

978. “Ānāpānassati, bhikkhave, bhāvitā bahulīkatā mahapphalā hoti mahānisaṃsā. Kathaṃ bhāvitā ca, bhikkhave, ānāpānassati kathaṃ bahulīkatā mahapphalā hoti mahānisaṃsā? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu ānāpānassatisahagataṃ satisambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti vivekanissitaṃ virāganissitaṃ nirodhanissitaṃ vossaggapariṇāmiṃ, ānāpānassatisahagataṃ dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti…pe… ānāpānassatisahagataṃ [P 5.0313] upekkhāsambojjhaṅgaṃ [T 5.0396] bhāveti vivekanissitaṃ virāganissitaṃ nirodhanissitaṃ vossaggapariṇāmiṃ. Evaṃ bhāvitā kho, bhikkhave, ānāpānassati evaṃ bahulīkatā mahapphalā hoti mahānisaṃsā”ti. Dutiyaṃ.

1. “Bhikkhus, mindfulness of breathing, when developed and cultivated, is of great fruit and great benefit. And how, bhikkhus, is mindfulness of breathing developed and cultivated so that it is of great fruit and great benefit? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu develops the enlightenment factor of mindfulness accompanied by mindfulness of breathing, based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and culminating in relinquishment. He develops the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena… he develops the enlightenment factor of equanimity accompanied by mindfulness of breathing, based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and culminating in relinquishment. In this way, bhikkhus, mindfulness of breathing, when so developed and so cultivated, is of great fruit and great benefit.” Second.

3. Suddhikasuttaṃ

977. The Simple Discourse

979. “Ānāpānassati, bhikkhave, bhāvitā bahulīkatā mahapphalā hoti mahānisaṃsā. Kathaṃ bhāvitā ca, bhikkhave, ānāpānassati kathaṃ bahulīkatā mahapphalā hoti mahānisaṃsā? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu araññagato vā rukkhamūlagato vā suññāgāragato vā nisīdati pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā ujuṃ kāyaṃ paṇidhāya parimukhaṃ satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā. So satova assasati, satova passasati…pe… ‘paṭinissaggānupassī assasissāmī’ti sikkhati, ‘paṭinissaggānupassī passasissāmī’ti sikkhati. Evaṃ bhāvitā kho, bhikkhave, ānāpānassati evaṃ bahulīkatā mahapphalā hoti mahānisaṃsā”ti. Tatiyaṃ.

979. “Monks, mindfulness of breathing, when developed and cultivated, is of great fruit and great benefit. And how, monks, is mindfulness of breathing developed and cultivated to be of great fruit and great benefit? Here, monks, a monk—having gone to the forest, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty dwelling—sits down; having folded his legs crosswise, set his body erect, and established mindfulness in front of him. Mindful he breathes out, mindful he breathes in... He trains thus: ‘Contemplating relinquishment, I will breathe out’; he trains thus: ‘Contemplating relinquishment, I will breathe in.’ In this way, monks, mindfulness of breathing, when so developed and so cultivated, is of great fruit and great benefit.” The Third.

4. Paṭhamaphalasuttaṃ

4. The First Discourse on the Fruit

980. “Ānāpānassati[V 3.0384][M 3.0273], bhikkhave, bhāvitā bahulīkatā mahapphalā hoti mahānisaṃsā. Kathaṃ bhāvitā ca, bhikkhave, ānāpānassati kathaṃ bahulīkatā mahapphalā hoti mahānisaṃsā? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu araññagato vā rukkhamūlagato vā suññāgāragato vā nisīdati pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā ujuṃ kāyaṃ paṇidhāya parimukhaṃ satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā. So satova assasati, satova passasati…pe… [T 5.0397] ‘paṭinissaggānupassī assasissāmī’ti sikkhati, ‘paṭinissaggānupassī passasissāmī’ti sikkhati. Evaṃ bhāvitā kho, bhikkhave, ānāpānassati evaṃ bahulīkatā mahapphalā hoti mahānisaṃsā. Evaṃ [P 5.0314] bhāvitāya kho, bhikkhave, ānāpānassatiyā evaṃ bahulīkatāya dvinnaṃ phalānaṃ aññataraṃ phalaṃ pāṭikaṅkhaṃ – diṭṭheva dhamme aññā, sati vā upādisese anāgāmitā”ti. Catutthaṃ.

980. “Monks, mindfulness of breathing, when developed and frequently practiced, is of great fruit, of great benefit. And how, monks, is mindfulness of breathing developed and frequently practiced so that it is of great fruit, of great benefit? Here, monks, a monk—having gone to the forest, or to the foot of a tree, or to a secluded place—sits down, having folded his legs crosswise, set his body erect, and established mindfulness in front of him. Mindful he breathes out, mindful he breathes in… He trains thus: ‘Contemplating relinquishment, I will breathe out’; he trains thus: ‘Contemplating relinquishment, I will breathe in.’ Indeed, monks, it is in this way that mindfulness of breathing, when developed and frequently practiced, is of great fruit, of great benefit. When mindfulness of breathing has been developed and frequently practiced in this way, monks, one of two fruits is to be expected: either final knowledge in this very life or, if there is a remnant of clinging, the state of a Non-returner.” The Fourth.

5. Dutiyaphalasuttaṃ

5. The Second Discourse on the Fruit

981. “Ānāpānassati, bhikkhave, bhāvitā bahulīkatā mahapphalā hoti mahānisaṃsā. Kathaṃ bhāvitā ca, bhikkhave, ānāpānassati kathaṃ bahulīkatā mahapphalā hoti mahānisaṃsā? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu araññagato vā rukkhamūlagato vā suññāgāragato vā nisīdati pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā ujuṃ kāyaṃ paṇidhāya parimukhaṃ satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā. So satova assasati, satova passasati…pe… ‘paṭinissaggānupassī assasissāmī’ti sikkhati, ‘paṭinissaggānupassī passasissāmī’ti sikkhati. Evaṃ bhāvitā kho, bhikkhave, ānāpānassati evaṃ bahulīkatā mahapphalā hoti mahānisaṃsā.

981. “Monks, mindfulness of breathing, when developed and frequently practiced, is of great fruit, of great benefit. And how, monks, is mindfulness of breathing developed and frequently practiced so that it is of great fruit, of great benefit? Here, monks, a monk—having gone to the forest, or to the foot of a tree, or to a secluded place—sits down, having folded his legs crosswise, set his body erect, and established mindfulness in front of him. Mindful he breathes out, mindful he breathes in… He trains thus: ‘Contemplating relinquishment, I will breathe out’; he trains thus: ‘Contemplating relinquishment, I will breathe in.’ Indeed, monks, it is in this way that mindfulness of breathing, when developed and frequently practiced, is of great fruit, of great benefit.”

“Evaṃ bhāvitāya kho, bhikkhave, ānāpānassatiyā evaṃ bahulīkatāya satta phalā sattānisaṃsā pāṭikaṅkhā. Katame satta phalā sattānisaṃsā? Diṭṭheva dhamme paṭikacca aññaṃ ārādheti; no ce diṭṭheva dhamme paṭikacca aññaṃ ārādheti. Atha maraṇakāle aññaṃ ārādheti; no ce diṭṭheva dhamme paṭikacca aññaṃ ārādheti[T 5.0398], no ce maraṇakāle aññaṃ ārādheti. Atha pañcannaṃ orambhāgiyānaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ parikkhayā antarāparinibbāyī hoti… upahaccaparinibbāyī hoti… asaṅkhāraparinibbāyī hoti… sasaṅkhāraparinibbāyī hoti… uddhaṃsoto [V 3.0385] hoti akaniṭṭhagāmī – evaṃ bhāvitāya [M 3.0274] kho, bhikkhave, ānāpānassatiyā evaṃ bahulīkatāya ime satta phalā sattānisaṃsā pāṭikaṅkhā”ti. Pañcamaṃ.

“Monks, when mindfulness of breathing is thus developed and thus frequently practiced, seven fruits and seven benefits are to be expected. What are the seven fruits and seven benefits? One attains final knowledge early on in this very life. If one does not attain final knowledge early on in this very life, then one attains final knowledge at the time of death. If one does not attain final knowledge early on in this very life and does not attain final knowledge at the time of death, then with the destruction of the five lower fetters, one becomes one who attains final Nibbāna in the interval… one becomes one who attains final Nibbāna upon landing… one becomes one who attains final Nibbāna without exertion… one becomes one who attains final Nibbāna with exertion… one becomes one who goes upstream, heading to the Akaniṭṭha realm. Monks, when mindfulness of breathing is thus developed and thus frequently practiced, these seven fruits and these seven benefits are to be expected.” The Fifth.

6. Ariṭṭhasuttaṃ

6. The Discourse to Ariṭṭha

982. Sāvatthinidānaṃ. Tatra kho bhagavā…pe… etadavoca – “bhāvetha no tumhe bhikkhave, ānāpānassati”nti? Evaṃ vutte āyasmā ariṭṭho bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “ahaṃ kho, bhante, bhāvemi ānāpānassati”nti. “Yathā [P 5.0315] kathaṃ pana tvaṃ, ariṭṭha, bhāvesi ānāpānassati”nti? “Atītesu me, bhante, kāmesu kāmacchando pahīno, anāgatesu me kāmesu kāmacchando vigato, ajjhattabahiddhā ajjhattaṃ bahiddhā (syā. kaṃ. pī. ka.) ca me dhammesu paṭighasaññā suppaṭivinītā. So sohaṃ (?) satova assasissāmi, satova passasissāmi. Evaṃ khvāhaṃ, bhante, bhāvemi ānāpānassati”nti.

982. At Sāvatthī. There the Blessed One… said this: “Monks, do you develop mindfulness of breathing?” When this was said, the Venerable Ariṭṭha said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, I do indeed develop mindfulness of breathing.” “But in what way, Ariṭṭha, do you develop mindfulness of breathing?” “Venerable sir, my sensual desire for past sensual pleasures is abandoned; my sensual desire for future sensual pleasures has vanished; and my perception of aversion toward internal and external phenomena is thoroughly dispelled. Mindful, I will breathe out; mindful, I will breathe in. It is in this way, venerable sir, that I develop mindfulness of breathing.”

“‘Atthesā, ariṭṭha, ānāpānassati, nesā natthī’ti vadāmi. Api ca, ariṭṭha, yathā ānāpānassati vitthārena paripuṇṇā hoti taṃ suṇāhi, sādhukaṃ manasi karohi; bhāsissāmī”ti. “Evaṃ, bhante”ti kho āyasmā ariṭṭho bhagavato paccassosi. Bhagavā etadavoca –

“This mindfulness of breathing exists, Ariṭṭha; I do not say that it does not exist. However, Ariṭṭha, listen and apply your mind well as to how mindfulness of breathing is fulfilled in detail; I will speak.” “Yes, venerable sir,” the Venerable Ariṭṭha replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:

“Kathañca, ariṭṭha, ānāpānassati vitthārena paripuṇṇā hoti? Idha, ariṭṭha, bhikkhu [T 5.0399] araññagato vā rukkhamūlagato vā suññāgāragato vā nisīdati pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā ujuṃ kāyaṃ paṇidhāya parimukhaṃ satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā. So satova assasati, satova passasati. Dīghaṃ vā assasanto ‘dīghaṃ assasāmī’ti pajānāti…pe… ‘paṭinissaggānupassī assasissāmī’ti sikkhati, ‘paṭinissaggānupassī passasissāmī’ti sikkhati. Evaṃ kho, ariṭṭha, ānāpānassati vitthārena paripuṇṇā hotī”ti. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

“And how, Ariṭṭha, is mindfulness of breathing fulfilled in detail? Here, Ariṭṭha, a monk, having gone to the forest, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty dwelling, sits down, folding his legs crosswise, setting his body erect, and establishing mindfulness in front of him. Mindful he breathes out, mindful he breathes in. Breathing out long, he knows, ‘I breathe out long.’… He trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out contemplating relinquishment’; he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in contemplating relinquishment.’ In this way, Ariṭṭha, mindfulness of breathing is fulfilled in detail.” The Sixth.

7. Mahākappinasuttaṃ

7. The Discourse with Mahākappina

983. Sāvatthinidānaṃ. Tena kho pana samayena āyasmā mahākappino bhagavato avidūre [V 3.0386] nisinno hoti pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā ujuṃ kāyaṃ paṇidhāya parimukhaṃ satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā. Addasā kho bhagavā āyasmantaṃ mahākappinaṃ avidūre nisinnaṃ pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā ujuṃ kāyaṃ paṇidhāya parimukhaṃ satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā. Disvāna bhikkhū āmantesi –

983. At Sāvatthī. On that occasion, the Venerable Mahākappina was sitting not far from the Blessed One, having folded his legs crosswise, set his body erect, and established mindfulness before him. The Blessed One saw the Venerable Mahākappina sitting not far away, having folded his legs crosswise, set his body erect, and established mindfulness before him. Having seen him, he addressed the bhikkhus:

“Passatha [M 3.0275] no tumhe, bhikkhave, etassa bhikkhuno kāyassa iñjitattaṃ vā phanditattaṃ vā”ti? “Yadāpi mayaṃ, bhante, taṃ āyasmantaṃ passāma saṅghamajjhe vā nisinnaṃ ekaṃ vā raho nisinnaṃ, tadāpi [P 5.0316] mayaṃ tassa āyasmato na passāma kāyassa iñjitattaṃ vā phanditattaṃ vā”ti.

“Bhikkhus, do you see any movement or trembling in this bhikkhu’s body?” “Venerable sir, whenever we see that venerable one seated in the midst of the Saṅgha or seated alone in seclusion, even then we do not see any movement or trembling in his body.”

“Yassa, bhikkhave, samādhissa bhāvitattā bahulīkatattā neva kāyassa iñjitattaṃ vā hoti phanditattaṃ vā, na cittassa iñjitattaṃ vā hoti phanditattaṃ vā, tassa so, bhikkhave, bhikkhu samādhissa nikāmalābhī akicchalābhī akasiralābhī. Katamassa [T 5.0400] ca, bhikkhave, samādhissa bhāvitattā bahulīkatattā neva kāyassa iñjitattaṃ vā hoti phanditattaṃ vā, na cittassa iñjitattaṃ vā hoti phanditattaṃ vā?

“Bhikkhus, it is because of having developed and made much of a certain concentration that there is no movement or trembling of the body, and no movement or trembling of the mind. That bhikkhu, bhikkhus, is an obtainer of that concentration at will, without difficulty, without trouble. And because of having developed and made much of what concentration is there no movement or trembling of the body, and no movement or trembling of the mind?

“Ānāpānassatisamādhissa, bhikkhave, bhāvitattā bahulīkatattā neva kāyassa iñjitattaṃ vā hoti phanditattaṃ vā, na cittassa iñjitattaṃ vā hoti phanditattaṃ vā. Kathaṃ bhāvite ca, bhikkhave, ānāpānassatisamādhimhi kathaṃ bahulīkate neva kāyassa iñjitattaṃ vā hoti phanditattaṃ vā, na cittassa iñjitattaṃ vā hoti phanditattaṃ vā?

“Bhikkhus, it is because of having developed and made much of the concentration of mindfulness of breathing that there is no movement or trembling of the body, and no movement or trembling of the mind. And how, bhikkhus, when the concentration of mindfulness of breathing is developed and made much of, is there no movement or trembling of the body, and no movement or trembling of the mind?”

“Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu araññagato vā rukkhamūlagato vā suññāgāragato vā nisīdati pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā ujuṃ kāyaṃ paṇidhāya parimukhaṃ satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā. So satova assasati, satova passasati…pe… ‘paṭinissaggānupassī assasissāmī’ti sikkhati, ‘paṭinissaggānupassī passasissāmī’ti sikkhati. Evaṃ bhāvite ca kho, bhikkhave, ānāpānassatisamādhimhi evaṃ bahulīkate neva kāyassa iñjitattaṃ vā hoti phanditattaṃ vā, na cittassa iñjitattaṃ vā hoti phanditattaṃ vā”ti. Sattamaṃ.

“Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu—gone to the forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty dwelling—sits down, folding his legs crosswise, holding his body erect, and establishing mindfulness before him. Mindful he breathes out, mindful he breathes in... He trains himself, ‘I will breathe out, contemplating relinquishment.’ He trains himself, ‘I will breathe in, contemplating relinquishment.’ When the concentration of mindfulness of breathing is developed and frequently practiced in this way, bhikkhus, there is neither movement nor trembling of the body, nor movement or trembling of the mind.” Seventh.

8. Padīpopamasuttaṃ

8. The Discourse on the Simile of the Lamp

984. “Ānāpānassatisamādhi[V 3.0387], bhikkhave, bhāvito bahulīkato mahapphalo hoti mahānisaṃso. Kathaṃ bhāvito ca, bhikkhave, ānāpānassatisamādhi kathaṃ bahulīkato mahapphalo hoti mahānisaṃso?

984. “Bhikkhus, the concentration of mindfulness of breathing, when developed and frequently practiced, is of great fruit and great benefit. And how, bhikkhus, is the concentration of mindfulness of breathing developed and frequently practiced so that it is of great fruit and great benefit?”

“Idha[P 5.0317], bhikkhave, bhikkhu araññagato vā rukkhamūlagato vā suññāgāragato vā nisīdati pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā ujuṃ [T 5.0401] kāyaṃ paṇidhāya parimukhaṃ [M 3.0276] satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā. So satova assasati, satova passasati. Dīghaṃ vā assasanto ‘dīghaṃ assasāmī’ti pajānāti…pe… ‘paṭinissaggānupassī assasissāmī’ti sikkhati, ‘paṭinissaggānupassī passasissāmī’ti sikkhati. Evaṃ bhāvito kho, bhikkhave, ānāpānassatisamādhi evaṃ bahulīkato mahapphalo hoti mahānisaṃso.

“Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu—gone to the forest, or to the foot of a tree, or to an empty dwelling—sits down, folding his legs crosswise, holding his body erect, and establishing mindfulness before him. Mindful, he breathes out; mindful, he breathes in. Breathing out long, he knows, ‘I am breathing out long’... He trains himself, ‘I will breathe out, contemplating relinquishment.’ He trains himself, ‘I will breathe in, contemplating relinquishment.’ When the concentration of mindfulness of breathing is developed and frequently practiced in this way, bhikkhus, it is of great fruit and great benefit.”

“Ahampi sudaṃ, bhikkhave, pubbeva sambodhā anabhisambuddho bodhisattova samāno iminā vihārena bahulaṃ viharāmi. Tassa mayhaṃ, bhikkhave, iminā vihārena bahulaṃ viharato neva kāyo kilamati na cakkhūni; anupādāya ca me āsavehi cittaṃ vimucci.

“Bhikkhus, I too, before my enlightenment, while not yet fully enlightened and still a Bodhisatta, frequently dwelled in this state. Bhikkhus, for me who frequently dwelled in this state, my body did not become fatigued, nor did my eyes; and without grasping, my mind was liberated from the taints.”

“Tasmātiha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu cepi ākaṅkheyya – ‘neva me kāyo kilameyya na cakkhūni, anupādāya ca me āsavehi cittaṃ vimucceyyā’ti, ayameva ānāpānassatisamādhi sādhukaṃ manasi kātabbo.

“Therefore, bhikkhus, should a bhikkhu wish: ‘May my body not become fatigued, may my eyes not become fatigued, and may my mind be liberated from the taints without grasping,’ this very concentration of mindfulness of breathing should be well attended to.”

“Tasmātiha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu cepi ākaṅkheyya – ‘ye me gehasitā sarasaṅkappā te pahīyeyyu’nti, ayameva ānāpānassatisamādhi sādhukaṃ manasi kātabbo.

“Therefore, bhikkhus, should a bhikkhu wish: ‘May my thoughts and intentions connected with the household life be abandoned,’ this very concentration of mindfulness of breathing should be well attended to.”

“Tasmātiha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu cepi ākaṅkheyya – ‘appaṭikūle paṭikūlasaññī vihareyya’nti, ayameva ānāpānassatisamādhi sādhukaṃ manasi kātabbo.

“Therefore, bhikkhus, should a bhikkhu wish: ‘May I dwell perceiving the repulsive in the unrepulsive,’ this very concentration of mindfulness of breathing should be well attended to.”

“Tasmātiha[V 3.0388], bhikkhave, bhikkhu cepi ākaṅkheyya – ‘paṭikūle appaṭikūlasaññī [T 5.0402] vihareyya’nti, ayameva ānāpānassatisamādhi sādhukaṃ manasi kātabbo.

“Therefore, bhikkhus, should a bhikkhu wish: ‘May I dwell perceiving the unrepulsive in the repulsive,’ this very concentration of mindfulness of breathing should be well attended to.”

“Tasmātiha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu cepi ākaṅkheyya – ‘paṭikūle ca appaṭikūle ca paṭikūlasaññī vihareyya’nti, ayameva ānāpānassatisamādhi sādhukaṃ manasi kātabbo.

“Therefore, bhikkhus, should a bhikkhu wish: ‘May I dwell perceiving the repulsive in both the repulsive and the unrepulsive,’ this very concentration of mindfulness of breathing should be well attended to.”

“Tasmātiha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu cepi ākaṅkheyya – ‘paṭikūle [P 5.0318] ca appaṭikūle ca appaṭikūlasaññī vihareyya’nti, ayameva ānāpānassatisamādhi sādhukaṃ manasi kātabbo.

“Therefore, bhikkhus, should a bhikkhu wish: ‘May I dwell perceiving the unrepulsive in both the repulsive and the unrepulsive,’ this very concentration of mindfulness of breathing should be well attended to.”

“Tasmātiha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu cepi ākaṅkheyya – ‘appaṭikūlañca paṭikūlañca tadubhayaṃ abhinivajjetvā upekkhako vihareyyaṃ sato sampajāno’ti, ayameva ānāpānassatisamādhi sādhukaṃ manasi kātabbo.

“Therefore, bhikkhus, should a bhikkhu wish: ‘Having avoided both the unrepulsive and the repulsive, may I dwell equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending,’ this very concentration of mindfulness of breathing should be well attended to.”

“Tasmātiha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu cepi ākaṅkheyya – ‘vivicceva kāmehi vivicca akusalehi dhammehi savitakkaṃ savicāraṃ vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja vihareyya’nti, ayameva ānāpānassatisamādhi sādhukaṃ manasi kātabbo.

Therefore, bhikkhus, in this Dispensation, if a bhikkhu should wish: ‘Secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, may I enter and dwell in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by initial thought and sustained thought, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion,’ then this very concentration by mindfulness of in-and-out breathing should be well attended to.

“Tasmātiha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu cepi ākaṅkheyya – ‘vitakkavicārānaṃ [M 3.0277] vūpasamā ajjhattaṃ sampasādanaṃ cetaso ekodibhāvaṃ avitakkaṃ avicāraṃ samādhijaṃ pītisukhaṃ dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja vihareyya’nti, ayameva ānāpānassatisamādhi sādhukaṃ manasi kātabbo.

Therefore, bhikkhus, in this Dispensation, if a bhikkhu should wish: ‘With the stilling of initial thought and sustained thought, may I enter and dwell in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without initial thought and sustained thought, and has rapture and happiness born of concentration,’ then this very concentration by mindfulness of in-and-out breathing should be well attended to.

“Tasmātiha bhikkhave, bhikkhu cepi ākaṅkheyya – ‘pītiyā ca [T 5.0403] virāgā upekkhako ca vihareyyaṃ sato ca sampajāno, sukhañca kāyena paṭisaṃvedeyyaṃ, yaṃ taṃ ariyā ācikkhanti – upekkhako satimā sukhavihārīti tatiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja vihareyya’nti, ayameva ānāpānassatisamādhi sādhukaṃ manasi kātabbo.

Therefore, bhikkhus, in this Dispensation, if a bhikkhu should wish: ‘With the fading away of rapture, may I dwell equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending, and experience happiness with the body; may I enter and dwell in that third jhāna of which the noble ones declare: “He is equanimous, mindful, and dwells happily,”’ then this very concentration by mindfulness of in-and-out breathing should be well attended to.

“Tasmātiha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu cepi ākaṅkheyya – ‘sukhassa ca pahānā dukkhassa ca pahānā [V 3.0389] pubbeva somanassadomanassānaṃ atthaṅgamā adukkhamasukhaṃ upekkhāsatipārisuddhiṃ catutthaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja vihareyya’nti, ayameva ānāpānassatisamādhi sādhukaṃ manasi kātabbo.

Therefore, bhikkhus, in this Dispensation, if a bhikkhu should wish: ‘With the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, may I enter and dwell in the fourth jhāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and has purity of mindfulness due to equanimity,’ then this very concentration by mindfulness of in-and-out breathing should be well attended to.

“Tasmātiha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu cepi ākaṅkheyya – ‘sabbaso rūpasaññānaṃ samatikkamā paṭighasaññānaṃ atthaṅgamā nānattasaññānaṃ amanasikārā ananto ākāsoti ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ upasampajja vihareyya’nti, ayameva ānāpānassatisamādhi sādhukaṃ manasi kātabbo.

Therefore, bhikkhus, in this Dispensation, if a bhikkhu should wish: ‘By completely transcending perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of sensory impingement, and by not attending to perceptions of diversity, perceiving “Space is infinite,” may I enter and dwell in the base of the infinity of space,’ then this very concentration by mindfulness of in-and-out breathing should be well attended to.

“Tasmātiha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu cepi ākaṅkheyya – ‘sabbaso ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ samatikkamma anantaṃ viññāṇanti [P 5.0319] viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ upasampajja vihareyya’nti, ayameva ānāpānassatisamādhi sādhukaṃ manasi kātabbo.

Therefore, bhikkhus, in this Dispensation, if a bhikkhu should wish: ‘Having completely transcended the base of infinite space, perceiving “Consciousness is infinite,” may I enter and dwell in the base of infinite consciousness,’ then this very concentration by mindfulness of in-and-out breathing should be well attended to.

“Tasmātiha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu cepi ākaṅkheyya – ‘sabbaso viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ samatikkamma natthi kiñcīti ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ upasampajja vihareyya’nti, ayameva ānāpānassatisamādhi sādhukaṃ manasi kātabbo.

Therefore, bhikkhus, in this Dispensation, if a bhikkhu should wish: ‘Having completely transcended the base of infinite consciousness, perceiving “There is nothing,” may I enter and dwell in the base of nothingness,’ then this very concentration by mindfulness of in-and-out breathing should be well attended to.

“Tasmātiha[T 5.0404], bhikkhave, bhikkhu cepi ākaṅkheyya – ‘sabbaso ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ samatikkamma nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ upasampajja vihareyya’nti, ayameva ānāpānassatisamādhi sādhukaṃ manasi kātabbo.

Therefore, bhikkhus, in this Dispensation, if a bhikkhu should wish: ‘Having completely transcended the base of nothingness, may I enter and dwell in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,’ then this very concentration by mindfulness of in-and-out breathing should be well attended to.

“Tasmātiha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu cepi ākaṅkheyya – ‘sabbaso nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ samatikkamma saññāvedayitanirodhaṃ upasampajja vihareyya’nti, ayameva ānāpānassatisamādhi sādhukaṃ manasi kātabbo.

Therefore, bhikkhus, in this Dispensation, if a bhikkhu should wish: ‘Having completely transcended the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, may I enter and dwell in the cessation of perception and feeling,’ then this very concentration by mindfulness of in-and-out breathing should be well attended to.

“Evaṃ bhāvite kho, bhikkhave, ānāpānassatisamādhimhi evaṃ bahulīkate, sukhaṃ ce vedanaṃ vedayati, sā ‘aniccā’ti pajānāti, ‘anajjhositā’ti pajānāti, ‘anabhinanditā’ti pajānāti; dukkhaṃ ce vedanaṃ vedayati, ‘sā aniccā’ti pajānāti, ‘anajjhositā’ti pajānāti, ‘anabhinanditā’ti [V 3.0390][M 3.0278] pajānāti; adukkhamasukhaṃ ce vedanaṃ vedayati, ‘sā aniccā’ti pajānāti, ‘anajjhositā’ti pajānāti, ‘anabhinanditā’ti pajānāti”.

Indeed, bhikkhus, when this concentration by mindfulness of in-and-out breathing has been developed and cultivated in this way, if he feels a pleasant feeling, he understands: ‘It is impermanent’; he understands: ‘It is not clung to’; he understands: ‘It is not delighted in.’ If he feels a painful feeling, he understands: ‘It is impermanent’; he understands: ‘It is not clung to’; he understands: ‘It is not delighted in.’ If he feels a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he understands: ‘It is impermanent’; he understands: ‘It is not clung to’; he understands: ‘It is not delighted in.’

“Sukhaṃ so sukhaṃ (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) ma. ni. 3.364 aṭṭhakathāṭīkā oloketabbā ce vedanaṃ vedayati, visaṃyutto naṃ vedayati; dukkhaṃ ce vedanaṃ vedayati, visaṃyutto naṃ vedayati; adukkhamasukhaṃ ce vedanaṃ vedayati, visaṃyutto naṃ vedayati. So kāyapariyantikaṃ vedanaṃ vedayamāno ‘kāyapariyantikaṃ vedanaṃ vedayāmī’ti pajānāti, jīvitapariyantikaṃ vedanaṃ vedayamāno ‘jīvitapariyantikaṃ vedanaṃ vedayāmī’ti pajānāti, ‘kāyassa bhedā uddhaṃ jīvitapariyādānā idheva sabbavedayitāni anabhinanditāni sītībhavissantī’ti pajānāti”.

If he feels a pleasant feeling, he feels it detached. If he feels a painful feeling, he feels it detached. If he feels a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he feels it detached. Experiencing a feeling limited to the body, he understands: ‘I am experiencing a feeling limited to the body.’ Experiencing a feeling limited to life, he understands: ‘I am experiencing a feeling limited to life.’ He understands: ‘After the breakup of the body, with the termination of life, all feelings that are experienced, not being delighted in, will become cool right here.’

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, telañca paṭicca, vaṭṭiñca paṭicca telappadīpo [T 5.0405] jhāyeyya, tasseva telassa ca vaṭṭiyā ca pariyādānā anāhāro nibbāyeyya; evameva kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu kāyapariyantikaṃ [P 5.0320] vedanaṃ vedayamāno ‘kāyapariyantikaṃ vedanaṃ vedayāmī’ti pajānāti, jīvitapariyantikaṃ vedanaṃ vedayamāno ‘jīvitapariyantikaṃ vedanaṃ vedayāmī’ti pajānāti, ‘kāyassa bhedā uddhaṃ jīvitapariyādānā idheva sabbavedayitāni anabhinanditāni sītībhavissantī’ti pajānātī”ti. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

Just as, bhikkhus, an oil lamp might burn in dependence on oil and a wick, and from the exhaustion of that oil and wick, being without fuel, it would be extinguished; so too, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu experiencing a feeling limited to the body understands: ‘I am experiencing a feeling limited to the body.’ Experiencing a feeling limited to life, he understands: ‘I am experiencing a feeling limited to life.’ He understands: ‘After the breakup of the body, with the termination of life, all feelings that are experienced, not being delighted in, will become cool right here.’ The eighth.

9. Vesālīsuttaṃ

9. The Discourse at Vesālī

985. Evaṃ me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā vesāliyaṃ viharati mahāvane kūṭāgārasālāyaṃ. Tena kho pana samayena bhagavā bhikkhūnaṃ anekapariyāyena asubhakathaṃ katheti, asubhāya vaṇṇaṃ bhāsati, asubhabhāvanāya vaṇṇaṃ bhāsati.

985. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Vesālī in the Great Wood, in the Hall with the Peaked Roof. At that time the Blessed One was speaking to the bhikkhus in many ways about the non-beautiful, praising the non-beautiful, praising the development of the meditation on the non-beautiful.

Atha kho bhagavā bhikkhū āmantesi – “icchāmahaṃ, bhikkhave, aḍḍhamāsaṃ paṭisallīyituṃ. Nāmhi kenaci upasaṅkamitabbo, aññatra ekena piṇḍapātanīhārakenā”ti. “Evaṃ, bhante”ti kho te bhikkhū bhagavato paṭissutvā nāssudha koci bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamati, aññatra ekena piṇḍapātanīhārakena.

Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “I wish, bhikkhus, to go into seclusion for half a month.
