Nor do those venerable ones, in this very life, realize for themselves with higher knowledge the goal of asceticism or the goal of brahminhood and abide in it.

“Ye ca kho keci, bhikkhave, samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā ‘idaṃ dukkha’nti yathābhūtaṃ pajānanti, ‘ayaṃ dukkhasamudayo’ti yathābhūtaṃ pajānanti, ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodho’ti yathābhūtaṃ pajānanti, ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā’ti yathābhūtaṃ pajānanti, te kho me, bhikkhave, samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā [M 3.0379] vā samaṇesu ceva samaṇasammatā brāhmaṇesu ca brāhmaṇasammatā, te [P 5.0433] ca panāyasmanto sāmaññatthañca brahmaññatthañca diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharantī”ti.

Bhikkhus, whatever ascetics or brahmins there may be who understand as it really is, ‘This is suffering,’ who understand as it really is, ‘This is the origin of suffering,’ who understand as it really is, ‘This is the cessation of suffering,’ and who understand as it really is, ‘This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering,’ they, bhikkhus, are acknowledged as ascetics among ascetics and as brahmins among brahmins. And those venerable ones, having realized it for themselves with higher knowledge, dwell having attained the goal of asceticism and the goal of brahminhood in this very life.

Idamavoca bhagavā. Idaṃ vatvāna sugato athāparaṃ etadavoca satthā –

The Blessed One said this. Having said this, the Well-Gone One, the Teacher, then said further:

“Ye dukkhaṃ nappajānanti, atho dukkhassa sambhavaṃ;

Yattha ca sabbaso dukkhaṃ, asesaṃ uparujjhati.

“Those who do not understand suffering, and also the origin of suffering, and where suffering ceases completely, without remainder;

“Tañca maggaṃ na jānanti, dukkhūpasamagāminaṃ;

Cetovimuttihīnā [T 5.0543] te, atho paññāvimuttiyā;

Abhabbā te antakiriyāya, te ve jātijarūpagā.

and do not know the path leading to the stilling of suffering. They are devoid of liberation of mind and also of liberation by wisdom; they are incapable of making an end; indeed, they are subject to birth and aging.

“Ye [V 3.0496] ca dukkhaṃ pajānanti, atho dukkhassa sambhavaṃ;

Yattha ca sabbaso dukkhaṃ, asesaṃ uparujjhati.

“But those who understand suffering, and also the origin of suffering, and where suffering ceases completely, without remainder;

“Tañca maggaṃ pajānanti, dukkhūpasamagāminaṃ;

Cetovimuttisampannā, atho paññāvimuttiyā;

Sabbā te antakiriyāya, na te jātijarūpagā”ti. dutiyaṃ;

and understand the path leading to the stilling of suffering. Endowed with liberation of mind and also with liberation by wisdom, they are capable of making an end; they are not subject to birth and aging.” Second.

3. Sammāsambuddhasuttaṃ

3. The Discourse on the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One

1093. Sāvatthinidānaṃ. Cattārimāni, bhikkhave, ariyasaccāni. Katamāni cattāri? Dukkhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ…pe… dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā ariyasaccaṃ – imāni kho, bhikkhave, cattāri ariyasaccāni. Imesaṃ kho, bhikkhave, catunnaṃ ariyasaccānaṃ yathābhūtaṃ abhisambuddhattā tathāgato ‘arahaṃ sammāsambuddho’ti vuccati.

1093. At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, there are these four noble truths. Which four? The noble truth of suffering… the noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering—these, bhikkhus, are the four noble truths. It is, bhikkhus, because the Tathāgata has fully awakened to these four noble truths as they really are that he is called ‘the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.’”

“Tasmātiha, bhikkhave, ‘idaṃ dukkha’nti yogo karaṇīyo…pe… ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā’ti yogo karaṇīyo”ti. Tatiyaṃ.

“Therefore, bhikkhus, an exertion should be made thus: ‘This is suffering.’… an exertion should be made thus: ‘This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.’” Third.

4. Arahantasuttaṃ

4. The Discourse on Arahants

1094. Sāvatthinidānaṃ. Ye hi keci, bhikkhave, atītamaddhānaṃ arahanto sammāsambuddhā yathābhūtaṃ abhisambujjhiṃsu, sabbe te cattāri ariyasaccāni yathābhūtaṃ [M 3.0380] abhisambujjhiṃsu. Ye [P 5.0434] hi yepi hi (bahūsu) keci, bhikkhave, anāgatamaddhānaṃ arahanto sammāsambuddhā yathābhūtaṃ abhisambujjhissanti, sabbe te cattāri ariyasaccāni yathābhūtaṃ abhisambujjhissanti. Ye hi keci, bhikkhave, etarahi arahanto sammāsambuddhā yathābhūtaṃ abhisambujjhanti, sabbe [T 5.0544] te cattāri ariyasaccāni yathābhūtaṃ abhisambujjhanti.

1094. At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, whatever Arahants, Perfectly Self-Enlightened Ones, in the past thoroughly understood as it truly is, all of them thoroughly understood the four Noble Truths as they truly are. Whatever Arahants, Perfectly Self-Enlightened Ones, in the future will thoroughly understand as it truly is, all of them will thoroughly understand the four Noble Truths as they truly are. Whatever Arahants, Perfectly Self-Enlightened Ones, in the present thoroughly understand as it truly is, all of them thoroughly understand the four Noble Truths as they truly are.”

“Katamāni cattāri? Dukkhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ, dukkhasamudayaṃ ariyasaccaṃ, dukkhanirodhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ, dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā ariyasaccaṃ. Ye hi, keci, bhikkhave, atītamaddhānaṃ [V 3.0497] arahanto sammāsambuddhā yathābhūtaṃ abhisambujjhiṃsu…pe… abhisambujjhissanti…pe… abhisambujjhanti, sabbe te imāni cattāri ariyasaccāni yathābhūtaṃ abhisambujjhanti.

“What are the four? The Noble Truth of suffering, the Noble Truth of the origin of suffering, the Noble Truth of the cessation of suffering, the Noble Truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering. Whatever Arahants, Perfectly Self-Enlightened Ones, in the past thoroughly understood… or will thoroughly understand… or are thoroughly understanding, all of them thoroughly understand these four Noble Truths as they truly are.”

“Tasmātiha, bhikkhave, ‘idaṃ dukkha’nti yogo karaṇīyo…pe… ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā’ti yogo karaṇīyo”ti. Catutthaṃ.

“Therefore, bhikkhus, an exertion should be made thus: ‘This is suffering.’… an exertion should be made thus: ‘This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.’” The Fourth.

5. Āsavakkhayasuttaṃ

5. The Discourse on the Destruction of the Taints

1095. “Jānatohaṃ, bhikkhave, passato āsavānaṃ khayaṃ vadāmi, no ajānato apassato. Kiñca, bhikkhave, jānato passato āsavānaṃ khayo hoti? ‘Idaṃ dukkha’nti, bhikkhave, jānato passato āsavānaṃ khayo hoti, ‘ayaṃ dukkhasamudayo’ti jānato passato āsavānaṃ khayo hoti, ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodho’ti jānato passato āsavānaṃ khayo hoti, ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā’ti jānato passato āsavānaṃ khayo hoti. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, jānato evaṃ passato āsavānaṃ khayo hoti.

1095. “Bhikkhus, I declare the destruction of the taints for one who knows and sees, not for one who does not know or see. And for one who knows and sees what, bhikkhus, does the destruction of the taints occur? ‘This is suffering’—for one who knows and sees this, bhikkhus, the destruction of the taints occurs. ‘This is the origin of suffering’—for one who knows and sees this, the destruction of the taints occurs. ‘This is the cessation of suffering’—for one who knows and sees this, the destruction of the taints occurs. ‘This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering’—for one who knows and sees this, the destruction of the taints occurs. Thus, bhikkhus, for one who knows thus and sees thus, the destruction of the taints occurs.”

“Tasmātiha, bhikkhave, ‘idaṃ dukkha’nti yogo karaṇīyo…pe… ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā’ti yogo karaṇīyo”ti. Pañcamaṃ.

“Therefore, bhikkhus, in this Dispensation, an exertion should be made thus: ‘This is suffering.’ … an exertion should be made thus: ‘This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.’” The fifth.

6. Mittasuttaṃ

6. The Discourse on Friends

1096. “Ye hi keci, bhikkhave, anukampeyyātha, ye ca sotabbaṃ maññeyyuṃ – mittā vā amaccā vā ñātī vā sālohitā vā [P 5.0435] – te vo, bhikkhave, catunnaṃ ariyasaccānaṃ yathābhūtaṃ abhisamayāya samādapetabbā nivesetabbā [T 5.0545] patiṭṭhāpetabbā.

1096. “Bhikkhus, whomever you might have compassion for, and whoever might think it worth listening to—whether friends, companions, relatives, or kinsmen—they should be exhorted, grounded, and established by you in the thorough understanding of the four noble truths as they really are.”

“Katamesaṃ [M 3.0381] catunnaṃ? Dukkhassa ariyasaccassa, dukkhasamudayassa ariyasaccassa, dukkhanirodhassa ariyasaccassa, dukkhanirodhagāminiyā paṭipadāya ariyasaccassa. Ye hi keci, bhikkhave, anukampeyyātha, ye ca sotabbaṃ maññeyyuṃ – mittā vā amaccā vā ñātī vā [V 3.0498] sālohitā vā te vo, bhikkhave, imesaṃ catunnaṃ ariyasaccānaṃ yathābhūtaṃ abhisamayāya samādapetabbā nivesetabbā patiṭṭhāpetabbā.

“Of which four? Of the noble truth of suffering, of the noble truth of the origin of suffering, of the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and of the noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering. Bhikkhus, whomever you might have compassion for, and whoever might think it worth listening to—whether friends, companions, relatives, or kinsmen—they should be exhorted, grounded, and established by you in the thorough understanding of these four noble truths as they really are.”

“Tasmātiha, bhikkhave, ‘idaṃ dukkha’nti yogo karaṇīyo…pe… ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā’ti yogo karaṇīyo”ti. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

“Therefore, bhikkhus, in this Dispensation, an exertion should be made thus: ‘This is suffering.’ … an exertion should be made thus: ‘This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.’” The sixth.

7. Tathasuttaṃ

7. The Discourse on the Real

1097. “Cattārimāni, bhikkhave, ariyasaccāni. Katamāni cattāri? Dukkhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ, dukkhasamudayaṃ ariyasaccaṃ, dukkhanirodhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ, dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā ariyasaccaṃ – imāni kho, bhikkhave, cattāri ariyasaccāni tathāni avitathāni anaññathāni; tasmā ‘ariyasaccānī’ti vuccanti.

1097. “Bhikkhus, there are these four noble truths. Which four? The noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering. Indeed, bhikkhus, these four noble truths are real, not unreal, and not otherwise; therefore, they are called ‘noble truths.’”

“Tasmātiha, bhikkhave, ‘idaṃ dukkha’nti yogo karaṇīyo…pe… ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā’ti yogo karaṇīyo”ti. Sattamaṃ.

“Therefore, bhikkhus, in this Dispensation, an exertion should be made thus: ‘This is suffering.’ … an exertion should be made thus: ‘This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering.’” The seventh.

8. Lokasuttaṃ

8. The Discourse on the World

1098. “Cattārimāni, bhikkhave, ariyasaccāni. Katamāni cattāri? Dukkhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ, dukkhasamudayaṃ ariyasaccaṃ, dukkhanirodhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ, dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā ariyasaccaṃ. Sadevake loke samārake sabrahmake sassamaṇabrāhmaṇiyā pajāya sadevamanussāya tathāgato ariyo; tasmā ‘ariyasaccānī’ti vuccanti”.

1098. “Bhikkhus, there are these four Noble Truths. What are the four? The Noble Truth of suffering, the Noble Truth of the origin of suffering, the Noble Truth of the cessation of suffering, and the Noble Truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering. In this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, with its devas and humans, the Tathāgata is noble; therefore, they are called ‘Noble Truths.’”

“Tasmātiha, bhikkhave, ‘idaṃ dukkha’nti yogo karaṇīyo…pe… ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā’ti yogo [T 5.0546] karaṇīyo”ti. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

“Therefore, bhikkhus, in this Dispensation, effort should be made thus: ‘This is suffering’… effort should be made thus: ‘This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering.’” The eighth.

9. Pariññeyyasuttaṃ

9. The Discourse on What Is to Be Fully Understood

1099. “Cattārimāni[V 3.0499][P 5.0436], bhikkhave, ariyasaccāni. Katamāni cattāri? Dukkhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ, dukkhasamudayaṃ ariyasaccaṃ, dukkhanirodhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ, dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā ariyasaccaṃ – imāni kho, bhikkhave, cattāri ariyasaccāni. Imesaṃ [M 3.0382] kho, bhikkhave, catunnaṃ ariyasaccānaṃ atthi ariyasaccaṃ pariññeyyaṃ, atthi ariyasaccaṃ pahātabbaṃ, atthi ariyasaccaṃ sacchikātabbaṃ, atthi ariyasaccaṃ bhāvetabbaṃ.

1099. “Bhikkhus, there are these four Noble Truths. What are the four? The Noble Truth of suffering, the Noble Truth of the origin of suffering, the Noble Truth of the cessation of suffering, and the Noble Truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering. These, bhikkhus, are the four Noble Truths. Among these four Noble Truths, bhikkhus, there is a Noble Truth to be fully understood, there is a Noble Truth to be abandoned, there is a Noble Truth to be realized, and there is a Noble Truth to be developed.”

“Katamañca, bhikkhave, ariyasaccaṃ pariññeyyaṃ? Dukkhaṃ, bhikkhave, ariyasaccaṃ pariññeyyaṃ, dukkhasamudayaṃ ariyasaccaṃ pahātabbaṃ, dukkhanirodhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ sacchikātabbaṃ, dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā ariyasaccaṃ bhāvetabbaṃ.

“And which, bhikkhus, is the Noble Truth to be fully understood? The Noble Truth of suffering, bhikkhus, is to be fully understood. The Noble Truth of the origin of suffering is to be abandoned. The Noble Truth of the cessation of suffering is to be realized. The Noble Truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering is to be developed.”

“Tasmātiha, bhikkhave, ‘idaṃ dukkha’nti yogo karaṇīyo…pe… ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā’ti yogo karaṇīyo”ti. Navamaṃ.

“Therefore, bhikkhus, in this Dispensation, effort should be made thus: ‘This is suffering’… effort should be made thus: ‘This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering.’” The ninth.

10. Gavampatisuttaṃ

10. The Discourse on Gavampati

1100. Ekaṃ samayaṃ sambahulā therā bhikkhū cetesu cetiyesu (syā.) viharanti sahañcanike sahajaniye (sī. syā. kaṃ.). Tena kho pana samayena sambahulānaṃ therānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ pacchābhattaṃ piṇḍapātapaṭikkantānaṃ maṇḍalamāḷe sannisinnānaṃ sannipatitānaṃ ayamantarākathā udapādi – “yo nu kho, āvuso, dukkhaṃ passati dukkhasamudayampi so passati, dukkhanirodhampi passati, dukkhanirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadampi passatī”ti.

1100. On one occasion, a number of elder bhikkhus were dwelling among the Cetis at Sahañcani. Now at that time, after their meal, on returning from their alms-round, a number of elder bhikkhus had gathered and were sitting together in the pavilion, when this discussion arose among them: “Friends, does one who sees suffering also see the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the path leading to the cessation of suffering?”

Evaṃ vutte āyasmā gavampati thero gavampatitthero (syā. kaṃ.) bhikkhū etadavoca – “sammukhā [T 5.0547] metaṃ, āvuso, bhagavato sutaṃ, sammukhā paṭiggahitaṃ – ‘yo[P 5.0437], bhikkhave, dukkhaṃ passati dukkhasamudayampi so passati, dukkhanirodhampi passati, dukkhanirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadampi passati. Yo dukkhasamudayaṃ passati dukkhampi so passati, dukkhanirodhampi passati, dukkhanirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadampi passati. Yo dukkhanirodhaṃ passati dukkhampi so passati, dukkhasamudayampi passati, dukkhanirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadampi [V 3.0500] passati. Yo dukkhanirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadaṃ passati dukkhampi so passati, dukkhasamudayampi passati, dukkhanirodhampi passatī’”ti. Dasamaṃ.

When this was said, the Venerable Gavampati, the elder, said to the elder bhikkhus: “Friends, I have heard this in the presence of the Blessed One, I have received it in his presence: ‘Bhikkhus, whoever sees suffering also sees the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the path leading to the cessation of suffering. Whoever sees the origin of suffering also sees suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the path leading to the cessation of suffering. Whoever sees the cessation of suffering also sees suffering, the origin of suffering, and the path leading to the cessation of suffering. Whoever sees the path leading to the cessation of suffering also sees suffering, the origin of suffering, and the cessation of suffering.’” The tenth.

Koṭigāmavaggo tatiyo.

The Third Chapter: The Koṭigāma Chapter

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary:

Dve vajjī sammāsambuddho, arahaṃ āsavakkhayo;

Mittaṃ tathā ca loko ca, pariññeyyaṃ gavampatīti.

Two on the Vajjis, the Perfectly Enlightened One, the Arahant, the Destruction of Taints; Friendship, the Real, the World, What Is to Be Fully Understood, and Gavampati.

4. Sīsapāvanavaggo

4. The Fourth Chapter: The Sīsapā Grove

1. Sīsapāvanasuttaṃ

1. The Discourse in the Sīsapā Grove

1101. Ekaṃ [T 5.0548][M 3.0383] samayaṃ bhagavā kosambiyaṃ viharati sīsapāvane siṃsapāvane (sī. pī.). Atha kho bhagavā parittāni sīsapāpaṇṇāni pāṇinā gahetvā bhikkhū āmantesi – “taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, katamaṃ nu kho bahutaraṃ – yāni vā mayā parittāni sīsapāpaṇṇāni pāṇinā gahitāni yadidaṃ upari sīsapāvane”ti? “Appamattakāni[P 5.0438], bhante, bhagavatā parittāni sīsapāpaṇṇāni pāṇinā gahitāni; atha kho etāneva bahutarāni yadidaṃ upari sīsapāvane”ti. “Evameva kho, bhikkhave, etadeva bahutaraṃ yaṃ vo mayā abhiññāya anakkhātaṃ. Kasmā cetaṃ, bhikkhave, mayā anakkhātaṃ? Na hetaṃ, bhikkhave, atthasaṃhitaṃ nādibrahmacariyakaṃ na nibbidāya na virāgāya na nirodhāya na upasamāya na abhiññāya na sambodhāya na nibbānāya saṃvattati; tasmā taṃ mayā anakkhātaṃ”.

1101. On one occasion, the Blessed One was dwelling in Kosambī, in the Sīsapā forest. Then the Blessed One, having taken a few Sīsapā leaves with his hand, addressed the bhikkhus: “What do you think, bhikkhus? Which is more numerous: these few Sīsapā leaves taken by me with my hand, or those which are in the Sīsapā forest above?” “Venerable Sir, the few Sīsapā leaves taken by the Blessed One with his hand are very few. Indeed, those which are in the Sīsapā forest above are far more numerous.” “Even so, bhikkhus, that which, having been directly known by me, has not been declared to you is far more. And why, bhikkhus, has this not been declared by me? Because, bhikkhus, it is not connected with benefit, it does not pertain to the fundamentals of the holy life, and it does not lead to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, to Nibbāna. Therefore, it has not been declared by me.”

“Kiñca, bhikkhave, mayā akkhātaṃ? ‘Idaṃ dukkha’nti, bhikkhave, mayā akkhātaṃ, ‘ayaṃ dukkhasamudayo’ti mayā akkhātaṃ, ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodho’ti mayā akkhātaṃ, ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā’ti mayā akkhātaṃ”.

“And what, bhikkhus, have I declared? I have declared, bhikkhus: ‘This is suffering.’ I have declared: ‘This is the origin of suffering.’ I have declared: ‘This is the cessation of suffering.’ I have declared: ‘This is the path of practice leading to the cessation of suffering.’”

“Kasmā [V 3.0501] cetaṃ, bhikkhave, mayā akkhātaṃ? Etañhi, bhikkhave, atthasaṃhitaṃ etaṃ ādibrahmacariyakaṃ etaṃ nibbidāya virāgāya nirodhāya upasamāya abhiññāya sambodhāya nibbānāya saṃvattati; tasmā taṃ mayā akkhātaṃ[T 5.0549].

“And why, bhikkhus, have I declared this? Because, bhikkhus, this is connected with benefit, this pertains to the fundamentals of the holy life, this leads to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, to Nibbāna. Therefore, I have declared it.”

“Tasmātiha, bhikkhave, ‘idaṃ dukkha’nti yogo karaṇīyo…pe… ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā’ti yogo karaṇīyo”ti. Paṭhamaṃ.

Therefore, monks, in this Dispensation, an exertion should be made thus: ‘This is suffering.’ … an exertion should be made thus: ‘This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.’ First.

2. Khadirapattasuttaṃ

2. Second: The Discourse on Acacia Leaves.

1102. “Yo, bhikkhave, evaṃ vadeyya – ‘ahaṃ dukkhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ yathābhūtaṃ anabhisamecca, dukkhasamudayaṃ ariyasaccaṃ yathābhūtaṃ anabhisamecca, dukkhanirodhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ yathābhūtaṃ anabhisamecca, dukkhanirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadaṃ ariyasaccaṃ yathābhūtaṃ anabhisamecca sammā dukkhassantaṃ karissāmī’ti – netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati.

1102. Monks, should anyone say thus: ‘Without having directly realized the noble truth of suffering as it really is, without having directly realized the noble truth of the origin of suffering as it really is, without having directly realized the noble truth of the cessation of suffering as it really is, without having directly realized the noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering as it really is, I will rightly make an end of suffering’—this is not possible.

“Seyyathāpi[M 3.0384], bhikkhave, yo evaṃ vadeyya – ‘ahaṃ khadirapattānaṃ vā saralapattānaṃ palāsapattānaṃ (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) vā āmalakapattānaṃ vā puṭaṃ [P 5.0439] karitvā udakaṃ vā tālapattaṃ vā āharissāmī’ti – netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati; evameva kho, bhikkhave, yo evaṃ vadeyya – ‘ahaṃ dukkhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ yathābhūtaṃ anabhisamecca…pe… dukkhanirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadaṃ ariyasaccaṃ yathābhūtaṃ anabhisamecca sammā dukkhassantaṃ karissāmī’ti – netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati.

Just as, monks, should someone say thus: ‘Having made a container of acacia leaves, or pine leaves, or myrobalan leaves, I will bring water or a bowl’—this is not possible; in this very same way, monks, should anyone say thus: ‘Without having directly realized the noble truth of suffering as it really is… without having directly realized the noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering as it really is, I will rightly make an end of suffering’—this is not possible.

“Yo ca kho, bhikkhave, evaṃ vadeyya – ‘ahaṃ dukkhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ yathābhūtaṃ abhisamecca, dukkhasamudayaṃ ariyasaccaṃ yathābhūtaṃ abhisamecca, dukkhanirodhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ yathābhūtaṃ abhisamecca, dukkhanirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadaṃ ariyasaccaṃ yathābhūtaṃ abhisamecca sammā dukkhassantaṃ karissāmī’ti – ṭhānametaṃ vijjati.

But whoever, monks, should say thus: ‘Having directly realized the noble truth of suffering as it really is, having directly realized the noble truth of the origin of suffering as it really is, having directly realized the noble truth of the cessation of suffering as it really is, having directly realized the noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering as it really is, I will rightly make an end of suffering’—this is possible.

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, yo evaṃ vadeyya – ‘ahaṃ padumapattānaṃ vā palāsapattānaṃ vā māluvapattānaṃ vā puṭaṃ karitvā udakaṃ vā tālapattaṃ vā āharissāmī’ti – ṭhānametaṃ vijjati; evameva kho, bhikkhave, yo evaṃ vadeyya – ‘ahaṃ dukkhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ yathābhūtaṃ abhisamecca [V 3.0502] …pe… dukkhanirodhagāminiṃ [T 5.0550] paṭipadaṃ ariyasaccaṃ yathābhūtaṃ abhisamecca sammā dukkhassantaṃ karissāmī’ti – ṭhānametaṃ vijjati.

Just as, monks, should someone say thus: ‘Having made a container of lotus leaves, or palāsa leaves, or māluvā leaves, I will bring water or a bowl’—this is possible; in this very same way, monks, should anyone say thus: ‘Having directly realized the noble truth of suffering as it really is… having directly realized the noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering as it really is, I will rightly make an end of suffering’—this is possible.

“Tasmātiha, bhikkhave, ‘idaṃ dukkha’nti yogo karaṇīyo…pe… ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā’ti yogo karaṇīyo”ti. Dutiyaṃ.

Therefore, monks, in this Dispensation, an exertion should be made thus: ‘This is suffering.’ … an exertion should be made thus: ‘This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.’ Second.

3. Daṇḍasuttaṃ

3. Third: The Discourse on the Stick.

1103. “Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, daṇḍo uparivehāsaṃ khitto sakimpi mūlena nipatati, sakimpi aggena nipatati; evameva kho, bhikkhave, avijjānīvaraṇā sattā taṇhāsaṃyojanā sandhāvantā saṃsarantā taṇhāsaṃyojanabandhā sandhāvatā (ka.) sakimpi asmā lokā paraṃ lokaṃ gacchanti, sakimpi parasmā lokā imaṃ lokaṃ āgacchanti. Taṃ kissa hetu? Adiṭṭhattā, bhikkhave, catunnaṃ ariyasaccānaṃ. Katamesaṃ catunnaṃ? Dukkhassa ariyasaccassa…pe… dukkhanirodhagāminiyā paṭipadāya ariyasaccassa.

1103. Just as, monks, a stick thrown up into the air falls sometimes on its base and sometimes on its tip; in the very same way, monks, beings veiled by ignorance and bound by the fetter of craving, transmigrating and wandering on, sometimes go from this world to another world, and sometimes come from another world to this world. For what reason is that? Because, monks, of not having seen the Four Noble Truths. Which four? The Noble Truth of suffering … the Noble Truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.

“Tasmātiha[P 5.0440], bhikkhave, ‘idaṃ dukkha’nti yogo karaṇīyo…pe… ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā’ti yogo karaṇīyo”ti. Tatiyaṃ.

Therefore, monks, in this Dispensation, an exertion should be made thus: ‘This is suffering.’ … an exertion should be made thus: ‘This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.’ Third.

4. Celasuttaṃ

4. Fourth: The Discourse on Cloth.

1104. “Āditte[M 3.0385], bhikkhave, cele vā sīse vā kimassa karaṇīya”nti? “Āditte, bhante, cele vā sīse vā, tasseva celassa vā sīsassa vā nibbāpanāya adhimatto chando ca vāyāmo ca ussāho ca ussoḷhī ca appaṭivānī ca sati ca sampajaññañca karaṇīya”nti.

1104. Monks, if one's cloth or head were on fire, what should be done?” “Venerable sir, if one's cloth or head were on fire, for the extinguishing of that very cloth or head, extraordinary desire, effort, exertion, endeavor, perseverance, mindfulness, and clear comprehension should be applied.”

“Ādittaṃ, bhikkhave, celaṃ vā sīsaṃ vā ajjhupekkhitvā amanasikaritvā anabhisametānaṃ catunnaṃ ariyasaccānaṃ yathābhūtaṃ abhisamayāya adhimatto chando ca vāyāmo ca ussāho [V 3.0503] ca ussoḷhī ca appaṭivānī ca sati [T 5.0551] ca sampajaññañca karaṇīyaṃ. Katamesaṃ catunnaṃ? Dukkhassa ariyasaccassa…pe… dukkhanirodhagāminiyā paṭipadāya ariyasaccassa.

Monks, having disregarded and paid no attention to a burning cloth or head, for the direct realization, as it truly is, of the Four Noble Truths that have not yet been directly realized, extraordinary desire, effort, exertion, endeavor, perseverance, mindfulness, and clear comprehension should be applied. Which four? The Noble Truth of suffering … the Noble Truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.

“Tasmātiha, bhikkhave, ‘idaṃ dukkha’nti yogo karaṇīyo…pe… ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā’ti yogo karaṇīyo”ti. Catutthaṃ.

Therefore, monks, in this Dispensation, an exertion should be made thus: ‘This is suffering.’ … an exertion should be made thus: ‘This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.’ Fourth.

5. Sattisatasuttaṃ

5. Fifth: The Discourse on the Hundred Spears.

1105. “Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, puriso vassasatāyuko vassasatajīvī. Tamenaṃ evaṃ vadeyya – ‘ehambho purisa, pubbaṇhasamayaṃ taṃ sattisatena hanissanti, majjhanhikasamayaṃ sattisatena hanissanti, sāyanhasamayaṃ sattisatena hanissanti. So kho tvaṃ, ambho purisa, divase divase tīhi tīhi sattisatehi haññamāno vassasatāyuko vassasatajīvī vassasatassa accayena anabhisametāni cattāri ariyasaccāni [P 5.0441] abhisamessasī’”ti.

1105. Monks, suppose there were a man with a life span of a hundred years, living for a hundred years. And someone were to say to him: ‘Come, good man, in the morning they will strike you with a hundred spears, at midday they will strike you with a hundred spears, and in the evening they will strike you with a hundred spears. And you, good man, being struck day after day by three hundred spears, with a life span of a hundred years, living for a hundred years, at the end of a hundred years you will realize the four noble truths that you have not yet realized.’”

“Atthavasikena, bhikkhave, kulaputtena alaṃ upagantuṃ. Taṃ kissa hetu? Anamataggoyaṃ, bhikkhave, saṃsāro; pubbā koṭi nappaññāyati sattippahārānaṃ asippahārānaṃ usuppahārānaṃ pharasuppahārānaṃ asippahārānaṃ pharasuppahārānaṃ (ka.). Evañcetaṃ, bhikkhave, assa. Na kho panāhaṃ, bhikkhave, saha dukkhena, saha domanassena catunnaṃ ariyasaccānaṃ abhisamayaṃ vadāmi; api cāhaṃ, bhikkhave, sahāva sukhena, sahāva somanassena catunnaṃ ariyasaccānaṃ abhisamayaṃ vadāmi. Katamesaṃ catunnaṃ? Dukkhassa ariyasaccassa…pe… dukkhanirodhagāminiyā paṭipadāya ariyasaccassa.

A clansman who desires his own welfare, monks, should accept this. For what reason? This saṃsāra, monks, is without discoverable beginning; a first point is not discerned of blows from spears, blows from swords, blows from arrows, and blows from axes. Even so, monks, would this be. Indeed, monks, I do not declare the realization of the four Noble Truths to be together with suffering and sorrow; rather, monks, I declare the realization of the four Noble Truths to be only together with happiness and joy. Of which four? Of the Noble Truth of suffering… of the Noble Truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering.

“Tasmātiha[M 3.0386], bhikkhave, ‘idaṃ dukkha’nti yogo karaṇīyo…pe… ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā’ti yogo karaṇīyo”ti. Pañcamaṃ.

“Therefore, monks, in this Dispensation, an exertion should be made thus: ‘This is suffering.’… an exertion should be made thus: ‘This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering.’” Fifth.

6. Pāṇasuttaṃ

6. The Discourse on Living Beings

1106. “Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, puriso yaṃ imasmiṃ jambudīpe tiṇakaṭṭhasākhāpalāsaṃ [T 5.0552] tacchetvā ekajjhaṃ saṃhareyya; ekajjhaṃ saṃharitvā sūlaṃ kareyya. Sūlaṃ karitvā ye mahāsamudde mahantakā [V 3.0504] pāṇā te mahantakesu sūlesu āvuneyya, ye mahāsamudde majjhimakā pāṇā te majjhimakesu sūlesu āvuneyya, ye mahāsamudde sukhumakā pāṇā te sukhumakesu sūlesu āvuneyya. Apariyādinnā ca, bhikkhave, mahāsamudde oḷārikā pāṇā assu.

1106. “Monks, suppose a man were to cut all the grass, wood, branches, and leaves in this Jambudīpa and gather them into a single pile. Having gathered them into a single pile, he would make stakes. Having made stakes, he would impale the large beings in the great ocean on large stakes, the medium-sized beings on medium-sized stakes, and the small beings on small stakes. And yet, monks, the large beings in the great ocean would not be exhausted.

“Atha imasmiṃ jambudīpe tiṇakaṭṭhasākhāpalāsaṃ parikkhayaṃ pariyādānaṃ gaccheyya. Ito bahutarā kho, bhikkhave, mahāsamudde sukhumakā pāṇā, ye na sukarā sūlesu āvunituṃ. Taṃ kissa hetu? Sukhumattā[P 5.0442], bhikkhave, attabhāvassa. Evaṃ mahā kho, bhikkhave, apāyo. Evaṃ mahantasmā kho, bhikkhave, apāyasmā parimutto diṭṭhisampanno puggalo ‘idaṃ dukkha’nti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti…pe… ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā’ti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti.

“Then the grass, wood, branches, and leaves in this Jambudīpa would come to an end, to utter consumption. Far more numerous than these, monks, are the minute beings in the great ocean, which are not easy to impale upon stakes. What is the reason for that? Because of the minuteness of their individual existence, monks. So vast, monks, is the plane of misery. Freed from such a vast plane of misery, monks, is a person accomplished in view, who understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’ … ‘This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering.’

“Tasmātiha, bhikkhave, ‘idaṃ dukkha’nti yogo karaṇīyo…pe… ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā’ti yogo karaṇīyo”ti. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

“Therefore, monks, in this Dispensation, an exertion should be made thus: ‘This is suffering’ … an exertion should be made thus: ‘This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering.’” Sixth.

7. Paṭhamasūriyasuttaṃ

7. The First Discourse on the Sun

1107. “Sūriyassa suriyassa (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.), bhikkhave, udayato etaṃ pubbaṅgamaṃ etaṃ pubbanimittaṃ, yadidaṃ – aruṇuggaṃ. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno catunnaṃ ariyasaccānaṃ yathābhūtaṃ abhisamayāya etaṃ pubbaṅgamaṃ etaṃ pubbanimittaṃ, yadidaṃ – sammādiṭṭhi. Tassetaṃ bhikkhave, bhikkhuno pāṭikaṅkhaṃ – ‘idaṃ dukkha’nti yathābhūtaṃ pajānissati…pe… ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā’ti yathābhūtaṃ pajānissati.

1107. “Monks, for the rising sun, this is the forerunner, this is the precursor, that is, the rising of the dawn. Even so, monks, for a monk, for the direct realization of the Four Noble Truths as they really are, this is the forerunner, this is the precursor, that is, right view. For that monk, monks, this is to be expected: he will understand as it really is, ‘This is suffering’ … ‘This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering.’

“Tasmātiha, bhikkhave, ‘idaṃ dukkha’nti [T 5.0553] yogo karaṇīyo…pe… ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā’ti yogo karaṇīyo”ti. Sattamaṃ.

“Therefore, monks, in this Dispensation, an exertion should be made thus: ‘This is suffering.’… an exertion should be made thus: ‘This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering.’” Seventh.

8. Dutiyasūriyasuttaṃ

8. The Second Discourse on the Sun

1108. “Yāvakīvañca[M 3.0387], bhikkhave, candimasūriyā loke nuppajjanti, neva tāva mahato ālokassa pātubhāvo hoti mahato obhāsassa. Andhatamaṃ tadā hoti andhakāratimisā[V 3.0505]. Neva tāva rattindivā rattidivā (ka.) paññāyanti, na māsaddhamāsā paññāyanti, na utusaṃvaccharā paññāyanti.

1108. “For as long, monks, as the moon and sun do not arise in the world, for so long there is no manifestation of great light, of great radiance. Then there is blinding darkness, a mass of darkness. For so long, night and day are not discerned, nor are months and half-months discerned, nor are seasons and years discerned.

“Yato ca kho, bhikkhave, candimasūriyā loke uppajjanti, atha mahato ālokassa pātubhāvo hoti mahato obhāsassa. Neva [P 5.0443] andhakāratamaṃ tadā hoti na andhakāratimisā. Atha rattindivā paññāyanti, māsaddhamāsā paññāyanti, utusaṃvaccharā paññāyanti. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, yāvakīvañca tathāgato loke nuppajjati arahaṃ sammāsambuddho, neva tāva mahato ālokassa pātubhāvo hoti mahato obhāsassa. Andhatamaṃ tadā hoti andhakāratimisā. Neva tāva catunnaṃ ariyasaccānaṃ ācikkhaṇā hoti desanā paññāpanā paṭṭhapanā vivaraṇā vibhajanā uttānīkammaṃ.

“But when, monks, the moon and sun arise in the world, then there is the manifestation of great light, of great radiance. Then there is no blinding darkness, no mass of darkness. Then night and day are discerned, months and half-months are discerned, and seasons and years are discerned. In the same way, monks, for as long as a Tathāgata—an Arahant, a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One—does not arise in the world, there is no manifestation of great light, of great radiance. Then there is blinding darkness, a mass of darkness. Then there is no declaring, teaching, making known, establishing, disclosing, analyzing, or making plain of the Four Noble Truths.

“Yato ca kho, bhikkhave, tathāgato loke uppajjati arahaṃ sammāsambuddho, atha mahato ālokassa pātubhāvo hoti mahato obhāsassa. Neva andhatamaṃ tadā hoti na andhakāratimisā. Atha kho catunnaṃ ariyasaccānaṃ ācikkhaṇā hoti desanā paññāpanā paṭṭhapanā vivaraṇā vibhajanā uttānīkammaṃ. Katamesaṃ catunnaṃ? Dukkhassa ariyasaccassa…pe… dukkhanirodhagāminiyā paṭipadāya ariyasaccassa[T 5.0554].

“But when, monks, a Tathāgata—an Arahant, a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One—arises in the world, then there is the manifestation of great light, of great radiance. Then there is no blinding darkness, no mass of darkness. Then there is the declaring, teaching, making known, establishing, disclosing, analyzing, and making plain of the Four Noble Truths. Of which four? Of the Noble Truth of suffering… of the Noble Truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering.

“Tasmātiha, bhikkhave, ‘idaṃ dukkha’nti yogo karaṇīyo…pe… ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā’ti yogo karaṇīyo”ti. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

“Therefore, monks, in this Dispensation, an exertion should be made thus: ‘This is suffering.’… an exertion should be made thus: ‘This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering.’” Eighth.

9. Indakhīlasuttaṃ

9. The Discourse on the City Pillar

1109. “Ye hi keci, bhikkhave, samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā ‘idaṃ dukkha’nti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānanti…pe… ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā’ti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānanti, te aññassa samaṇassa vā brāhmaṇassa vā mukhaṃ ullokenti olokenti (sī. syā.) – ‘ayaṃ nūna bhavaṃ jānaṃ jānāti, passaṃ passatī’”ti.

1109. “Monks, whatever ascetics or brahmins do not understand as it really is: ‘This is suffering’ … do not understand as it really is: ‘This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering,’ they look up to the face of another ascetic or brahmin, thinking: ‘Surely this venerable one knows what is to be known and sees what is to be seen.’

“Seyyathāpi[M 3.0388], bhikkhave, tūlapicu vā kappāsapicu vā lahuko vātūpādāno same bhūmibhāge [V 3.0506] nikkhitto. Tamenaṃ puratthimo [P 5.0444] vāto pacchimena saṃhareyya, pacchimo vāto puratthimena saṃhareyya, uttaro vāto dakkhiṇena saṃhareyya, dakkhiṇo vāto uttarena saṃhareyya. Taṃ kissa hetu? Lahukattā, bhikkhave, kappāsapicuno. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, ye hi keci samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā ‘idaṃ dukkha’nti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānanti…pe… ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā’ti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānanti, te aññassa samaṇassa vā brāhmaṇassa vā mukhaṃ ullokenti – ‘ayaṃ nūna bhavaṃ jānaṃ jānāti, passaṃ passatī’ti. Taṃ kissa hetu? Adiṭṭhattā, bhikkhave, catunnaṃ ariyasaccānaṃ.

“Just as, monks, a light tuft of silk-cotton or a tuft of cotton, being fuel for the wind, placed on a level stretch of ground, might be carried westward by an eastern wind, eastward by a western wind, southward by a northern wind, or northward by a southern wind. What is the reason for that? Because of the lightness, monks, of the cotton tuft. In the very same way, monks, whatever ascetics or brahmins do not understand as it really is: ‘This is suffering’ … do not understand as it really is: ‘This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering,’ they look up to the face of another ascetic or brahmin, thinking: ‘Surely this venerable one knows what is to be known and sees what is to be seen.’ What is the reason for that? Because, monks, of not having seen the Four Noble Truths.

“Ye ca kho keci, bhikkhave, samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā ‘idaṃ dukkha’nti yathābhūtaṃ pajānanti…pe… ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā’ti yathābhūtaṃ pajānanti, te na aññassa samaṇassa vā brāhmaṇassa [T 5.0555] vā mukhaṃ ullokenti – ‘ayaṃ nūna bhavaṃ jānaṃ jānāti, passaṃ passatī’”ti.

Whatever ascetics or brahmins, monks, understand as it really is: ‘This is suffering’ … understand as it really is: ‘This is the path of practice leading to the cessation of suffering,’ they do not look up to the face of another ascetic or brahmin, thinking: ‘Surely this venerable one knows what is to be known and sees what is to be seen.’

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, ayokhīlo vā indakhīlo vā gambhīranemo sunikhāto acalo asampakampī. Puratthimāya cepi disāya āgaccheyya bhusā vātavuṭṭhi, neva saṅkampeyya neva naṃ saṅkampeyya (sī. pī.) na sampakampeyya na sampacāleyya; pacchimāya cepi disāya…pe… uttarāya cepi disāya…pe… dakkhiṇāya cepi disāya āgaccheyya bhusā vātavuṭṭhi, neva saṅkampeyya na sampakampeyya na sampacāleyya. Taṃ kissa hetu? Gambhīrattā, bhikkhave, nemassa sunikhātattā indakhīlassa. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, ye ca kho keci samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā ‘idaṃ dukkha’nti yathābhūtaṃ pajānanti…pe… ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā’ti yathābhūtaṃ pajānanti, te na aññassa samaṇassa vā brāhmaṇassa vā mukhaṃ ullokenti – ‘ayaṃ nūna bhavaṃ jānaṃ jānāti, passaṃ passatī’ti. Taṃ kissa hetu? Sudiṭṭhattā, bhikkhave, catunnaṃ ariyasaccānaṃ. Katamesaṃ catunnaṃ? Dukkhassa [P 5.0445] ariyasaccassa…pe… dukkhanirodhagāminiyā paṭipadāya ariyasaccassa.

Just as, monks, an iron post or a gatepost has a deep foundation, is well-planted, immovable, and unshakable. Even if a fierce storm with rain were to come from the eastern direction, it would not shake, tremble, or sway; if from the western direction... from the northern direction... or if a fierce storm with rain were to come from the southern direction, it would not shake, tremble, or sway. For what reason? Because, monks, of the depth of the foundation and because the gatepost is well-planted. In the same way, monks, whatever ascetics or brahmins understand as it really is: ‘This is suffering’ … ‘This is the path of practice leading to the cessation of suffering,’ they do not look up to the face of another ascetic or brahmin, thinking: ‘Surely this venerable one knows what is to be known and sees what is to be seen.’ For what reason? Because, monks, the Four Noble Truths have been well seen. Which four? The Noble Truth of suffering… the Noble Truth of the path of practice leading to the cessation of suffering.

“Tasmātiha, bhikkhave, ‘idaṃ dukkha’nti yogo karaṇīyo…pe… ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā’ti yogo karaṇīyo”ti. Navamaṃ.

Therefore, monks, you should apply effort towards this: ‘This is suffering’… you should apply effort towards this: ‘This is the path of practice leading to the cessation of suffering.’ Ninth.

10. Vādatthikasuttaṃ

10. The Discourse on the Debater

1110. “Yo [V 3.0507][M 3.0389] hi koci, bhikkhave, bhikkhu ‘idaṃ dukkha’nti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti…pe… ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā’ti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, puratthimāya cepi disāya āgaccheyya samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā vādatthiko [T 5.0556] vādagavesī – ‘vādamassa āropessāmī’ti, taṃ vata sahadhammena saṅkampessati vā sampakampessati vā sampacālessati vāti – netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati. Pacchimāya cepi disāya…pe… uttarāya cepi disāya…pe… dakkhiṇāya cepi disāya āgaccheyya samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā vādatthiko vādagavesī – ‘vādamassa āropessāmī’ti, taṃ vata sahadhammena saṅkampessati vā sampakampessati vā sampacālessati vāti – netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati.

1110. Monks, whatever monk understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’… ‘This is the path of practice leading to the cessation of suffering,’ then if an ascetic or a brahmin should come from the eastern direction, desiring a debate, searching for a debate, thinking: ‘I will challenge his view,’ that he could, with just cause, cause him to shake, tremble, or be agitated—this is not possible. If from the western direction… if from the northern direction… if from the southern direction an ascetic or a brahmin should come, desiring a debate, searching for a debate, thinking: ‘I will challenge his view,’ that he could, with just cause, cause him to shake, tremble, or be agitated—this is not possible.

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, silāyūpo soḷasa kukkuko. Tassassu aṭṭha kukku heṭṭhā nemaṅgamā, aṭṭha kukku uparinemassa. Puratthimāya cepi disāya āgaccheyya bhusā vātavuṭṭhi, neva saṅkampeyya na sampakampeyya na sampacāleyya; pacchimāya cepi disāya…pe… uttarāya cepi disāya…pe… dakkhiṇāya cepi disāya āgaccheyya bhusā vātavuṭṭhi, neva saṅkampeyya na sampakampeyya na sampacāleyya. Taṃ kissa hetu? Gambhīrattā, bhikkhave, nemassa sunikhātattā silāyūpassa. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, yo hi koci bhikkhu ‘idaṃ dukkha’nti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti…pe… ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā’ti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti; puratthimāya [P 5.0446] cepi disāya āgaccheyya samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā vādatthiko vādagavesī ‘vādamassa āropessāmī’ti, taṃ vata sahadhammena saṅkampessati vā sampakampessati vā sampacālessati vāti – netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati. Pacchimāya cepi disāya…pe… uttarāya [T 5.0557] cepi disāya…pe… dakkhiṇāya cepi disāya āgaccheyya samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā vādatthiko vādagavesī – ‘vādamassa āropessāmī’ti, taṃ vata sahadhammena saṅkampessati vā sampakampessati vā sampacālessati vāti – netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati. Taṃ kissa hetu? Sudiṭṭhattā, bhikkhave, catunnaṃ ariyasaccānaṃ. Katamesaṃ catunnaṃ? Dukkhassa ariyasaccassa…pe… dukkhanirodhagāminiyā paṭipadāya ariyasaccassa.

Monks, it is just as if there were a stone pillar sixteen cubits long. Eight cubits would be sunk into its foundation, and eight cubits would be above the foundation. If a fierce wind and rain were to come from the eastern direction, it would not shake, nor tremble, nor sway. If from the western direction… if from the northern direction… if from the southern direction a fierce wind and rain were to come, it would not shake, nor tremble, nor sway. For what reason? Because, monks, the foundation is deep and the stone pillar is well-planted. So too, monks, whatever monk understands according to reality, ‘This is suffering’… ‘This is the path of practice leading to the cessation of suffering’; if from the eastern direction an ascetic or a brahmin, desiring a debate, seeking a debate, should come thinking, ‘I will challenge his view,’ that he could rightfully cause him to shake, or cause him to tremble, or cause him to sway—this is not possible. If from the western direction… if from the northern direction… if from the southern direction an ascetic or a brahmin, desiring a debate, seeking a debate, should come thinking, ‘I will challenge his view,’ that he could rightfully cause him to shake, or cause him to tremble, or cause him to sway—this is not possible. For what reason? Because, monks, the Four Noble Truths are well-seen. Which four? The Noble Truth of Suffering… the Noble Truth of the path of practice leading to the cessation of suffering.

“Tasmātiha[V 3.0508], bhikkhave, ‘idaṃ dukkha’nti yogo karaṇīyo…pe… ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā’ti yogo karaṇīyo”ti. Dasamaṃ.

Therefore, monks, in this Dispensation, you should apply effort towards this: ‘This is suffering.’ … you should apply effort towards this: ‘This is the path of practice leading to the cessation of suffering.’ Tenth.

Sīsapāvanavaggo catuttho.

The fourth chapter, the Sīsapāvana Chapter.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary verse thereof:

Sīsapā [M 3.0390] khadiro daṇḍo, celā sattisatena ca;

Pāṇā suriyūpamā dvedhā, indakhīlo ca vādinoti.

Sīsapā, Khadira, Daṇḍa, Celā, and Sattisata; Pāṇā, the two Sūriyūpamā suttas, Indakhīla, and Vādī.

5. Papātavaggo

5. 5. The Chapter on the Precipice

1. Lokacintāsuttaṃ

1. 1. The Discourse on Thoughts About the World

1111. Ekaṃ [T 5.0558] samayaṃ bhagavā rājagahe viharati veḷuvane kalandakanivāpe. Tatra kho bhagavā bhikkhū āmantesi – “bhūtapubbaṃ, bhikkhave, aññataro puriso rājagahā nikkhamitvā ‘lokacintaṃ [P 5.0447] cintessāmī’ti yena sumāgadhā pokkharaṇī tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā sumāgadhāya pokkharaṇiyā tīre nisīdi lokacintaṃ cintento. Addasā kho, bhikkhave, so puriso sumāgadhāya pokkharaṇiyā tīre caturaṅginiṃ senaṃ caturaṅginisenaṃ (ka.) bhisamuḷālaṃ bhisamūlālaṃ (pī. ka.) pavisantaṃ. Disvānassa etadahosi – ‘ummattosmi nāmāhaṃ, vicetosmi nāmāhaṃ! Yaṃ loke natthi taṃ mayā diṭṭha’”nti.

1111. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling in Rājagaha, in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place. On that occasion, the Blessed One addressed the monks: 'Monks, in a time past, a certain man, having departed from Rājagaha thinking, "I will contemplate thoughts about the world," approached the Sumāgadhā pond. Having approached, he sat down on the bank of the Sumāgadhā pond, contemplating thoughts about the world. Monks, that man saw, on the bank of the Sumāgadhā pond, a four-limbed army entering a lotus stalk. Having seen this, the thought occurred to him: "I must be mad, I must be deranged! I have seen that which does not exist in the world."'

“Atha kho so, bhikkhave, puriso nagaraṃ pavisitvā mahājanakāyassa ārocesi – ‘ummattosmi nāmāhaṃ, bhante, vicetosmi nāmāhaṃ, bhante! Yaṃ loke natthi taṃ mayā diṭṭha’”nti. “Kathaṃ pana tvaṃ, ambho purisa, ummatto kathaṃ viceto? Kiñca loke natthi yaṃ tayā diṭṭha”nti? “Idhāhaṃ, bhante, rājagahā nikkhamitvā ‘lokacintaṃ cintessāmī’ti yena sumāgadhā pokkharaṇī tenupasaṅkamiṃ; upasaṅkamitvā sumāgadhāya pokkharaṇiyā tīre nisīdiṃ lokacintaṃ cintento. Addasaṃ khvāhaṃ, bhante, sumāgadhāya pokkharaṇiyā tīre caturaṅginiṃ senaṃ bhisamuḷālaṃ [V 3.0509] pavisantaṃ. Evaṃ khvāhaṃ, bhante, ummatto evaṃ viceto. Idañca loke natthi yaṃ mayā [T 5.0559] diṭṭha”nti. “Taggha tvaṃ, ambho purisa, ummatto taggha viceto. Idañca loke natthi yaṃ tayā diṭṭha”nti.

“Then, Bhikkhus, that man, having entered the city, announced to the great crowd of people: ‘Sirs, I am indeed mad; sirs, I am indeed deranged! That which does not exist in the world has been seen by me.’ ‘How then, O man, are you mad? How are you deranged? And what is it that does not exist in the world, which has been seen by you?’ ‘Sirs, here, having departed from Rājagaha thinking, “I will contemplate the world,” I approached the Sumāgadhā pond. Having approached, I sat on the bank of the Sumāgadhā pond, contemplating the world. Sirs, on the bank of the Sumāgadhā pond I saw a four-limbed army entering a lotus-root stalk. Thus indeed, sirs, I am mad; thus I am deranged. And this, which has been seen by me, does not exist in the world.’ ‘Indeed, O man, you are mad; indeed, you are deranged. And this, which has been seen by you, does not exist in the world.’”

“Taṃ kho pana, bhikkhave, so puriso bhūtaṃyeva addasa, no abhūtaṃ. Bhūtapubbaṃ, bhikkhave, devāsurasaṅgāmo samupabyūḷho ahosi. Tasmiṃ kho pana, bhikkhave, saṅgāme devā jiniṃsu, asurā parājiniṃsu. Parājitā [M 3.0391] ca [P 5.0448] kho, bhikkhave, asurā bhītā bhisamuḷālena asurapuraṃ pavisiṃsu devānaṃyeva mohayamānā.

“Bhikkhus, that man indeed saw what was real, not what was unreal. Formerly, Bhikkhus, a battle between devas and asuras was arrayed. In that battle, Bhikkhus, the devas were victorious, and the asuras were defeated. And being defeated, Bhikkhus, the asuras, terrified, entered the city of the asuras by means of a lotus-root stalk, deluding the devas.”

“Tasmātiha, bhikkhave, mā lokacintaṃ cintetha – ‘sassato loko’ti vā ‘asassato loko’ti vā, ‘antavā loko’ti vā ‘anantavā loko’ti vā, ‘taṃ jīvaṃ taṃ sarīra’nti vā ‘aññaṃ jīvaṃ aññaṃ sarīra’nti vā, ‘hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā’ti vā ‘na hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā’ti vā, ‘hoti ca na ca hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā’ti vā, ‘neva hoti na na hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā’ti vā. Taṃ kissa hetu? Nesā, bhikkhave, cintā atthasaṃhitā nādibrahmacariyakā na nibbidāya na virāgāya na nirodhāya na upasamāya na abhiññāya na sambodhāya na nibbānāya saṃvattati.

“Therefore, Bhikkhus, do not contemplate the world, thinking: ‘The world is eternal’ or ‘the world is not eternal’; ‘the world is finite’ or ‘the world is infinite’; ‘the life-principle is the same as the body’ or ‘the life-principle is one thing and the body another’; ‘a being exists after death’ or ‘a being does not exist after death’; ‘a being both exists and does not exist after death’ or ‘a being neither exists nor does not exist after death.’ For what reason? Because, Bhikkhus, this contemplation is not connected with the goal, is not fundamental to the holy life, and does not lead to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to awakening, or to Nibbāna.”

“Cintentā kho tumhe, bhikkhave, ‘idaṃ dukkha’nti cinteyyātha…pe… ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā’ti cinteyyātha. Taṃ kissa hetu? Esā, bhikkhave, cintā atthasaṃhitā esā ādibrahmacariyakā esā nibbidāya virāgāya nirodhāya upasamāya abhiññāya [T 5.0560] sambodhāya nibbānāya saṃvattati.

“When you contemplate, Bhikkhus, you should contemplate: ‘This is suffering’… you should contemplate: ‘This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering.’ For what reason? Because, Bhikkhus, this contemplation is connected with the goal, it is fundamental to the holy life, and it leads to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to awakening, and to Nibbāna.”

“Tasmātiha, bhikkhave, ‘idaṃ dukkha’nti yogo karaṇīyo…pe… ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā’ti yogo karaṇīyo”ti. Paṭhamaṃ.

“Therefore, Bhikkhus, exertion should be made concerning ‘This is suffering’… exertion should be made concerning ‘This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering.’”

2. Papātasuttaṃ

2. The Discourse on the Precipice

1112. Ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā rājagahe viharati gijjhakūṭe pabbate. Atha kho bhagavā bhikkhū [V 3.0510] āmantesi – “āyāma, bhikkhave, yena paṭibhānakūṭo tenupasaṅkamissāma divāvihārāyā”ti. “Evaṃ, bhante”ti kho te bhikkhū bhagavato paccassosuṃ. Atha [P 5.0449] kho bhagavā sambahulehi bhikkhūhi saddhiṃ yena paṭibhānakūṭo tenupasaṅkami. Addasā kho aññataro bhikkhu paṭibhānakūṭe mahantaṃ papātaṃ. Disvāna bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “mahā vatāyaṃ, bhante, papāto subhayānako, bhante, papāto. Atthi nu kho, bhante, imamhā papātā añño papāto mahantataro ca bhayānakataro cā”ti? “Atthi kho, bhikkhu, imamhā papātā añño papāto mahantataro ca bhayānakataro cā”ti.

1112. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha, on Vulture Peak Mountain. Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Come, bhikkhus, let us go to Paṭibhānakūṭa for the day’s abiding.” “Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One, together with many bhikkhus, went to Paṭibhānakūṭa. A certain bhikkhu saw a great precipice at Paṭibhānakūṭa. Having seen it, he said to the Blessed One: “Truly, venerable sir, this precipice is vast; venerable sir, this precipice is terrifying. Is there, venerable sir, another precipice more vast and more terrifying than this one?” “There is, bhikkhu, another precipice more vast and more terrifying than this one.”

“Katamo [M 3.0392] pana, bhante, imamhā papātā añño papāto mahantataro ca bhayānakataro cā”ti? “Ye hi keci, bhikkhave, samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā ‘idaṃ dukkha’nti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānanti, ‘ayaṃ dukkhasamudayo’ti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānanti, ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodho’ti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānanti, ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā’ti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānanti, te jātisaṃvattanikesu saṅkhāresu abhiramanti, jarāsaṃvattanikesu saṅkhāresu abhiramanti[T 5.0561], maraṇasaṃvattanikesu saṅkhāresu abhiramanti, sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsasaṃvattanikesu saṅkhāresu abhiramanti. Te jātisaṃvattanikesu saṅkhāresu abhiratā jarāsaṃvattanikesu saṅkhāresu abhiratā maraṇasaṃvattanikesu saṅkhāresu abhiratā sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsasaṃvattanikesu saṅkhāresu abhiratā jātisaṃvattanikepi saṅkhāre abhisaṅkharonti, jarāsaṃvattanikepi saṅkhāre abhisaṅkharonti, maraṇasaṃvattanikepi saṅkhāre abhisaṅkharonti, sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsasaṃvattanikepi saṅkhāre abhisaṅkharonti. Te jātisaṃvattanikepi saṅkhāre abhisaṅkharitvā jarāsaṃvattanikepi saṅkhāre abhisaṅkharitvā maraṇasaṃvattanikepi saṅkhāre abhisaṅkharitvā sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsasaṃvattanikepi saṅkhāre abhisaṅkharitvā jātipapātampi papatanti, jarāpapātampi papatanti, maraṇapapātampi papatanti, sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsapapātampi [P 5.0450] papatanti. Te na parimuccanti jātiyā jarāya maraṇena sokehi paridevehi dukkhehi domanassehi upāyāsehi. ‘Na parimuccanti dukkhasmā’ti vadāmi”.

“But what, venerable sir, is another precipice more vast and more terrifying than this one?” “Bhikkhus, whatever ascetics or brahmins do not understand as it actually is: ‘This is suffering’; do not understand as it actually is: ‘This is the origin of suffering’; do not understand as it actually is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; do not understand as it actually is: ‘This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering’—they delight in volitional formations that lead to birth, delight in volitional formations that lead to aging, delight in volitional formations that lead to death, delight in volitional formations that lead to sorrow, lamentation, pain, distress, and despair. Delighting in volitional formations that lead to birth, delighting in volitional formations that lead to aging, delighting in volitional formations that lead to death, delighting in volitional formations that lead to sorrow, lamentation, pain, distress, and despair, they generate volitional formations that lead to birth, generate volitional formations that lead to aging, generate volitional formations that lead to death, generate volitional formations that lead to sorrow, lamentation, pain, distress, and despair. Having generated volitional formations that lead to birth, having generated volitional formations that lead to aging, having generated volitional formations that lead to death, having generated volitional formations that lead to sorrow, lamentation, pain, distress, and despair, they fall into the precipice of birth, fall into the precipice of aging, fall into the precipice of death, fall into the precipice of sorrow, lamentation, pain, distress, and despair. They are not freed from birth, aging, death, sorrows, lamentations, pains, distresses, and despairs. I say: ‘They are not freed from suffering.’”

“Ye ca kho keci, bhikkhave, samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā ‘idaṃ dukkha’nti yathābhūtaṃ pajānanti…pe… ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā’ti yathābhūtaṃ pajānanti, te jātisaṃvattanikesu saṅkhāresu nābhiramanti, jarāsaṃvattanikesu saṅkhāresu nābhiramanti, maraṇasaṃvattanikesu [V 3.0511] saṅkhāresu nābhiramanti, sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsasaṃvattanikesu [T 5.0562] saṅkhāresu nābhiramanti. Te jātisaṃvattanikesu saṅkhāresu anabhiratā, jarāsaṃvattanikesu saṅkhāresu anabhiratā, maraṇasaṃvattanikesu saṅkhāresu anabhiratā, sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsasaṃvattanikesu saṅkhāresu anabhiratā, jātisaṃvattanikepi saṅkhāre nābhisaṅkharonti, jarāsaṃvattanikepi saṅkhāre nābhisaṅkharonti, maraṇasaṃvattanikepi saṅkhāre nābhisaṅkharonti, sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsasaṃvattanikepi [M 3.0393] saṅkhāre nābhisaṅkharonti. Te jātisaṃvattanikepi saṅkhāre anabhisaṅkharitvā, jarāsaṃvattanikepi saṅkhāre anabhisaṅkharitvā, maraṇasaṃvattanikepi saṅkhāre anabhisaṅkharitvā, sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsasaṃvattanikepi saṅkhāre anabhisaṅkharitvā, jātipapātampi nappapatanti, jarāpapātampi nappapatanti, maraṇapapātampi nappapatanti, sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsapapātampi nappapatanti. Te parimuccanti jātiyā jarāya maraṇena sokehi paridevehi dukkhehi domanassehi upāyāsehi. ‘Parimuccanti dukkhasmā’ti vadāmi”.

“Bhikkhus, those ascetics or brahmins who understand as it actually is: ‘This is suffering’… who understand as it actually is: ‘This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering’—they do not delight in volitional formations that lead to birth, they do not delight in volitional formations that lead to aging, they do not delight in volitional formations that lead to death, they do not delight in volitional formations that lead to sorrow, lamentation, pain, distress, and despair. Not delighting in volitional formations that lead to birth, not delighting in volitional formations that lead to aging, not delighting in volitional formations that lead to death, not delighting in volitional formations that lead to sorrow, lamentation, pain, distress, and despair, they do not generate volitional formations that lead to birth, they do not generate volitional formations that lead to aging, they do not generate volitional formations that lead to death, they do not generate volitional formations that lead to sorrow, lamentation, pain, distress, and despair. Not having generated volitional formations that lead to birth, not having generated volitional formations that lead to aging, not having generated volitional formations that lead to death, not having generated volitional formations that lead to sorrow, lamentation, pain, distress, and despair, they do not fall into the precipice of birth, they do not fall into the precipice of aging, they do not fall into the precipice of death, they do not fall into the precipice of sorrow, lamentation, pain, distress, and despair. They are freed from birth, aging, death, sorrows, lamentations, pains, distresses, and despairs. I say: ‘They are freed from suffering.’”

“Tasmātiha, bhikkhave, ‘idaṃ dukkha’nti yogo karaṇīyo…pe… ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā’ti yogo karaṇīyo”ti. Dutiyaṃ.

“Therefore, bhikkhus, an exertion should be made to realize: ‘This is suffering’… an exertion should be made to realize: ‘This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering.’”

3. Mahāpariḷāhasuttaṃ

3. The Great Conflagration

1113. “Atthi, bhikkhave, mahāpariḷāho nāma nirayo. Tattha yaṃ kiñci cakkhunā rūpaṃ passati, aniṭṭharūpaññeva passati [P 5.0451] no iṭṭharūpaṃ; akantarūpaññeva passati no kantarūpaṃ; amanāparūpaññeva passati no manāparūpaṃ. Yaṃ kiñci sotena saddaṃ suṇāti…pe… yaṃ [T 5.0563] kiñci kāyena phoṭṭhabbaṃ phusati…pe… yaṃ kiñci manasā dhammaṃ vijānāti, aniṭṭharūpaññeva vijānāti no iṭṭharūpaṃ; akantarūpaññeva vijānāti no kantarūpaṃ; amanāparūpaññeva vijānāti no manāparūpa”nti.

1113. “Bhikkhus, there is a hell named the Great Conflagration. There, whatever form one sees with the eye, one sees only a disagreeable form, not an agreeable form; one sees only an undesirable form, not a desirable form; one sees only a displeasing form, not a pleasing form. Whatever sound one hears with the ear… whatever tangible object one feels with the body… whatever mental phenomenon one cognizes with the mind, one cognizes only a disagreeable phenomenon, not an agreeable phenomenon; one cognizes only an undesirable phenomenon, not a desirable phenomenon; one cognizes only a displeasing phenomenon, not a pleasing phenomenon.”

Evaṃ vutte aññataro bhikkhu bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “mahā vata so, bhante, pariḷāho, sumahā vata so, bhante, pariḷāho! Atthi nu kho, bhante, etamhā pariḷāhā añño pariḷāho [V 3.0512] mahantataro ceva bhayānakataro cā”ti? “Atthi kho, bhikkhu, etamhā pariḷāhā añño pariḷāho mahantataro ca bhayānakataro cā”ti.

When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said this to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, that conflagration is indeed great; venerable sir, that conflagration is indeed very great! But, venerable sir, is there another conflagration greater and more frightening than this conflagration?” “There is, bhikkhu, another conflagration greater and more frightening than this conflagration.”

“Katamo pana, bhante, etamhā pariḷāhā añño pariḷāho mahantataro ca bhayānakataro cā”ti? “Ye hi keci, bhikkhave, samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā ‘idaṃ dukkha’nti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānanti…pe… ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā’ti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānanti, te jātisaṃvattanikesu saṅkhāresu abhiramanti…pe… abhiratā…pe… abhisaṅkharonti…pe… abhisaṅkharitvā jātipariḷāhenapi pariḍayhanti, jarāpariḷāhenapi pariḍayhanti, maraṇapariḷāhenapi pariḍayhanti, sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsapariḷāhenapi pariḍayhanti[M 3.0394]. Te na parimuccanti jātiyā jarāya maraṇena sokehi paridevehi dukkhehi domanassehi upāyāsehi. ‘Na parimuccanti dukkhasmā’ti vadāmi”.

“But what, Venerable Sir, is that other burning which is greater and more frightening than this burning?” “Bhikkhus, whatever ascetics or brahmins do not understand as it really is, ‘This is suffering’… do not understand as it really is, ‘This is the path of practice leading to the cessation of suffering’—they delight in formations that lead to rebirth… delighting… they fabricate… having fabricated, they are burned by the burning of birth, they are burned by the burning of aging, they are burned by the burning of death, they are burned by the burning of sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. They are not released from birth, from aging, from death, from sorrows, from lamentations, from pains, from griefs, from despairs. They are not released from suffering, I say.”

“Ye ca kho keci, bhikkhave, samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā ‘idaṃ dukkha’nti yathābhūtaṃ pajānanti…pe… ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā’ti [T 5.0564] yathābhūtaṃ pajānanti. Te jātisaṃvattanikesu saṅkhāresu nābhiramanti…pe… anabhiratā…pe… nābhisaṅkharonti…pe… anabhisaṅkharitvā jātipariḷāhenapi na pariḍayhanti, jarāpariḷāhenapi na pariḍayhanti, maraṇapariḷāhenapi na pariḍayhanti, sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsapariḷāhenapi na pariḍayhanti. Te parimuccanti jātiyā jarāya [P 5.0452] maraṇena sokehi paridevehi dukkhehi domanassehi upāyāsehi. ‘Parimuccanti dukkhasmā’ti vadāmi”.

“Bhikkhus, whatever ascetics or brahmins there may be who understand as it really is, ‘This is suffering’… who understand as it really is, ‘This is the path of practice leading to the cessation of suffering’—they do not delight in formations that lead to rebirth… not delighting… they do not fabricate… not fabricating, they are not burned by the torment of birth, nor by the torment of aging, nor by the torment of death, nor by the torment of sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair. They are freed from birth, aging, and death; from sorrows, lamentations, pains, displeasures, and despairs. They are freed from suffering, I say.”

“Tasmātiha, bhikkhave, ‘idaṃ dukkha’nti yogo karaṇīyo…pe… ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā’ti yogo karaṇīyo”ti. Tatiyaṃ.

“Therefore, Bhikkhus, effort should be made [to understand]: ‘This is suffering’… effort should be made [to understand]: ‘This is the path of practice leading to the cessation of suffering.’”

4. Kūṭāgārasuttaṃ

4. The Discourse on the Gabled House

1114. “Yo hi, bhikkhave yo ca kho bhikkhave (syā. ka.), evaṃ vadeyya – ‘ahaṃ dukkhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ yathābhūtaṃ anabhisamecca…pe… dukkhanirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadaṃ ariyasaccaṃ yathābhūtaṃ anabhisamecca sammā dukkhassantaṃ karissāmī’ti – netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati.

1114. “Bhikkhus, if anyone were to say: ‘Without having thoroughly understood the noble truth of suffering as it really is… without having thoroughly understood the noble truth of the path of practice leading to the cessation of suffering as it really is, I will rightly make an end of suffering’—this is not possible.

“Seyyathāpi[V 3.0513], bhikkhave, yo evaṃ vadeyya – ‘ahaṃ kūṭāgārassa heṭṭhimaṃ gharaṃ akaritvā uparimaṃ gharaṃ āropessāmī’ti – netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati; evameva kho, bhikkhave, yo evaṃ vadeyya – ‘ahaṃ dukkhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ yathābhūtaṃ anabhisamecca…pe… dukkhanirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadaṃ ariyasaccaṃ yathābhūtaṃ anabhisamecca sammā dukkhassantaṃ karissāmī’ti – netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati.

“Just as, Bhikkhus, if someone were to say: ‘Without having built the lower story of a gabled house, I will set up the upper story’—this is not possible; even so, Bhikkhus, if someone were to say: ‘Without having thoroughly understood the noble truth of suffering as it really is… without having thoroughly understood the noble truth of the path of practice leading to the cessation of suffering as it really is, I will rightly make an end of suffering’—this is not possible.

“Yo ca kho, bhikkhave, evaṃ vadeyya – ‘ahaṃ dukkhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ yathābhūtaṃ abhisamecca…pe… dukkhanirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadaṃ ariyasaccaṃ yathābhūtaṃ abhisamecca sammā dukkhassantaṃ karissāmī’ti – ṭhānametaṃ vijjati.

“But, Bhikkhus, if anyone were to say: ‘Having thoroughly understood the noble truth of suffering as it really is… having thoroughly understood the noble truth of the path of practice leading to the cessation of suffering as it really is, I will rightly make an end of suffering’—this is possible.

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, yo evaṃ vadeyya – ‘ahaṃ kūṭāgārassa heṭṭhimaṃ gharaṃ [T 5.0565] karitvā uparimaṃ gharaṃ āropessāmī’ti – ṭhānametaṃ vijjati; evameva kho[M 3.0395], bhikkhave, yo evaṃ vadeyya – ‘ahaṃ dukkhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ yathābhūtaṃ abhisamecca…pe… dukkhanirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadaṃ ariyasaccaṃ yathābhūtaṃ abhisamecca sammā dukkhassantaṃ karissāmī’ti – ṭhānametaṃ vijjati.

“Just as, Bhikkhus, if someone were to say, ‘Having built the lower story of a gabled house, I will then erect the upper story’—this is indeed possible; in the same way, Bhikkhus, if someone were to say, ‘Having thoroughly understood the noble truth of suffering as it really is… having thoroughly understood the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering as it really is, I will rightly make an end to suffering’—this is indeed possible.

“Tasmātiha[P 5.0453], bhikkhave, ‘idaṃ dukkha’nti yogo karaṇīyo…pe… ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā’ti yogo karaṇīyo”ti. Catutthaṃ.

“Therefore, Bhikkhus, here effort should be made to realize: ‘This is suffering’… effort should be made to realize: ‘This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering.’”

5. Vālasuttaṃ

5. The Discourse on Hair

1115. Ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā vesāliyaṃ viharati mahāvane kūṭāgārasālāyaṃ. Atha kho āyasmā ānando pubbaṇhasamayaṃ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya vesāliṃ piṇḍāya pāvisi. Addasā kho āyasmā ānando sambahule licchavikumārake santhāgāre upāsanaṃ karonte, dūratova sukhumena tāḷacchiggaḷena asanaṃ atipātente, poṅkhānupoṅkhaṃ pokhānupokhaṃ (syā. kaṃ.) avirādhitaṃ. Disvānassa etadahosi – “sikkhitā vatime licchavikumārakā, susikkhitā vatime licchavikumārakā; yatra hi nāma dūratova sukhumena tāḷacchiggaḷena asanaṃ atipātessanti poṅkhānupoṅkhaṃ avirādhita”nti.

1115. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Vesālī, in the Great Wood, in the Gabled Hall. Then, in the morning, Venerable Ānanda dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered Vesālī for alms. Venerable Ānanda saw a number of Licchavi youths at the assembly hall, practicing archery, shooting arrows from a distance through a fine keyhole, shaft after shaft without error. Seeing this, it occurred to him: “These Licchavi youths are trained indeed, well-trained indeed, that they can shoot arrows from a distance through a fine keyhole, shaft after shaft without error.”

Atha [V 3.0514] kho āyasmā ānando vesāliṃ piṇḍāya caritvā pacchābhattaṃ piṇḍapātapaṭikkanto yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho āyasmā ānando bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “idhāhaṃ, bhante, pubbaṇhasamayaṃ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya vesāliṃ piṇḍāya pāvisiṃ[T 5.0566]. Addasaṃ khvāhaṃ, bhante sambahule licchavikumārake santhāgāre upāsanaṃ karonte dūratova sukhumena tāḷacchiggaḷena asanaṃ atipātente poṅkhānupoṅkhaṃ avirādhitaṃ’. Disvāna me etadahosi – “sikkhitā vatime licchavikumārakā, susikkhitā vatime licchavikumārakā; yatra hi nāma dūratova sukhumena tāḷacchiggaḷena asanaṃ atipātessanti poṅkhānupoṅkhaṃ avirādhita”nti.

Then, Venerable Ānanda, having wandered for alms in Vesālī and returned from the alms-round after his meal, approached the Blessed One. Having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One: “Venerable Sir, here, in the morning, having dressed and taken my bowl and robe, I entered Vesālī for alms. I saw, Venerable Sir, many Licchavi youths in the assembly hall practicing archery, shooting an arrow from a distance through a fine keyhole, shaft after shaft, without error. Having seen this, this thought occurred to me: ‘Indeed, these Licchavi youths are trained! Indeed, these Licchavi youths are well-trained, in that they shoot an arrow from a distance through a fine keyhole, shaft after shaft, without error!’”

“Taṃ [P 5.0454] kiṃ maññasi, ānanda, katamaṃ nu kho dukkarataraṃ vā durabhisambhavataraṃ vā – yo dūratova sukhumena tāḷacchiggaḷena asanaṃ atipāteyya poṅkhānupoṅkhaṃ avirādhitaṃ, yo vā sattadhā bhinnassa vālassa koṭiyā koṭiṃ paṭivijjheyyā”ti? “Etadeva, bhante, dukkaratarañceva durabhisambhavatarañca yo [M 3.0396] vā yo (sī.) sattadhā bhinnassa vālassa koṭiyā koṭiṃ paṭivijjheyyā”ti. “Atha kho atha kho te (syā. kaṃ.), ānanda, duppaṭivijjhataraṃ paṭivijjhanti, ye ‘idaṃ dukkha’nti yathābhūtaṃ paṭivijjhanti…pe… ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā’ti yathābhūtaṃ paṭivijjhanti”.

“What do you think, Ānanda? Which is more difficult, more difficult to accomplish: that one should shoot an arrow from a distance through a fine keyhole, shaft after shaft, without error, or that one should pierce the tip of a horse-tail hair split sevenfold with another tip?” “Venerable sir, this is more difficult and more difficult to accomplish: that one should pierce the tip of a horse-tail hair split sevenfold with another tip.” “But indeed, Ānanda, they penetrate what is more difficult to penetrate, those who penetrate ‘This is suffering’ as it truly is… ‘This is the path of practice leading to the cessation of suffering’ as it truly is.”

“Tasmātihānanda, ‘idaṃ dukkha’nti yogo karaṇīyo…pe… ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā’ti yogo karaṇīyo”ti. Pañcamaṃ.

“Therefore, Ānanda, in this Dispensation, exertion should be made thus: ‘This is suffering.’ … Exertion should be made thus: ‘This is the path of practice leading to the cessation of suffering.’” The Fifth.

6. Andhakārasuttaṃ

6. The Discourse on Darkness

1116. “Atthi, bhikkhave, lokantarikā aghā asaṃvutā andhakārā andhakāratimisā, yatthamimesaṃ candimasūriyānaṃ evaṃmahiddhikānaṃ evaṃ mahānubhāvānaṃ ābhāya nānubhontī”ti.

1116. “Bhikkhus, there are the world-interstice hells—miserable, unenclosed, dark, a blind gloom—where the light of this moon and sun, so mighty and so powerful, is not experienced.”

Evaṃ vutte aññataro bhikkhu bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “mahā vata so, bhante, andhakāro, sumahā vata so, bhante, andhakāro! Atthi [T 5.0567] nu kho, bhante, etamhā andhakārā añño [V 3.0515] andhakāro mahantataro ca bhayānakataro cā”ti? “Atthi kho, bhikkhu, etamhā andhakārā añño andhakāro mahantataro ca bhayānakataro cā”ti.

When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, that darkness is great indeed, exceedingly great indeed! Is there, venerable sir, another darkness greater and more frightening than this darkness?” “There is, bhikkhu, another darkness greater and more frightening than this darkness.”

“Katamo pana, bhante, etamhā andhakārā añño andhakāro mahantataro ca bhayānakataro cā”ti? “Ye hi keci, bhikkhu, samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā ‘idaṃ dukkha’nti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānanti…pe… ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī [P 5.0455] paṭipadā’ti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānanti, te jātisaṃvattanikesu saṅkhāresu abhiramanti…pe… abhiratā…pe… abhisaṅkharonti…pe… abhisaṅkharitvā jātandhakārampi papatanti, jarandhakārampi papatanti, maraṇandhakārampi papatanti, sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsandhakārampi papatanti. Te na parimuccanti jātiyā jarāya maraṇena sokehi paridevehi dukkhehi domanassehi upāyāsehi. ‘Na parimuccanti dukkhasmā’ti vadāmi”.

“But what, venerable sir, is the other darkness that is greater and more frightening than this darkness?” “Bhikkhu, whatever ascetics or brahmins do not understand as it truly is, ‘This is suffering,’ … ‘This is the path of practice leading to the cessation of suffering,’ they delight in formations that lead to rebirth. Delighting in them, they generate them; having generated them, they fall into the darkness of birth, they fall into the darkness of aging, they fall into the darkness of death, they fall into the darkness of sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. They are not freed from birth, aging, and death; from sorrows, lamentations, pains, griefs, and despairs. They are not freed from suffering, I say.”

“Ye ca kho keci, bhikkhu, samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā ‘idaṃ dukkha’nti yathābhūtaṃ pajānanti…pe… ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā’ti yathābhūtaṃ pajānanti, te jātisaṃvattanikesu saṅkhāresu nābhiramanti…pe… anabhiratā…pe… nābhisaṅkharonti…pe… anabhisaṅkharitvā jātandhakārampi nappapatanti[M 3.0397], jarandhakārampi nappapatanti, maraṇandhakārampi nappapatanti, sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsandhakārampi nappapatanti. Te parimuccanti jātiyā jarāya maraṇena sokehi paridevehi [T 5.0568] dukkhehi domanassehi upāyāsehi. ‘Parimuccanti dukkhasmā’ti vadāmi”.

“Bhikkhu, whatever ascetics or brahmins understand as it truly is, ‘This is suffering,’ … ‘This is the path of practice leading to the cessation of suffering,’ they do not delight in formations that lead to rebirth. Not delighting in them, they do not generate them; not having generated them, they do not fall into the darkness of birth, they do not fall into the darkness of aging, they do not fall into the darkness of death, they do not fall into the darkness of sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. They are freed from birth, aging, and death; from sorrows, lamentations, pains, griefs, and despairs. They are freed from suffering, I say.”

“Tasmātiha, bhikkhave, ‘idaṃ dukkha’nti yogo karaṇīyo…pe… ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā’ti yogo karaṇīyo”ti. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

“Therefore, bhikkhus, in this Dispensation, exertion should be made thus: ‘This is suffering.’ … Exertion should be made thus: ‘This is the path of practice leading to the cessation of suffering.’” The Sixth.

7. Paṭhamachiggaḷayugasuttaṃ

7. The First Discourse on the Yoke with a Hole

1117. “Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, puriso mahāsamudde ekacchiggaḷaṃ yugaṃ pakkhipeyya. Tatrāpissa kāṇo kacchapo. So vassasatassa vassasatassa accayena sakiṃ sakiṃ ummujjeyya. Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, api nu kho kāṇo kacchapo vassasatassa vassasatassa [V 3.0516] accayena sakiṃ sakiṃ ummujjanto amusmiṃ ekacchiggaḷe yuge gīvaṃ paveseyyā”ti? “Yadi [P 5.0456] nūna, bhante, kadāci karahaci dīghassa addhuno accayenā”ti.

1117. “Suppose, bhikkhus, a man were to throw a yoke with a single hole into the great ocean, and there were a blind turtle. That turtle would surface only once every hundred years. What do you think, bhikkhus? Would that blind turtle, surfacing only once every hundred years, insert its neck into that yoke with a single hole?” “It might, venerable sir, if at all, only after a very long time.”

“Khippataraṃ kho so, bhikkhave, kāṇo kacchapo vassasatassa vassasatassa accayena sakiṃ sakiṃ ummujjanto amusmiṃ ekacchiggaḷe yuge gīvaṃ paveseyya, na tvevāhaṃ, bhikkhave, sakiṃ vinipātagatena bālena vinītagatena bahulena (ka.) manussattaṃ vadāmi”.

“Sooner, bhikkhus, would that blind turtle, surfacing only once every hundred years, insert its neck into that yoke with a single hole, than I say that a fool who has once gone to a state of ruin would regain human existence.”

Taṃ kissa hetu? Na hettha, bhikkhave, atthi dhammacariyā, samacariyā, kusalakiriyā, puññakiriyā. Aññamaññakhādikā ettha, bhikkhave, vattati dubbalakhādikā. Taṃ kissa hetu? Adiṭṭhattā, bhikkhave, catunnaṃ ariyasaccānaṃ. Katamesaṃ catunnaṃ? Dukkhassa ariyasaccassa…pe… dukkhanirodhagāminiyā paṭipadāya ariyasaccassa.

“For what reason? Here, bhikkhus, there is no practice of the Dhamma, no righteous conduct, no doing of wholesome deeds, no doing of meritorious deeds. Here, bhikkhus, mutual devouring prevails, the devouring of the weak prevails. For what reason? Because, bhikkhus, of not having seen the four noble truths. Which four? The noble truth of suffering… the noble truth of the path of practice leading to the cessation of suffering.”

“Tasmātiha, bhikkhave, ‘idaṃ dukkha’nti yogo karaṇīyo…pe… ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā’ti yogo karaṇīyo”ti. Sattamaṃ.

“Therefore, bhikkhus, in this Dispensation, exertion should be made thus: ‘This is suffering.’ … Exertion should be made thus: ‘This is the path of practice leading to the cessation of suffering.’” The Seventh.

8. Dutiyachiggaḷayugasuttaṃ

8. The Second Discourse on the Yoke with a Hole

1118. “Seyyathāpi[M 3.0398], bhikkhave, ayaṃ mahāpathavī ekodakā assa. Tatra [T 5.0569] puriso ekacchiggaḷaṃ yugaṃ pakkhipeyya. Tamenaṃ puratthimo vāto pacchimena saṃhareyya, pacchimo vāto puratthimena saṃhareyya, uttaro vāto dakkhiṇena saṃhareyya, dakkhiṇo vāto uttarena saṃhareyya. Tatrassa kāṇo kacchapo. So vassasatassa vassasatassa accayena sakiṃ sakiṃ ummujjeyya. Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, api nu kho kāṇo kacchapo vassasatassa vassasatassa accayena sakiṃ sakiṃ ummujjanto [P 5.0457] amusmiṃ ekacchiggaḷe yuge gīvaṃ paveseyyā”ti? “Adhiccamidaṃ, bhante, yaṃ so kāṇo kacchapo vassasatassa vassasatassa accayena sakiṃ sakiṃ ummujjanto amusmiṃ ekacchiggaḷe yuge gīvaṃ paveseyyā”ti.

1118. “Monks, suppose this great earth were to become a single mass of water, and a man were to cast a yoke with a single hole into it. The east wind would carry it to the west, the west wind would carry it to the east, the north wind would carry it to the south, and the south wind would carry it to the north. And there, there were a blind turtle. It would surface once after every hundred years. What do you think of this, monks? Would that blind turtle, surfacing once after every hundred years, insert its neck into that yoke with a single hole?” “It would only be by a rare coincidence, Venerable Sir, that the blind turtle, surfacing once after every hundred years, would insert its neck into that yoke with a single hole.”

“Evaṃ adhiccamidaṃ, bhikkhave, yaṃ manussattaṃ labhati. Evaṃ adhiccamidaṃ, bhikkhave, yaṃ tathāgato loke uppajjati arahaṃ sammāsambuddho. Evaṃ adhiccamidaṃ, bhikkhave, yaṃ tathāgatappavedito [V 3.0517] dhammavinayo loke dibbati. Tassidaṃ tayidaṃ (?), bhikkhave, manussattaṃ laddhaṃ, tathāgato loke uppanno arahaṃ sammāsambuddho, tathāgatappavedito ca dhammavinayo loke dibbati.

“In the same way, monks, it is by a rare coincidence that one obtains the human state. In the same way, monks, it is by a rare coincidence that a Tathāgata, an Arahant, a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, arises in the world.
